case_title: Silvassa Cement Products Pvt. Ltd. vs. Noor India Buildcon Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Silvassa Cement Products Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor; Respondent Noor India Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial operational supply of cement products by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on operational debt asserted in Form 5. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board Resolution passed on 28.09.2018 authorizing Manager Praveen Kumar B. Mundra to file and defend legal proceedings under the IBC. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board Resolution dated 28.09.2018 (Exhibit A, Page 16); Form 5 application signed by two advocates (Mr. Niraj Shah and Mr. Dhruv K. Dave) without an accompanying notarization or date recorded on the form. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court II; NCLT dismissed the application on 15.06.2020 as non-maintainable due to lack of applicant signature/notarization without ruling on the substantive debt and default.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC can be dismissed at the threshold as non-maintainable due to procedural defects in signatures and notarization without affording statutory opportunity to cure defects under the proviso to Section 9(5)(ii).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Incompleteness of an insolvency application is distinct from statutory non-maintainability, and an adjudicating authority cannot dismiss a petition for technical defects without providing mandatory statutory notice to cure them. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 9(5)(ii) of the IBC imposes a mandatory statutory obligation on the Adjudicating Authority to issue a notice giving the applicant seven days to rectify defects before rejecting an application as incomplete. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a petition is backed by a valid corporate board resolution and executed by authorized legal counsel, procedural lapses such as missing verification dates or lack of notarization constitute curable defects rather than incurable jurisdictional bars. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the application as non-maintainable without issuing the mandatory defect notice under the proviso to Section 9(5), necessitating a remand for procedural cure and merits adjudication.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, setting aside the impugned order dated 15.06.2020 and remitting the case back to NCLT Ahmedabad to afford the Appellant opportunity to rectify defects in Form 5 and thereafter decide admission on merits.
summary: Silvassa Cement Products Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the dismissal of its Section 9 IBC petition by NCLT Ahmedabad. The NCLT had rejected the petition on non-maintainability because Form 5 was signed by advocates without dates or notarization, rather than the manager authorized by the Board Resolution dated 28.09.2018. The NCLAT set aside the dismissal, holding that procedural defects and incompleteness must be distinguished from non-maintainability. Under the mandatory proviso to Section 9(5)(ii), the Adjudicating Authority was obligated to provide seven days' notice to cure technical defects before dismissing the petition. The case was remitted for rectification and merits adjudication.

case_title: Sri D. Srinivasa Rao vs. Vaishnovi Infratech Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sri D. Srinivasa Rao is the Operational Creditor; Respondent Vaishnovi Infratech Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of operational services and execution of works by the Operational Creditor for the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of crystallized unpaid operational debt. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8(1) dispatched via speed post; limited notice by Adjudicating Authority delivered on 14.11.2019 at the exact same postal address. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Copy of Section 8 demand notice (Pages 52-54), speed post postal receipt (Page 55), postal tracking article bearing official endorsement 'addressee refused service' (Page 57), and proof of service of NCLT notice at the identical address (Page 93). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 application before NCLT Hyderabad Bench; NCLT rejected the application on 09.06.2020 on the ground that the mandatory Section 8 demand notice was returned unserved.
legal_issues: Whether the deliberate refusal by a Corporate Debtor to accept delivery of a Section 8 demand notice constitutes valid and effective service for initiating CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Deliberate refusal to accept delivery of a mandatory pre-litigation statutory demand notice constitutes valid legal service, precluding the defaulting party from taking advantage of its own evasive conduct. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Delivery contemplated under Section 8(1) is a mandatory condition precedent for a Section 9 application; however, when an addressee actively refuses delivery at a correct address, the statutory requirement of delivery is deemed satisfied by legal fiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Postal authority endorsements stating 'addressee refused service' establish willful evasion, which is distinct from non-delivery caused by incorrect addresses, non-existent premises, or neutral external failures. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor deliberately refused service to evade insolvency consequences, and the Adjudicating Authority erred in treating refusal as non-delivery; the statutory mandate under Section 8(1) stood fulfilled.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, setting aside the rejection order dated 09.06.2020 and remanding the matter to NCLT Hyderabad to consider admission under Section 9 of the IBC after giving the Corporate Debtor an opportunity to settle.
summary: Sri D. Srinivasa Rao challenged an order of NCLT Hyderabad rejecting his Section 9 IBC application against Vaishnovi Infratech Ltd. on the ground that the mandatory Section 8 demand notice had returned unserved. On examining postal records, the NCLAT found that the postal envelope bore the explicit endorsement 'addressee refused service', whereas tribunal notice sent to the identical address was accepted. The NCLAT held that deliberate refusal to accept delivery constitutes good and effective service in law, and a defaulting corporate debtor cannot benefit from its own obstructionist conduct. Setting aside the dismissal, the Appellate Tribunal remanded the matter to NCLT for admission.

case_title: Ravindra Chaturvedi (Liquidator of Excel Glasses Ltd.) vs. Kopran Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ravindra Chaturvedi, Liquidator of Excel Glasses Ltd.; Respondent is Kopran Ltd. (Applicant in MA before NCLT). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claims administration and disbursement of dues regarding ex-workmen and creditor Kopran Ltd. during liquidation proceedings of Excel Glasses Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Competing claims regarding legitimate operational dues of workmen versus disbursements to applicant Kopran Ltd. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Miscellaneous Application MA 148/KOB/2020 in IBA 258/Chennai Bench filed during ongoing liquidation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's counter and reply affidavits filed before the Adjudicating Authority, specifically paragraph 3 (page 163) and paragraph 11 (page 173), explaining the procedural and legal position on payments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench dismissed MA 148/KOB/2020 on 10.12.2020 as non-maintainable, but recorded adverse findings in paragraph 24 alleging criminal collusion between the liquidator and Kopran Ltd. to defeat ex-workers' claims; Liquidator appealed against these remarks.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is legally justified in recording disparaging findings of collusive fraud and misconduct against a Court-appointed Liquidator when dismissing a miscellaneous application on procedural non-maintainability.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Judicial and quasi-judicial tribunals must refrain from recording disparaging or defamatory character strictures against court-appointed officers unless an express finding of criminal intent or intentional wrongdoing is established by undeniable evidence on record. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inquiries into procedural non-maintainability under the IBC do not authorize the Adjudicating Authority to draw unfounded inferences of criminal conspiracy or professional collusion against an Insolvency Professional. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Even where an application lacks merit, is vexatious, or suffers from procedural flaws such as non-joinder of necessary parties, such deficiencies do not establish a meeting of minds or complicity bordering on criminal misconduct. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The disparaging observations in paragraph 24 branding the Liquidator as collusive and tainted lacked evidential foundation and caused severe prejudice, warranting their complete judicial expunction.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the collusive remarks in paragraph 24 of the NCLT order dated 10.12.2020 are expunged and deleted from the record, with a direction to drop any contemplated consequential action against the Liquidator.
summary: Ravindra Chaturvedi, Liquidator of Excel Glasses Ltd., appealed to NCLAT Chennai challenging disparaging remarks recorded in paragraph 24 of an NCLT Kochi order dated 10.12.2020. The NCLT had dismissed an application filed by Kopran Ltd. as non-maintainable, but observed that the Liquidator acted in collusion with Kopran Ltd. to defeat the legitimate dues of ex-workmen. The NCLAT held that the NCLT's strictures were wholly unwarranted, noting that procedural missteps or frivolous applications do not justify branding an Insolvency Professional as a criminal collaborator. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and ordered the expunction and deletion of the offending remarks.

case_title: Supertech Township Project Ltd. vs. Inderpal Singh Khandpur HUF
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Supertech Township Project Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (real estate developer); Respondent Inderpal Singh Khandpur HUF is an individual allottee/homebuyer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project and allotment of residential units to homebuyers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged defaults in construction and delivery of allotted units, prompting allottee class-action initiation under Section 7. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency Amendment Ordinance introduced the minimum threshold of 100 allottees or 10% of total allottees for Section 7 real estate petitions; Supreme Court directed status quo in WP(C) No. 26/2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's website failed to provide complete allottee registers; NCLT ordered disclosure of details of 100 allottees or 1/10th of total project allottees on 08.12.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 proceedings initiated; NCLT directed the Corporate Debtor to furnish allottee details to enable the applicant to meet the amended statutory threshold; Corporate Debtor appealed contending violation of Supreme Court status-quo orders.
legal_issues: Whether an order directing a real estate Corporate Debtor to disclose allottee data to facilitate compliance with the Section 7 numerical threshold infringes the Corporate Debtor's legal rights or violates Supreme Court status-quo directions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Directing a corporate entity to disclose statutory records to enable stakeholders to meet collective class-action thresholds does not infringe any vested legal right or prejudice the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory threshold requirements under the Section 7 proviso require transparency; Supreme Court status quo orders on initiating or continuing CIRP do not prohibit supplying information mandated by regulatory frameworks and RERA disclosures. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where developer websites do not maintain transparent lists of allottees, tribunals possess incidental authority to compel disclosure to facilitate statutory compliance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Real estate developers and regulators are under an existing legal obligation to display allottee particulars; directing disclosure facilitates legitimate class-action compliance and causes no legal prejudice.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without merit; the Corporate Debtor is directed to display complete particulars of allottees on its website within two weeks and provide necessary information to the Respondent upon request.
summary: Supertech Township Project Ltd. challenged an NCLT order directing it to provide an allottee, Inderpal Singh Khandpur HUF, with information regarding 100 allottees or 1/10th of total allottees to enable compliance with the amended threshold for real estate class action under Section 7 of the IBC. The developer contended that the directive violated Supreme Court status-quo orders in WP(C) No. 26/2020 and infringed its rights. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that providing transparency regarding allottees does not trigger CIRP or cause legal prejudice, and directed the company to publish allottee details on its website within two weeks.

case_title: Aster Technologies Pvt. Ltd. vs. Solas Fire Safety Equipment Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Aster Technologies Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is Solas Fire Safety Equipment Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of requisite goods and services by the Operational Creditor pursuant to purchase orders placed by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed is an unpaid amount of Rs. 4.35 lakhs; default followed an unfulfilled commitment made via letter dated 13.03.2018 promising to clear dues within 30 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on 04.10.2019; Corporate Debtor responded via Reply dated 13.12.2019 disputing the claim. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's letter dated 13.03.2018 acknowledging delayed payments due to client delays and poor funds flow at year-end, promising clearance within 30 days; subsequent Reply to Demand Notice dated 13.12.2019 contradicting the earlier admission. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 184/BB/2020 was filed before NCLT Bengaluru Bench, which disposed of the petition on 09.09.2020 by directing the unserved Corporate Debtor to settle the small claim of Rs. 4.35 lakhs rather than admitting CIRP.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 9 of the IBC can dispose of an application by directing an unserved Corporate Debtor to settle the debt merely on the ground that the debt amount is small (Rs. 4.35 lakhs), rather than adjudicating upon service, completeness of the application, debt, and default as prescribed by law.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot sidestep the statutory framework of the IBC by disposing of an insolvency application with an order directing settlement merely because the claimed debt is small or the respondent has not appeared; it is bound to either admit or reject the application based on statutory criteria once service is effected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9 of the IBC, if the respondent has been duly served and fails to appear, the Adjudicating Authority is mandatorily required to examine whether the application is complete and whether there is an operational debt due and default; if complete, it must be admitted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance with notice and procedural service requirements under the IBC; the tribunal must satisfy itself regarding proper service of notice before proceeding to determine debt, default, and completeness of the petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Disposing of a Section 9 petition by directing an unserved respondent to settle the claim is improper and contrary to law; the order must be set aside and the petition remanded for fresh consideration on merits.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 09.09.2020 is set aside. CP (IB) No. 184/BB/2020 is restored to the file of NCLT Bengaluru Bench with a direction to hear the parties and decide the Section 9 application as per law. Parties directed to appear on 27th January, 2021. Appeal disposed of.
summary: Aster Technologies Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order disposing of its Section 9 IBC petition for Rs. 4.35 lakhs with directions to the unserved Corporate Debtor, Solas Fire Safety Equipment Pvt. Ltd., to settle the claim. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority cannot dispose of a petition by mandating settlement simply due to a small claim value. The Tribunal must ensure service and determine debt, default, and completeness under Section 9. Setting aside the impugned order, NCLAT remanded the matter back for adjudication on merits.

case_title: Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd. vs. Anish Niranjan Nanavaty & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant is Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Resolution Professional Anish Niranjan Nanavaty of Corporate Debtor Reliance Infratel Limited; other respondents include Doha Bank Q.P.S.C. and indirect lenders/COC members. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Reliance Infratel Limited involving indirect lenders admitted as financial creditors and resolution plan approval. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Approval of resolution plan following CIRP; monetary claim distributions are contested based on creditor categorization. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan unanimously approved by COC; approved by Adjudicating Authority via impugned order dated 03.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Plan unanimously approved by COC; pending applications IA Nos. 1960 of 2019 and 3055 of 2019 challenging the RP's recognition of indirect lenders as Financial Creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court-1) approved the Resolution Plan on 03.12.2020 while explicitly stipulating that payment distributions to creditors would be subject to the final outcome of pending interim applications IA Nos. 1960/2019 and 3055/2019.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in approving a Resolution Plan unanimously passed by the Committee of Creditors while keeping the distribution of proceeds subject to the outcome of pending interlocutory applications regarding creditor status and admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors approving a resolution plan is non-justiciable save for limited statutory parameters under Sections 30(2) and 61(3); an Adjudicating Authority can approve a plan while expressly conditioning creditor distributions on the final outcome of pending interlocutory adjudications. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 approval paired with Section 30(2) review requires conformity with legal provisions, but the pendency of applications disputing creditor categorization does not impede plan approval if distributions are explicitly tied to their eventual outcome. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of any established non-conformity with Section 30(2) conditions or violation of extant law in the unanimously approved resolution plan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no illegality in approving the Resolution Plan subject to pending applications; the appeal is disposed of directing NCLT to decide the pending IAs expeditiously within three weeks.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with directions to the Adjudicating Authority to decide pending IA Nos. 1960 of 2019 and 3055 of 2019 with utmost expedition, preferably within three weeks, and reconsider the distribution aspect under the impugned order if necessitated by the outcome.
summary: Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd. challenged the NCLT Mumbai order dated 03.12.2020 approving the Resolution Plan for Reliance Infratel Limited, contending that interlocutory applications filed by Doha Bank and others questioning creditor recognition remained undecided. NCLAT held that the commercial wisdom of the COC in approving the plan unanimously is paramount and subject only to limited review under Sections 30(2) and 61(3). Since the NCLT expressly subjected distribution to the outcome of pending applications, the approval was legally sound. The appeal was disposed of with directions to expedite the pending IAs within three weeks.

case_title: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II, Rourkela vs. Sumit Binani & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II, Rourkela (EPFO); Respondent No. 1 is Sumit Binani (RP/Liquidator of M/s Adhunik Metaliks Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Liberty House Group Metal Two Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP and subsequent resolution/liquidation process involving provident fund claims against the Corporate Debtor, Adhunik Metaliks Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory dues claimed towards employees' provident fund; resolution plan approved on 17.07.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved on 17.07.2018; liquidation ordered on 09.07.2019; liquidation order set aside and plan restored by NCLAT on 03.03.2020; present appeal filed in 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence showing Appellant approached the Liquidator with claims, who declined as his role ceased upon restoration of the Resolution Plan by NCLAT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench approved the Resolution Plan on 17.07.2018, later ordered liquidation on 09.07.2019, which was overturned by NCLAT restoring the plan on 03.03.2020; Appellant challenged the original approval order dated 17.07.2018 in 2021.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal challenging an order approving a resolution plan passed more than two years prior is barred by limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC despite intervening liquidation and restoration proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, an appeal must be preferred within 30 days, extendable by at most 15 days upon sufficient cause; this statutory limitation is rigid and cannot be bypassed due to intervening collateral orders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) confers jurisdiction on the Appellate Tribunal to condone delay up to a maximum period of 15 days only; beyond 45 days, the Tribunal has no power to condone delay. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict computation of the period of limitation from the date of the impugned order, disregarding extraneous subsequent developments where the appellant slept over its statutory appellate rights. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order having been passed on 17.07.2018 and remaining un-appealed within the statutory period, the present appeal is hopelessly barred by limitation.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as time-barred.
summary: The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II, Rourkela challenged the NCLT Cuttack Bench order dated 17.07.2018 approving the resolution plan for Adhunik Metaliks Ltd., arguing that subsequent liquidation orders and eventual plan restoration by NCLAT prevented earlier challenge. NCLAT held that under Section 61(2) of the IBC, appeals must be filed within 30 days, condonable only up to 15 days. Intervening proceedings do not excuse the delay in challenging the original order. The appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation.

case_title: Asher Ebrahim Melamed vs. Mr. Soumitra Banerjee & Anr.
appeal_number: Contempt Case (AT) No. 05 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 100 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Contempt Applicant is Asher Ebrahim Melamed; Alleged Contemnors/Respondents are Soumitra Banerjee and Shampa Banerjee (management of the company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate dispute involving allegations of oppression and mismanagement and management of company properties. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged non-compliance and violation of an interim status-quo/restraint order dated 25.04.2018 regarding company expenditure and asset management. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interim restraint order passed on 25.04.2018; Company Appeal (AT) No. 100 of 2018 finally disposed of on merits on 12.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Allegations that contemnors kept company property vacant causing financial losses and subsequently leased it to a disreputable entity in violation of the interim order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Appeal (AT) No. 100 of 2018 was disposed of on merits on 12.03.2020 upholding the NCLT order permitting the company to liquidate assets; contempt application filed thereafter alleging breach of the interlocutory order.
legal_issues: Whether a contempt application alleging willful violation of an interim order of an appellate tribunal remains maintainable before the appellate tribunal after the main appeal has been disposed of on merits and the interim order has merged into the final order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Interlocutory orders merge into the final order upon substantive disposal of the main appeal, and independent contempt proceedings for interim violations will not be entertained by the appellate forum where proceedings have returned to the primary adjudicatory body. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Doctrine of merger dictates that an interlocutory restraint order ceases to operate independently once final judgment on the subject matter is pronounced. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consideration of whether the main proceeding stands concluded and whether an alternative effective remedy lies before the executing or lower forum (NCLT) handling ongoing liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the interim order merged into the final order dated 12.03.2020 and liquidation is pending before the NCLT, the contempt application before NCLAT is not entertained, with liberty granted to approach the NCLT.
operative_order: Contempt Case (AT) No. 05 of 2020 stands disposed of with liberty to the Applicant to move an application before the NCLT.
summary: Asher Ebrahim Melamed filed a contempt petition alleging that Soumitra Banerjee and another breached an interim order dated 25.04.2018 by leasing company assets. NCLAT noted that the substantive Company Appeal (AT) No. 100 of 2018 had already been disposed of on 12.03.2020 upholding liquidation of assets. Applying the doctrine of merger, NCLAT held that the interim order merged with the final order and, as liquidation proceedings were underway before the NCLT, the contempt petition could not be entertained by NCLAT. The petition was disposed of with liberty to approach NCLT.

case_title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. M/s S. Kumars Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant is Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (trustee of EARC SC Trust 35); Corporate Debtor/Respondent is M/s S. Kumars Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities extended to the Corporate Debtor resulting in outstanding financial debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial debt; Section 7 application filed and pending admission. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed; NCLT passed order on 02.03.2020 deferring admission to 15.04.2021 to explore settlement; matter remained unheard. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pleadings and records demonstrating debt and default under Section 7 of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench, Court No.-II deferred the Section 7 petition via order dated 02.03.2020 to 15.04.2021 for settlement talks, leading the Financial Creditor to appeal against prolonged delay and violation of statutory timelines.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can repeatedly defer a Section 7 IBC application for over a year for settlement talks, contrary to the mandatory 14-day timeline prescribed under Section 7(4) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority must strictly adhere to the statutory timeframe under Section 7(4) of the IBC and cannot keep an insolvency admission petition pending for prolonged periods merely to explore non-fructifying settlement efforts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(4) of the IBC stipulates a period of 14 days for the Adjudicating Authority to ascertain the existence of default and decide upon admission or rejection of a Section 7 application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Satisfaction of the Adjudicating Authority as to the completeness of the Section 7 application and existence of debt and default on merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While granting opportunity for amicable settlement is not per se invalid, the Adjudicating Authority must adhere to statutory provisions and proceed to admit or reject the application on merits if settlement does not fructify.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with a request to the Adjudicating Authority to list the matter in the coming week and, if parties do not report settlement, pass an order of admission or otherwise on merit after ascertaining debt, default, and completeness. Order to be communicated forthwith.
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 02.03.2020 that adjourned its Section 7 petition against M/s S. Kumars Ltd. to 15.04.2021 for settlement discussions. NCLAT held that while encouraging settlement is permissible, the Adjudicating Authority cannot disregard the statutory 14-day mandate in Section 7(4) of the IBC. The NCLT was directed to list the petition in the following week and decide on admission or rejection on merits if no settlement is reported.

case_title: Vikash Gautamchand Jain vs. Hemant Shantilal Shah & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vikash Gautamchand Jain, Resolution Professional of Care Office Equipment Limited; Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are Hemant Shantilal Shah and another, promoters/erstwhile directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Care Office Equipment Limited wherein a resolution plan received 99.6% COC approval and was submitted for NCLT approval. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default during CIRP; liquidation value and valuation reports prepared under statutory regulations. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved with 99.6% voting share by the COC; Adjudicating Authority passed impugned directions on 15.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports and liquidation value submitted to NCLT in a sealed cover; erstwhile directors are neither MSME promoters, COC members, nor Resolution Applicants. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court No. 2 directed the RP on 15.12.2020 to file the liquidation value and valuation report and provide copies to the promoters/erstwhile directors; RP appealed this disclosure order.
legal_issues: Whether erstwhile directors and promoters who are neither resolution applicants nor COC members are legally entitled to receive copies of the confidential valuation report and liquidation value during the CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Valuation reports and liquidation values prepared during CIRP carry statutory confidentiality under the IBC and IBBI Regulations and are not routinely disclosable to erstwhile directors/promoters who are neither MSME applicants nor COC members. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 35 of the CIRP Regulations and governing IBC provisions restrict dissemination of valuation metrics to protect commercial integrity; entitlement of non-participating promoters must be strictly evaluated within statutory limits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of locus and qualification—promoters who are not Resolution Applicants, MSME exceptions, or COC members lack standing to access valuation data. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the RP complied with filing reports before the NCLT and the promoters' legal entitlement to confidential valuations was disputed, NCLT was directed to re-examine the disclosure order within the statutory framework of the IBC.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with directions to the Adjudicating Authority to take a re-look at its order directing supply of liquidation value and valuation reports to Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in light of the IBC and relevant IBBI Regulations.
summary: Vikash Gautamchand Jain, RP of Care Office Equipment Ltd., challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad order directing him to provide the liquidation value and valuation reports to erstwhile promoters/directors. NCLAT observed that the Resolution Plan had already been approved by 99.6% vote share of the COC, and the erstwhile directors were neither MSME promoters, COC members, nor Resolution Applicants. Emphasizing the confidentiality of valuation data under the IBC and IBBI Regulations, NCLAT directed the Adjudicating Authority to reconsider its direction to provide the confidential reports.

case_title: Ranjeet Kumar Verma vs. Committee of Creditors of Straight Edge Contract Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ranjeet Kumar Verma (Erstwhile IRP); Respondent is Committee of Creditors of Straight Edge Contract Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), acting through its Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Replacement of the Interim Resolution Professional by the Committee of Creditors during Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory voting requirement of 66% under Section 22(2); replacement resolution was passed with 100% COC vote share. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution passed by COC during statutory CIRP replacing the IRP with Mr. Ankit Sinha as Resolution Professional. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting records showing 100% COC vote share in favor of replacing the Appellant; COC was constituted by the Appellant himself. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: COC resolved to replace Appellant IRP with Ankit Sinha under Section 22; Appellant challenged his replacement before NCLAT alleging collusion and that COC members were related to the Corporate Debtor.
legal_issues: Whether an Interim Resolution Professional has a vested legal right or locus standi under the IBC to challenge his replacement by the Committee of Creditors passed with requisite majority under Section 22.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Interim Resolution Professional has no vested legal right to continue in office and lacks locus standi to challenge a resolution of the Committee of Creditors replacing him under Section 22 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 22 of the IBC, the Committee of Creditors possesses the absolute statutory prerogative by a minimum 66% voting share to appoint the IRP as RP or replace him with another RP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of legal injury; an IRP is an officer of the court and not a stakeholder in the CIRP, and cannot challenge the composition of a COC that he himself constituted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The replacement having been approved by 100% voting share of the COC, the appellant suffered no invasion of any legal right; hence the appeal is non-maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable.
summary: Ranjeet Kumar Verma, erstwhile IRP of Straight Edge Contract Pvt. Ltd., appealed against his replacement by the Committee of Creditors with 100% vote share, alleging the COC was related to the Corporate Debtor and acted collusively. NCLAT held that Section 22 vests complete power in the COC to replace an IRP with the requisite 66% majority. The IRP has no vested right to continue, is not a stakeholder, lacks locus standi to maintain the appeal, and cannot impeach the validity of a COC he constituted. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vs. Om Shree Krishan Enterprises & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Financial Creditor Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd.; Respondents are Om Shree Krishan Enterprises and another. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial facility and enforcement of security interest against corporate assets/security by the Financial Creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaults arising in connection with pending CP No. (IB) 391/ALD/2018 and interlocutory stay on security interest enforcement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned interim stay order passed by NCLT on 22.12.2020 expiring on 29.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interim application IA No. 352/2020 filed by respondents on medical grounds seeking adjournment and stay on security enforcement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Allahabad Bench) granted an interim stay on 22.12.2020 in IA No. 352/2020 restraining the Financial Creditor from enforcing security interest until 29.01.2021; Financial Creditor appealed against the stay.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate challenge against a short interim stay order restraining enforcement of security interest should be entertained when the substantive interim application is actively listed for early determination before the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate intervention against an interlocutory order granting a temporary stay on security enforcement is unwarranted when the order is of limited duration and the primary forum is seized of the substantive application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interlocutory case management orders granting short adjournments on medical grounds do not call for interference where statutory rights can be fully agitated before the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the immediate prejudice versus the short duration of the interim stay order set to expire within days. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appropriate relief is to direct the Adjudicating Authority to decide the creditor's objections and dispose of the interim application within a specified expeditious timeframe.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with a direction to the Adjudicating Authority to consider the objections raised by the Financial Creditor regarding enforcement of security interest and dispose of IA No. 352/2020 at the earliest, preferably within two weeks.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. appealed against an interim order dated 22.12.2020 passed by NCLT Allahabad in CP No. (IB) 391/ALD/2018 (IA No. 352/2020) staying the enforcement of its security interest until 29.01.2021. Noting that the interim order was granted on medical grounds and due to expire shortly, NCLAT declined to interfere with the interlocutory stay. Instead, the Appellate Tribunal disposed of the appeal by directing the NCLT to consider the bank's objections and decide IA No. 352/2020 expeditiously, preferably within two weeks.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vs. Atul Kumar Kansal, Resolution Professional, Universal Buildwel Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Financial Creditor Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd.; Respondent is Atul Kumar Kansal, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Universal Buildwel Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the IBC initiated via a Section 7 application that had been pending since 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in the context of the underlying financial debt leading to CIRP; approval of the Resolution Plan under Section 31 has been pending consideration since November 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application initiated in 2018; Section 31 application for approval of Resolution Plan pending before the Adjudicating Authority since November 2019; impugned order listed the Company Petition on 18.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record indicating prolonged pendency of the Section 31 plan approval application since November 2019 without disposal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Special Bench, Court-II) merely listed the petition on 18.01.2021; Appellant approached NCLAT seeking expeditious determination of the pending Section 31 approval application.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is required to dispose of an application for approval of a Resolution Plan under Section 31 of the IBC in an expeditious manner where the CIRP and Section 31 application have remained pending since November 2019.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory timelines under the IBC are essential to the object of the Code, and applications for approval of resolution plans under Section 31 must be prioritized and decided expeditiously by the Adjudicating Authority rather than being subjected to routine administrative adjournments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC mandates that the Adjudicating Authority shall promptly consider and determine whether an approved plan complies with statutory criteria to either approve or reject it, preserving the economic value of the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the timeline of procedural delay, specifically that the plan approval had remained undecided for over a year since November 2019. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because protracted delays undermine the CIRP framework, the Adjudicating Authority must be directed to dispose of the Section 31 plan approval application with utmost expedition.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of by requesting the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi, Special Bench, Court-II) to dispose of the application under Section 31 of the IBC with utmost expedition, preferably within two weeks.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. appealed against an administrative listing order of NCLT New Delhi regarding Universal Buildwel Pvt. Ltd., pointing out that the Section 31 plan approval application had been pending since November 2019 while the underlying Section 7 petition dated back to 2018. Stressing the necessity of strict adherence to IBC timelines, NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the Adjudicating Authority to decide the Section 31 application with utmost expedition, preferably within two weeks.

case_title: M/s. L&T Finance Ltd. vs. M/s. Essar Shipping Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Financial Creditor M/s. L&T Finance Ltd.; Respondent is Corporate Debtor M/s. Essar Shipping Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Extension of financial facilities/debt and subsequent insolvency proceedings initiated under the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of the financial debt by the Corporate Debtor resulting in the initiation of insolvency proceedings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Pleadings completed before the Adjudicating Authority with rejoinder filed by the Appellant; appeal heard by NCLAT on 28.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showing completion of pleadings, including the filing of the rejoinder by the Appellant, establishing that the petition was ripe for final hearing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The insolvency application remained pending before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench despite completion of pleadings; Appellant approached NCLAT seeking directions for an early and expeditious determination on merits.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should direct the Adjudicating Authority to hear and dispose of an insolvency petition on an expedited basis once the pleadings are complete and the matter is ripe for final consideration.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In furtherance of the time-bound nature and primary objectives of the IBC, where pleadings are complete and the petition is ripe for determination, the Adjudicating Authority is obligated to hear and dispose of the proceedings expeditiously without undue delay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The summary scheme of the IBC mandates that applications must not linger indefinitely once pleadings are closed, ensuring swift dispute resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ascertainment that all requisite pleadings, including the rejoinder, are formally placed on record and served between the parties. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The matter being ripe for adjudication, an expedited timeline must be fixed for the Adjudicating Authority to dispose of the case on merits.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with a request to the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) to accord consideration to the matter and ensure it is disposed of expeditiously, preferably within two weeks. Rejoinder to be served on the Respondent during the course of the day if not already served.
summary: M/s. L&T Finance Ltd. preferred an appeal before NCLAT seeking expeditious disposal of its insolvency proceedings against M/s. Essar Shipping Ltd. pending before NCLT Ahmedabad. Noting that the Appellant had filed its rejoinder and the case was fully ripe for final consideration, NCLAT disposed of the appeal by requesting the Adjudicating Authority to ensure final disposal on merits expeditiously, preferably within two weeks, and directed service of the rejoinder if not already completed.

case_title: Rajnish Jain vs. BVN Traders & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rajnish Jain is the Promoter and Managing Director of the suspended Board of Jain Mfg (India) Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 3 BVN Traders is an alleged Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 Anupam Tiwari is the Resolution Professional (replacing IRP Manoj Kumar Singh). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: BVN Traders (through partner Dilip Kapoor) advanced loan funds for working capital requirements against deposit of original title deed of Plot No. Y, 7/190(1), Swaroop Nagar, Kanpur, carrying agreed interest at 18% per annum repayable within one month. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 80,00,000/- advanced as loan with 18% per annum interest, where repayment was assured within one month from 15.08.2018 and remained unpaid, leading to an FIR on 21.10.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9 on 22.02.2019; Public Announcement on 24.02.2019; Form C claim filed by BVN Traders on 07.03.2019; First CoC meeting held on 23.03.2019 admitting BVN Traders with 30.6% voting share; RP replaced on 14.05.2019; CA No. 142/ALD/2019 filed under Section 60(5) in 2019; NCLT interim order on 19.08.2019; fourth CoC meeting on 30.08.2019; NCLT impugned order on 23.01.2020; seventh CoC on 14.02.2020; eighth CoC on 18.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form C claim with ledger extracts, bank statements showing RTGS fund transfers, deposit of original title deeds, WhatsApp communications confirming the 18% interest loan, and an admission email dated 02.09.2018 from Appellant requesting return of title deeds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP on 22.02.2019; IRP collated BVN Traders' claim as a Financial Debt; Appellant filed CA No. 142/ALD/2019 under Section 60(5) challenging BVN's status; NCLT Allahabad on 23.01.2020 dismissed the application declaring BVN Traders a Financial Creditor relying on CoC majority voting.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors possesses adjudicatory power under the IBC to determine or vote upon whether a creditor is a Financial Creditor or an Operational Creditor; whether a Resolution Professional can suo motu reclassify an admitted financial creditor's claim under the guise of updating the list of claims; and whether an advance for working capital carrying 18% per annum interest against title deeds constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Determination of creditor status as financial or operational is purely a question of statutory interpretation and application of law to facts, falling exclusively within the adjudicatory realm of the Adjudicating Authority, and cannot be delegated to or decided by the Committee of Creditors under the cloak of commercial wisdom or majority voting; nor can a Resolution Professional suo motu reclassify an already collated and admitted claim under the guise of updating the claim list. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1)(b) and 25(2)(e) authorize collation, verification, and updation by adding subsequent claims, but do not empower an IRP/RP to sit in review of admitted claims or reclassify status; commercial wisdom under Section 30(4) and Section 28 is confined to business feasibility and viability, not legal adjudication of debt status. Section 5(8) requires disbursement of money against consideration for the time value of money, which includes loans advanced with interest for working capital. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct fund flows substantiated by bank RTGS statements, security creation via deposit of title deeds, and electronic communications demonstrating agreed interest rates conclusively establish disbursement for time value of money. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: BVN Traders is a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8); NCLT's final conclusion was valid on facts though its reliance on CoC voting was legally flawed; and all subsequent CoC resolutions attempting to eliminate BVN Traders and withdraw CIRP under Section 12A were void and non-est.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Impugned order declaring BVN Traders as Financial Creditor upheld, while setting aside the Adjudicating Authority's reasoning relying on CoC voting. Resolutions of the 4th, 7th, and 8th CoC meetings attempting to reclassify and eliminate BVN Traders and approving Section 12A withdrawal are declared beyond jurisdiction and directed to be ignored. Copy of judgment directed to be forwarded to the Chairperson, IBBI for necessary action. No orders as to costs.
summary: An appeal was filed by the suspended director challenging NCLT Allahabad's dismissal of CA No. 142/2019, which affirmed BVN Traders as a Financial Creditor of Jain Mfg (India) Pvt Ltd based partly on a CoC majority vote. The NCLAT held that determining whether a claimant is a financial or operational creditor is an adjudicatory question governed by statutory law, outside the commercial wisdom or voting mandate of the CoC. Furthermore, a Resolution Professional cannot reclassify an admitted claim under the guise of updating claims. On merits, an advance of Rs. 80 lakhs at 18% interest against title deeds satisfies Section 5(8). The appellate tribunal upheld BVN Traders' status and invalidated CoC resolutions seeking its exclusion.

case_title: Brookefield Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Shailaja Iyer & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: First Appellant is Brookefield Technologies Pvt Ltd; Second Appellant is Pawan Kumar Jain (Director); First Respondent is Shailaja Iyer (shareholder/former director); Respondents 2 to 4 are other shareholders/directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operating business of private tech company where Respondent No. 1 originally held 45% equity; company availed a term loan of Rs. 1.85 crore from Karur Vysya Bank backed by collateral of a jointly-owned property; company subsequently issued rights shares on 25.04.2016 which diluted Respondent No. 1's shareholding to 9%. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression/mismanagement grievance arising from alleged illegal dilution of shareholding from 45% to 9% following unaccepted rights issue offer of 25.04.2016 open for 18 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Alleged resignation of Respondent No. 1 dated 05.04.2016; Board Meeting accepting resignation on 13.04.2016; DIR-12 filed 13.04.2016; Rights offer dated 25.04.2016; Civil Suit O.S. No. 3554 of 2016 filed before City Civil Court Bangalore and dismissed; CP No. 110/BB/2019 filed on 04.04.2019; IA No. 170 of 2020 for waiver filed in 2020; NCLT Bengaluru waiver order passed on 05.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resignation letter, emails dated 13.04.2016 expressing parting ways, Form DIR-12, Rights Issue letter of offer dated 25.04.2016, joint purchase deed of White Field property dated 07.08.2013, and judgment of 39th Addl. City Civil Judge dismissing OS No. 3554/2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP No. 110/BB/2019 alleging oppression/mismanagement and IA No. 170/2020 seeking waiver under Section 244(1); NCLT Bengaluru granted waiver on 05.06.2020 holding that a prima facie case was established and meritorious litigation cannot be thrown out at the threshold.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT properly exercised its discretion under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant a waiver of shareholding qualifications to maintain a petition under Section 241 alleging illegal dilution of equity from 45% to 9%; and whether prior civil court proceedings regarding director resignation create an issue estoppel or res judicata bar against maintaining an oppression and mismanagement petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal possesses discretionary judicial power under the proviso to Section 244(1) to grant waiver of minimum qualification requirements where a substantial or significant shareholder makes out a bona fide prima facie grievance of oppression, especially where the reduction of shareholding below statutory thresholds is itself the impugned act of oppression. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proviso to Section 244(1) read with Section 241 allows waiver based on objective facts of hardship and substantiality; civil court bar under Section 430 reinforces that civil courts lack jurisdiction over oppression and mismanagement, meaning civil findings on directorship do not extinguish tribunal jurisdiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: At the threshold waiver stage, the Tribunal does not conduct a final trial on merits but determines whether the petition is prima facie meritorious, non-frivolous, and raises triable issues of oppressive conduct. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The reduction of equity from 45% to 9% via a challenged rights issue justifies granting waiver under Section 244(1); preliminary objections regarding estoppel, delay, and resignation can be adjudicated at the final hearing without barring admission.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Impugned order of NCLT Bengaluru dated 05.06.2020 waiving compliance with Section 244(1) and admitting CP No. 110/BB/2019 is upheld. Appellants granted liberty to raise all legal and factual contentions at the final hearing before NCLT. No costs.
summary: Appellants appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order allowing an application under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, waiving the 10% shareholding threshold in favour of Respondent No. 1 to pursue an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241. Respondent No. 1 alleged her 45% shareholding was fraudulently diluted to 9% via an improper rights issue after her contentious removal as director. The NCLAT held that the statutory waiver power is equitable and discretionary, properly exercised when the petitioner's shareholding reduction below the qualifying threshold is the core oppressive grievance. Holding that civil court findings did not bar NCLT's exclusive jurisdiction, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: KVR Industries Private Limited vs. P.P. Bafna Ventures Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is KVR Industries Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is P.P. Bafna Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor represented by authorized signatory Praful Prakash Bafna). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt transaction wherein Financial Creditor claimed default in payment of debt exceeding Rs. 12.45 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial debt default to the tune of Rs. 12.45 crores forming subject of Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 204/7/AMR/2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interim status quo order passed on 02.12.2019; Section 9 petition by Eshwar Enterprises admitted on 12.02.2020; Section 7 petition disposed of on 13.02.2020 directing claim submission before IRP; Section 9 matter settled and withdrawn on 21.02.2020; Financial Creditor filed IA Nos. 41 & 42 of 2020 on 21.02.2020; Corporate Debtor filed IA Nos. 51 & 52 of 2020 in February/March 2020 and IA No. 62 of 2020 on 13.03.2020; Financial Creditor filed reaffirmation affidavit on 09.05.2020 and withdrawal memo on 29.05.2020; NCLT impugned order passed on 08.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Restoration applications (IA 41 & 42/2020) bearing disputed signatures, comparison with General Affidavit and Vakalatnama in CP 204/2019, unilateral forensic expert report dated 02.03.2020 from Truth Labs alleging forged/transplanted signatures, and subsequent reverifying affidavit by Praful Prakash Bafna dated 09.05.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP/204/2019 had been closed suo motu on 13.02.2020 due to parallel Section 9 admission; following settlement of the Section 9 petition, Financial Creditor sought restoration via IAs 41 and 42; Corporate Debtor alleged forged signatures seeking criminal inquiry under Section 340 CrPC; NCLT Amaravati permitted withdrawal of IAs 41 and 42, suo motu restored CP/204/2019, and held it lacked criminal jurisdiction regarding perjury.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to initiate preliminary inquiry and criminal prosecution under Section 340 read with Section 195(1)(b) of the CrPC for alleged forgery of pleadings; whether the Adjudicating Authority has inherent power under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules and Section 424 Companies Act to suo motu restore a Section 7 petition previously closed due to a separate operational creditor CIRP that subsequently got settled; and whether Section 340 CrPC proceedings were expedient in the interest of justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 424(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, the NCLT and NCLAT are deemed Civil Courts for the purposes of Section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the CrPC, possessing jurisdiction to conduct preliminary inquiry under Section 340 CrPC; however, initiation of such prosecution is discretionary and warranted only when deliberate falsehood affecting administration of justice is evident and inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice, not to satisfy private tactical vendettas. Furthermore, tribunals possess inherent powers to suo motu restore an insolvency petition disposed of due to parallel CIRP proceedings that were subsequently withdrawn. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(4) explicitly designates tribunal proceedings as judicial proceedings under IPC Sections 193 and 228, conferring jurisdiction under Section 195 CrPC. Under Section 340 CrPC, the threshold requirement of 'expedient in the interests of justice' requires a prima facie case of conscious and deliberate fabrication resulting in injury or illicit advantage, which was absent where the deponent reaffirmed the substantive contents. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unilateral private handwriting reports obtained without tribunal sanction lack conclusive weight; in the absence of mens rea, illicit gain, or false substantive pleadings, variance in signature does not justify criminal perjury proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in concluding it lacked criminal jurisdiction under Section 340 CrPC, but correctly restored the Section 7 petition; on merits, holding a Section 340 inquiry was inexpedient, justifying the final dismissal of the Corporate Debtor's criminal applications.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of. Suo motu restoration of CP (IB) No. 204/7/AMR/2019 and dismissal of IA Nos. 41, 42, and 62 of 2020 affirmed. Observations of the Adjudicating Authority stating it lacked jurisdiction to entertain Section 340 CrPC proceedings are set aside, and IA Nos. 51 and 52 of 2020 are substantively disposed of as not expedient in the interest of justice. No order as to costs.
summary: Corporate Debtor appealed against an order of NCLT Amaravati which suo motu restored a Section 7 petition filed by P.P. Bafna Ventures Pvt. Ltd. and dismissed applications seeking criminal prosecution under Section 340 CrPC against the creditor's signatory for allegedly forged signatures on restoration petitions. The NCLAT held that while NCLT is deemed a Civil Court under Section 424(4) of the Companies Act with jurisdiction under Section 340 CrPC, prosecution is only warranted when deliberate falsehood is demonstrated and expedient in the interest of justice. Finding no fraudulent intent or falsehood in substantive claims, the NCLAT affirmed the restoration of the Section 7 petition and closed the criminal applications.

case_title: Rajendra Narottamdas Sheth & Anr. vs. Chandra Prakash Jain & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Rajendra Narottamdas Sheth and Heenaben Rajendra Kumar Sheth are suspended directors of Corporate Debtor R.K. Infratel Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Chandra Prakash Jain (IRP); Respondent No. 2 is Union Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan and working capital credit facilities aggregating Rs. 20,26,50,000/- sanctioned across multiple accounts between 2009 and 2013 for rolling out dark fibre broadband and leased lines in Surat. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 24,62,98,391/- as of 31.03.2019; date of default/NPA declared was 30.09.2014. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30.09.2014; Loan recall notice issued on 01.10.2014; OA No. 656 of 2015 filed before DRT; Section 7 petition filed on 25.04.2019 (registered 29.04.2019); NCLT Ahmedabad admitted CIRP on 01.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debit balance confirmation letter dated 07.04.2016 signed by Corporate Debtor; regular credit entries from April 2016 to May 2018; letter dated 17.11.2018 acknowledging outstanding liabilities; admission in Corporate Debtor's NCLT reply that it deposited Rs. 316.53 lakhs post-NPA (including Rs. 154.67 lakhs under 'cut-back' arrangement from 12.06.2017 onwards) and a total of Rs. 776.67 lakhs from 2013-14 onwards; general power of attorney dated prior to IBC in favour of Chief Manager Praveen Kumar Gupta. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 324/NCLT/AHM/2019 filed on 25.04.2019; Corporate Debtor opposed on limitation and power of attorney competence; NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the application on 01.06.2020 holding debt acknowledged within limitation.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of IBC filed in 2019 is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act where default/NPA occurred on 30.09.2014, in light of balance confirmations under Section 18 and repayments under Section 19; whether deductions made by a bank under a 'cut-back' arrangement constitute part-payments of debt under Section 19; and whether a General Power of Attorney executed prior to the enactment of the IBC validly authorizes an officer to initiate Section 7 proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 apply to Section 7 IBC applications by virtue of Section 238A, meaning written acknowledgments of liability or payments made on account of debt/interest within the three-year period compute a fresh period of limitation from the date of acknowledgment or payment; further, a comprehensive pre-IBC General Power of Attorney authorizing legal proceedings empowers a bank official to file an insolvency petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Article 137 prescribes a 3-year limitation triggered from the date of default/NPA (which foundational date does not shift), Sections 18 and 19 extend the computation of the prescribed period under Section 2(j) and Section 3. Payments made under a 'cut-back' arrangement with the debtor's consent qualify fully as payments made on account of debt under Section 19. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Signed balance confirmation letters coupled with bank statements and pleadings admitting ledger deposits and installment payments post-NPA provide sufficient legal foundation for extension of limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was filed well within limitation due to continuous acknowledgments and part-payments up to 2018–2019; the attorney holder possessed valid authority; and natural justice was not infringed.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Order of Adjudicating Authority admitting Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 324/NCLT/AHM/2019 and initiating CIRP against R.K. Infratel Ltd. is upheld. No orders as to costs.
summary: Suspended directors of R.K. Infratel Ltd. challenged the admission of a Section 7 IBC application by Union Bank of India, contending the debt was barred by limitation since the account was classified as an NPA on 30.09.2014, and asserting the bank official lacked authority under a pre-IBC power of attorney. The NCLAT held that a comprehensive general power of attorney validly authorized the filing, and that by virtue of Section 238A, Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act apply to IBC proceedings. Given written balance confirmations in 2016 and 2018 and continuous part-payments (including via cut-back arrangements), a fresh limitation period commenced, making the 2019 petition timely.

case_title: J.M. Housing Limited & Ors. vs. Surender Kumar Gupta & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is J.M. Housing Ltd.; Appellants 2 to 4 are Ankur Aggarwal, Neeraj Jindal, and Rupesh Kumar Gupta (Shareholders/Directors); Respondents 1 to 3 are Surender Kumar Gupta, Anita Gupta, and Nikyta Gupta (Petitioners holding 36.65% shares); Respondents 4 to 8 are other related entities and family members. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development business involving the J.M. Florence project in Noida and industrial park development by subsidiary Durga Enterprises Pvt. Ltd., involving substantial bank facilities and commercial inventories. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of siphoning and diversion of company funds, unauthorized sale of properties/plots, and illegal allocation of 8 flats without petitioner consent; outstanding liabilities included Rs. 68.37 crores (earlier Rs. 99.25 crores) to Punjab & Sind Bank and over Rs. 106 crores to Noida/Greater Noida authorities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 1 resigned as director on 01.11.2016; settlement deed dated 19.04.2017; CP/133/2020 filed on 14.08.2020; petition listed for hearing on 05.10.2020; impugned ex-parte ad-interim restraint order passed on 05.10.2020; appeal decided on 18.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: WhatsApp group created by Bench Officer on the afternoon of 05.10.2020 where Appellants 2 and 3 exited before hearing; erroneous entry in order sheet listing Appellants 2-4 as 'Advocates'; audited balance sheets as of 31.03.2019; bank credit facility records; and settlement deed dated 19.04.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents 1-3 filed CP/133/2020 under Sections 241-242; NCLT New Delhi Court-II on first listing (05.10.2020) simultaneously issued notice and granted ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining Appellants from selling any company properties or altering shareholding; Appellants appealed on breach of natural justice.
legal_issues: Whether an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining a real estate development company from selling its property/stock-in-trade and altering shareholding, passed on the first day of listing while directing issuance of notice, violates the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem) under Section 420(1) and Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An ex-parte ad-interim restraint order entailing severe civil consequences that paralyze an ongoing commercial enterprise's ordinary trade cannot be passed without providing a reasonable and effective opportunity of hearing in accordance with the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(1) and Section 424 of the Companies Act mandate that tribunals must adhere to principles of natural justice; while interim powers under Section 241/242 are broad, orders causing grave disruption require reasoned consideration after adequate notice, in alignment with Rules 37-48 of NCLT Rules. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the order sheet erroneously records parties as appearing through counsel due to clerical mistake and parties had no functional access to virtual hearing links, the order must be treated as ex-parte and legally defective for want of procedural fair play. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ad-interim restraint order paralyzed the company's housing project operations and was passed in violation of natural justice, necessitating remand for de novo hearing on merits.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned ad-interim order dated 05.10.2020 passed in CP/133/2020 set aside. Matter remitted to NCLT New Delhi Court-II for de novo consideration and dispassionate adjudication on merits after providing adequate opportunity of hearing to all parties. Stay application I.A. No. 2556/2020 closed. No costs.
summary: Appellants appealed against an ex-parte ad-interim order of NCLT New Delhi Court-II in CP/133/2020 which restrained real estate firm J.M. Housing Ltd. and its directors from selling any company property or altering shareholding. The order was passed on the very first day of listing while directing registry notice, despite Appellants not being represented due to virtual hearing link anomalies and clerical listing errors. The NCLAT held that imposing blanket restraint orders that jeopardize commercial operations and stock-in-trade without affording a proper hearing violates audi alteram partem and statutory mandates under Sections 420 and 424 of the Companies Act. The appellate tribunal set aside the order and remitted the dispute for de novo hearing.

case_title: Anubhav Anilkumar Agarwal vs. Bank of India & Anr.
appeal_number: Review Application (AT) No. 15 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1504 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant Anubhav Anilkumar Agarwal is the suspended director of Corporate Debtor/Guarantor RNA Corp. Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Bank of India (Financial Creditor); Chamber Constructions Pvt. Ltd. is a co-guarantor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by Bank of India backed by corporate guarantees executed by RNA Corp. Pvt. Ltd. and Chamber Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (Deed of Guarantee dated 09.12.2013). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to simultaneous claims of identical debt amounts admitted against both the guarantor entities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against co-guarantor Chamber Constructions in CP No. 3962/IBC/NCLT/MB/MAH/2018; Section 7 petition admitted against RNA Corp; NCLAT dismissed original appeal CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 1504 of 2019 on 07.02.2020; Review Application (AT) No. 15 of 2020 decided on 07.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Guarantee dated 09.12.2013 executed by Chamber Constructions, list of admitted creditors and CoC report of Chamber Constructions confirming admission of the identical debt claim, and Para 14 of the original NCLAT judgment dated 07.02.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 application against RNA Corp.; on appeal, NCLAT dismissed CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 1504/2019 on 07.02.2020 finding no proof of guarantee by Chamber Constructions; Applicant filed Review Application No. 15/2020 under Rule 11 asserting error apparent on the face of the record under the Piramal doctrine.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT possesses statutory or inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 or Section 420 of the Companies Act, 2013 to review its own final judgment on merits and reappraise evidence.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Power of review is not an inherent power and cannot be exercised by an appellate tribunal unless expressly conferred by statute; Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 is confined to procedural rectifications and preventing abuse of process, and cannot be invoked as an appeal in disguise to reconsider findings of fact or revisit judgments on merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 confers rectification power exclusively on the NCLT and not the Appellate Tribunal; Rule 11 inherent powers cannot be enlarged to create substantive review jurisdiction or substitute a finding arrived at upon appreciation of evidence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An alleged misreading of documentary evidence (such as a Deed of Guarantee or admission list) that requires re-examination or elaborate reappraisal does not constitute an error apparent on the face of the record amenable to correction under inherent powers. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Even if the tribunal's factual finding in the original judgment was erroneous, substituting it would exceed jurisdiction under Rule 11, rendering the review application untenable.
operative_order: Review Application dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: Applicant filed a review application under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 seeking review of the NCLAT's judgment dated 07.02.2020, which had affirmed the admission of a Section 7 IBC application against corporate guarantor RNA Corp. Pvt. Ltd. The Applicant contended that the tribunal committed an error apparent on the face of the record by overlooking the guarantee deed of co-guarantor Chamber Constructions Pvt. Ltd., thereby violating the Piramal bar against duplicate CIRPs for identical claims. The NCLAT dismissed the application, holding that review is a statutory creature not inherently available under Rule 11, and inherent powers cannot be utilized to reappraise evidence or sit in appeal over earlier findings.

case_title: Apya Capital Services Private Limited vs. Guardian Homes Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Apya Capital Services Pvt. Ltd. is an Operational Creditor (financial advisory service provider); Respondent Guardian Homes Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (real estate developer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Engagement letter dated 08.11.2017 to provide debt syndication, structuring, and financial advisory services to raise funding between Rs. 200–450 Crores, stipulating a professional fee of 1% of total facilities arranged, leading to KKR India Asset Finance Pvt. Ltd. sanctioning a Rs. 280 Crore facility for project 'Cityscapes'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of balance professional advisory fees amounting to Rs. 2,05,00,000/- plus taxes out of total billed fee of Rs. 2,80,00,000/-; Rs. 75,00,000/- paid on 25.01.2019, leaving default of Rs. 2,05,00,000/- (with at least Rs. 75,00,000/- unconditionally admitted by Corporate Debtor). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Engagement letter executed 08.11.2017; mandate letters dated 03.04.2018 and 03.09.2018; sanction letter by lender dated 16.10.2018; invoices raised on 16.01.2019, 30.01.2019, 27.02.2019, and 20.04.2019; demand notice under Section 8 issued on 20.05.2019; NCLT Mumbai order of dismissal on 03.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Engagement letter dated 08.11.2017; proforma invoice dated 20.04.2019; Corporate Debtor's letter dated 02.05.2019 acknowledging liability up to Rs. 1.5 Crores and requesting revised full invoice for Rs. 75 Lakhs; Section 8 demand notice dated 20.05.2019 to which no statutory reply was sent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 application CP No. 3113/I&B/2019; NCLT Mumbai dismissed it on 03.01.2020 finding lack of debt and clear deficiency of service under Section 5(6)(b).
legal_issues: Whether a unresponded Section 8 demand notice where the Corporate Debtor admitted an outstanding payable balance of Rs. 75 Lakhs in prior correspondence constitutes a pre-existing dispute regarding deficiency of service under Section 5(6)(b); and whether a dispute merely regarding the quantum of operational debt justifies the dismissal of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where an operational debt meets the statutory threshold and liability is partially admitted, a dispute relating solely to the quantum of debt does not justify rejection of an application under Section 9; in the absence of pre-existing arbitration, suit, or a contemporaneous response to the Section 8 notice, self-serving claims of deficiency in service cannot bar CIRP admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Dispute' under Section 5(6)(b) requires a real, substantial pre-existing contest regarding quality of goods or service; an unaccepted unilateral settlement offer or arbitrary fee-withholding does not establish a bona fide pre-existing dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mutual extension of mandates and continued engagement beyond an initial indicative term vitiate claims that time was strictly of essence; an admission in writing of balance fees (Rs. 75 Lakhs) establishes default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in finding deficiency in service and absence of debt; default was clear and admission of the application was mandatory.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned order of NCLT Mumbai dated 03.01.2020 set aside. Adjudicating Authority directed to admit the application under Section 9 of the IBC after granting an opportunity to the Corporate Debtor to settle the claim. No order as to costs.
summary: Operational Creditor Apya Capital Services appealed the dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application by NCLT Mumbai, which had held there was a deficiency of service in raising funds for Corporate Debtor Guardian Homes Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that the Corporate Debtor had admitted liability of at least Rs. 75 lakhs in pre-notice correspondence and failed to respond to the Section 8 demand notice. Disputes regarding quantum or delays that were mutually accommodated do not constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6)(b). The appeal was allowed and NCLT was directed to admit the insolvency petition after giving the debtor an opportunity to settle.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of LEEL Electricals Ltd. vs. Leel Electricals Ltd. Through its IRP, Arvind Mittal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Committee of Creditors of LEEL Electricals Ltd. represented through State Bank of India; Respondent is Leel Electricals Ltd. represented through its Interim Resolution Professional Arvind Mittal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing CIRP of corporate debtor LEEL Electricals Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Replacement of IRP Arvind Mittal voted on by CoC with 78.28% majority voting share. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced; First CoC meeting held wherein resolution to confirm IRP as RP received 0% votes; Second CoC meeting e-voting concluded where IRP garnered only 8% votes, while resolution to replace IRP with Gangaram Agarwal secured 78.28% votes; CoC filed application under Section 22(3); NCLT Allahabad adjourned hearing to 20.01.2021 by order dated 14.12.2020 granting IRP time to file objections. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting results of first and second CoC meetings; email dated 26.11.2020 by IRP asserting Section 22 replacement can only happen in the first meeting; resolution passed with 78.28% voting share in favour of Gangaram Agarwal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC applied to NCLT Allahabad under Section 22(3) to replace IRP; NCLT on 14.12.2020 adjourned the case to 20.01.2021 directing IRP to file a reply affidavit; CoC appealed against the delay and procedural indulgence granted to the IRP.
legal_issues: Whether the replacement of an Interim Resolution Professional by the Committee of Creditors under Section 22 of the IBC requires adjudicatory inquiry or granting an opportunity to the IRP to file objections; and whether such replacement is non-justiciable under the commercial wisdom of the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The replacement of an Interim Resolution Professional by a Resolution Professional under Section 22 of the IBC is an unreviewable commercial decision of the Committee of Creditors, and the outgoing IRP has no locus standi or vested legal right to oppose the replacement or file objections before the Adjudicating Authority. 2.
