STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 16(5) read with Section 22, the IRP's tenure continues strictly until an RP is appointed under Section 22; Section 27 applies to replacement of an already appointed RP and not to the initial replacement of an IRP. Protracted proceedings under Section 27 are unwarranted when replacing an IRP under Section 22. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of a valid CoC resolution approved by more than the required 66% majority voting share is conclusive, leaving no adjudicatory discretion to the tribunal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in entertaining objections from the IRP and adjourning the CIRP, warranting immediate appointment of the CoC-approved RP.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned order of NCLT Allahabad dated 14.12.2020 set aside. Adjudicating Authority directed to carry forward CIRP with Mr. Gangaram Agarwal discharging functions as Resolution Professional in accordance with the CoC resolution. Order to be communicated forthwith.
summary: The Committee of Creditors of LEEL Electricals Ltd. appealed an adjournment order passed by NCLT Allahabad that allowed the Interim Resolution Professional time to file objections against his replacement by a new Resolution Professional under Section 22 of the IBC. The NCLAT set aside the order and allowed the appeal, ruling that the substitution of an IRP under Section 22 is an unfettered commercial decision of the CoC requiring at least a 66% vote share, which is not subject to judicial review. The outgoing IRP possesses no legal right to resist replacement, and tribunals must not prolong the CIRP by inviting replies or treating Section 22 appointments under Section 27.

case_title: Bhim Sain Goyal vs. The American Swan Lifestyle Co. Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Bhim Sain Goyal is the Interim Resolution Professional of American Swan Lifestyle Co. Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor under CIRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Conduct and statutory administration of CIRP within the 180-day timeframe under Section 12 of IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exclusion of 167 days sought from the ordinary CIRP period of 180 days due to COVID-19 pandemic restrictions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Nationwide lockdown imposed on 25.03.2020; CoC resolved on 09.09.2020 recommending exclusion of lockdown period; NCLT New Delhi Court-II on 23.10.2020 granted exclusion of only 68 days while denying 167 days; NCLAT appeal decided on 15.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Orders of the Supreme Court in Suo Motu Writ Petition (Civil) No. 3/2020 extending limitation; local movement restrictions in the NCR region impacting operations of the corporate debtor's registered office; resolution and recommendation of CoC dated 09.09.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IRP applied to NCLT New Delhi Court-II for exclusion of 167 days from CIRP period; NCLT passed an unreasoned order on 23.10.2020 allowing only 68 days, prompting the IRP to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the period of disruption caused by the COVID-19 nationwide lockdown and severe movement curbs in the National Capital Region (from 20.03.2020 to 02.09.2020) should be excluded from the statutory 180-day CIRP period under Section 12 of the IBC in light of the Supreme Court's suo motu extension orders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Uncontrollable time lost during a pandemic lockdown that physically disables an insolvency professional and team from functioning must be excluded from the computation of the statutory CIRP period to protect the viability of the resolution process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the Supreme Court's order under Articles 141 and 142 in Suo Motu WP (C) No. 3/2020 directly governs judicial filing limitation, the equitable spirit behind it applies to statutory timelines under Section 12 of the IBC; orders rejecting exclusion must provide plausible, speaking reasons. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Official lockdowns and regional pandemic restrictions establish sufficient impossibility of performance to warrant time exclusion when recommended by the CoC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority's order was non-speaking; the entire period from 20.03.2020 to 02.09.2020 is liable to be excluded.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned order of NCLT New Delhi dated 23.10.2020 set aside. Exclusion of time from 20th March, 2020 to 2nd September, 2020 granted in reckoning the initial 180-day CIRP period. IRP directed to proceed with expedition, with liberty to seek further extension from NCLT if needed. Order to be communicated forthwith.
summary: The Interim Resolution Professional of American Swan Lifestyle Co. Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an unreasoned order of NCLT New Delhi Court-II which granted an exclusion of only 68 days instead of the requested 167 days from the initial 180-day CIRP timeline due to COVID-19 disruptions. The NCLAT held that the impugned decision was a non-speaking order and that the spirit of the Supreme Court's suo motu limitation extensions applied to alleviate hardships caused by pandemic-induced lockdowns and movement curbs in the NCR. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the NCLT order and allowed full exclusion from 20.03.2020 to 02.09.2020.

case_title: Sumilon Polyester Pvt. Ltd. vs. Parikh Packaging Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Sumilon Polyester Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (supplier of CC PET and CC MET-PET films); Respondent M/s Parikh Packaging Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (packaging converter). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Longstanding business engagement involving continuous supply of CC PET and CC MET-PET packaging films by Appellant to Respondent under recurrent purchase orders and credit terms. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under Section 9 totaled Rs. 19,07,560/- (comprising Rs. 11,83,255/- balance under invoice dated 04.09.2018 of total value Rs. 38,83,169/-, plus debit notes of Rs. 5,96,234/- dated 28.02.2019 and Rs. 1,28,071/- dated 08.04.2019). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Complaints regarding quality raised in Nov/Dec 2017; email exchange throughout Dec 2017–Jan 2018; subsequent supply invoice dated 04.09.2018; first demand notice issued on 19.04.2018 with reply; second statutory demand notice issued under Section 8 followed by corporate debtor's reply dated 18.07.2019; NCLT dismissal order dated 20.03.2020; NCLAT judgment pronounced on 23.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 02.01.2018 acknowledging defect complaint and agreeing to take back 9116.4 kg unused film; email dated 04.01.2019 citing Rs. 11.5 lakh loss due to lamination failures and loss of client Dabur; email dated 08.02.2019 directing cessation of all business with Appellant due to quality failures; ledger accounts showing intermittent running account payments of Rs. 87,78,462/- between 01.02.2018 and 05.02.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 656/9/NCLT/AHM/2019 under Section 9; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed the application on 20.03.2020 on the grounds of pre-existing quality disputes and issuance of debit notes.
legal_issues: Whether the email exchanges documenting substandard materials, return of goods, and debit notes constitute a bona fide 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9 of the IBC; and whether payments made across an ongoing running account establish the conclusive settlement of prior quality disputes.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 cannot be maintained if a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of goods or services exists prior to the issuance of the demand notice under Section 8, and ongoing business quality contestations across connected transactions preclude insolvency admission where the defense is neither frivolous, spurious, nor a moonshine defense. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Section 8(2)(a) read with Section 9(5) and the Mobilox doctrine, the threshold for determining a dispute requires only a plausible contention demonstrating real controversy touching liability or quality; dispute is not strictly confined to isolated invoices if systemic quality contestations remain open on running ledger accounts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous email trails rejecting supplies, returning consignments, intimating consequential losses, and debiting accounts constitute sufficient credible evidence of a pre-existing dispute. Running ledger payments do not establish settlement of a dispute unless explicitly tied to full and final adjustment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor demonstrated an active, unresolved pre-existing dispute regarding product adhesion failures, justifying the rejection of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Impugned order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dated 20.03.2020 dismissing the Section 9 petition is affirmed. No orders as to costs. Liberty reserved for Appellant to pursue recovery before an appropriate competent civil forum.
summary: Operational Creditor Sumilon Polyester Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench regarding unpaid amounts on a film consignment invoice from September 2018 and subsequent debit notes totaling Rs. 19,07,560/-. The Corporate Debtor had consistently raised disputes concerning poor adhesion in the supplied CC PET/MET-PET films, which resulted in unusable packaging laminates, return of 9116.4 kg of material, client cancellation from Dabur, and issuance of debit notes. The NCLAT, applying the Supreme Court's Mobilox Innovations and Innoventive Industries jurisprudence, held that the email records evidenced a genuine, continuous, and non-frivolous pre-existing dispute that preceded the Section 8 demand notice. Running account ledger entries did not establish complete compromise, and the appeal was accordingly dismissed.

case_title: Mr. Kishore Katare vs. Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kishore Katare is a shareholder and director of Katare Spinning Mills Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Bank of India (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Vitthal M. Dahake (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of India sanctioned a term loan facility of Rs. 9,00,00,000/- and cash credit facility of Rs. 6,00,00,000/- on 14.08.2013 (total credit exposure availed Rs. 25 Crores) for modernization of spinning units, working capital, and installation of a solar power project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 23,90,64,696.69/- (including interest and expenses) claimed up to 28.08.2018; date of NPA declared was 31.03.2015 and date of default occurred was stated as 30.06.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 31.03.2015; Deeds of Acknowledgment executed on 31.08.2015; OTS proposals sent on 01.04.2017, 21.11.2017, 04.01.2018, 09.07.2018, and 14.09.2020; Section 7 petition filed on 30.08.2018; NCLT Mumbai admission order passed on 17.07.2020; appeal decided on 21.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 1 application Part-IV; Deeds of Acknowledgment of Debt and Securities dated 31.08.2015; multiple written One-Time Settlement (OTS) offers proposing lump-sum payments ranging from Rs. 6 Crores to Rs. 15.5 Crores; part-payments of Rs. 3.24 Crores and Rs. 3 Crores across installments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank of India filed CP No. 3460/IBC/NCLT/MB/MAH/2018 under Section 7 on 30.08.2018; Corporate Debtor did not raise the issue of limitation before NCLT; NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted CIRP on 17.07.2020; Appellant appealed on the ground of limitation relying on the Supreme Court's Babulal Gurjar ruling.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 IBC application filed on 30.08.2018 is barred by limitation when the loan account was declared NPA on 31.03.2015/30.06.2015, in view of successive written OTS settlement proposals offering part payments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act; and whether the judgment in Babulal Vardharji Gurjar bars acknowledgment of debt under OTS proposals.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Repeated, voluntary written settlement offers and One-Time Settlement (OTS) proposals acknowledging liability and offering lump-sum payments constitute valid acknowledgments of debt within the meaning of Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, thereby extending the period of limitation for maintaining an insolvency application under Section 7 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act is applicable to Section 7 petitions; the dictum in Babulal Vardharji Gurjar does not exclude the operation of acknowledgment of debt where the creditor places concrete written admissions, signed OTS proposals, and part-payments on record. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted letters issued by corporate debtors proposing revised payment terms, seeking interest waivers, and remitting upfront deposits provide unequivocal documentary evidence of debt acknowledgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the corporate debtor continuously acknowledged debt through written OTS offers between 2015 and 2018, the Section 7 petition was filed within the extended limitation period.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Impugned order dated 17.07.2020 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court No. II admitting Section 7 application and initiating CIRP against Katare Spinning Mills Limited is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Bank of India against Katare Spinning Mills Limited for a default exceeding Rs. 23.90 Crores, contending that the petition was barred by limitation as it was filed in August 2018 following an NPA classification in March 2015. The NCLAT affirmed the admission, holding that the Corporate Debtor had repeatedly and unequivocally acknowledged its indebtedness through written OTS proposals submitted in 2017 and 2018, accompanied by substantial part-payments. Such conduct constitutes valid acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, rendering Babulal Gurjar inapplicable and keeping the petition timely.

case_title: M/s. Neesa Infrastructure Limited vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Neesa Infrastructure Limited (Corporate Debtor/Corporate Applicant represented by promoter Sanjay Gupta); Respondents 1 to 4 are Financial Creditors (State Bank of India, Indian Overseas Bank, Central Bank of India, Small Industries Development Bank of India). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Substantial banking and credit facilities extended by consortium of institutional lenders for industrial infrastructure operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete default in debt servicing leading to NPA classification on 30.04.2014, recovery recovery claims in DRT OA No. 53/2015, and SARFAESI auction realized at Rs. 13,68,58,600/-; balance sheet of 31.03.2016 recorded deferred tax liability of Rs. 10,34,37,089/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30.04.2014; SARFAESI sale certificate issued 27.10.2017; SPA executed on 05.12.2017; Section 10 application CP No. (IB) 61/10/NCLT/AHM/2018 filed; NCLT rejection order passed on 17.09.2020; NCLAT judgment pronounced on 23.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 6 petition disclosures; Special Power of Attorney dated 05.12.2017 executed by Neelu Gupta misstating shareholding as 4,50,000 shares whereas promoter register showed 3,30,000 shares; absence of audited financials post-2016; non-disclosure of unsecured debt metrics; list of 241 operational debtors without quantified defaults. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Promoter Sanjay Gupta filed Section 10 application on behalf of corporate debtor as all directors were disqualified under Section 164 of Companies Act; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejected the petition on 17.09.2020 citing lack of Special Resolution under Section 10(3)(c), fabricated shareholding figures, disqualified status, and mala fide abuse to stall pending DRT/SARFAESI actions.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate insolvency application under Section 10 of the IBC can be instituted by disqualified promoters without passing a Special Resolution of shareholders under Section 10(3)(c); and whether Section 10 can be invoked mala fide merely to impose a Section 14 moratorium to thwart bank recovery and SARFAESI enforcement proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 10 of the IBC cannot be maintained by promoters without strict compliance with statutory preconditions, including a valid Special Resolution passed by shareholders under Section 10(3)(c); the IBC cannot be deployed as an abusive device by disqualified management solely to invoke a moratorium and stall lawful debt recovery proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10(3)(c) is mandatory; corporate applicants cannot bypass shareholder approval. Disqualification of all directors under Section 164 of the Companies Act does not empower promoters to initiate CIRP unilaterally on discrepant and fabricated powers of attorney. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Material contradictions between sworn power of attorney declarations and statutory promoter share records, suppression of debt schedules, and evasion of tax filings reveal lack of bona fides. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 10 application was fraudulent, lacked statutory authority, and was rightly rejected by the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dated 17.09.2020 rejecting CP No. (IB) 61/10/NCLT/AHM/2018 affirmed. No orders as to costs.
summary: Disqualified promoters of Neesa Infrastructure Limited appealed against the rejection of their Section 10 IBC corporate debtor petition by NCLT Ahmedabad. The application was filed by a promoter on the basis of an inaccurate Special Power of Attorney, claiming all company directors stood disqualified under Section 164 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, emphasizing that passing a Special Resolution by shareholders under Section 10(3)(c) is mandatory. The Tribunal observed that the corporate applicant presented fabricated shareholding details, omitted debt schedules, and filed the petition with the mala fide intent of securing a moratorium under Section 14 to stall pending SARFAESI and DRT recovery actions.

case_title: Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Amit Gupta & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. is a stakeholder/creditor; Respondent No. 1 is Amit Gupta (Resolution Professional of Unimark Remedies Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Unimark Remedies Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondents 3 & 4 are ICICI Bank and Corporation Bank (CoC Members). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing CIRP valuation and resolution proceedings concerning pharmaceutical firm Unimark Remedies Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arising in corporate insolvency resolution with CIRP exceeding 550 days, involving disputed valuations of tangible and pharmaceutical intangible assets. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP admitted on 03.04.2018; initial valuers appointed under Regulation 27; Corporation Bank challenged valuation via MA 1406/2019; split division bench verdict referred to third member who ordered fresh intangible valuation on 28.01.2020; NCLAT declined interference in CA 418/2020; NCLT regular bench order on 24.02.2020; impugned NCLT Mumbai order passed on 19.11.2020 in IA 1141/2020; appeal dismissed on 23.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Initial valuation reports by Delta and R&C valuing intangible assets at Nil; Order of third Member (Judicial) dated 28.01.2020 directing fresh valuation of intangibles by GAA Advisory LLP; CoC resolutions endorsing GAA Advisory valuation; Resolution Plan submitted to NCLT for approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Split bench verdict on valuation was settled by third member on 28.01.2020; subsequent regular bench attempted to appoint its own valuers on 24.02.2020; NCLT Mumbai Bench on 19.11.2020 allowed IA 1141/2020 permitting RP to proceed with GAA Advisory as approved by CoC majority; Appellant appealed challenging the valuation continuity.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in upholding the continuation and report of an independent valuer (GAA Advisory LLP) approved by the majority CoC to value intangible assets, instead of directing fresh valuation de novo after CIRP had elapsed over 550 days.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In CIRP proceedings that have experienced substantial delay, the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in endorsing an independent valuer's report to evaluate corporate assets should not be derailed by hyper-technical challenges or dissenting minority creditors where the process conforms to judicial directions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 27 of the IBBI CIRP Regulations read with Section 31 requires objective determination of fair and liquidation values; tribunals should avoid continuous re-valuation shuttling that frustrates time-bound resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an independent valuer was appointed pursuant to the binding directions of a third referee Member and the majority CoC adopted the resulting intangible valuation alongside existing tangible valuations, no prejudice is established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's direction to proceed with GAA Advisory avoided further delay in an already extended CIRP (>550 days), warranting non-interference.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without admission. Order of NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 19.11.2020 in IA 1141 of 2020 is maintained. No costs.
summary: Appellant Omkara ARC appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order allowing IA 1141/2020, which directed the Resolution Professional of Unimark Remedies Ltd. to proceed with the valuation conducted by GAA Advisory LLP as approved by the CoC majority. Corporation Bank (holding ~7% vote share) had continuously disputed valuations of pharmaceutical intangible assets, resulting in a split verdict, reference to a third member, and conflicting bench directions. Noting that the CIRP had already exceeded 550 days and the Resolution Plan was pending approval before the NCLT, the NCLAT held that reopening valuation afresh at the instance of a dissenting stakeholder would frustrate time-bound resolution. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited vs. Committee of Creditors of Jai Hind Projects Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. is the assignee of financial facilities from L&T Finance Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is the CoC of Jai Hind Projects Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is Parthiv Parikh (RP); Respondent No. 3 is Premnarayan Ramanand Tripathi (IRP); Respondent No. 4 is Parixit Irrigation Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Assignment of loan facility by original lender L&T Finance Ltd. to Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vide Deed of Assignment dated 29.03.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities of the Corporate Debtor, regarding which Bombay High Court had passed an interim injunction on 04.06.2018 in Chamber Summons No. 827/2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court injunction dated 04.06.2018; Section 7 CIRP admitted on 02.11.2018; loan assignment on 29.03.2019; Resolution Plan approved by NCLT on 19.03.2020; Appellant's email inquiries to IRP/RP sent on 18.04.2020 and 19.04.2020; claim formally submitted by Appellant on 15.06.2020; IA No. 487 of 2020 rejected on 29.09.2020; NCLAT appeal decided on 23.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of assignment dated 29.03.2019; emails exchanged between Appellant and RP in April 2020 indicating written approval orders were awaited; Form C claim filed on 15.06.2020; order dated 19.03.2020 approving resolution plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application CP(IB) No. 172/2018 was admitted against Jai Hind Projects Ltd. on 02.11.2018; resolution plan was approved by NCLT Ahmedabad on 19.03.2020; Appellant filed its claim on 15.06.2020 and filed IA 487/2020 to review/recall the approval order; NCLT rejected IA 487/2020 on 29.09.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor who acquired debt via assignment during CIRP can file a claim after the Resolution Plan has already been approved by the Adjudicating Authority; and whether an approved resolution plan can be recalled or opened up to admit belated claims.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a Resolution Plan has received statutory approval from the Adjudicating Authority, the CIRP reaches culmination and no fresh claims can be entertained or admitted by the Resolution Professional; belated claims submitted after plan approval cannot undo completed resolution processes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: CIRP is an in rem public proceeding governed by strict public notices and statutory time windows; a creditor is bound to submit claims within the designated framework, and Section 14 moratorium supersedes prior individual execution proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof that a claim was submitted nearly three months after the formal approval of the resolution plan by the NCLT conclusively extinguishes the applicant's right to participate in CIRP distributions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A claim submitted on 15.06.2020 following plan approval on 19.03.2020 cannot be entertained, and the refusal to recall the approved plan is legally sound.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without admission. Order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dated 29.09.2020 rejecting IA No. 487 of 2020 is affirmed. No costs.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank appealed against an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejecting its application (IA No. 487 of 2020) to review and recall an order dated 19.03.2020 that approved a Resolution Plan for Jai Hind Projects Ltd. The Appellant, which had taken assignment of the debt from L&T Finance in March 2019, lodged its claim before the Resolution Professional only on 15.06.2020. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that CIRP is initiated by public notice and culminates upon approval of the resolution plan. Once a plan has been formally approved by the Adjudicating Authority, fresh claims cannot be entertained, and the clock cannot be turned back to admit belated claimants.

case_title: Jay Overseas Pvt. Ltd. vs. George Samuel, RP of Jason Decor Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Jay Overseas Pvt. Ltd. is a prospective Resolution Applicant; Respondent No. 1 is George Samuel (RP of Jason Decor Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Indian Overseas Bank (sole Financial Creditor constituting 100% of CoC). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of corporate debtor Jason Decor Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory CIRP period of 180 days expired on 15.06.2020; 68 days of lockdown exclusion expired on 28.08.2020; subsequent 90-day extension granted on 26.11.2020; CoC rejected original plan on 11.11.2020 and recommended liquidation; RP filed Section 33 application on 24.11.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9/7 CP (IB) 257/2019 admitted on 19.12.2019; CoC rejected plan on 11.11.2020; Section 33 liquidation application filed 24.11.2020; revised plan Annexure P/6 submitted; NCLT Ahmedabad rejected IA 886/2020 on 09.12.2020 as premature; NCLAT hearing and disposal on 23.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Revised Resolution Plan submitted by Appellant (Annexure P/6, page 46) providing a drastically improved financial offer; CoC minutes dated 11.11.2020; statement of Indian Overseas Bank (100% CoC) consenting before NCLAT to evaluate the revised plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC resolved to liquidate the debtor and RP filed Section 33 application; Appellant filed IA 886/2020 seeking directions to submit a revised plan; NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the application on 09.12.2020 as premature and unmaintainable since CoC was functus officio; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority ought to direct the Committee of Creditors to consider an improved, revised Resolution Plan where the formal liquidation order under Section 33 has not yet been passed and the sole financial creditor (100% CoC) expresses consent to evaluate the plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The primary objective of the IBC is resolution and preservation of the corporate debtor as a going concern, avoiding liquidation wherever possible; hence, prior to the formal passing of a liquidation order under Section 33, a improved resolution plan may be placed before the CoC for consideration if the CoC consents. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An application under Section 33 pending disposal does not create an irreversible statutory bar preventing the CoC from exercising its commercial wisdom to reconsider an improved plan in the interest of corporate revival. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consent of the 100% voting share financial creditor to consider the revised offer provides sufficient justification to bypass formalistic procedural objections. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in dismissing the application as premature; remitting the plan for CoC consideration advances the Code's core objective of avoiding corporate death.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned order dated 09.12.2020 set aside. Resolution Professional directed to process the revised Resolution Plan (Annexure P/6) and place it before the Committee of Creditors for consideration on its merits, with freedom to accept or proceed with liquidation. Order communicated forthwith.
summary: Resolution Applicant Jay Overseas appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order dismissing its application (IA 886/2020) to place a revised, significantly improved Resolution Plan before the CoC of Jason Decor Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had rejected the application as premature because the CoC had previously voted for liquidation and filed an application under Section 33. Before the NCLAT, Indian Overseas Bank (holding 100% CoC voting rights) agreed to consider the revised proposal. Emphasizing that the foremost objective of the IBC is the revival of the Corporate Debtor and prevention of liquidation, the NCLAT set aside the dismissal order and directed the RP to submit the revised plan to the CoC for evaluation.

case_title: Mohan Lal Jain vs. Lalit Modi & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mohan Lal Jain (Liquidator of Kaliber Associates Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Lalit Modi; Respondents 2 to 45 are other private parties/creditors; Respondent No. 46 is the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution and Liquidation proceedings involving avoidance transactions, preferential transfers, and fraudulent trading under Sections 43 and 66 of IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Specific impugned avoidance transactions and fraudulent transfers challenged by the Liquidator under CA 1342/2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CA 1342/2019 filed by Liquidator; NCLT impugned order passed on 27.02.2020; NCLAT interim order arraying MCA on 06.11.2020; final appeal decided on 16.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's report and forensic transaction audit records detailing preferential transfers and wrongful trading forming the bedrock of CA 1342/2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed CA 1342/2019 under Sections 43 and 66; NCLT New Delhi Bench on 27.02.2020 refused to adjudicate, holding it was beyond its scope to examine such transactions and directing that explanations be submitted to investigating agencies; Liquidator appealed against this abdication of statutory power.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) has the statutory duty and exclusive jurisdiction under Sections 43, 60(5), and 66 of the IBC to adjudicate applications regarding preferential transactions and fraudulent trading, or whether it can abdicate this duty by relegating the matter to investigating agencies or the MCA.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) is statutorily mandated to adjudicate applications concerning preferential transactions (Section 43) and fraudulent/wrongful trading (Section 66); it cannot abdicate its adjudicatory authority or delegate such determination to external investigating agencies or the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 43, 65, 66, and 69 of the IBC confer express jurisdiction upon the NCLT to investigate and determine civil avoidance matters, fraudulent initiation, and fraudulent dealings; delegating these statutory functions constitutes an error of jurisdiction contrary to the Supreme Court's ruling in Embassy Property Developments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an avoidance application contains specific allegations supported by transactional material, the NCLT must evaluate the responses on merits rather than declining jurisdiction based on differing factual versions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's refusal to examine the transactions in CA 1342/2019 was legally unsustainable, requiring an expeditious judicial determination within two months.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned order of NCLT New Delhi dated 27.02.2020 in CA 1342/2019 set aside and modified with a direction that the Adjudicating Authority shall inquire into the alleged preferential and fraudulent transactions in accordance with law with expedition, preferably within two months. Order communicated forthwith.
summary: The Liquidator of Kaliber Associates Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi Bench disposing of CA 1342/2019, where the tribunal refused to adjudicate allegations of preferential transactions and fraudulent trading under Sections 43 and 66 of the IBC, stating that examining such disputes was beyond its scope and should be addressed to investigating agencies. Citing the Supreme Court's decision in Embassy Property Developments, the NCLAT held that the NCLT is statutorily empowered and obligated to determine matters concerning avoidance transactions and fraudulent trading. The Adjudicating Authority cannot abdicate its jurisdiction to police or investigating authorities, and the matter was remitted for decision on merits within two months.

case_title: Madanlal Balmukund Karwa Company & Ors. vs. New Phaltan Sugar Works Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Madanlal Balmukund Karwa Company (CA 1021/2020), Madanlal Trading Company (CA 1022/2020), and Pawan Trading Company (CA 1023/2020) (Creditors/Lenders); Respondents are Corporate Debtor New Phaltan Sugar Works Ltd., CoC, and successful Resolution Applicant Shri Dutt India Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business loans and commercial advances extended by Appellants to the Corporate Debtor, funded via third-party borrowings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of commercial advances; claims filed before IRP were rejected for lack of supporting documents on 21.05.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claim rejected by IRP on 21.05.2019; CIRP extended by 90 days on 11.09.2019; miscellaneous applications MA 3431/2019, 3430/2019, and 3429/2019 filed seeking claim acceptance; Resolution Plan approved by CoC with 100% vote share; NCLT Mumbai approved plan on 11.11.2019; NCLAT appeals dismissed on 04.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: IRP rejection communication dated 21.05.2019 for absence of proof; order of NCLT dated 11.09.2019 granting 90-day extension; subsequent applications seeking to introduce supporting documents turned down for delay; criminal proceedings and arrest of partner in CA 1023/2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants failed to substantiate claims within the statutory window; NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed their applications (MA Nos. 3429, 3430, 3431 of 2019) on grounds of delay and approved the resolution plan on 11.11.2019; Appellants challenged the plan approval.
legal_issues: Whether creditors whose claims were rejected by the IRP for lack of documentary evidence can seek de novo admission of their claims at a belated stage after the CoC and Adjudicating Authority have approved a Resolution Plan under Section 31; and whether an extension of the CIRP period grants creditors a renewed right to submit proof of claims.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory timelines for submission and verification of claims during CIRP are mandatory; once a Resolution Plan has received unanimous CoC approval and been sanctioned by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31, the process culminates and rejected claimants cannot reopen CIRP or tender proof belatedly. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An extension of the CIRP timeline under Section 12 granted for concluding the resolution process does not resurrect expired stages for claim collation or grant defaulting creditors a fresh window to substantiate claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A claimant who fails to furnish supporting documentary evidence to the IRP within prescribed periods and suffers dismissal of interlocutory applications cannot impeach the final resolution plan on equitable grounds of personal hardship or criminal detention. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Reopening the CIRP after plan approval is impermissible in law, rendering the appeals meritless.
operative_order: Appeals dismissed at the threshold. Approval of the Resolution Plan submitted by Shri Dutt India Pvt. Ltd. by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 11.11.2019 is upheld. No orders as to costs.
summary: Appellants filed three connected appeals challenging an order dated 11.11.2019 of NCLT Mumbai Bench that approved the Resolution Plan of Shri Dutt India Pvt. Ltd. for Corporate Debtor New Phaltan Sugar Works Ltd. (approved unanimously by 100% CoC vote). The IRP had rejected the Appellants' claims in May 2019 due to lack of supporting evidence, and subsequent applications to introduce proof were dismissed by NCLT for latches. Appellants pleaded personal hardship, arrest, and reliance on a 90-day CIRP extension. The NCLAT held that timelines under the IBC are sacrosanct; a general CIRP extension does not reopen claim collation, and CIRP cannot be reopened de novo once a resolution plan has crossed culmination.

case_title: K. Venugopalan Nair vs. Rita Venugopal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant K. Venugopalan Nair is the Ex-Managing Director of Dewa Projects Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Rita Venugopal (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Dr. K.S. Venugopal (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt investment/advances extended by Financial Creditors to Dewa Projects Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial debt giving rise to Section 7 admission. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT admission order passed on 13.09.2019; initial 30-day appeal period expired on 14.10.2019; 15-day condonable period expired on 30.10.2019; national COVID lockdown imposed on 23.03.2020; appeal filed before NCLAT on 26.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Paragraph 19 of NCLT order establishing service of notice delivered on 25.06.2019 via courier receipt and acknowledgment; appeal filing date of 26.11.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditors filed Section 7 petition; NCLT Kochi Bench admitted petition on 13.09.2019, imposing moratorium and appointing IRP; Ex-MD filed appeal on 26.11.2020 seeking condonation of delay citing lack of service and COVID limitation suspensions.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT has the statutory power under Section 61(2) of the IBC or Section 238A read with the Limitation Act to condone an appeal delay exceeding the maximum condonable window of 15 days where the limitation expired prior to the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation scheme prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC is self-contained and mandatory; an appeal preferred beyond the initial 30 days plus the discretionary 15-day extended period cannot be condoned by invoking Section 238A or general Limitation Act provisions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) specifically regulates appellate limitation and its max 15-day condonation limit; where limitation expired in October 2019 (well before the March 2020 COVID suspension orders), the appeal is incurably time-barred. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Official tribunal records establishing successful delivery of courier notice and postal acknowledgment disprove unsubstantiated allegations of breach of natural justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was filed with an incurable delay exceeding four months beyond the outer condonable limit, requiring dismissal.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed as barred by limitation along with all pending interlocutory applications (including IA No. 2825 of 2020). No orders as to costs.
summary: The Ex-Managing Director of Dewa Projects Pvt. Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Kochi Bench dated 13.09.2019 admitting a Section 7 IBC petition by financial creditors. The appeal was filed on 26.11.2020. The Appellant claimed breach of natural justice and sought the benefit of COVID-19 limitation tolling orders. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as barred by limitation, noting that the 30-day statutory window and the 15-day discretionary extension under Section 61(2) expired in October 2019, months before the onset of the pandemic. As Section 61(2) constitutes a complete and overriding code for appeals, general provisions of the Limitation Act cannot be imported via Section 238A to condone delay beyond 15 days.

case_title: GABS Megacorp Ltd. vs. Sutanu Sinha and Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is GABS Megacorp Ltd. (the successful auction purchaser/bidder of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Sutanu Sinha (Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 represents the Stakeholders/Lenders. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern during the liquidation process in favour of the Appellant for a total sale consideration of Rs. 1654.77 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The 90-day period under Regulation 44 for depositing full sale consideration expired on 03-12-2020 without Appellant depositing payment by 30-11-2020; default in timely completion of liquidation/sale proceeds payment due to pending judicial adjudication on waiver of interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation commenced on 26-07-2019; initial liquidation completion timeline was 24-10-2020; voting lines on interest waiver concluded on 03-12-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes recorded on 08-12-2020 and voting results showing the Lenders and Stakeholders Committee approved interest waiver by 91.59% majority (Annexures 6 and 7 of the Counter Affidavit); table computing 271 days of judicial delay from 25-03-2020 to 21-12-2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench passed an order granting partial extension (orders dated 29-09-2020 read with 11-11-2020) but failed to exclude the time consumed in prosecuting legal applications, prompting appeal to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the period consumed in litigation and judicial intervention seeking waiver of interest and completion of sale under the liquidation process can be excluded under Regulation 47A read with Regulation 44 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time consumed in bona fide legal proceedings before judicial authorities to resolve bottlenecks in an asset sale during liquidation must be excluded from the statutory liquidation timeline to advance the objectives of value maximization. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 47A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 permits exclusion of time lost due to events beyond the control of the liquidator/purchaser, including periods spent under judicial intervention and pandemic disruptions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unanimous or supermajority approval (91.59%) of the Lenders and Stakeholders Committee consenting to an interest waiver and extension of time serves as conclusive justification for the tribunal to grant exclusion in the interest of justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The 271-day period from 25-03-2020 to 21-12-2020 constituted judicial intervention and was rightfully excluded, extending the liquidation deadline to 22-07-2021 and granting 90 days from 22-12-2020 to deposit the remaining purchase price.
operative_order: Appeals are allowed; exclusion of 271 days w.e.f. 25-03-2020 to 21-12-2020 granted; liquidation process extended until 22-07-2021; Appellant directed to pay Rs. 1654.77 Crores (minus advance payment) within 90 days from 22-12-2020, with no interest charged if paid within 30 days.
summary: GABS Megacorp Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Hyderabad which failed to account for litigation time while granting an extension to conclude the sale of the Corporate Debtor during liquidation. With the Stakeholders Committee having approved an interest waiver by 91.59%, the NCLAT held that the 271 days consumed in judicial intervention from 25 March 2020 to 21 December 2020 must be excluded under Regulation 47A. The Tribunal extended the liquidation period to 22 July 2021 and granted the Appellant 90 days from 22 December 2020 to deposit the remaining consideration of Rs. 1654.77 Crores without interest if paid within 30 days.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Rosewood Trexim Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shailendra Singh
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Committee of Creditors of Corporate Debtor Rosewood Trexim Pvt. Ltd., acting through Resolution Professional Mr. Shailendra Singh. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of the Corporate Debtor requiring completion within statutory timelines under Section 12 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Expiry/exhaustion of the mandatory 180-day CIRP period during lockdown disruptions and medical incapacity of the Resolution Professional. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Professional fell ill on 01-09-2020, tested COVID-19 positive on 18-09-2020; attempted virtual CoC meeting on 24-09-2020; tested negative on 02-10-2020; issued notice for 8th CoC meeting on 05-10-2020; CoC meeting held on 08-10-2020 resolving to seek exclusion. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Medical reports and quarantine records (Annexures A8 and A9, pages 63-70) establishing the RP's COVID-19 infection and physical incapacitation, alongside the unanimous 100% resolution passed at the 8th CoC meeting on 08-10-2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi, Principal Bench) dismissed IA 4719 of 2020 on 19-11-2020, refusing to exclude the lockdown and medical quarantine period from the CIRP period.
legal_issues: Whether the period of nationwide lockdown coupled with the Resolution Professional's medical incapacitation due to COVID-19 contraction can be excluded from the statutory CIRP period under Section 12 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unforeseen statutory lockdowns and personal physical incapacitation of an insolvency professional caused by a pandemic justify exclusion of time from the mandatory CIRP period to prevent hardship and preserve the resolution process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory time limits under Section 12 of the IBC must be applied purposively; the CoC does not become defunct or dissolved automatically upon expiration of timelines when nationwide lockdowns and medical incapacitation halt operations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented medical evidence of infection and strict home isolation constitutes sufficient proof of physical impossibility to conduct CIRP proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in strictly compounding hardship; 203 days from 15-03-2020 to 04-10-2020 must be excluded from the 180-day CIRP timeline, coupled with a 90-day extension.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 19-11-2020 is set aside; exclusion of 203 days w.e.f. 15-03-2020 to 04-10-2020 from the CIRP period is granted, and an extension of 90 days is allowed with directions to expedite the CIRP.
summary: The Committee of Creditors of Rosewood Trexim Pvt. Ltd., through its RP, challenged the NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of an application seeking exclusion of time and extension of the CIRP timeline. The RP had been incapacitated after testing positive for COVID-19 in September 2020 during the nationwide pandemic disruptions, and the CoC unanimously voted to seek an extension. Setting aside the NCLT order, the NCLAT held that the CoC is not deemed dissolved and that unexpected medical quarantine and lockdown warrant mitigating hardship. The Tribunal allowed the exclusion of 203 days and granted a 90-day extension to conclude the CIRP.

case_title: Lifestyle Magazines Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. In Re
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Lifestyle Magazines Pvt. Ltd. (Transferor Company) and Jindal Diamonds Pvt. Ltd. (Transferee Company), both closely held private limited companies. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed Scheme of Amalgamation between the Transferor and Transferee companies under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-applicable (corporate restructuring matter with zero debt default; companies had no secured or unsecured creditors). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application for dispensation of meetings was dismissed by NCLT Special Bench New Delhi on 19-06-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Nil creditors certificate, and written No Objection Certificates (NOCs) submitted via sworn affidavits by all shareholders (two shareholders of the Transferor Company and three shareholders of the Transferee Company, who were also their directors). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench New Delhi on 19-06-2020 refused to exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to dispense with calling meetings of the shareholders of the merging companies.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the power and discretion to dispense with convening meetings of equity shareholders in a scheme of amalgamation when all shareholders of closely held private companies give their written consent via affidavits and there are no creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Convening formal meetings of equity shareholders for a scheme of amalgamation can be dispensed with where all shareholders of closely held entities have unanimously provided unconditional consent through affidavits and there are no creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with inherent powers under Rule 11 do not mandate the futile formality of physical meetings when 100% written consent by affidavit is demonstrably on record. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Sworn affidavits containing No Objection Certificates from 100% of the shareholders establish complete compliance with the statutory requirement to consider and approve a scheme. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Compelling closely held companies facing financial difficulties to conduct formal shareholder meetings when all members are directors who consented on affidavit causes unnecessary financial hardship, justifying dispensation.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned orders dated 19-06-2020 are set aside to the extent of directing shareholder meetings; the matter is remanded to the NCLT to consider the Scheme of Amalgamation without insisting on convening meetings of the shareholders.
summary: Lifestyle Magazines Pvt. Ltd. and Jindal Diamonds Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Special Bench New Delhi order declining to dispense with meetings of shareholders for their proposed Scheme of Amalgamation. Both companies were closely held private entities with no secured or unsecured creditors, and all shareholders (two in the transferor and three in the transferee) had submitted consent affidavits/NOCs. Citing established precedents, the NCLAT held that requiring formal meetings imposed unnecessary financial burdens where 100% consent had already been furnished on affidavit. The Tribunal set aside the requirement and remanded the matter to NCLT to proceed with sanctioning the scheme.

case_title: Vijayalakshmi Enterprises vs. Malabar Hotels Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vijayalakshmi Enterprises (alleged Financial Creditor / Disputed Creditor); Respondent is Malabar Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported financial facility/loan claimed by the Appellant against the Corporate Debtor, which was disputed and unadjudicated. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact amount not crystalized; claim was rejected in its entirety by the Resolution Professional during a prior CIRP of the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan of the Corporate Debtor was approved by NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai on 17-09-2018 with Clause (9) addressing disputed creditors; subsequent Section 7 petition dismissed on 05-05-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Extract of the approved Resolution Plan (page 170) and Clause (9) of the NCLT approval order dated 17-09-2018, stipulating that claims of disputed creditors (including Appellant) shall be paid based on the outcome of adjudication of legal proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Division Bench-I dismissed the Appellant's Section 7 petition on 05-05-2020 on grounds that debt was not crystalized and Section 7 does not constitute adjudication of disputed claims.
legal_issues: Whether triggering a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 of the IBC constitutes 'adjudication of legal proceedings' to determine and recover an unliquidated, disputed claim preserved under an approved Resolution Plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC cannot be invoked as a substitute for civil recovery or suit-based adjudicatory proceedings to determine disputed, unliquidated claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The phrase 'outcome of adjudication of legal proceedings' in a resolution plan saving clause contemplates suits, arbitrations, or civil adjudications, and cannot be interpreted to include Section 7 IBC applications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Section 7 requires existence of a clear, crystalized, and undisputed financial debt and default; an unadjudicated disputed claim rejected by the RP does not meet the standard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Proceedings under the IBC are exclusively designed for insolvency resolution, not money claim adjudication; hence the Section 7 application was legally untenable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merit, without precluding the Appellant from seeking appropriate legal remedies before a competent civil or arbitral forum subject to legal exceptions.
summary: Vijayalakshmi Enterprises appealed an order of NCLT Chennai dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against Malabar Hotels Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant's claim had previously been rejected by the RP, but an approved Resolution Plan provided that disputed creditors would be paid based on the outcome of the adjudication of legal proceedings. The Appellant argued this entitled it to file under Section 7. Rejecting this contention, the NCLAT affirmed that Section 7 proceedings are meant solely for insolvency resolution, not for adjudicating disputed monetary claims, which must be determined by a civil court or arbitral tribunal.

case_title: Seroco Lighting Industries Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ravi Kapoor, RP for Arya Filaments Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Seroco Lighting Industries Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / promoter-connected person); Respondent No. 1 is Ravi Kapoor (Resolution Professional of Arya Filaments Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor, an MSME). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and approval of a resolution plan by the Appellant for the revival of Corporate Debtor Arya Filaments Pvt. Ltd. under Section 31 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact financial figures not stated; Appellant sought downward revision/modification of its payment obligations under the approved plan citing post-approval financial stress and COVID-19 slowdown. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sole resolution plan was approved by the Adjudicating Authority; Appellant subsequently filed IA No. 96 of 2020 seeking revision, which was dismissed on 23-10-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor was registered as an MSME; records established that the Appellant, being a promoter/connected person, had prior intimate knowledge of the financial conditions and operations of the Corporate Debtor before bidding. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad dismissed IA No. 96 of 2020 on 23-10-2020 with costs, holding that the Resolution Applicant cannot claim ignorance of financial health or withdraw/modify an approved plan.
legal_issues: Whether a Successful Resolution Applicant of an MSME Corporate Debtor can seek modification, revision, or withdrawal of an approved Resolution Plan under Section 61(3) of the IBC citing financial distress or lack of knowledge of financial condition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Successful Resolution Applicant cannot modify, revise, or withdraw an approved Resolution Plan once sanctioned, as approved resolution plans are binding and inviolable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Post-approval revision of a resolution plan on the ground of financial hardship does not constitute a 'material irregularity' within the scope of Section 61(3) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A resolution applicant connected as a promoter or insider to an MSME Corporate Debtor cannot plead lack of knowledge regarding the financial status of the entity to justify plan alteration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of the modification application was legally valid; however, general economic slowdown due to COVID-19 warranted waiver of punitive costs imposed by the NCLT.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed on merits; however, the impugned order is modified to the extent of setting aside and waiving off the costs imposed by the Adjudicating Authority in view of the COVID-19 pandemic and MSME status.
summary: Seroco Lighting Industries Pvt. Ltd., the successful resolution applicant and connected promoter entity for MSME corporate debtor Arya Filaments Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Ahmedabad (Indore Bench) order rejecting its application (IA 96 of 2020) to revise its approved resolution plan due to financial distress. The NCLAT affirmed that successful resolution applicants are legally barred from withdrawing or revising an approved resolution plan and that alleged financial distress is not a material irregularity under Section 61(3). The Tribunal dismissed the appeal on merits but waived the costs imposed by the NCLT in light of pandemic-induced hardships.

case_title: Prole Hotels Pvt. Ltd. Through Erstwhile Director Sh. Vijay Kumar Kashinath Fadke vs. The Greater Bombay Co-operative Bank Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Prole Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, also referred as Parole Hotels Pvt. Ltd.) through its erstwhile Director Vijay Kumar Kashinath Fadke; Respondent No. 1 is The Greater Bombay Co-operative Bank Ltd. (Financial Creditor), alongside the Resolution Professional, Resolution Applicant, and Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/loan facilities advanced by the Financial Creditor against which a Recovery Certificate had been issued, leading to CIRP of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details stemmed from an unpaid claim covered under a Recovery Certificate; exact numerical figures were not specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 27-06-2019, NCLT permitted Appellant to take immediate steps to settle with the Financial Creditor; CoC subsequently approved the Resolution Plan with 100% voting; NCLT approved the plan on 06-10-2020 subject to an additional affidavit. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order dated 27-06-2019 (Annexure-10, p. 116) granting liberty to settle; communication at page 120 showing Financial Creditor's conditional offer to withdraw cases upon payment under the Recovery Certificate; failure of the Appellant to tender payment or settle. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the Resolution Plan on 06-10-2020; Appellant appealed under Section 61 alleging RP-creditor connivance and readiness to pay.
legal_issues: Whether an approved Resolution Plan sanctioned by 100% voting share of the Committee of Creditors can be interfered with under Section 61(3) of the IBC based on unsubstantiated allegations of connivance and belated offers of settlement by an erstwhile director.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is non-justiciable and not amenable to judicial review in the absence of demonstrable material irregularity under Section 61(3) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory grounds for challenging an approved plan under Section 61(3) of the IBC are strictly circumscribed to material irregularity in exercise of powers during CIRP or contravention of law, and do not extend to reviewing business decisions of the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mere assertions of willingness to settle without tangible proof of payment or compliance with prior settlement liberties granted by the adjudicating authority fail to establish any procedural illegality or infirmity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the CoC approved the plan with 100% voting and the Appellant failed to take settlement steps despite prior opportunities, no ground for interference was established.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.
summary: Prole Hotels Pvt. Ltd., represented by its erstwhile director Vijay Kumar Kashinath Fadke, challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order approving a Resolution Plan with 100% voting share of the CoC, alleging connivance between the RP and the Financial Creditor and asserting a readiness to settle outstanding dues. The NCLAT held that the commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving a resolution plan is not amenable to judicial review. Furthermore, the Appellant had failed to take steps toward settlement despite earlier opportunities granted by the NCLT. Finding no material irregularity under Section 61(3) of the IBC, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Anil N. Surwade & Ors. vs. Prashant Jain, Resolution Professional, Sejal Glass Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Anil N. Surwade and other employees of the Corporate Debtor (Operational Creditors); Respondent is Prashant Jain, Resolution Professional of Sejal Glass Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment contracts and claims for outstanding wages/employee dues during the CIRP of Sejal Glass Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid employee and operational dues; specific figures not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claims submitted and admitted by the Resolution Professional during the CIRP; NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed Appellants' application on 28-09-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admitted claims of the Appellants as operational creditors on the records of the Resolution Professional; application by employees demanding inspection/access to CoC meetings and resolution plans submitted for approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench (Special Bench, Court No. II) on 28-09-2020 rejected the Appellants' application seeking access to CoC proceedings and resolution plans on the ground that employees have limited interest restricted to their admitted claims.
legal_issues: Whether Operational Creditors/employees whose claims have been admitted by the Resolution Professional have any statutory right under the IBC to access CoC proceedings, participate in CoC deliberations, or inspect submitted Resolution Plans on par with the suspended Board of Directors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Operational Creditors possess no statutory entitlement under the IBC to participate in Committee of Creditors deliberations or access confidential resolution plans, their legal interest being strictly restricted to the satisfaction and distribution of their admitted claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory framework under Section 24 of the IBC strictly defines the composition and invitees of CoC meetings; operational creditors cannot be placed on equal footing with the suspended Board of Directors to demand access to CIRP discussions and resolution plans. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once an Operational Creditor's claim has been verified and admitted by the Resolution Professional, no legal basis remains to enlarge their procedural role into CoC deliberations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: An application by employees seeking access to confidential CoC meetings and resolution plans is not maintainable under the IBC, and its dismissal by the NCLT was legally sound.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit, with the clarification that the dismissal shall not affect the Appellants' legal rights regarding their admitted monetary claims.
summary: Employees of Sejal Glass Ltd. (acting as Operational Creditors) appealed an order of the NCLT Mumbai Bench which rejected their application seeking access to CoC proceedings and inspection of submitted Resolution Plans. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's view, ruling that operational creditors have a limited interest restricted to the distribution and satisfaction of their admitted claims. Holding that operational creditors cannot claim parity with the suspended Board of Directors to access confidential CoC deliberations or resolution plans, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal while preserving the Appellants' rights regarding their admitted claims.

case_title: Sanjeev Kumar vs. Aithent Technologies Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sanjeev Kumar, Ex-Director of Web Data Systems Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Appellant); Aithent Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor/Respondent No. 1); and Rajesh Lihala, Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor leased basement and ground floor premises situated at Plot No. 8 & 9, Electronic City, Sector 18, Gurgaon, Haryana, vide Lease Deed dated 15.06.2015. Alongside the lease, Operational Creditor provided specialized IT infrastructure facilities and services including a 550 KVA DG Set for uninterrupted power supply, UPS maintenance, technical support equipment, network/voice ports, and consumables. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under Part-IV of Form 5 was an operational debt amounting to Rs. 54,73,536/-, with the date of default asserted as 19.02.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on 27.09.2018. Corporate Debtor issued its reply on 08.10.2018 raising disputes regarding part-vacation of the premises and forfeiture of security deposit. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor produced emails dated 23.03.2018, 06.04.2018, and 13.09.2018 showing ongoing disputes concerning vacation of the basement, non-adjustment of Rs. 11,29,000/- security deposit, and damages; Operational Creditor produced invoices spanning pages 119 to 177 for DG set diesel, multi-skilled technicians, Paytm device repairs, and water tankers, along with Master Service Agreement terms demonstrating service provisions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP(IB) No. 288/KB/2019 under Section 9 before NCLT Kolkata Bench; NCLT admitted the petition on 13.03.2020 holding that undisputed dues for electricity, diesel, sewer, and water charges exceeded Rs. 1 Lakh and constituted provision of services under Section 5(21).
legal_issues: Whether the application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable where the claim arises out of a lease agreement coupled with provision of infrastructure services, and whether such ancillary dues (electricity, diesel, water, and sewer charges) qualify as operational debt under Section 5(21) distinguishing the precedent in M. Ravindranath Reddy vs. G. Kishan & Ors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a commercial transaction goes beyond a pure landlord-tenant relationship and encompasses the active supply and maintenance of specialized infrastructure and utility facilities directly facilitating the corporate debtor's business operations, outstanding dues for such operational facilities constitute an operational debt under the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) broadly defines 'operational debt' as a claim in respect of the provision of goods or services; electricity, diesel for generators, sewer, and water charges provided in furtherance of business operations constitute 'services' within this definition and are not precluded by rulings governing pure lease rental claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal established that where invoices demonstrate distinct charges for supply of utilities and technical services exceeding the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh and remain undisputed on their factual incurrence, the debt fulfills the statutory requirements for admission under Section 9. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded (by a 2:1 majority) that NCLT Kolkata properly distinguished M. Ravindranath Reddy, correctly identified undisputed service-related debts exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh, and rightly admitted the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The majority affirmed the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated 13.03.2020 in CP(IB) No. 288/KB/2019; the appeal was dismissed, interim orders vacated, with no order as to costs.
summary: Corporate Debtor Web Data Systems Pvt. Ltd. challenged an NCLT Kolkata order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Aithent Technologies Pvt. Ltd. for default amounting to Rs. 54,73,536/- arising under a lease deed and infrastructure arrangement. The Corporate Debtor argued that lease rentals do not constitute operational debt as per M. Ravindranath Reddy and that pre-existing disputes existed. The NCLAT majority held that the relationship exceeded a simple tenancy because the creditor provided specialized utilities and services (diesel, power backup, technical support, water), and undisputed service dues exceeded the Rs. 1 Lakh threshold under Section 5(21) of the IBC. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Chalasani Venkateswara Rao & Ors. vs. United Telecoms Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Chalasani Venkateswara Rao (Appellant No. 1/Director/Shareholder), Mrs. C. Padmavathi (Appellant No. 2), Dr. Chalasani Sandhya Rao (Appellant No. 3) vs. United Telecoms Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company) and Dr. Potluri Raja Mohan Rao along with other directors/shareholders (Respondents No. 2 to 12). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and shareholding dispute within a closely-held family company incorporated on 17.03.1994; Appellants held undisputed shareholdings of 8.93%, 8.10%, and 8.52% respectively (total 25.55% of paid-up capital), with a further disputed claim of holding 42.76% under a testamentary will. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 seeking to declare void board resolutions passed between March 2017 and April 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Petitioners executed a General Power of Attorney on 04.04.2019 in favour of Appellant No. 1; Company Petition CP No. 82/BB/2019 filed before NCLT Bengaluru on 30.04.2019; subsequent confirmatory affidavits and GPA executed on 03.09.2019 and 04.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Executed notarized GPA dated 04.04.2019 empowering Appellant No. 1 to sign, verify, and consent to legal proceedings; joint Vakalatnama signed by all three Appellants filed with the petition; balance sheets for FY 2016-17 and 2017-18 evidencing 25.55% joint shareholding. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed IA No. 317 of 2019 challenging maintainability; NCLT Bengaluru dismissed CP No. 82/BB/2019 on 18.10.2019 holding that written consent under Section 244 was not annexed with the petition, GPA execution was doubtful, and qualification threshold was unmet.
legal_issues: Whether non-annexure of written consent under Section 244(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 81(2) of NCLT Rules, 2016 at the time of presenting a petition under Section 241 is fatal to maintainability, and whether a Power of Attorney holder can validly accord consent and execute a petition on behalf of co-shareholders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The requirement of obtaining consent of supporting members prior to filing an oppression and mismanagement petition is a matter of substantive compliance rather than rigid form; failure to annex such written consent or GPA with the initial petition does not ipso facto invalidate the proceeding and constitutes a curable procedural irregularity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 244(2) mandates 'obtaining' written consent but does not prescribe that it must be annexed to the petition; Rule 81(2) of NCLT Rules is directory and governed by Rule 58, ensuring non-compliance does not vitiate proceedings absent a miscarriage of justice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A broad consensus approach must govern the evaluation of shareholder consent; where supporting shareholders sign the Vakalatnama, do not dispute the authorization, and confirm authority via subsequent affidavits/GPAs, valid prior consent stands established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Appellants indisputably held 25.55% of paid-up capital (satisfying the 1/10th threshold) and valid authority was conferred via GPA dated 04.04.2019, the petition satisfied Section 244(1)(a) and was fully maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed; the NCLT Bengaluru order dated 18.10.2019 in IA No. 317 of 2019 in CP No. 82/BB/2019 was set aside; CP No. 82/BB/2019 was restored and remanded back to NCLT Bengaluru for disposal on merits, directing parties to appear on 11.11.2020 without costs.
summary: Appellants holding 25.55% paid-up capital of United Telecoms Ltd. filed a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241-242. Appellant No. 1 filed the joint petition based on a GPA executed by his wife and daughter, but omitted annexing the GPA to the petition. NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the petition as unmaintainable under Section 244. Setting aside the dismissal, NCLAT held that Section 244(2) requires obtaining consent, not necessarily annexing it at filing; Rule 81(2) of the NCLT Rules is directory by virtue of Rule 58. Since the Appellants fulfilled the 10% shareholding threshold and confirmed authorization via signed Vakalatnamas and affidavits, the defect was cured, rendering the petition maintainable.

case_title: R. Narayanasamy vs. The Registrar of Companies, Tamil Nadu
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: R. Narayanasamy, Shareholder and Managing Director of Shri Laxmi Spinners Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant) vs. The Registrar of Companies, Tamil Nadu, Coimbatore (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Shri Laxmi Spinners Pvt. Ltd., incorporated on 27.09.1978 for textile manufacturing, yarn, and ginning, owned 5.6 acres of land and a 17,000 sq. ft. mill facility, but had completely shut down manufacturing operations due to power failures and labor issues. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to file statutory annual returns and balance sheets for financial years 2014-15 through 2017-18; reported Nil income and Nil tax across four consecutive assessment years. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ROC issued Section 248(1) show-cause notice on 11.05.2018 (claimed received on 16.07.2018); second notice issued on 06.07.2018; company replied on 24.07.2018; strike-off order passed on 29.08.2018 and published in Form STK-7 on 31.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Company filed reply dated 24.07.2018 expressly admitting that it was non-functional and had halted all operations for several years; filed Income Tax returns showing gross total income as 'Nil' for AYs 2014-15, 2015-16, 2016-17, and 2017-18; absence of any contemporaneous commercial invoices, ledgers, or banking operations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed appeal CA/06/2020 under Section 252(3) before NCLT Chennai Bench; NCLT dismissed the appeal on 05.05.2020 finding the company was dormant, non-operational, and without cogent grounds for revival.
legal_issues: Whether the Registrar of Companies lawfully exercised jurisdiction under Section 248(1)(c) to strike off the company, and whether the non-operational status and admitted failure to file returns disentitle the company from relief under the 'otherwise just' standard of Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Administrative striking off under Section 248 is legally validated when the statutory condition of non-operation for two immediately preceding financial years is established, and restoration under Section 252(3) on the ground of 'otherwise just' requires demonstrable, bona fide commercial viability supported by contemporaneous evidence rather than speculative revival claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The words 'carrying on business or in operation' under Section 252(3) require active commercial enterprise at the time of striking off; the phrase 'otherwise just' cannot be utilized to circumvent regular corporate compliance obligations where the management voluntarily abandons business and defaults on statutory filings without seeking dormant status under Section 455. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Categorical admissions of complete cessation of operations in statutory replies coupled with 'Nil' income tax returns for consecutive years constitute conclusive proof that the company was not in operation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: ROC strictly adhered to procedural safeguards, and in the absence of credible proof of business or valid justification for multi-year non-compliance, the dismissal of the restoration petition by NCLT was unassailable.
operative_order: Per Technical Member Dr. Alok Srivastava: Company Appeal (AT) No. 171 of 2020 was dismissed, upholding NCLT Chennai Bench's order dated 05.05.2020 without costs; note submitted to Acting Chairperson due to split opinion (Member Judicial dissenting) to refer the appeal to a third member.
summary: Shri Laxmi Spinners Pvt. Ltd. was struck off the Register of Companies by ROC Tamil Nadu under Section 248 for failing to carry on business and omiting annual returns for over two consecutive financial years. The Managing Director appealed under Section 252(3), citing infrastructural assets, past power shortages, and pending litigations as 'otherwise just' reasons for revival. In his opinion, Technical Member Dr. Alok Srivastava dismissed the appeal, holding that the company conceded non-operation with Nil income tax returns across multiple years and failed to show any active business or seek dormant status under Section 455, thereby affirming NCLT Chennai's dismissal.

case_title: Facor Alloys Limited & Anr. vs. Bhuvan Madan & Ors. (with Toplight Corporate Management Pvt. Ltd. vs. Bhuvan Madan & Ors.)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Facor Alloys Ltd. and Vineet Infin Pvt. Ltd. (Appellants in CA 340/2020 / Minority shareholders in subsidiary FPL); Toplight Corporate Management Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant in CA 462/2020 / Dissenting Financial Creditor); Bhuvan Madan (RP of Corporate Debtor FACL / Respondent No. 1); REC Ltd. (Lead Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 2); Sterlite Power Transmission Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / Respondent No. 3); and Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. (FACL), corporate guarantor holding 86.09% equity in its power-generating subsidiary, Facor Power Ltd. (FPL). 3.
