DEFAULT METRICS: Debt default by principal borrower FPL and guarantor FACL to consortium lenders led by REC Ltd., leading to approved Resolution Plan providing Rs. 270 Crores total consideration and NCD allocations. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC meeting on 11.11.2019 evaluated independent valuation; CoC approved Sterlite's Resolution Plan on 13.11.2019 with 95.15% voting share; NCLT Cuttack Bench approved the plan under Section 31 on 30.01.2020 in CP (IB) No. 157/CTB/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports by two independent valuers assessing FACL's liquidation value at Rs. 305 Crores, including Rs. 95 Crores specifically attributable to its 86.09% shareholding in FPL; pledge agreements permitting REC to invoke shares of FPL; CoC voting records showing Toplight Corporate abstained/did not vote. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeals filed before NCLAT challenging NCLT Cuttack Bench order dated 30.01.2020 approving the Resolution Plan on grounds that plan illegally dealt with subsidiary assets and discriminated against dissenting financial creditors.
legal_issues: Whether an approved resolution plan can deal with and transfer the corporate debtor's shareholding in a subsidiary company under Section 18(f)(v), and whether offering dissenting financial creditors liquidation value in debentures while assenting creditors receive cash and debentures violates Section 30(2)(b) or Regulation 38.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Shares held by a corporate debtor in a subsidiary company are legitimate assets of the corporate debtor under Section 18(f)(v) which vest in the successful resolution applicant, and resolution plans may extinguish related-party claims to allow acquisition on a clean slate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC guarantees dissenting financial creditors a minimum safety net equal to the liquidation value under Section 53(1); it does not prohibit the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom from according distinct payout structures to assenting versus dissenting classes so long as the statutory minimum is met. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: CIRP Regulation amendments operate prospectively; the 27.11.2019 amendment requiring priority in payment to dissenting financial creditors does not apply to resolution plans voted upon prior to its notification (13.11.2019). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan conformed with Section 30(2) as independent valuation factored subsidiary shares, the commercial wisdom of 95.15% CoC majority was unassailable, and dissenting creditors received their full entitled liquidation value.
operative_order: Both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 340 of 2020 and No. 462 of 2020) were held to be devoid of merit and dismissed without costs; the approval order of NCLT Cuttack Bench dated 30.01.2020 was affirmed.
summary: Appellants challenged the approval of Sterlite Power Transmission Ltd.'s resolution plan for Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. (FACL). Minority shareholders of subsidiary Facor Power Ltd. (FPL) argued that dealing with FPL's assets was unauthorized, while Toplight Corporate claimed discrimination between assenting and dissenting financial creditors regarding cash disbursements. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, ruling that FACL's 86.09% equity in FPL is an asset under Section 18(f)(v) that resolves with the debtor. Furthermore, Section 30(2)(b) guarantees only the minimum liquidation value to dissenting creditors, leaving distribution terms to the CoC's commercial wisdom, and the amended priority rule of Regulation 38 applies prospectively.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Athena Energy Ventures Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Financial Creditor/Appellant); Athena Energy Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor/Corporate Debtor/Respondent); Athena Chattisgarh Power Ltd. (Principal Borrower). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium loan facility under Common Loan Agreement dated 30.03.2011 (amended 31.03.2015 and 01.09.2016) sanctioned to Athena Chattisgarh Power Ltd. for Rs. 3,069.68 Crores (Rs. 2,769.19 Crores disbursed), secured by a corporate guarantee executed by Athena Energy Ventures Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayment by the Principal Borrower, with outstanding dues as on 31.08.2018 exceeding thousands of crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition against Principal Borrower admitted on 15.05.2019 in CP(IB) No. 616/07/HDB/2018; Section 7 petition against Corporate Guarantor filed in CP(IB) No. 466/07/HDB/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Guarantee Agreements and financial sanction letters executed by Respondent; admitted default in debt servicing under the amended consortium loan agreement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad rejected CP(IB) No. 466/7/HDB/2019 on 04.03.2020 relying on Piramal Enterprise Ltd., holding that a second Section 7 application cannot be admitted against the corporate guarantor for the identical debt and default.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable against a Corporate Guarantor when a Section 7 application on the identical set of debt and default has already been admitted against the Principal Borrower, and whether the ruling in Vishnu Kumar Agarwal vs. Piramal Enterprise Ltd. bars simultaneous CIRP proceedings against both borrower and guarantor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act and the scheme of the IBC, the liability of a principal borrower and corporate guarantor is co-extensive; simultaneous CIRP proceedings can be initiated and maintained against both for the same debt and default, subject to accounting and adjustment against double recovery at the distribution stage. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(2) and Section 60(3) of the IBC (as amended by Act 26 of 2018 retrospective from 06.06.2018) expressly contemplate simultaneous insolvency or liquidation proceedings of a corporate debtor and its corporate guarantor before the very same Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Initiation of CIRP against one entity does not extinguish or render the debt 'not due or payable' by the guarantor; the obligation to pay persists until full satisfaction is received by the creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench departed from the dictum in Piramal (which omitted consideration of amended Section 60(2) and addressed two co-guarantors), set aside the impugned rejection, and ruled that financial creditors can proceed simultaneously against both principal borrower and guarantor.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed; NCLT Hyderabad Bench order dated 04.03.2020 was quashed and set aside; CP(IB) No. 466/7/HDB/2019 was restored to file with directions to admit the application, proceed under the IBC, and appoint the same IRP/RP handling the Principal Borrower's CIRP.
summary: State Bank of India appealed the rejection of its Section 7 petition against Corporate Guarantor Athena Energy Ventures Pvt. Ltd., which NCLT Hyderabad had dismissed based on Vishnu Kumar Agarwal vs. Piramal Enterprises Ltd. because CIRP had already commenced against the Principal Borrower. The NCLAT held that the liability of borrower and guarantor is co-extensive under Section 128 of the Contract Act and that Section 60(2) & (3) of the IBC explicitly allows simultaneous CIRP proceedings before the same NCLT Bench. Debt is not extinguished merely by filing claims in the borrower's CIRP, as adjustments occur at distribution. The appeal was allowed and the petition restored for admission.

case_title: Promila Taneja vs. Surendri Design Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Promila Taneja (Landlord/Operational Creditor/Appellant) vs. Surendri Design Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent/Tenant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lease of commercial shop premises (Shop No. 101, Galaxy Mall, Silokhera, Sector 15, Gurugram) for running an apparels showroom under a lease agreement dated 01.02.2016 having a 36-month lock-in period. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default of unpaid monthly lease rent following unilateral cessation of payment by the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor sent lease termination emails on 18.08.2017 and 12.09.2017; Appellant issued Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC on 06.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email trail dated 18.08.2017 and 12.09.2017 evidencing that Corporate Debtor suffered severe business losses due to demonetization and Supreme Court orders relocating liquor vends near highways (which forced changes to mall entryways), citing frustration and premature lease termination. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Landlord filed C.P. (IB) No. 394/Chd/Hry/2018 under Section 9 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench; NCLT dismissed the application on twin grounds that rent is not an operational debt (per M. Ravindranath Reddy) and that a pre-existing dispute existed.
legal_issues: Whether arrears of commercial lease rent fall within the definition of 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC, and whether external definitions from the Consumer Protection Act and CGST Act can be imported via Section 3(37) of the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Arrears of rent arising from a lease of immovable property do not constitute an operational debt under the IBC, as leasing real estate does not amount to the provision of goods or services. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(37) of the IBC strictly limits external statutory definitions to specified enactments; hence, definitions of 'services' in the Consumer Protection Act or CGST Act cannot be imported into Section 5(21). Furthermore, while Section 5(8)(d) explicitly classifies financial/capital leases as financial debt, the legislature intentionally omitted lease rents from operational debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-existing dispute is established where communications terminating the contract and disputing liability pre-date the Section 8 demand notice, rendering the legality of termination a matter for civil trial rather than summary insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Reaffirming M. Ravindranath Reddy and distinguishing Anup Shushil Dubey, the bench concluded lease rent is not an operational debt, and the existence of a prior dispute fully barred the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs, affirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh Bench) dismissing C.P. (IB) No. 394/Chd/Hry/2018.
summary: Appellant landlord filed a Section 9 application claiming unpaid lease rentals from tenant Surendri Design Pvt. Ltd. for shop space in Galaxy Mall. NCLT Chandigarh dismissed the application on grounds of pre-existing dispute and holding rent outside the ambit of operational debt. On appeal, Appellant cited Anup Shushil Dubey to argue commercial leases constitute services under CGST and Consumer Protection laws. The NCLAT reaffirmed its three-member bench ruling in M. Ravindranath Reddy, holding that leasing immovable property is neither goods nor services, external statutory definitions cannot be imported under Section 3(37), and prior lease termination emails proved a pre-existing dispute.

case_title: Amrit Kumar Agrawal vs. Tempo Appliances Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amrit Kumar Agrawal (Appellant/Purported Financial Creditor); Tempo Appliances Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Guarantor/Corporate Debtor); and Tempo Appliances India Ltd. (Principal Borrower). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan of Rs. 1,50,00,000/- advanced under an MoU dated 22.09.2017 to Principal Borrower at 18% interest p.a.; upon dishonor of cheques, a subsequent Settlement Agreement dated 16.01.2020 was executed solely between Appellant and Respondent corporate guarantor to settle liabilities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Cheques issued under the Settlement Agreement totaling Rs. 86 Lakhs principal balance plus Rs. 22 Lakhs calculated interest were dishonored upon presentation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheques of Rs. 86 Lakhs and Rs. 18 Lakhs bounced on 20.09.2019 and 20.10.2019; Section 138 NI Act proceedings initiated; Settlement Agreement executed on 16.01.2020; subsequent post-dated settlement cheques dishonored. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Memorandum of Understanding dated 22.09.2017; two dishonored post-dated cheques; Settlement Agreement dated 16.01.2020 superseding the original MoU without joining the principal borrower. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 7 application against Respondent; NCLT New Delhi Bench-V dismissed the petition on 28.09.2020 holding that default under a settlement agreement does not constitute financial debt.
legal_issues: Whether the obligation to pay an outstanding liability arising under a Settlement Agreement (following dishonor of cheques) constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC so as to entitle the creditor to initiate CIRP under Section 7.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A mere obligation to pay arising from a breach of a settlement agreement does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8) absent a direct disbursement of money to the debtor against consideration for the time value of money. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The core requirement of Section 5(8) is a disbursal against the time value of money; entering into a novated compromise or settlement agreement where no fresh funds are borrowed does not create a financial debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the agreement relied upon supersedes previous loan documents and demonstrates that the corporate debtor did not receive any disbursal of borrowing from the creditor, the transaction fails the legal test of Section 5(8). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Dishonor of cheques issued under a settlement agreement may provide grounds for civil recovery or NI Act prosecution, but cannot trigger CIRP under Section 7 because the IBC is not a recovery mechanism.
operative_order: The appeal was held devoid of merit and dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT New Delhi Bench-V order dated 28.09.2020.
summary: Appellant advanced a loan to Tempo Appliances India Ltd. secured by a guarantee from Tempo Appliances Pvt. Ltd. When initial repayment cheques bounced, the Appellant and guarantor executed a Settlement Agreement dated 16.01.2020 for Rs. 86 Lakhs plus Rs. 22 Lakhs interest, superseding the original loan MoU. Cheques issued pursuant to the settlement were also dishonored, prompting the Appellant to file a Section 7 petition against the guarantor. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal of the petition, holding that a breach of a settlement agreement does not involve a disbursement against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and insolvency proceedings cannot be utilized for debt recovery.

case_title: Hindustan Oil Exploration Company vs. Erstwhile Committee of Creditors of JEKPL Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Hindustan Oil Exploration Company (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant/Appellant) vs. Erstwhile Committee of Creditors of JEKPL Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 2); and JEKPL Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of JEKPL Pvt. Ltd. in CP No. (IB) 24/ALD/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Implementation of approved resolution plan requiring Successful Resolution Applicant to infuse Rs. 123 Crores for resolution within 30 days of approval. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by NCLT on 04.02.2020; 30-day funding deadline expired on 05.03.2020; CoC filed Section 60(5) application; NCLT granted extension until 30.09.2020 by order dated 09.09.2020 in IA No. 208/2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Disruption of business operations and capital liquidity caused by the nationwide COVID-19 pandemic; CoC consent and approval allowing extended payment timelines without claiming prejudice; prior dismissal of Appellant's appeal against plan approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant challenged NCLT Allahabad Bench order dated 09.09.2020 extending the implementation deadline on the ground that the CoC was functus officio and connived to accept a revised plan.
legal_issues: Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant whose bid was rejected has the legal locus standi to challenge subsequent timeline extensions and implementation variations granted to the successful resolution applicant by the Adjudicating Authority and the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsuccessful resolution applicant has no legal standing (locus standi) to challenge the implementation, timeline extensions, or consensual modifications granted to an approved resolution plan once its own challenge against plan approval has attained finality. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) confers jurisdiction on the Adjudicating Authority to facilitate the effective implementation of an approved resolution plan, including accommodating practical exigencies such as pandemic disruptions when agreed upon by stakeholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To question plan implementation, a party must establish a subsisting legal right or demonstrable prejudice; third-party contenders eliminated from the resolution process suffer no actionable prejudice when creditors consent to time extensions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial stakeholders agreed to the extensions due to COVID-19 economic hardships; the appellant was completely out of the fray and lacked standing to intermeddle.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed in limine without costs, affirming the NCLT Allahabad Bench order dated 09.09.2020 in IA No. 208/2020.
summary: Hindustan Oil Exploration Company, an unsuccessful resolution applicant, challenged an NCLT Allahabad order that extended the deadline for the successful resolution applicant to infuse Rs. 123 Crores under an approved plan for JEKPL Pvt. Ltd. until 30.09.2020. Appellant contended the CoC was functus officio and could not renegotiate terms after its own bid was rejected for lacking upfront payment. Dismissing the appeal in limine, NCLAT held that once an unsuccessful bidder's challenge to plan approval is dismissed, it has no locus standi to question subsequent implementation extensions agreed upon by creditors to mitigate COVID-19 disruptions.

case_title: Naveen Kumar Jain vs. Committee of Creditors of K.D.K Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Naveen Kumar Jain (Interim Resolution Professional/Appellant) vs. Committee of Creditors of K.D.K Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (Respondents), with Indian Bank as the sole Financial Creditor (100% voting share). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Administration and CIRP process of K.D.K Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fixation and payment of Interim Resolution Professional fees determined by the CoC at Rs. 50,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Committee of Creditors resolved with 100% majority to replace the IRP under Section 22 and fix fees under Regulation 33(3). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC voting record showing 100% vote share by sole financial creditor Indian Bank resolving to replace the IRP; resolution fixing IRP fee at Rs. 50,000/- pursuant to statutory regulations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IRP filed an application under Section 60(5) before NCLT Court-V New Delhi seeking to stay his replacement and challenge fee fixation; NCLT dismissed the application; IRP appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the replacement of an Interim Resolution Professional by a 100% vote of the Committee of Creditors under Section 22 and the fixation of IRP expenses under Regulation 33(3) are subject to judicial review.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The replacement of an Interim Resolution Professional under Section 22 and the fixation of CIRP fees under regulatory provisions fall squarely within the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors and are non-justiciable outside the narrow scope of statutory illegality. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22 empowers the CoC to replace an IRP by a requisite vote of 66%; where a sole financial creditor votes with 100% voting share, the statutory threshold is fully satisfied and admits no judicial second-guessing. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance with Regulation 33(3) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations by the CoC in fixing fees at a specific figure (Rs. 50,000/-) precludes adjudicatory interference absent patent arbitrariness. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial decision of the CoC to substitute the professional and cap fees is beyond the pale of judicial review, rendering the appeal baseless.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs, affirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Court-V New Delhi).
summary: Naveen Kumar Jain, serving as Interim Resolution Professional of K.D.K Enterprises Pvt. Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi rejecting his application under Section 60(5) to stay his replacement and enhance his fee. The sole financial creditor, Indian Bank, holding 100% voting share, resolved under Section 22 to replace him and fixed his professional fee at Rs. 50,000/- pursuant to IBBI Regulation 33(3). Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT affirmed that the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding the replacement of the resolution professional and fixation of fees is non-justiciable and falls outside the purview of judicial review.

case_title: Amit Katyal vs. Meera Ahuja & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amit Katyal, Promoter/Director of Jasmine Buildmart Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Mrs. Meera Ahuja and Mrs. Ruby Sachdev through POA holder Hemant Ahuja (Respondents No. 1-3/Financial Creditors/Home Buyers); and Jugraj Singh Bedi (IRP/Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking and allotment of Flat No. C-1101 (5,800 sq. ft.) in 'Krish Provence' project, Gurgaon, under an Apartment Buyer Agreement dated 07.08.2012 for a total consideration of Rs. 3,80,10,000/- on a construction-linked plan, with delivery scheduled within 36 months plus a 6-month grace period (by February 2016). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Home buyers paid Rs. 2,75,55,186/- (approx. 72.5% of total cost) up to August 2013; Corporate Debtor claimed outstanding unpaid installments of Rs. 58,93,394/- and purported cancellation on 26.06.2015, while Home Buyers claimed default on failure to deliver possession by February 2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Promised possession deadline: 07.02.2016; Developer applied for Occupation Certificate on 03.07.2019 (granted 29.10.2019); Section 7 petition filed on 06.12.2018 claiming Rs. 6,93,02,755/-. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's reply dated 22.11.2018 admitting internal finishing and flooring were still ongoing past the scheduled delivery; developer accepted VAT payment of Rs. 3,00,615/- on 30.01.2017 and maintained active ledger accounts as late as 25.10.2018 without charging interest, disproving prior cancellation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III admitted the Section 7 petition on 28.11.2019 in CP (IB) No. 1722/ND/2018 holding the developer committed default in completing construction within the stipulated timeline.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application filed by home buyers was barred by limitation, whether non-payment of subsequent installments during inordinate construction delay constitutes default by allottees, and whether the petition was liable to be dismissed under Section 65 as a fraudulent and malicious initiation by speculative buyers.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In real estate purchase agreements, default occurs when the developer fails to complete construction and deliver possession within the contractually stipulated timeframe; allottees who withhold further installments due to substantial delay and failure of the developer to issue milestone notices cannot be deemed defaulting or speculative purchasers. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For the purposes of Article 137 of the Limitation Act, the right to sue for home buyers under Section 7 accrues upon failure to hand over possession by the promised date; Section 65 cannot be deployed to stifle genuine insolvency proceedings absent clear prima facie proof of malicious intent to defraud or extort. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a developer accepts statutory tax dues and maintains account ledgers long after an alleged cancellation, the defense of prior cancellation fails; additionally, failure to adhere to mandatory postal stage notices under a construction-linked plan bars the developer from claiming allottee default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor committed default by failing to deliver possession by February 2016, the petition filed in December 2018 was within the 3-year limitation period, and the Section 7 admission by NCLT was unimpeachable.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT New Delhi Bench-III order dated 28.11.2019 admitting CP (IB) No. 1722/ND/2018 under Section 7 of the IBC.
summary: Corporate Debtor Jasmine Buildmart Pvt. Ltd. challenged an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 application filed by allottees who had paid Rs. 2,75,55,186/- towards an apartment in Gurgaon. The developer alleged that the buyers defaulted on installments leading to cancellation in 2015, and argued the petition was time-barred and malicious under Section 65. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the developer defaulted by failing to deliver possession by February 2016, making the December 2018 filing well within limitation. The court found the buyers stopped payments due to persistent construction delays, the developer failed to follow contractual stage-notice mandates, and the buyers were genuine allottees.

case_title: Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Yashomati Hospitals Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (Assignee of South Indian Bank / Financial Creditor / Appellant) vs. Yashomati Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial facilities comprising a consortium term loan of Rs. 15 Crores (sanctioned 26.02.2009 via Consortium Agreement dated 25.03.2009 with SBI) and an independent separate overdraft facility of Rs. 1.35 Crores granted by South Indian Bank in 2011; debts assigned to Pegasus on 30.03.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred and account classified as NPA by South Indian Bank on 30.01.2014; Section 7 application claimed an outstanding default of Rs. 15,43,83,042.73. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NPA declared on 30.01.2014; part repayments of Rs. 3.47 Crores on 28.11.2014 and Rs. 53 Lakhs on 03.12.2014; debt acknowledgment certificate on 20.11.2015; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 144/BB/2017 filed on 23.11.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered assignment deed dated 30.03.2016; bank ledger entries establishing part payments in late 2014; High Court records in WP 52886-52887/2015 showing interim stays obtained by debtor were exclusively against SBI, not SIB. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor filed IA 69 of 2019 challenging maintainability due to High Court proceedings; NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the Section 7 petition on 10.10.2019 granting liberty to refile after High Court adjudication.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition by an individual consortium lender is barred or rendered unmaintainable by High Court stay orders issued solely against another consortium lender in SARFAESI proceedings, and whether an applicant must be afforded an opportunity to cure formatting defects to plead facts establishing limitation under Section 18 and Section 19 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual bank or its assignee within a consortium lending structure retains an independent legal entitlement to initiate CIRP under Section 7, and writ orders issued against other consortium members in distinct SARFAESI proceedings cannot impede its statutory insolvency remedy. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5) of the IBC read with Section 3 of the Limitation Act requires the Adjudicating Authority to examine whether debt is legally enforceable and within limitation; where an application omits complete limitation particulars, the proviso to Section 7(5) and inherent powers mandate giving the applicant an opportunity to cure defects and produce evidence of part-payment or acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If part-repayments under Section 19 or acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act are evidenced by bank statements and court pleadings, the creditor must be permitted to amend Form 1 to incorporate them. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in abdicating jurisdiction and dismissing the petition pending unrelated High Court litigation; the petition was maintainable and required remand to decide limitation after rectifying Form 1.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed; the NCLT Bengaluru order dated 10.10.2019 in IA No. 69 of 2019 in CP (IB) No. 144/BB/2017 was set aside; IA 69/2019 was dismissed; CP (IB) No. 144/BB/2017 was restored and remanded with directions to permit Pegasus to amend Form 1 and determine limitation on merits.
summary: Pegasus ARC, as assignee of South Indian Bank, appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order dismissing its Section 7 application against Yashomati Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. NCLT had dismissed the petition pending adjudication of writ proceedings before the Karnataka High Court relating to SARFAESI actions initiated by lead bank SBI. NCLAT set aside the dismissal, holding that SIB was not a party to the High Court stay orders and had independent claims, including an unlinked overdraft facility. Furthermore, because the creditor alleged part-repayments and acknowledgments saving limitation under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, NCLAT remanded the matter, directing NCLT to allow Pegasus to cure defects in Form 1 and decide admission on merits.

case_title: A. Balakrishnan vs. Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: A. Balakrishnan, Director of M/s Prasad Properties and Investments Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Guarantor/Corporate Debtor); Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Assignee Financial Creditor); and L.V. Shyam Sundar (IRP/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities originally sanctioned by Indbank Housing Ltd. (IBHL) to three borrower entities (Gemini Arts, Green Gardens, and Mahalaxmi Properties) secured by corporate guarantee and equitable mortgage of immovable property by Prasad Properties; debts assigned to Kotak Mahindra Bank on 13.10.2006. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Facilities classified as NPA in November 1997; compromise decree entered on 26.03.2007; Debt Recovery Certificates issued by DRT on 20.06.2017; Section 7 petition claimed an aggregate default of Rs. 835,93,52,369/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account classified as NPA: November 1997; High Court consent decree: 26.03.2007; SARFAESI notices: 2007-2008; DRT Recovery Certificates issued: 20.06.2017; Section 7 application filed: 05.10.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 1 filed under Section 7 omitted specifying any date of default; Recovery Certificates dated 20.06.2017 issued under Section 31A of the RDDBFI Act pursuant to the 2007 compromise decree. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Kotak Mahindra Bank filed CP/1352/IB/2018; NCLT Chennai Division Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 20.09.2019 holding the defense of the corporate debtor to be spurious bluster.
legal_issues: Whether the issuance of a Debt Recovery Certificate by a Debt Recovery Tribunal gives rise to a fresh cause of action or triggers a new limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act for initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for initiating corporate insolvency under Section 7 is governed residually by Article 137 of the Limitation Act and runs from the original date of default (or NPA classification); the issuance of a recovery certificate or decree does not constitute a continuing wrong or provide a fresh starting point of limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: IBC proceedings are not execution proceedings for enforcing court decrees or DRT recovery certificates; therefore, the obtaining of a recovery certificate does not revive an already time-barred debt under Section 238A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In accordance with Vashdeo R. Bhojwani, issuance of a recovery certificate finalizes and injures the right rather than renewing the limitation clock; omission of the default date in Form 1 cannot shield a petition where the underlying debt defaulted two decades earlier. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the original default occurred in November 1997, the claim was barred by limitation under Article 137, rendering the Section 7 application time-barred and unsustainable.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed; NCLT Chennai order dated 20.09.2019 was quashed and set aside; CP/1352/IB/2018 was dismissed; CIRP was set aside with directions to restore management to the directors, and CIRP expenses were saddled upon Kotak Mahindra Bank.
summary: Director of Prasad Properties and Investments Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Chennai order admitting Kotak Mahindra Bank's Section 7 petition claiming over Rs. 835 Crores. The underlying debts had been classified as NPA in 1997, followed by a consent decree in 2007 and DRT Recovery Certificates in June 2017. Kotak argued the recovery certificates furnished a fresh cause of action. NCLAT reversed the admission, ruling that limitation runs from the original default date under Article 137, the IBC is not an execution forum, and recovery certificates do not create a fresh trigger date (a ruling later overturned by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 689 of 2021, which held recovery certificates do trigger a fresh limitation period of 12 years).

case_title: Shubha Sharma vs. Mansi Brar Fernandes & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shubha Sharma, Former Director of Gayatri Infraplanner Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Mansi Brar Fernandes (Respondent No. 1/Purported Financial Creditor); and Manish Sukhani (IRP/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: MOU dated 06.04.2016 for provisional allotment of 4 apartments (6,740 sq. ft.) in 'Gayatri Life', Noida Extension, for Rs. 1,03,78,521/-, wherein Respondent paid Rs. 35 Lakhs upfront, with an irrevocable compulsory buyback clause obligating builder to return Rs. 35 Lakhs plus Rs. 65 Lakhs premium within 12 months. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor issued two post-dated cheques totaling Rs. 1,00,00,000/-, which were dishonored upon presentation; Respondent claimed financial debt of Rs. 1,02,50,000/- including 28% interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MOU executed 06.04.2016; extensions executed on 07.04.2017 and 07.10.2017 (extending to 06.10.2018); Section 7 petition filed on 18.03.2019; reserved on 04.12.2019; admitted on 02.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU clauses 5(b), 7, and 8 showing compulsory buyback and lack of any construction-linked payment schedule for the balance Rs. 68.78 Lakhs; Section 138 NI Act complaint filed by Respondent; Form 1 misstating debt disbursed as Rs. 1,02,50,000/- instead of Rs. 35 Lakhs and omitting default date. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 02.01.2020 holding that amounts raised from allottees under real estate projects constitute financial debt under Section 5(8)(f).
legal_issues: Whether an investor under an assured return/compulsory buyback agreement qualifies as a genuine 'allottee' and 'financial creditor' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, or is a speculative investor precluded from triggering CIRP under Section 7.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual who enters into an agreement containing compulsory buyback provisions with guaranteed exorbitant premiums, lacks interest in obtaining physical possession, and undertakes no construction-linked obligations is a speculative investor, not an 'allottee' or 'financial creditor' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The explanation to Section 5(8)(f) incorporates definitions from RERA; an allottee must intend to acquire commercial or residential units; where the core transaction is an assured return investment disguised as provisional allotment, it does not qualify as a financial debt under the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Pioneer Urban Land, tribunals must pierce the transaction structure; total absence of stage-wise payment schedules, delivery covenants, combined with post-dated cheques for double the principal and pursuit of Section 138 NI Act remedies demonstrate speculative investment rather than genuine home-buying. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Respondent was a speculative investor; the Rs. 35 Lakhs paid was not a financial debt under Section 5(8)(f), making the Section 7 petition unmaintainable.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed; the NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench order dated 02.01.2020 was set aside; the Section 7 application was dismissed; Corporate Debtor was released from moratorium, and management restored to the Board of Directors.
summary: Former Director of Gayatri Infraplanner Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by Mansi Brar Fernandes. The applicant had paid Rs. 35 Lakhs under an MOU for 4 apartments that included an irrevocable compulsory buyback clause for Rs. 1 Crore within 12 months. Following cheque dishonor, the applicant initiated Section 138 proceedings and Section 7 CIRP. Setting aside the admission, NCLAT held that the MOU was an investment contract rather than a genuine agreement for sale. Applying Pioneer Urban Land, the Tribunal ruled that speculative investors seeking exorbitant returns are not genuine allottees under Section 5(8)(f) and cannot invoke Section 7.

case_title: Vintage Hotels Private Limited & Anr. vs. Ahamed Nizar Moideen Kunhi Kunhimahin
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vintage Hotels Pvt. Ltd. and Kunhibi Layinchirapurakkal Saithumada, MD (Appellants) vs. Ahamed Nizar Moideen Kunhi Kunhimahin (Respondent/Transferee Shareholder). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of shares in Vintage Hotels Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent purchased 20,000 equity shares from T. Shahul Hameed for Rs. 39,15,000/- on 10.04.2015, and 12,500 equity shares from P.A. Ibrahim Haji for Rs. 24,46,875/- on 30.06.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Refusal by the Board of Directors vide letter dated 30.10.2015 to register share transfers and rectify the register of members. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share purchase agreements and affidavits executed on 10.04.2015 and 30.06.2015; share transfer forms (Form SH-4) lodged with company on 13.08.2015; Board rejection letter issued on 30.10.2015; NCLT allowed petition on 16.10.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share Purchase Agreements and Indemnity Bonds/Sworn Affidavits from both transferors affirming original certificates were lost and requesting duplicate certificates directly to the transferee; cheques proving full payment; refusal letter citing failure to attend board meetings, pending criminal complaints, and absence of physical certificates. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed CP No. 1 of 2016 under Section 58 before NCLT Bengaluru; NCLT allowed the petition on 16.10.2018 ordering registration of shares and register rectification.
legal_issues: Whether a company can arbitrarily refuse to register a share transfer under Section 58 when original share certificates are lost and transferors submit indemnity bonds and sworn affidavits requesting duplicate certificates, and whether personal disputes justify board refusal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The board's discretionary power to refuse share transfers must be exercised reasonably, bona fide, and in the company's objective interest; refusal cannot be based on arbitrary, capricious, or collateral personal disputes between management and the transferee. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 56 requires delivery of share certificates with transfer deeds, Rule 6(2)(a) of the Companies Rules permits duplicate certificates upon submission of proof of loss and indemnities; a company cannot exploit the absence of physical certificates to block transfers when transferors furnish adequate indemnities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Allegations of hostility, non-attendance at meetings, or criminal complaints do not constitute valid corporate grounds under Section 58(5) to deny statutory transfer rights when lawful consideration, transfer forms, and sworn indemnity deeds are submitted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Board's refusal letter dated 30.10.2015 was legally unsustainable, and NCLT correctly directed rectification of the register.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs; NCLT Bengaluru order dated 16.10.2018 was affirmed; Respondent directed to submit remaining formal documentation within 3 weeks, and the Company directed to effect registration and register rectification within 3 weeks thereafter.
summary: Vintage Hotels Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order directing it to register the transfer of 32,500 equity shares in favor of Ahamed Nizar and rectify its member register. The company had rejected the transfer on grounds that original share certificates were not enclosed and the transferee had ongoing personal/criminal disputes with directors. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the transferors had duly submitted sworn affidavits and indemnity bonds confirming the certificates were lost and requesting duplicate issuance under Rule 6(2)(a). The board's refusal based on personal rancor and missing certificates was arbitrary and contrary to Section 58 of the Companies Act.

case_title: Anuj Khanna vs. Wishwa Naveen Traders & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anuj Khanna, Ex-Director of Cosmic Export Solutions (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor) vs. Wishwa Naveen Traders (Proprietorship / Operational Creditor / Respondent No. 1) and Cosmic Export Solutions (India) Pvt. Ltd. through IRP (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Custom clearance services provided by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor between 2015 and 2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default of Rs. 18,09,541.92 (consisting of Rs. 14,59,308/- principal and Rs. 3,50,233.92/- interest at 24% p.a.). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheques dishonored on 22.02.2019 and 20.03.2019; Debtor sent suspension email on 05.03.2019 and legal notices on 06.03.2019 and 28.03.2019; Creditor issued Section 138 notice on 17.04.2019; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 22.04.2019; Section 9 petition filed on 24.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 05.03.2019 suspending services for lack of accounting transparency; legal notices dated 06.03.2019 and 28.03.2019 proving Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 14,17,000/- into personal accounts of Creditor's employees (Yadav, Prajapati, Malhotra, Dhawan) and demanded ledger reconciliation; Creditor admitted receipt of Rs. 14,17,000/- but unconvincingly claimed it was for out-of-pocket expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 petition on 13.02.2020 holding that defenses raised were spurious bluster outside Section 5(6).
legal_issues: Whether pre-demand communications and legal notices detailing disputed accounting reconciliations and uncredited payments made to employees of the operational creditor establish a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 5(6) of the IBC barring Section 9 admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 9 application must be rejected if there is a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding debt quantum or accounting treatment raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice; the definition of dispute under Section 5(6) is illustrative and not exhaustive. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) bars CIRP when an operational creditor receives notice of an existing plausible controversy; IBC proceedings cannot serve as a summary recovery mechanism for disputed accounting ledgers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the doctrine of vicarious liability, payments made to key employees on the principal's instruction cannot be unilaterally dismissed as personal transactions; where the creditor concedes receiving funds but claims they were for unverified out-of-pocket expenses without contractual support, a substantial plausible dispute exists under the Mobilox standard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Multiple legal notices and stop-payment instructions pre-dating the Section 8 notice clearly established a genuine pre-existing dispute, rendering the Section 9 petition unmaintainable.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed; NCLT Mumbai order dated 13.02.2020 in C.P. No. 2431/I&BP/2019 was set aside; CIRP against the Corporate Debtor was quashed, and NCLT was directed to determine IRP expenses without costs.
summary: Corporate Debtor's director appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 application filed by custom clearance agent Wishwa Naveen Traders claiming Rs. 18,09,541/-. The Corporate Debtor demonstrated that prior to the Section 8 demand notice, it had suspended the creditor's services and issued legal notices regarding uncredited payments of Rs. 14,17,000/- made to the creditor's key employees. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission, holding that Section 5(6) is inclusive and the pre-notice correspondence, stop-payment instructions, and admitted but uncredited payments established a genuine, non-spurious pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox test.

case_title: Registrar of Companies, West Bengal vs. Goouksheer Farm Fresh Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Registrar of Companies, West Bengal (Appellant) vs. Goouksheer Farm Fresh Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company) and Sanjeev Jhunjhunwala, IRP of Respondent No. 1 (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regulatory striking off of Goouksheer Farm Fresh Pvt. Ltd. under Section 248 for non-filing of balance sheets since 31.03.2015 and annual returns since 31.03.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory non-compliance under Sections 92 and 137; NCLT ordered restoration without payment of statutory late filing fees and penalties. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against the struck-off company on 13.12.2019 in CP (IB) No. 1582/KB/2019; IRP filed restoration petition CP No. 183/KB/2020; NCLT allowed restoration and waived fees on 22.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Struck-off company records showing persistent failure to submit annual filings; MCA online portal structure demonstrating statutory fee generation under Section 403. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata allowed CP No. 183/KB/2020 under Section 252(3) to facilitate CIRP, but directed ROC not to levy any statutory fees or penalties because the company was in CIRP.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT possesses statutory power or inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11/14 of the NCLT Rules to grant a blanket waiver of statutory filing fees and additional penalties mandated under Section 403 of the Companies Act, 2013 when restoring a company to the register under Section 252(3).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adjudicating authorities cannot invoke inherent or procedural powers to waive mandatory statutory filing fees and penalties in the absence of express statutory authorization. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 403(1) read with Rule 12 of the Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014 constitutes an exhaustive, self-contained mandatory code governing fees; neither Rule 11 nor Rule 14 of the NCLT Rules can override express statutory fiscal requirements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: While an IRP has locus to seek company restoration under Section 252(3) to complete CIRP, ongoing CIRP does not grant statutory immunity from mandatory compliance fees upon revival. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT's direction restoring the company was sound, but the direction restraining ROC from levying statutory fees/penalties was ultra vires and must be quashed.
operative_order: The appeal was allowed; the portion of NCLT Kolkata's order dated 22.01.2020 directing ROC not to levy any fee/penalty was set aside; restoration under Section 252(3) was upheld subject to payment of all prescribed statutory fees, late fees, and penalties without costs.
summary: ROC West Bengal appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order that restored Goouksheer Farm Fresh Pvt. Ltd. under Section 252(3) to facilitate an ongoing CIRP while directing the ROC to waive all statutory filing fees and penalties. The ROC argued that Section 403 mandates payment of prescribed and additional fees for belated filings without any waiver provision. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT held that Section 403 and the relevant fee rules are mandatory and self-contained. NCLT cannot invoke its inherent powers under Rule 11 or Rule 14 to waive statutory fees simply because the corporate debtor is in CIRP. The fee-waiver direction was set aside.

case_title: Alanda Media & Entertainments Pvt. Ltd. vs. V. Ravi Prakash & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Alanda Media & Entertainments Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant) vs. V. Ravi Prakash (Respondent No. 1 / Petitioner No. 1), M.K.V.N. Murthy (Respondent No. 2 / Petitioner No. 2), and Associated Broadcasting Company Pvt. Ltd. along with other shareholders/directors (Respondents No. 3-10). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance and shareholding in Associated Broadcasting Company Pvt. Ltd., a closely-held company comprising only 6 total shareholders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement petition filed under Sections 241-242; Petitioner No. 1 held 5,00,000 shares and Petitioner No. 2 held 1,40,000 shares. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company petition filed jointly; Applications challenging maintainability (IA Nos. 811, 828, and 929 of 2019) dismissed by NCLT Hyderabad on 30.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share register showing company had 6 shareholders total; Petitioner No. 1 alone constituted more than one-tenth of total members; Petitioner No. 2 did not sign the petition and written consent was omitted. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants challenged maintainability on grounds that Petitioner No. 2 failed to sign and written consent under Section 244(2) read with Rule 81 was not annexed; NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the objections; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the non-annexure of written consent under Section 244(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 81 of the NCLT Rules by a co-petitioner entails threshold dismissal of an oppression and mismanagement petition when the first petitioner independently qualifies under Section 244(1)(a).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Non-compliance with procedural rules regarding the annexure of written consent under Section 244(2) does not warrant threshold dismissal; such procedural defects are curable and cannot defeat substantive statutory rights. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 244(2) governs obtaining consent, whereas Rule 81 of the NCLT Rules is directory by operation of Rule 58, which provides that procedural defaults do not invalidate proceedings absent a miscarriage of justice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Chalasani Venkateswara Rao, where an individual petitioner holds more than one-tenth of the total membership (1 of 6 shareholders), that petitioner has independent standing under Section 244(1)(a) irrespective of defective co-petitioner joinder. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT Hyderabad properly dismissed the objections; the petition met the statutory qualification threshold.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed in limine without costs, upholding the NCLT Hyderabad order dated 30.01.2020 in IA Nos. 811, 828, and 929 of 2019.
summary: Alanda Media challenged an NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing its applications questioning the maintainability of a Sections 241-242 petition filed by V. Ravi Prakash and another shareholder. Appellant argued that the co-petitioner did not sign the petition and written consent was omitted, violating Section 244(2) and Rule 81 of NCLT Rules. Dismissing the appeal in limine, NCLAT reaffirmed its ruling in Chalasani Venkateswara Rao that non-annexure of consent is a curable irregularity under Rule 58. Moreover, because the company had only 6 members in total, the first petitioner independently met the 1/10th membership threshold under Section 244(1)(a).

case_title: Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund vs. Royal Brushes Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (Financial Creditor/Appellant) vs. Royal Brushes Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lending/credit facilities advanced to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayment occurred on 01.07.2001; subsequent OTS proposal made in 2006 for Rs. 353 Lakhs (revised 07.07.2006) was revoked on 13.12.2006. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Date of default: 01.07.2001; OTS revoked: 13.12.2006; Section 7 application CP IB-902/I&BP/MB/2019 filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's failed OTS compromise letters from 2006 and loan default classification records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Special Bench Court-III dismissed the Section 7 petition on 18.03.2020 as barred by limitation under Article 137.
legal_issues: Whether a failed and revoked One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal/debt restructuring extends limitation or provides a continuing cause of action to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC eighteen years after the date of default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act runs strictly from the date of default or NPA declaration; failed and aborted restructuring settlements do not create a continuing cause of action. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications are governed by Article 137 (3-year period); the date of default anchors the accrual of the right to sue and cannot be shifted by subsequent aborted negotiations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Babulal Vardharji Gurjar and Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave, limitation begins running when default occurs; computing time from the failure of a 2006 settlement still renders an application filed in 2019 hopelessly time-barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was barred by limitation, warranting threshold dismissal.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs; liberty was reserved to pursue appropriate legal remedies for debt recovery before competent forums.
summary: Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its Section 7 petition against Royal Brushes Pvt. Ltd. on limitation grounds. The date of default occurred on 01.07.2001, and the appellant argued that an OTS proposal submitted and revoked in 2006 provided a continuing cause of action. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that limitation under Article 137 runs from the date of default and does not reset due to aborted settlement discussions. Even if calculated from the 2006 revocation, the 2019 application was time-barred (the broader doctrine on acknowledgment was subsequently qualified by the Supreme Court in Dena Bank and Laxmi Pat Surana).

case_title: The Dy. Commissioner of Customs DEEC (Monitoring Cell) vs. Vandana Garg
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deputy Commissioner of Customs DEEC (Monitoring Cell) (Appellant/Operational Creditor) vs. Vandana Garg (Resolution Professional of M/s Jyoti Structures Ltd. / Corporate Debtor / Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory customs duty claims arising out of export/import monitoring against the Corporate Debtor, Jyoti Structures Ltd.. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Belated customs claim submitted with an application seeking condonation of delay of 1,111 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT approved Resolution Plan on 27.03.2019 in MA No. 1129/2019 in CP (IB) 1137/MB/2017; Appellant submitted claim and sought recall long after approval. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate books of accounts and records of approved Resolution Plan finalized by the CoC and NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Customs Department filed application for condoning 1,111 days delay and recalling the plan approval order dated 27.03.2019; NCLT Mumbai rejected the application as unmaintainable; Customs Department appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory authority can submit claims or seek recall of an approved resolution plan after its sanction by the Committee of Creditors and the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31(1) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful resolution applicant is entitled to take over the corporate debtor on a clean slate; no unsubmitted or belated claims can be entertained after the resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) makes an approved resolution plan binding on all stakeholders, including central and local statutory authorities; entertaining claims after plan approval violates the certainty mandate of the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Supreme Court's Essar Steel doctrine, a resolution applicant cannot be faced with undecided 'hydra-headed' liabilities post-approval; applicants must know the exact quantum of debt to tailor their resolution plans. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A delay of 1,111 days in filing claims after resolution plan approval cannot be condoned, and NCLT rightly dismissed the application.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Mumbai order rejecting the application to recall the approval order in CP (IB) 1137/MB/2017.
summary: The Customs Department appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its application seeking condonation of a 1,111-day delay in submitting customs claims against Jyoti Structures Ltd. and seeking recall of the resolution plan approved on 27.03.2019. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, holding that under Section 31(1) an approved resolution plan binds all stakeholders, including statutory authorities. A successful resolution applicant acquires the debtor on a clean slate and cannot be subjected to sudden, unadjudicated liabilities post-approval.

case_title: Vijay Kumar Singh vs. Anil Kumar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Vijay Kumar Singh was a Shareholder/Director of Suspended Board of M/s Newgen Speciality Plastics Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 Anil Kumar was Resolution Professional (subsequently appointed Liquidator); Respondents No. 2 to 6 were Financial Creditors/CoC members (including Punjab National Bank, Exim Bank, Hero Fincorp, Intec Capital, HDFC Bank); Respondent No. 7 M/s Dynamic Star Security & Allied Services was Operational Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was an MSME manufacturer/exporter of plastic products which availed credit facilities from various lenders and contracted security/manpower services from Respondent No. 7. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default leading to CIRP initiation under Section 9; Corporate Debtor suffered continuous cash losses with depleted working capital and Rs. 16.18 Crores book debts written off in FY 2017-18. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 19.11.2018; 180-day period ended on 17.05.2019; NCLT extended CIRP by 90 days ending on 16.08.2019; CoC voted for liquidation via e-voting on 22-24.06.2019; RP filed CA No. 452/2019 under Section 33(2) on 01.07.2019; Joint Lenders' Meeting passed resolution to replace RP on 25.11.2019; CoC filed CA No. 962/2019 on 16.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th CoC meetings establishing no resolution plan submitted within deadlines; E-voting sheets showing 100% vote for liquidation; Minutes of Joint Lenders' Meeting dated 25.11.2019 stating CIRP was not conducted in the desired manner and resolving replacement of RP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition admitted on 19.11.2018; on 06.01.2020, NCLT New Delhi (Bench-III) rejected CoC's CA No. 962/2019 seeking replacement of RP and allowed RP's CA No. 452/2019 ordering liquidation and appointing RP as Liquidator.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in appointing the Resolution Professional as the Liquidator under Section 34 of the IBC despite the Committee of Creditors passing a resolution to replace the Resolution Professional prior to the passing of the liquidation order, and whether the order directing liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC was valid in the absence of any approved resolution plan within the statutory period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the Committee of Creditors resolves to replace the Resolution Professional prior to the passing of an order of liquidation, the Adjudicating Authority must give effect to the CoC's intent by substituting the insolvency professional rather than appointing the outgoing Resolution Professional as Liquidator, even if the formal prerequisites under Section 34(4) are not strictly met, because the Liquidator functions in a fiduciary capacity for creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27 and Section 34 read with Section 60(5) of the IBC empower the Adjudicating Authority to replace a Resolution Professional when the CoC has expressed lack of confidence in the RP prior to the liquidation order being made; the CoC's prerogative to replace the professional survives until the liquidation order is actually passed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court does not require conclusive proof or sit in judgment on the veracity of the creditors' specific factual allegations of mismanagement against the RP; a recorded decision of lenders showing loss of trust and expressing that CIRP was not conducted in the desired manner is sufficient to warrant substitution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidation order under Section 33 was unassailable due to non-receipt of any resolution plan within statutory timelines; however, dismissing the CoC's application for replacement of the RP was erroneous, necessitating remittance to appoint a substitute Liquidator.
operative_order: The liquidation order passed by the Adjudicating Authority is maintained; the order dismissing CA No. 962/C-III/ND/2019 is set aside; the matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to appoint another Insolvency Professional (Mr. Sandeep Kr. Bhat as proposed by CoC, or another IP nominated by IBBI) as Liquidator replacing Respondent No. 1, with appropriate directions for handover of charge.
summary: An appeal was filed by the suspended Director of M/s Newgen Speciality Plastics Ltd. challenging the NCLT New Delhi's order directing liquidation of the Corporate Debtor and dismissing the CoC's application to replace the Resolution Professional (RP) as Liquidator. The NCLAT upheld the liquidation order since no resolution plan was submitted within the extended 270-day CIRP period. However, the Tribunal held that because the CoC had formally resolved in a Joint Lenders' Meeting prior to the liquidation order that the CIRP was not conducted satisfactorily and sought replacement of the RP, the Adjudicating Authority should have honored the creditors' commercial mandate and substituted the RP under Section 27 and Section 34 of the IBC. The matter was remitted to appoint a new Liquidator.

case_title: Piyush Periwal vs. Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (SASF)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Piyush Periwal was Promoter/Shareholder of National Plywood Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor); Respondent Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (SASF) was Financial Creditor as Assignee of IDBI; National Boards Ltd. (NBL) was Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IDBI extended term loan facility of Rs. 32 Million to NBL on 27.03.1997, for which the Corporate Debtor executed a Corporate Guarantee on 16.07.1997; debts assigned to SASF on 30.09.2004. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by NBL led IDBI to recall loan on 09.11.2001 and invoke Corporate Guarantee on 03.12.2001 demanding Rs. 5,42,94,868/- with interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First BIFR reference No. 160/2001 filed on 02.03.2001 and dismissed on 25.06.2002; Second BIFR reference No. 259/2003 filed on 21.02.2003 (registered 01.07.2003) and abated on SICA repeal on 01.12.2016; Section 7 petition filed on 12.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan recall notice dated 09.11.2001; Guarantee invocation notice dated 03.12.2001; BIFR order dated 25.06.2002; BIFR registration letter dated 01.07.2003; Letter of acknowledgment of liability by Principal Borrower dated 20.12.2016; Recovery Certificate dated 05.01.2005 issued by DRT Guwahati in OA No. 27/2002. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition filed before NCLT Guwahati (CP (IB) No. 23/GB/2018); NCLT admitted petition on 26.08.2019 rejecting plea of limitation; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 25.11.2019; Supreme Court remanded matter in Civil Appeal No. 9142/2019 on 20.01.2020 for fresh consideration.
legal_issues: Whether the application under Section 7 of the IBC filed against the Corporate Guarantor was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and whether the period during which a registered BIFR reference was pending prior to its dismissal as time-barred can be excluded under Section 22(1) of SICA.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A reference received, registered, and assigned a case number by the BIFR constitutes an inquiry under Section 16 of SICA, entitling the creditor to statutory suspension and exclusion of time under Section 22(1) of SICA from the limitation period until its formal dismissal, even if subsequently dismissed for delay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(1) of SICA suspends legal proceedings against the debtor and guarantors once an inquiry is underway; Regulation 19(7) of BIFR Regulations (deeming a reference not made) applies only where registration is declined at the threshold scrutiny stage, not where a reference is registered, numbered, and later dismissed by a Bench. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Computation of limitation excludes periods protected by Section 22(1) of SICA; the unexcluded interval between dismissal of the first reference and filing of the second reference (241 days), combined with the interval from SICA's repeal to filing under Section 7 (831 days), totaled 1,072 days, falling within the 3-year limitation period. Furthermore, acknowledgment of debt by the principal borrower binds the corporate guarantor whose liability is co-extensive. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: SASF's Section 7 application was filed well within the three-year limitation period prescribed under Article 137 of the Limitation Act read with Section 238A IBC.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 26.08.2019 passed by NCLT Guwahati admitting the Section 7 petition is affirmed, and the appeal is dismissed without costs.
summary: Promoter of Corporate Guarantor National Plywood Industries Ltd. appealed against NCLT Guwahati's order admitting SASF's Section 7 IBC petition, claiming it was barred by limitation as guarantee invocation occurred on 03.12.2001 while CIRP was triggered on 12.03.2019. The NCLAT held that the first reference before BIFR was duly registered before dismissal, warranting statutory exclusion under Section 22(1) of SICA. Accounting for the non-excluded gap between references (241 days) and post-SICA repeal duration (831 days), the total effective period was 1,072 days, which is within the 3-year limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act. The liability was further reinforced by the principal borrower's acknowledgment. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: K.S. Sreenivasan vs. Landmark Housing Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant K.S. Sreenivasan claimed to be Financial Creditor; Respondent Landmark Housing Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd. was Corporate Debtor engaged in real estate development. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties executed an Agreement for Sale dated 03.04.2015 for 1,89,299 sq. ft. of saleable area in 'Torrence' project at pre-launch price of Rs. 3,000/sq. ft. Appellant paid Rs. 5 Lakhs advance with balance Rs. 56,73,97,000/- payable in stages. Agreement contained a buyback covenant under which Corporate Debtor was to repurchase area at Rs. 4,535/sq. ft. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant claimed a financial debt of Rs. 29,05,73,965/- (representing the differential price of Rs. 1,535/sq. ft. across 1,89,299 sq. ft.) with 12.5% interest; no date of disbursement of Rs. 29.05 Crores or specific default date was pleaded in Form 1. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed on 03.04.2015; Corporate Debtor issued three cheques dated 22.02.2016, 22.08.2016, 22.02.2017; Corporate Debtor sent letters dated 22.02.2017 and 07.02.2019; Legal notice demanding payment issued on 13.02.2019; Section 7 petition filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement for Sale dated 03.04.2015; three uncashed cheques totaling Rs. 29,05,73,965/-; letter dated 07.02.2019 stating cheques were compensation for surrendering right of purchase; absence of bank proof showing disbursal beyond Rs. 5 Lakhs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 7 application before NCLT Chennai; NCLT dismissed petition holding Appellant disbursed only Rs. 5 Lakhs against Rs. 56.78 Crores commitment and could not enforce reciprocal buyback promise, meaning Rs. 29.05 Crores was not a financial debt.
legal_issues: Whether an unfulfilled buyback agreement for real estate where the creditor paid only a token advance constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(f) or 5(8)(g) of the IBC, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to examine disbursement and the nature/quantum of debt under Section 7.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A claim arising from a reciprocal buyback contract cannot be characterized as a 'financial debt' unless there has been actual disbursement of money having commercial effect of borrowing or consideration for time value of money, and a party who fails to fulfill primary payment obligations cannot claim default on a reciprocal repurchase promise under insolvency law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Financial debt' under Section 5(8) requires disbursement of debt against consideration for the time value of money; a claim for differential upside margin in real estate buyback is not a derivative transaction under Section 5(8)(g), nor does an unperformed forward sale qualify under Section 5(8)(f) without underlying financing disbursement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority is obligated to ascertain whether the claimed debt is payable in fact and law; issuing cheques as compensation for surrender of purchase rights does not substantiate disbursement against the time value of money. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant failed to establish disbursement of the claimed Rs. 29,05,73,965/- or any actionable default by Corporate Debtor, justifying dismissal of the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing the Section 7 application. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the dismissal of his Section 7 IBC application by NCLT Chennai against a real estate developer. The Appellant entered into an agreement to purchase saleable area for Rs. 56.78 Crores but paid only Rs. 5 Lakhs, and subsequently claimed Rs. 29.05 Crores with interest as financial debt based on a buyback clause and three cheques issued for differential pricing. The NCLAT held that the transaction involved reciprocal obligations which the Appellant failed to perform. The claimed differential amount was compensation for surrendering purchase rights rather than an amount disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8). The dismissal was affirmed.

case_title: Omega Icehill Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Anil Agarwal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants were Omega Icehill Pvt. Ltd. (Company), Herman Johan Oonk, Harm Jan Oonk (representing foreign majority Omega Group holding 53%), and Tushar Kant Jindal; Respondent Anil Agarwal was promoter, First Director, and removed Managing Director holding 5,000 shares (0.04%). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint Venture between Netherlands-based Omega Engineering Holding BV and Indian partnership Friends Refrigeration and Associates (FRA) incorporated on 11.11.2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of oppression and mismanagement regarding illegal ouster and termination of MD; issued and paid-up capital of Rs. 12,26,33,970/-; Respondent individually held 0.04%, with family holding 2.93% (and beneficial interest in corporate shareholder Kurinji Metals holding 30.42%). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting notice issued on 06.05.2019; Board resolution removing Respondent as MD passed on 14.05.2019; Company Petition CP No. 102/ND/2019 along with Section 244 waiver IA filed in May 2019; NCLT granted waiver on 22.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint Venture Agreement dated 20.01.2010; Article 52 of Articles of Association reserving MD appointment/removal powers to controlling shareholders; Notice dated 06.05.2019; Minutes of Board Meeting dated 14.05.2019; consent affidavits filed by family members. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed petition under Sections 241-242 and IA under Section 244 before NCLT New Delhi; NCLT allowed waiver application holding the petition raised triable issues of oppression; Appellants appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal correctly exercised its discretion under Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 in granting a waiver of the qualifying shareholding threshold to a minority shareholder/founding Managing Director alleging wrongful removal by the Board in violation of the Articles of Association.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory threshold of 10% shareholding under Section 244(1)(a) may be waived by the Tribunal where exceptional and compelling circumstances exist, such as where a founding promoter-director managing the company is ousted without following the Articles of Association and the shareholding structure concentrates all remaining equity among majority groups, rendering it impossible to meet numerical thresholds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 244 enables the Tribunal to waive statutory prerequisites on application; consent affidavits of family members filed during proceedings constitute valid consent under Section 244(2) for reckoning collective support. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: At the stage of Section 244 waiver, the Tribunal evaluates whether a prima facie case of oppression/mismanagement is shown under the principles laid down in Cyrus Investments, without conducting a conclusive inquiry into the underlying merits of the petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The summary ouster of the long-standing Managing Director by the Board contrary to the AoA, in a closely held venture where majority power precludes minority coalition, constitutes an exceptional circumstance warranting grant of waiver.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT New Delhi order dated 22.07.2020 granting waiver under Section 244. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellants appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order granting Respondent Anil Agarwal a waiver under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 to pursue an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242. The Respondent, a founding director and Managing Director holding 0.04% individually and 2.93% with family, was abruptly removed as Managing Director by the Board of Directors. The NCLAT held that because the removal allegedly contravened Article 52 of the AoA and the majority foreign group controlled the venture, exceptional and compelling circumstances existed as enunciated in Cyrus Investments. The waiver was upheld and the appeal dismissed.

case_title: Akhil R. Kothakota & Ors. vs. M/s. Tierra Farm Assets Company Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Akhil R. Kothakota and Madadi Rinda were secured debenture holders; Respondent M/s Tierra Farm Assets Company Pvt. Ltd. was a private limited company and debenture issuer; Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. was Debenture Trustee. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debenture Trust Deed executed on 17.12.2015 mortgaging Schedule II properties; Appellant No. 1 allotted 225 secured NCDs for Rs. 45 Lakhs; Appellant No. 2 allotted 75 secured NCDs for Rs. 15 Lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in quarterly interest payments from 31.03.2018 onwards; total claimed amount Rs. 56,24,460/- for Appellant No. 1 and Rs. 18,74,820/- for Appellant No. 2 (including principal, interest, default interest, and 3% prepayment penalty). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interest paid until 01.01.2018; default occurred from 31.03.2018; demand/redemption notices sent between April and September 2018; legal notice issued on 31.10.2018; CP No. 73/BB/2019 filed on 09.11.2019; NCLT order passed on 17.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture Trust Deed dated 17.12.2015; Allotment Letters dated 21.03.2017 and 30.03.2017; written reply before NCLT admitting default in paying interest on NCDs and claiming financial distress. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed petition under Section 71(10) of Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Bengaluru; NCLT disposed of petition by granting the company six months' provisional time to explore settlement without ordering redemption.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has the discretion under Section 71(10) of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant time to explore settlement based on financial distress instead of directing immediate redemption of debentures and payment of overdue interest upon established default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 71(10) of the Companies Act, 2013, upon an admitted failure by a company to pay interest or redeem debentures on maturity, the Tribunal has a statutory duty to order forthwith redemption and repayment, and lacks statutory authority to defer relief based on the company's financial distress. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 71(10) read with Section 71(8) is mandatory in nature; the power conferred on the Tribunal is coupled with a duty to enforce the repayment obligation rather than granting arbitrary moratoriums to explore non-binding settlements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An admission of default in the company's pleadings satisfies the evidentiary requirement under Rule 73 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, precluding any requirement to assess the commercial viability or financial status of the debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's direction granting six months to explore settlement was ultra vires Section 71(10), warranting an order directing repayment within a defined period.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with a specific direction to the Respondent Company to repay the amounts due and payable to the Appellants within a period of two months from the date of judgment, failing which Appellants are at liberty to take appropriate legal steps in accordance with law; IA No. 706/2020 closed; no costs.
summary: Debenture holders filed an appeal against the order of NCLT Bengaluru, which disposed of their Section 71(10) Companies Act petition by granting the defaulting company six months to explore settlement due to financial distress rather than directing repayment.
