The NCLAT held that Section 71(10) read with Section 71(8) does not permit the Tribunal to evaluate financial distress or grant exploratory settlement periods when default is admitted. The statutory duty requires ordering forthwith redemption and repayment of principal and interest. The NCLAT modified the order and directed the company to repay all dues within two months.

case_title: Ratna Singh & Anr. vs. Theme Export Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Ratna Singh and Brijinder Singh were Ex-Directors holding 8% equity in Theme Export Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 was Theme Export Pvt. Ltd. through Liquidator Vikram Bajaj; Respondent No. 2 was Nandini Singh, Director holding 92% equity; Bank of Baroda was lead Financial Creditor (98.10% CoC share). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was an export company that availed Rs. 25 Crores credit facilities from Bank of Baroda secured by factory and assets; Operational Creditor Ratan Singh provided services/goods. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on operational debt triggered Section 9 CIRP; credit facilities of Rs. 25 Crores defaulted; revenues fell from ~Rs. 100 Crores (FY 2015-16) to ~Rs. 30 Crores (FY 2018-19). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petition admitted on 29.08.2019; 1st CoC meeting on 28.09.2019; 2nd CoC meeting on 04.11.2019 resolving liquidation with 98.5% vote; NCLT liquidation order passed on 29.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Ex-accountant's disclosure of asset transfers; plant inspection revealing dismantled plant and machinery; lack of financial statements since 31.03.2017; forensic audit initiated with M/s K.R.A and Company under Sections 43, 45, 66; 2nd CoC minutes dated 04.11.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor initiated CIRP on 29.08.2019; on 29.07.2020, NCLT New Delhi (Court V) allowed RP's CA No. 121/ND/2019 and ordered liquidation based on CoC's 98.5% majority vote.
legal_issues: Whether a liquidation order passed under Section 33 of the IBC based on the commercial wisdom of 98.5% of the Committee of Creditors can be challenged under Section 61(4) by former directors on allegations of inter-se director fraud, oppression, and mismanagement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against a liquidation order under Section 61(4) of the IBC is strictly limited to grounds of material irregularity or fraud committed in relation to the liquidation order itself, and disputes concerning past management fraud or oppression cannot invalidate a valid liquidation decision made by the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(4) restricts appellate jurisdiction over liquidation orders; the commercial wisdom of the CoC to liquidate an unviable business is non-justiciable. IBC proceedings cannot be converted into oppression and mismanagement proceedings under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appellants failed to establish any material irregularity or fraud pertaining to the CoC's voting process or the liquidation order; allegations regarding diversion of assets are properly addressable via avoidance and fraudulent trading applications under Sections 43-51 and Section 66 during liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in ordering liquidation on the basis of 98.5% CoC vote, warranting dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The liquidation order dated 29.07.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi is upheld and the appeal is dismissed without costs; copy of order directed to be sent to IBBI and Bank of Baroda.
summary: Former directors of Theme Export Pvt. Ltd. challenged the NCLT New Delhi order directing liquidation under Section 33 IBC, alleging that the majority director committed fraud, siphoned corporate funds, and caused business closure. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 61(4) of the IBC, a liquidation order can only be assailed on proof of material irregularity or fraud committed in relation to the liquidation order itself. The CoC had resolved by 98.5% majority that business revival was impossible due to dismantled machinery and absence of accounts. Allegations of past managerial fraud fall under avoidance proceedings under Sections 43 to 66 or separate company law remedies, not as grounds to overturn CoC's commercial decision to liquidate.

case_title: Slipco Constructions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Yogesh Gupta, Liquidator of Kohinoor Power Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Slipco Constructions Pvt. Ltd. was a contractor/third-party equipment owner; Respondent Yogesh Gupta was Liquidator of Kohinoor Power Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sub-contract for constructing a 110-meter RCC chimney at Corporate Debtor's power plant site, originally awarded to Tecpro Infra Projects Ltd. and continued by Appellant after site takeover. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor ousted Appellant's personnel, detained plant and machinery, and defaulted on payment; no direct monetary insolvency default between Appellant and CD was adjudicated. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Civil dispute arose in 2013; Title Suit No. 11/2013 filed by CD; Money Suit No. 05/2013 filed by Appellant; Court Commissioner inventory report submitted on 02.05.2017; CIRP initiated on 03.08.2018; liquidation order passed thereafter; NCLT rejected equipment release on 15.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Commissioner Report dated 02.05.2017 detailing inventoried equipment locked in a container with keys deposited in Civil Court; injunction orders in Misc. Appeal No. 466/2013; Liquidator's admission in Reply that equipment belonged to Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA (IB) 19/KB/2019 before NCLT Kolkata seeking return of equipment from Corporate Debtor's site; NCLT rejected application directing Appellant to first have the Civil Court injunction vacated.
legal_issues: Whether third-party assets lying at a corporate debtor's project site form part of the liquidation estate under Section 36 of the IBC, and whether pre-existing civil court proceedings and injunctions bar the third party from seeking custody of its assets during liquidation proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Assets owned by a third party in the possession of the Corporate Debtor do not form part of the liquidation estate under Section 36(4) of the IBC, and pre-existing civil proceedings concerning custody of such assets are not barred by Section 33(5) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(5) bars fresh suits against the corporate debtor upon liquidation but does not extinguish pre-CIRP pending suits; under Section 35(1)(k), the liquidator possesses the power and duty to defend and participate in pending suits to facilitate appropriate orders regarding non-debtor property. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the liquidator explicitly concedes that inventoried equipment belongs to a third party and is excluded by Section 36(4), no proprietary claim of the Corporate Debtor survives to justify withholding property. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in outright dismissing the application; the appropriate relief is granting liberty to the equipment owner to seek release from the concerned Civil Court holding the keys, with the Liquidator cooperating in the application.
operative_order: The impugned order is modified; appeal disposed of granting liberty to the Appellant to approach the Civil Court (Senior Division, Seraikella) for return of its construction equipment, and directing the Liquidator to appropriately respond and cooperate before the Civil Court; no costs.
summary: Appellant Slipco Constructions challenged an order of NCLT Kolkata dismissing its application for the release of construction equipment stored at the site of Kohinoor Power Pvt. Ltd. (in liquidation). The equipment had been inventoried by a Court Commissioner in a pre-CIRP 2013 money suit and locked in a container with keys deposited with the Civil Court. The Liquidator admitted the equipment did not belong to the Corporate Debtor. The NCLAT held that under Section 36(4) IBC, third-party assets do not form part of the liquidation estate, and Section 33(5) does not extinguish pre-existing suits. The NCLAT modified the order, granting liberty to Appellant to apply to the Civil Court for release of its assets, with the Liquidator instructed to support the request.

case_title: M/s. Sowil Limited vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Sowil Limited was an Indian public limited company and prospective bidder; Respondent No. 1 was Competition Commission of India (CCI); Respondent No. 2 was Hexagon Geosystems India Pvt. Ltd. (equipment vendor and competing bidder); Respondent No. 3 was RDSO, Ministry of Railways. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: RDSO floated a tender on 26.06.2019 for monitoring railway ballast beds using Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) technology; Appellant sought to procure rolling stock mounted GPR equipment from Respondent No. 2 to participate in tender. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant alleged price gouging/abuse where Respondent No. 2 quoted Rs. 4,86,40,005/-, which was 200% higher than foreign market rate of Rs. 1,41,69,824/-, offering only a 17% discount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tender floated 26.06.2019; RDSO provided clarification to CCI on 02.06.2020; CCI passed Section 26(2) closure order on 26.08.2020; appeal heard and decided on 04.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email quote showing markups of 80% on spares and doubled training costs; RDSO reply dated 02.06.2020 establishing presence of at least 4 other global manufacturers (Zetica, Ground Control, SIC Infraconsult, Loram). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed information under Section 19(1)(a) alleging abuse of dominance under Section 4; CCI dismissed information under Section 26(2) holding no prima facie case existed.
legal_issues: Whether the Competition Commission of India was required to order a Director General investigation under Section 26(1) without the informant defining a relevant market, where multiple global suppliers existed in the market and the vendor was also a direct competitor in the tender.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An allegation of abuse of dominant position under Section 4 cannot be sustained without prima facie evidence establishing dominance in a properly delineated relevant market, especially where multiple global competitors operate in the same product segment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19 and Section 26(2) empower the Commission to close an information at the threshold if no prima facie contravention is revealed; the burden of establishing prima facie dominance rests initially upon the informant rather than the Commission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Market presence of multiple international equipment manufacturers confirmed by the procurement authority negates the assertion that an entity commands dominant market power capable of operating independently of competitive forces. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Informant failed to establish dominance or a prima facie case under Section 4, as it simply approached its own competitor after failing to negotiate desired pricing, justifying threshold dismissal without DG investigation.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the admission stage without being admitted; no order as to costs.
summary: Sowil Limited appealed under Section 53B of the Competition Act, 2002 against CCI's Section 26(2) order closing an information filed against Hexagon Geosystems for alleged abuse of dominance under Section 4. Sowil alleged Hexagon quoted excessive prices for GPR equipment required for an RDSO railway tender. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Sowil failed to delineate a relevant market or establish dominance. Information obtained from RDSO proved that at least four other international manufacturers offered the technology in India, disproving dominance. Sowil merely attempted to procure equipment from a commercial rival and failed to demonstrate any anti-competitive abuse.

case_title: Sundaram Brake Linings Ltd. & Ors. vs. Competition Commission of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants were Sundaram Brake Linings Ltd. and its officials Mr. S. Balaji and Mr. P. Bose; Respondent No. 1 was Competition Commission of India; Respondent No. 2 was Chief Materials Manager, South Eastern Railway. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Procurement of brake linings by South Eastern Railway subject to competition enquiry in Reference Case No. 3 (and others) of 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Commission investigated anti-competitive conduct and passed an adverse order on 10.07.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Primary substantive order passed by CCI on 10.07.2020; Appellants filed Competition Appeal (AT) No. 19/2020; rectification application under Section 38 filed before CCI on 21.09.2020; CCI dismissed rectification application on 08.10.2020; Section 53B appeal filed and decided on 23.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 38 application dated 21.09.2020 seeking deletion of sentence in Para 47(16) referencing a meeting at Hotel Piccadelly, Lucknow and modification in Para 33(i); CCI order dated 08.10.2020 holding no error apparent on the face of the record. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After filing substantive Appeal No. 19/2020 against CCI's primary order dated 10.07.2020, Appellants sought rectification from CCI under Section 38(2)(b); upon CCI's refusal, Appellants filed the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Competition Commission of India has the jurisdiction or propriety to entertain an application for rectification of an order under Section 38 of the Competition Act, 2002 during the pendency of a statutory appeal challenging that same order before the Appellate Tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An original adjudicatory authority should refrain from altering or entertaining rectification proceedings in respect of an order that is already subject to appellate review before a superior appellate tribunal, as the entire record is sub judice before the appellate court. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 38 of the Competition Act permits amendment only for mistakes apparent from the record; by analogous jurisprudence (such as Section 420(2) of Companies Act, 2013), rectification powers cannot be exercised once an appeal is instituted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an appeal is actively pending before the appellate tribunal, errors on the record must be raised before the appellate forum rather than through parallel rectification proceedings below. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCI rightly rejected the rectification application, and the appellate tribunal will not interfere with such refusal when the main order is already challenged in a pending appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interference in the impugned order, with liberty granted to Appellants to point out any errors or mistakes apparent from the record in the main pending appeal (Competition Appeal (AT) No. 19 of 2020); no costs.
summary: Sundaram Brake Linings Ltd. appealed under Section 53B against CCI's order rejecting its application under Section 38 for rectification of an earlier order dated 10.07.2020. The Appellants sought deletion of specific factual sentences regarding an alleged meeting in Lucknow while their substantive appeal against the primary order was already pending before NCLAT. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that once an order is under challenge before an appellate forum, the original authority cannot amend or alter its order. The Appellants were granted liberty to advance all arguments regarding factual errors before the appellate court in their pending appeal.

case_title: M/s Quippo Energy Ltd. vs. M/s Soundararaja Mills Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Quippo Energy Ltd. was Operational Creditor; Respondent M/s Soundararaja Mills Limited was Corporate Debtor operating a textile unit at Karaikal, Pondicherry. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties executed two Lease Agreements (dated 05.01.2015 with addendum dated 20.09.2015, and dated 20.01.2016) for gas-based power generation equipment, along with two corresponding Service Agreements for manpower. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed total outstanding operational debt of Rs. 1,17,65,461/- (comprising principal amount of Rs. 1,13,29,658/- and 18% interest of Rs. 4,35,803/- calculated from the last invoice dated 01.02.2019); last payment received was Rs. 9,56,160/- via RTGS on 06.10.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Business dealings ran from February 2015 to 13.12.2018; Section 8 demand notice issued on 20.04.2019; Corporate Debtor issued detailed notice of dispute/reply denying liability on 28.04.2019; Section 9 petition CP IBA/868/2019 filed thereafter; NCLT Chennai dismissed petition on 23.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's email dated 09.06.2018 detailing generator trippings; Corporate Debtor's Debit Note No. SRMAO/B/C68/18-19 dated 28.11.2018 for Rs. 55,53,730/- raised for generator breakdowns and higher power costs from Tamil Nadu Electricity Board; email dated 28.11.2018 where Operational Creditor resisted the debit note and agreed to send ledgers for reconciliation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application before NCLT Division Bench Chennai; NCLT rejected the petition on 23.12.2019 holding that a pre-existing dispute regarding deficiency of service and debit notes existed prior to the demand notice.
legal_issues: Whether the pre-CIRP exchange of emails and issuance of debit notes regarding equipment failure, supply tripping, and service deficiency constitutes a plausible 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) read with Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC justifying rejection of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC, an application must be rejected if notice of a pre-existing dispute exists prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice under Section 8, provided the defense raised is plausible, supported by evidence, and not spurious, hypothetical, or a mere bluster. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The definition of 'dispute' under Section 5(6) encompasses complaints relating to quality of goods or service deficiency; disputes over deductions, unadjusted debit notes, and uncalibrated performance raised prior to the Section 8 notice fall squarely within this threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Mobilox Innovations test, the adjudicating authority is not required to examine whether the defense will ultimately succeed on merits, but merely whether there is a plausible contention requiring investigation evidenced by contemporaneous pre-notice correspondence and debit notes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The record demonstrated pre-existing disputes regarding service tripping, procurement of alternative grid power, and rival claims on debit notes raised in November 2018 before the Section 8 demand notice dated 20.04.2019, warranting dismissal of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the order of the NCLT Division Bench, Chennai dated 23.12.2019.
summary: Operational Creditor Quippo Energy Ltd. appealed against NCLT Chennai's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application seeking Rs. 1.17 Crores under equipment lease and service agreements from Corporate Debtor Soundararaja Mills Ltd. The Corporate Debtor resisted the demand relying on correspondence and a debit note for Rs. 55.53 Lakhs issued on 28.11.2018 for frequent generator tripping and breach of minimum generation hours, which forced reliance on costlier grid electricity. The NCLAT held that these contemporaneous exchanges occurring months prior to the Section 8 notice established a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) and Mobilox Innovations principles, rendering the petition unmaintainable.

case_title: UCO Bank vs. Mr. G. Ramachandran, Resolution Professional, M/s. Sai Regency Power Corporation Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant UCO Bank was Financial Creditor maintaining bank accounts; Respondent G. Ramachandran was Resolution Professional of M/s Sai Regency Power Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Kamang Dam Hydro Power Pvt. Ltd. and J.R. Power Pvt. Ltd. were group companies. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor maintained two Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDRs) with UCO Bank which were offered in 2011 as security for two vehicle loans and two demand loans of Rs. 50,00,000/- each sanctioned to group companies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: During the CIRP moratorium, UCO Bank on 09.07.2019 adjusted the Corporate Debtor's Fixed Deposits and accrued interest aggregating to Rs. 2,07,31,503/- against outstanding vehicle and group company loans; RP demanded refund of Rs. 2,27,94,706/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 against Corporate Debtor on 27.03.2019; public notice published in Tamil and English (Business Standard) on 30.03.2019; UCO Bank debited/appropriated FDRs on 09.07.2019; RP issued demand letter on 06.12.2019; NCLT order passed on 29.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Copy of English newspaper publication dated 30.03.2019; RP notice dated 06.12.2019 citing Section 14 and Section 17(d); bank statements showing appropriation of Fixed Deposit account Nos. 19050310045848 and 19050310046265. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed M.A. No. 39/2020 in IBA/92/2019 before NCLT Special Bench Chennai; NCLT directed UCO Bank to refund and restore the credited sum of Rs. 2,27,94,706/- to the Corporate Debtor's account to facilitate resolution.
legal_issues: Whether a lending bank is entitled to adjust and set off the Corporate Debtor's fixed deposits against outstanding loan obligations of the Corporate Debtor and its sister entities during the subsistence of a CIRP moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, and whether ignorance of CIRP initiation protects such appropriation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a moratorium is declared under Section 14 of the IBC upon admission of a CIRP petition, no creditor or financial institution is permitted to recover, appropriate, or set off any amounts from the accounts or fixed deposits of the Corporate Debtor towards past dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 imposes an absolute statutory prohibition on recovery and encumbrance enforcement during CIRP; Section 17(d) mandates financial institutions maintaining debtor accounts to act strictly on the instructions of the Resolution Professional. Provisions governing mutual set-off under Section 173 and asset exclusions under Section 36(4)(b) apply strictly to liquidation proceedings and cannot justify appropriation during CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Public announcement in prescribed newspapers constitutes constructive notice to all entities; lack of actual knowledge of CIRP initiation is legally irrelevant to the operation of the statutory moratorium under Section 14. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: UCO Bank's debit and appropriation of the Corporate Debtor's fixed deposits violated Section 14, rendering the NCLT's order directing refund and restoration unassailable.
operative_order: Delay condoned via IA No. 2038/2020; the appeal is dismissed without costs, maintaining the Adjudicating Authority's order directing UCO Bank to restore the credit to the Corporate Debtor's account.
summary: UCO Bank appealed against the NCLT Chennai order directing it to refund Rs. 2,27,94,706/- adjusted from the Fixed Deposits of Corporate Debtor Sai Regency Power Corporation Pvt. Ltd. during CIRP against outstanding vehicle loans and third-party group company loans. The bank contended it had no knowledge of CIRP and claimed a right of set-off under Section 173 and Section 36(4)(b) IBC. The NCLAT held that public announcement in newspapers constituted valid notice and lack of subjective knowledge is immaterial. Following settled law in Indian Overseas Bank v. Dinkar T. Venkatsubramaniam, the Tribunal held that Section 14 absolutely bars any creditor from appropriating or recovering funds from the debtor's accounts during moratorium, with set-off rules applicable only at liquidation. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s Arihant Unitech Realty Projects Limited vs. Nil
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Arihant Unitech Realty Projects Limited was Transferor Company; North Town Estates Private Limited was Transferee Company in a proposed Scheme of Amalgamation. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate restructuring through a Scheme of Amalgamation between Transferor Company and Transferee Company under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural default of 201 days delay in filing the second motion Company Scheme Petition after the submission of the Chairman's reports on meetings of equity shareholders and unsecured creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Shareholders' meeting held on 23.05.2019; Unsecured Creditors' meeting held on 16.05.2019; Chairman reports submitted within time; second motion petition due within 7 days of report filing; petition filed with delay on 24.01.2020 via MA/102/2020; NCLT Chennai dismissed delay condonation application on 13.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Chairman reports certifying unanimous approval of the amalgamation scheme by equity shareholders and unsecured creditors of both companies; affidavit detailing internal compliance pre-occupations and closure of audits as reason for delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed MA/102/2020 in CA/216 & 217/CAA/2018 before NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai seeking condonation of 201 days delay in presenting the second motion petition; NCLT dismissed the application on 13.02.2020 holding causes were not unavoidable; Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal should adopt a justice-oriented and liberal approach in condoning delay in presenting a second motion company petition for sanction of a scheme of amalgamation under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, where the delay is not tainted by mala fides.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In applications for condonation of procedural delay in corporate amalgamation and arrangement proceedings, tribunals must adopt a pragmatic, liberal, and justice-oriented approach, and where the explanation does not smack of mala fides or gross contumacy, procedural delay should be condoned to prevent an aberration of justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Timelines prescribed under company court rules for filing second-stage petitions following meeting reports are directory and procedural; they should not be rigidly applied to thwart substantive corporate restructuring approved unanimously by stakeholders under Sections 230-232. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-occupation with internal compliance, account finalization, and corporate audit closure constitutes a bona fide explanation in the absence of opposing prejudice or mala fides. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in taking an overly technical approach; the 201-day delay was adequately explained and non-fatal to the amalgamation petition.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed without costs; the impugned order dated 13.02.2020 in MA/102/2020 is set aside; the delay of 201 days in filing the Company Scheme Petition is condoned; MA/102/2020 is allowed; IA No. 2309/2020 closed with direction to file certified copy within three weeks.
summary: Arihant Unitech Realty Projects Ltd. appealed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against an order of NCLT Chennai which dismissed its application for condonation of 201 days delay in filing a second motion company petition to sanction an amalgamation scheme. The NCLT had rejected the plea on grounds that internal compliance and audit finalization were not unavoidable causes. The NCLAT reversed the order and condoned the delay, holding that tribunals must apply a pragmatic and justice-oriented approach to procedural delays where there is no evidence of mala fides, especially when equity shareholders and unsecured creditors had already unanimously approved the restructuring scheme.

case_title: M/s. Venkateswara Agencies vs. Competition Commission of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Venkateswara Agencies was a proprietorship agricultural machinery dealer in Andhra Pradesh; Respondent No. 1 was Competition Commission of India; Respondent No. 2 was Kerala Agro Machinery Corporation Ltd. (KAMCO), a machinery manufacturer based in Kerala. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dealership Agreement dated 28.09.2006 for distribution and service of power tillers, power reapers, and power stone cutters in designated districts of Andhra Pradesh, renewed periodically until 31.03.2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Contractual grievances alleging arbitrary refusal by KAMCO to supply new machinery/spares and unauthorized appointment of competing dealers in Appellant's territory; Appellant filed civil suit OS (IA) No. 1593/2019 before District Judge and initiated criminal proceedings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed on 28.09.2006; dealership operated through 31.03.2018; supplies established in November-December 2016; information Case No. 38/2019 filed before CCI; CCI passed Section 26(2) dismissal on 05.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Dealership Agreement dated 28.09.2006 containing Clause 7(a)(ii) reserving manufacturer's right to appoint additional dealers; market share data indicating pan-India distribution without state-specific exclusivity; proof of supplies in late 2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed information under Section 19(1)(a) alleging abuse of dominant position under Section 4; CCI dismissed the information under Section 26(2) finding no prima facie anti-competitive conduct or abuse; Appellant appealed under Section 53B.
legal_issues: Whether a manufacturer appointing additional distributors within a territory in terms of an express non-exclusive contract clause and disputes arising from supply curtailment constitutes an abuse of dominant position under Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Pure contractual and commercial disputes between a manufacturer and an authorized dealer cannot be dressed up as competition law violations in the absence of demonstrable dominant position and abusive or exclusionary practices in the relevant market. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause reserving the right to appoint additional non-exclusive dealers improves intra-brand competition and enhances consumer choice; it does not constitute an anti-competitive practice or denial of market access under the Competition Act, 2002. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where market share data fails to establish market dominance and the commercial contract permits non-exclusive dealer appointments and termination upon 90 days' notice, no prima facie case of abuse is established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The disputes are civil and contractual in nature; the CCI properly closed the information under Section 26(2) without ordering a Director General investigation.
operative_order: Delay condoned via IA No. 40/2020; the appeal is dismissed at the admission stage; Compensation Application No. 02/2020 is disposed of as not surviving.
summary: Appellant Venkateswara Agencies, an authorized agricultural machinery dealer, appealed against the CCI's Section 26(2) order closing an information filed against manufacturer KAMCO under Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002. Appellant alleged that KAMCO abused its dominance by appointing new dealers within Appellant's assigned territory and withholding machinery supplies. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, affirming the CCI's findings that the dealership agreement explicitly allowed the appointment of multiple non-exclusive dealers, which in fact fostered intra-brand competition. The Tribunal held that ordinary contractual disputes between a principal and dealer cannot be converted into competition law infractions without establishing statutory dominance and abusive conduct.

case_title: IIFCL Mutual Fund vs. Committee of Creditors of GVR Infra & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant IIFCL Mutual Fund was an assenting Secured Financial Creditor holding 3.94% voting share in CoC; Respondent No. 1 was Committee of Creditors of GVR Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); UVARC was Successful Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of GVR Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. involving total admitted financial claims of Rs. 2,271.08 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor resulted in resolution plan resolving Rs. 2,271.08 Crores in debt for a total payout of Rs. 352 Crores; Appellant's admitted claim was Rs. 86,09,59,759/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Revised resolution plan approved by 67.97% voting share at 16th CoC meeting; post-approval, Appellant filed MA No. 99/2020 in C.P. No. 941/IB/2018 before NCLT Chennai; NCLT approved resolution plan and dismissed MA No. 99/2020; appeal decided on 02.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting sheet showing Appellant voted in favor of UVARC's resolution plan; resolution plan provision earmarking Rs. 135 Crores as a contingent payout to four secured creditors in respect of uninvoked bank guarantees to keep Corporate Debtor a going concern. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority approved UVARC's resolution plan under Section 31 and dismissed Appellant's MA No. 99/2020 challenging the distribution mechanism; Appellant appealed under Section 61(3).
legal_issues: Whether a secured financial creditor who voted in favor of an approved resolution plan can subsequently challenge the distribution mechanism and contingency fund allocation approved by the Committee of Creditors under Section 61(3) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial creditor who assents to and votes in favor of a resolution plan is estopped from subsequently assailing the approved plan or questioning the distribution mechanism determined by the Committee of Creditors in exercise of its commercial wisdom. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial review of an approved resolution plan under Section 30(2) and Section 61(3) is strictly circumscribed and does not allow tribunals to trespass into the collective commercial and business decisions of the CoC regarding debt allocation and contingency funds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Allocation of funds toward uninvoked bank guarantees to preserve the corporate debtor as a going concern represents a valid commercial decision within the CoC's statutory domain; no violation of Section 53 or material irregularity under Section 61(3) was established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant suffered no actionable prejudice as an assenting creditor, rendering its challenge to the approved resolution plan impermissible and devoid of merit.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the threshold stage without costs.
summary: IIFCL Mutual Fund, a secured financial creditor with 3.94% voting share in the CoC of GVR Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Chennai order approving the resolution plan of UVARC and dismissing its application (MA No. 99/2020). The Appellant challenged the distribution mechanism, alleging that the allocation of a Rs. 135 Crore contingency fund for uninvoked bank guarantees among four other secured creditors was inequitable and violated Section 53 IBC. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the threshold, holding that the Appellant had assented to and voted for the resolution plan and was therefore estopped from disputing it. The distribution mechanism and contingency allocations fall squarely within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the CoC.

case_title: Hemant Sharma, Resolution Professional of Global Softech Ltd. vs. Nil
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Hemant Sharma was Resolution Professional of Global Softech Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Global Softech Ltd. involving prospective resolution applicants seeking to submit resolution plans following expression of interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory 180-day CIRP period (inclusive of lockdown) expired on 24.07.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated; initial 180-day period expired on 24.07.2020; nationwide lockdown imposed on 23.03.2020; UT of Dadra & Nagar Haveli lockdown extended to 31.08.2020; Maharashtra State lockdown extended to 30.09.2020; NCLT Ahmedabad passed order on 15.10.2020 granting partial exclusion of 68 days (23.03.2020 to 31.05.2020); NCLAT order passed on 02.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Government of Maharashtra lockdown extension notification dated 30.09.2020 (Annexure A-9); UT Administration of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu lockdown notification dated 31.08.2020 (Annexure A-8); corporate records showing registered office in Dadra & Nagar Haveli and corporate office in Maharashtra. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed application before NCLT Ahmedabad (Court 2) seeking exclusion of lockdown period from 25.03.2020 to 15.09.2020; NCLT partially allowed application by excluding only 68 days (up to 31.05.2020); RP appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the period of COVID-19 lockdown restrictions prevailing in the specific states/territories where the Corporate Debtor's registered office and corporate office are situated should be excluded from the computation of the statutory CIRP period under Section 12 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In computing statutory timelines for CIRP under Section 12 of the IBC, the entire period during which commercial activities are paralyzed by government-mandated lockdown restrictions in the jurisdictions where the corporate debtor operates must be excluded to prevent defeating the code's resolution objectives. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 timelines are designed to facilitate resolution; applying rigid cut-offs while governmental containment orders prevent prospective resolution applicants from submitting plans contradicts the statutory objective of value maximization. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Official executive notifications demonstrating continuation of severe pandemic lockdown restrictions beyond central guidelines suffice to justify exclusion for the full duration of disruption. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in restricting exclusion to 31.05.2020; the entire duration from 25.03.2020 to 15.09.2020 was liable to be excluded.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 15.10.2020 is set aside; the period from 25.03.2020 till 15.09.2020 is excluded from the 180-day CIRP period; the extended 90-day period under Section 12(3) shall commence only after the expiry of the excluded 180-day period; IA Nos. 2563/2020, 2564/2020, and 2565/2020 disposed of.
summary: Resolution Professional of Global Softech Ltd. appealed against NCLT Ahmedabad's order which granted an exclusion of only 68 days (23.03.2020 to 31.05.2020) from the CIRP timeline due to COVID-19, despite the RP requesting an exclusion up to 15.09.2020. The RP demonstrated that the company's registered office in Dadra & Nagar Haveli and corporate office in Maharashtra were subjected to state-level lockdown extensions through September 2020, stalling prospective applicants from submitting resolution plans. The NCLAT set aside the impugned order and granted full exclusion of the period from 25.03.2020 to 15.09.2020 from the initial 180-day CIRP timeframe, clarifying that any further 90-day extension would begin thereafter.

case_title: Narinder Bhushan Aggarwal vs. M/s. Little Bee International Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Narinder Bhushan Aggarwal was Liquidator (erstwhile RP); Respondent was M/s Little Bee International Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings following failure of corporate insolvency resolution of M/s Little Bee International Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation ordered under Section 33(1)(a) of IBC; dispute confined to liquidator's monthly remuneration and expense funding during liquidation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 8th CoC meeting held on 25.11.2019 approving liquidation fee structure by 69.48% voting share; NCLT Chandigarh passed liquidation and fee order on 26.02.2019 [sic, 2020]; appeal decided on 18.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution passed at the 8th CoC meeting dated 25.11.2019 approved with 69.48% vote share fixing remuneration at Rs. 50,000/- per month or as per IBBI regulation sliding scales, and approving escrow funding of liquidation expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh passed order on 26.02.2019 directing liquidator remuneration to be calculated strictly as per Regulation 4(2) and (3) rather than Regulation 39D, holding Regulation 39D was inapplicable because liquidation was ordered under Section 33(1)(a); Liquidator appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors possesses the jurisdiction to fix the remuneration and liquidation expenses of the Liquidator under Regulation 39D of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 when the liquidation order is passed under Section 33(1)(a) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the Committee of Creditors approves the remuneration and liquidation expenses of the liquidator with the requisite statutory voting majority, such commercial decision falls squarely within the ambit of Regulation 39D, and the Adjudicating Authority cannot substitute such determination with default scales under Regulation 4(2) and (3). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The specific section under which the liquidation order is passed (such as Section 33(1)(a)) does not exclude the operation of Regulation 39D; Regulation 4 scales apply solely in default of a valid CoC determination under Regulation 39D. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of CoC minutes establishing a valid resolution passed with over 66% majority approving liquidator remuneration conclusively satisfies the statutory requirements under Regulation 39D. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in denying applicability of Regulation 39D, warranting modification of the order to align with the CoC's resolution.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order is set aside to the limited extent of remuneration of the liquidator; it is directed that the liquidator's remuneration shall be governed strictly in accordance with the recommendation of the Committee of Creditors.
summary: Liquidator Narinder Bhushan Aggarwal appealed against an order of NCLT Chandigarh which held that his remuneration was governed by the default percentage slabs under Regulation 4(2) and (3) of the Liquidation Process Regulations instead of the fee structure approved by the CoC under Regulation 39D, solely because liquidation was ordered under Section 33(1)(a) of the IBC. The NCLAT set aside the impugned portion of the order, holding that where the CoC with the requisite voting majority (69.48%) determines the fee and expenses of the liquidator, such resolution falls squarely within the purview of Regulation 39D regardless of which IBC provision initiated liquidation. The CoC's determination was restored.

case_title: Gururaj S. Kulkarni & Ors. vs. Gujarat NRE Coke Ltd. (In Liquidation) Through Liquidator Mr. Sumit Binani
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants were Gururaj S. Kulkarni and other employee representatives of Gujarat NRE Coke Ltd.; Respondent was Gujarat NRE Coke Ltd. (in liquidation) represented by Liquidator Sumit Binani; Secured Creditors formed the stakeholder committee. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 sponsored by shareholders for reviving the Corporate Debtor during liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was ordered into liquidation on 11.01.2018; multiple attempts to approve a revival scheme failed with secured creditors repeatedly rejecting compromise proposals. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation order passed on 11.01.2018; initial 90-day period for proposing a Section 230 scheme expired in 2018; over two years elapsed under liquidation; NCLT Kolkata dismissed reconsideration application on 09.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Techno-Economic Viability (TEV) Study submitted by shareholders/employees; minutes of meetings of secured creditors recording explicit rejection of the compromise scheme despite the TEV Study. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Employee representatives filed application before NCLT Kolkata seeking to compel reconsideration of the rejected Section 230 compromise scheme in light of a new TEV Study; NCLT dismissed the application on 09.06.2020; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can direct creditors to reconsider a Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 after the expiry of the statutory 90-day liquidation period and after the secured creditors have explicitly rejected the scheme including an accompanying TEV Study.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be foisted upon unwilling secured creditors by judicial direction where the creditors have considered and rejected the proposal, nor can liquidation proceedings be prolonged indefinitely beyond statutory limits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While revival of a corporate debtor is favored under the IBC, the statutory window of 90 days to achieve a Section 230 compromise during liquidation cannot be enlarged indefinitely to force repeated reconsiderations absent a change in material circumstances. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mere addition of a TEV Study to a previously rejected scheme does not constitute a compelling change in circumstances when the creditors have formally considered and rejected the scheme with the study. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The application was filed over two years after the liquidation order and was rightfully dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 09.06.2020.
summary: Employee representatives of Gujarat NRE Coke Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order dismissing their application to direct secured creditors to reconsider a Section 230 Companies Act revival scheme on the strength of a new Techno-Economic Viability (TEV) Study. The Corporate Debtor had been in liquidation since January 2018, and its secured creditors had repeatedly rejected the shareholders' compromise proposals. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that more than two years had elapsed since the liquidation order—well beyond the 90-day timeframe for Section 230 schemes—and that courts cannot force a compromise scheme upon unwilling financial stakeholders who have already evaluated and rejected it.

case_title: M/s Quippo Energy Ltd. vs. M/s Soundararaja Mills Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Quippo Energy Ltd. (Appellant/Operational Creditor) and M/s Soundararaja Mills Limited (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two Lease Agreements dated 05.01.2015 (with addendum dated 20.09.2015) and 20.01.2016 for leasing gas-based power generation equipment, along with two corresponding Service Agreements dated 05.01.2015 and 20.01.2016 for manpower supply to operate the units at Karaikal, Pondicherry. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of INR 1,13,29,658/- as principal along with 18% interest per annum amounting to INR 4,35,803/-, totaling INR 1,17,65,461/-, with default accruing after the last part payment of INR 9,56,160/- on 06.10.2018 and the last invoice raised on 01.02.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice was issued in Form 3 and Form 4 on 20.04.2019; the Corporate Debtor issued its reply notice disputing the claim on 28.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor relied on email communications dated 09.06.2018 noting frequent trippings in breach of the 8,400-hour contractual guarantee, email and debit note SRMAO/B/C68/18-19 dated 28.11.2018 for INR 55,53,730/- regarding power failure/EB purchase costs, and reconciliation email dated 30.05.2018; Operational Creditor relied on debtor email dated 19.07.2018 setting a tentative repayment schedule of INR 28 Lakhs per month from July to October 2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application CP IBA/868/2019 before NCLT Division Bench, Chennai; NCLT dismissed the application on 23.12.2019 citing a pre-existing dispute under the principles of Mobilox Innovations.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the Section 9 application on the ground of a pre-existing dispute raised prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected where the Corporate Debtor demonstrates the existence of a genuine, plausible pre-existing dispute supported by contemporaneous documentary evidence predating the statutory demand notice, rather than a spurious or afterthought defence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The definition of 'dispute' under Section 5(6) read with Section 9(5)(ii)(d) encompasses breaches of contractual performance standards and deficiency of service, including unadjusted debit notes raised for failure to meet agreed operating hours and performance guarantees prior to the statutory notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the threshold laid down in Mobilox Innovations v. Kirusa Software, the Adjudicating Authority is required only to examine whether there is a plausible contention requiring further investigation that is not patently feeble or an assertion of fact unsupported by evidence, without delving into the final merits of the dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because contemporaneous emails and debit notes dated 28.11.2018 explicitly established a bona fide dispute regarding generator trippings, deficiency in service, and counter-debit reconciliation prior to the Section 8 notice dated 20.04.2019, the Section 9 petition was untenable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 231 of 2020 is dismissed as devoid of merit. No order as to costs.
summary: Quippo Energy Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Soundararaja Mills Limited for alleged unpaid lease and service charges totaling INR 1,17,65,461/-. The Corporate Debtor had raised contemporaneous objections on 28.11.2018 concerning frequent generator tripping and failure to guarantee 8,400 hours of continuous power supply, supported by a debit note for INR 55,53,730/-. Affirming the NCLT's decision under the Mobilox Innovations standard, NCLAT held that substantial documentary evidence demonstrated a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding deficiency of service prior to the Section 8 demand notice, thereby justifying the dismissal of the Section 9 application.

case_title: UCO Bank vs. Mr. G. Ramachandran, Resolution Professional of M/s Sai Regency Power Corporation Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: UCO Bank (Appellant/Financial Creditor) and Mr. G. Ramachandran, Resolution Professional of M/s Sai Regency Power Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor held two Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDRs) with UCO Bank and had secured vehicle loans; in 2011, the Corporate Debtor provided these FDRs as security for demand loans of Rs. 50,00,000/- each sanctioned by UCO Bank to group companies M/s Kamang Dam Hydro Power Pvt. Ltd. and M/s J.R. Power Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: On 09.07.2019, post-initiation of CIRP, UCO Bank unilaterally liquidated and adjusted the Corporate Debtor's FDR accounts (Nos. 19050310045848 and 19050310046265) amounting to Rs. 2,07,31,503/- plus interest, totaling an adjusted sum of Rs. 2,27,94,706/- against outstanding vehicle and group company loans. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 27.03.2019 under Section 7; public announcement was published in Business Standard on 30.03.2019; the Resolution Professional issued a demand letter for restitution of funds on 06.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Public notices in English (Business Standard) and Tamil, Resolution Professional's letter dated 06.12.2019 citing NCLAT ruling in Indian Overseas Bank v. Dinkar T. Venkatsubramaniam, and bank debit vouchers showing unilateral set-off during moratorium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed M.A. No. 39 of 2020 in IBA/92/2019 before NCLT Chennai; on 29.05.2020, NCLT directed UCO Bank to refund and restore the credit of Rs. 2,27,94,706/- to the Corporate Debtor's account to facilitate the resolution process.
legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor/bank is entitled to unilaterally appropriate or set off fixed deposit receipts of a Corporate Debtor against outstanding loan dues during the CIRP moratorium under Section 14, and whether lack of actual knowledge of CIRP initiation protects such set-off.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a moratorium under Section 14 comes into force upon commencement of CIRP, no creditor or financial institution is legally permitted to recover, appropriate, or set off any amounts from the bank accounts or deposits of the corporate debtor towards its dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 imposes an absolute prohibition on recovery or appropriation; provisions relating to mutual credit and set-off under Section 36(4)(b) or Section 173 apply solely during liquidation proceedings and have no application during the CIRP moratorium. Under Section 17(d), financial institutions must act strictly on the instructions of the Resolution Professional. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The operation of the statutory moratorium under Section 14 is automatic by operation of law upon admission of the petition; absence or lack of personal knowledge of the public announcement is legally irrelevant and cannot validate a prohibited recovery. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: UCO Bank's post-CIRP adjustment of the FDRs directly violated the statutory moratorium under Section 14, warranting the direction to immediately restore and credit the full amount to the Corporate Debtor's account.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 761 of 2020 along with I.A. No. 2038 of 2020 is dismissed. The order of NCLT Chennai directing the refund and restoration of Rs. 2,27,94,706/- to the Corporate Debtor's account is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: UCO Bank challenged the NCLT Chennai order directing it to refund Rs. 2,27,94,706/- to the account of Corporate Debtor Sai Regency Power Corporation Pvt. Ltd., which the bank had unilaterally adjusted during CIRP from the Corporate Debtor's Fixed Deposits against vehicle loans and demand loans granted to group companies. The bank contended it lacked knowledge of the CIRP admission and possessed a right to set off. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under Section 14 of the IBC, moratorium operates automatically and completely bars any creditor from appropriating or recovering funds from the debtor's account, rendering set-off provisions inapplicable during CIRP.

case_title: Arihant Unitech Realty Projects Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Arihant Unitech Realty Projects Limited (Appellant/Transferor Company) and North Town Estates Private Limited (Transferee Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Scheme of Amalgamation formulated under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 for the merger of Arihant Unitech Realty Projects Limited into North Town Estates Private Limited in the interest of stakeholders, employees, and creditors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural limitation delay: failure to file the second-motion Company Petition within the prescribed 7-day period following the filing of the Chairman's reports, culminating in an overall delay of 201 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Meetings of Equity Shareholders and Unsecured Creditors convened on 23.05.2019 and 16.05.2019 respectively; the second-motion Company Petition was filed on 24.01.2020 along with a condonation application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Reports of the Chairman demonstrating unanimous approval of the Scheme by equity shareholders and unsecured creditors; notices served on statutory authorities; averments in paragraph 4 of MA/102/2020 establishing that delay arose from preoccupation with statutory internal compliance and closure of corporate audits/accounts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Transferor Company filed MA/102/2020 in CA/216 & 217/CAA/2018 before NCLT Division Bench-I, Chennai seeking condonation of 201 days delay; NCLT dismissed the application on 13.02.2020 holding that the reasons did not constitute unavoidable causes.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal erred in rejecting an application for condonation of a 201-day delay in filing the second-motion petition under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, where the delay resulted from audit closure and lacked mala fides.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In matters concerning condonation of delay, judicial tribunals must adopt a pragmatic, lenient, and justice-oriented approach rather than a pedantic one; where the explanation offered demonstrates due diligence and is devoid of mala fides, delay ought to be condoned to prevent an aberration of justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural timelines governing company scheme petitions under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 are directory in nature, designed to facilitate corporate arrangements, and should not be applied rigidly to thwart substantive corporate restructuring approved unanimously by stakeholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The length of the delay cannot be the sole measure of negligence; rather, the test is whether the suitor demonstrated gross inaction or mala fides. Preoccupation with statutory audit and account finalization constitutes a bona fide explanation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's finding that internal audit and accounting compliance did not explain the delay was erroneous and unsustainable; the 201 days delay was condoned to secure the ends of justice.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 162 of 2020 is allowed. The impugned order dated 13.02.2020 in MA/102/2020 in CA/216 & 217/CAA/2018 is set aside, MA/102/2020 is allowed, and delay of 201 days is condoned. Appellant directed to submit certified copy of impugned order within three weeks. No costs.
summary: Arihant Unitech Realty Projects Limited appealed against an order of NCLT Chennai rejecting its application (MA/102/2020) for condonation of a 201-day delay in filing a second-motion company petition for sanctioning a Scheme of Amalgamation with North Town Estates Private Limited. The meetings of shareholders and creditors had unanimously approved the scheme, but filing was delayed due to internal audit closures and statutory compliances. Overturning NCLT's rejection, NCLAT held that tribunals must adopt a pragmatic and justice-oriented approach toward condonation of delay where no mala fides exist, condoned the 201-day delay, and allowed the appeal without costs.

case_title: IIFCL Mutual Fund vs. Committee of Creditors of GVR Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IIFCL Mutual Fund (Appellant/Financial Creditor having 3.94% voting share in CoC) and Committee of Creditors of GVR Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. along with Successful Resolution Applicant UVARC and Resolution Professional (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lending/financial debt extended to Corporate Debtor GVR Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd.; admission of Appellant's financial claim and consideration of a revised resolution plan submitted by UVARC in the CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total admitted claims of Financial Creditors stood at Rs. 2,271.08 Crores, to be settled under the plan for Rs. 352 Crores; Appellant's admitted financial claim was Rs. 86,09,59,759/-; resolution plan allocated Rs. 135 Crores exclusively as a contingency fund for uninvoked bank guarantees among four secured creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Revised resolution plan approved by 67.97% voting majority of the CoC during its 16th meeting; Appellant subsequently filed M.A. No. 99 of 2020 in C.P. No. 941/IB/2018 challenging the allocation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan voting records showing Appellant assented to and voted in favour of the resolution plan; CoC minutes and Resolution Professional's explanation confirming that the Rs. 135 Crore allocation was a contingent commercial payout to maintain the Corporate Debtor as a going concern. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed M.A. No. 99 of 2020 seeking equal revision of the resolution fund among secured financial creditors; NCLT Chennai approved the resolution plan and dismissed M.A. 99 of 2020 holding that Appellant, having voted in favour of the plan, could not challenge the distribution mechanism.
legal_issues: Whether an assenting financial creditor who voted in favour of a resolution plan can subsequently challenge the distribution mechanism and contingency fund allocation approved by the Committee of Creditors under Section 61(3) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The distribution mechanism and allocation of resolution proceeds, including contingent allocations to keep a corporate debtor a going concern, fall within the exclusive commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors and are non-justiciable under the limited scope of judicial review. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial scrutiny of an approved resolution plan under Section 30(2) by the Adjudicating Authority and Section 61(3) by the Appellate Tribunal is restricted strictly to statutory compliances and material irregularities; it does not empower tribunals to trespass upon the commercial business decisions of the CoC majority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying K. Shashidhar v. IOB and CoC of Essar Steel v. Satish Kumar Gupta, an assenting financial creditor that exercised its franchise to approve a resolution plan is legally estopped from challenging its terms, absent any violation of Section 30(2) or proof of material irregularity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The allocation of Rs. 135 Crores for contingent bank guarantees was a valid exercise of commercial wisdom, and an assenting member cannot challenge the plan or claim discrimination under Section 53.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 938 of 2020 is dismissed in limine at the threshold stage. No order as to costs.
summary: IIFCL Mutual Fund, holding a 3.94% voting share in the CoC of GVR Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT order approving UVARC's resolution plan and rejecting its application (MA No. 99 of 2020) that demanded equal redistribution of a Rs. 135 Crore contingency fund earmarked for uninvoked bank guarantees. The Appellant had voted in favor of the plan during the 16th CoC meeting. Affirming the dismissal, NCLAT held that the distribution matrix forms an integral part of the commercial wisdom of the CoC, and an assenting financial creditor is estopped from challenging the approved plan under Section 61(3) of the IBC.

case_title: K. Bapaiah vs. Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K. Bapaiah (Appellant/Promoter and Erstwhile Director of Corporate Debtor) and Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. (ARCIL, sole Financial Creditor with 100% voting share in CoC) along with Ms. Santhanam Jayashree (Liquidator of Anandram Developers Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities assigned to ARCIL, leading to default and insolvency of Corporate Debtor Anandram Developers Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claim of Rs. 90 Crores asserted by ARCIL; Appellant paid Rs. 4,08,06,591/- via DD dated 10.12.2019 and Rs. 91,93,481/- via transfer on 23.01.2020 (totaling Rs. 5 Crores) pursuant to an alleged one-time settlement (OTS). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 06.06.2018; CIRP extended on 04.12.2018 and 26 days excluded on 08.03.2019; statutory CIRP period expired without any resolution plan; Section 33 liquidation application filed on 24.04.2019; MA 463/2019 decided on 31.12.2019; liquidation order passed on 11.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ARCIL's submission confirming that the promoter defaulted on subsequent payments under the OTS, causing the settlement to fail; failure of the parties to file an application complying with Section 12A of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed M.A. No. 463 of 2019 under Section 33; Appellant filed M.A. No. 732 of 2019 and Section 60(5) application pleading settlement; NCLT Chennai rejected the intervention and passed liquidation order on 11.02.2020 appointing Ms. Santhanam Jayashree as Liquidator.
legal_issues: Whether an order of liquidation passed under Section 33 can be set aside based on an unconsummated private settlement between the promoter and the sole financial creditor without following the statutory withdrawal procedure under Section 12A.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon expiry of the statutory period prescribed under Section 12 without the approval of any resolution plan, liquidation under Section 33 is a mandatory statutory consequence that cannot be averted by an incomplete or failed private settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once a Committee of Creditors is constituted, any termination of CIRP or withdrawal of proceedings pursuant to a settlement can only occur strictly in compliance with Section 12A of the IBC, requiring an application through the Resolution Professional and 90% voting approval. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A mere assertion of an ongoing settlement or part-payment where the creditor confirms that the settlement has fallen through due to default does not stay statutory liquidation proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In the absence of a viable resolution plan within the statutory CIRP period and non-compliance with Section 12A, the Adjudicating Authority had no alternative but to order liquidation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 306 of 2020 is dismissed. The liquidation order dated 11.02.2020 passed by NCLT Chennai is affirmed.
summary: K. Bapaiah, erstwhile director of Anandram Developers Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Chennai liquidation order dated 11.02.2020, asserting that an OTS had been reached with ARCIL (the sole financial creditor) with Rs. 5 Crores paid out of a Rs. 90 Crore debt. ARCIL countered that the settlement had failed due to default on subsequent installments. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that because the statutory CIRP timeframe under Section 12 expired without any resolution plan and no formal withdrawal process was initiated under Section 12A, liquidation under Section 33 was the inevitable statutory outcome.

case_title: Hemant Sharma, Resolution Professional of Global Softech Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Hemant Sharma, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Global Softech Ltd. (Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Global Softech Ltd. where two Prospective Resolution Applicants responded to the Expression of Interest (EoI) and required time to submit plans due to pandemic disruption. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory timeline limitation: expiration of initial 180-day CIRP period on 24.07.2020 during the nationwide COVID-19 lockdown. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Professional sought exclusion of the lockdown period from 25.03.2020 to 15.09.2020 (175 days); NCLT restricted exclusion to 68 days (23.03.2020 to 31.05.2020). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Government of Maharashtra lockdown extension order extending restrictions until 30.09.2020 (Annexure A-9), and Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu UT Administration order extending lockdown restrictions up to 31.08.2020 (Annexure A-8), establishing cessation of commercial operations at the Corporate Office (Maharashtra) and Registered Office (Dadra & Nagar Haveli). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed application before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court 2 seeking 175 days exclusion; on 15.10.2020, NCLT partly allowed exclusion for only 68 days, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in restricting the exclusion of the COVID-19 lockdown period to 68 days instead of excluding the actual operational lockdown period extending up to 15.09.2020 for computing the statutory CIRP period under Section 12.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For computing the statutory periods of 180/270 days under Section 12 of the IBC, the entire period during which commercial and resolution activities remain paralyzed due to state or regional lockdown restrictions must be excluded to fulfill the Code's objective of resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory time limits under Section 12 must be harmonized with extraordinary force majeure events; artificially truncating the exclusion period when executive lockdown orders are demonstrably active defeats the paramount objective of corporate revival. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of official state/UT government gazettes demonstrating localized administrative lockdowns at the corporate and registered office locations suffices to establish impossibility of commercial operations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Professional made out sufficient grounds establishing that disruption continued through 15.09.2020, entitling the CIRP to full exclusion from 25.03.2020 to 15.09.2020.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 942 of 2020 is allowed. Impugned order dated 15.10.2020 is set aside. The period from 25.03.2020 to 15.09.2020 is excluded from the computation of 180 days of CIRP, and the 90-day extension under Section 12 shall commence only upon completion of the adjusted 180 days. I.A. Nos. 2563/2020, 2564/2020, and 2565/2020 disposed of.
summary: Hemant Sharma, Resolution Professional of Global Softech Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad which granted only 68 days of lockdown exclusion (23.03.2020 to 31.05.2020) instead of the requested period up to 15.09.2020. The RP demonstrated that official orders extended lockdown in Maharashtra (corporate office) and Dadra & Nagar Haveli (registered office) well past May 2020, disrupting resolution efforts from prospective applicants. Setting aside the NCLT order, NCLAT directed that the entire period from 25.03.2020 to 15.09.2020 be excluded from the 180-day CIRP period, clarifying that any further 90-day extension will begin only after the adjusted 180 days elapse.

case_title: Sandeep Sharma & Anr. vs. Sunil Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sandeep Sharma & Anr., suspended members of the Board of Directors of Corporate Debtor M/s Vas Data Services Pvt. Ltd. (Appellants) and Sunil Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional along with CoC (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Vas Data Services Pvt. Ltd., involving evaluation of resolution plans and meetings of the Committee of Creditors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural dispute regarding conduct of CIRP; Appellants sought to relegate CIRP back to the stage of issuing fresh Expression of Interest (EoI) and voiding meetings from the 7th CoC meeting onward. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Professional requested a confidentiality undertaking from Appellants on 24.06.2020; undertaking furnished on 01.07.2020 and plan copy supplied; CoC met on 10.07.2020 and approved the Resolution Plan on 06.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Execution of confidentiality undertaking on 01.07.2020, receipt of resolution plan copy prior to CoC voting, and demands by suspended directors for video recordings and minutes of CoC meetings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed application before NCLT New Delhi Court-III alleging procedural irregularities and withholding of information; NCLT dismissed the application on 18.09.2020 holding that the appropriate stage to raise legal objections is during approval under Section 31.
legal_issues: Whether suspended directors are entitled to annul CoC meetings and restart the CIRP de novo from the EoI stage after receiving a copy of the resolution plan prior to its CoC approval.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Suspended directors who have been provided copies of the proposed resolution plan upon furnishing confidentiality undertakings cannot scuttle the CIRP or rewind it to the EoI stage under the pretext of procedural irregularity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory scheme under Sections 30 and 31 provides that objections to a resolution plan approved by the CoC must be raised before the Adjudicating Authority when the plan is presented for approval under Section 31, rather than through interlocutory applications disrupting CIRP timelines. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An application by suspended management seeking de novo resolution proceedings will be treated as an abuse of process where evidence establishes that the plan was furnished beforehand and the prayer is designed merely to frustrate statutory timelines. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants failed to demonstrate any material irregularity; their appropriate legal remedy is to raise genuine legal objections before the Adjudicating Authority when the plan is considered under Section 31.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 989 of 2020 is dismissed in limine with liberty to Appellants to present genuine legal objections before the Adjudicating Authority at the stage of Section 31 consideration.
summary: Suspended directors of Vas Data Services Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing their application to set aside CoC proceedings from the 7th meeting onwards and restart the CIRP de novo with a fresh EoI. The directors alleged non-receipt of information and minutes. Finding that the RP provided the resolution plan on 01.07.2020 following a confidentiality undertaking prior to the CoC's approval of the plan on 06.08.2020, NCLAT dismissed the appeal in limine. It ruled that the petition was a tactic to protract the process, affirming that any valid legal objections to the plan must be presented before the NCLT during Section 31 approval proceedings.

case_title: Liberty Steels SBQ Limited vs. Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi, Liquidator of M/s SBQ Steels Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Liberty Steels SBQ Limited (Appellant), Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi (Liquidator of M/s SBQ Steels Limited, Respondent No. 1), SBQ Steels Limited (in Liquidation, Respondent No. 2), and Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing liquidation process and auction/sale of assets of Corporate Debtor SBQ Steels Limited under the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural dispute regarding urgent hearing of an interlocutory application (dated 06.11.2020) concerning the liquidation sale process. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application mentioned for urgent listing before NCLT Chennai on 09.11.2020; NCLT orally posted the hearing to 17.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interlocutory application Annexure-11 dated 06.11.2020 and urgent oral mentioning before NCLT Chennai on 09.11.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by NCLT Chennai's oral direction scheduling the urgent interlocutory application to 17.12.2020 instead of granting an immediate hearing, the Appellant appealed directly to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should adjudicate substantive contentions on appeal against a mere oral listing direction of the Adjudicating Authority, or remand the application for an expeditious hearing on the merits.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not entertain or rule upon substantive rights and contentions where the order appealed from is merely an oral administrative listing direction; the court of first instance must first decide the application on its merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 contemplates appellate review of adjudicatory determinations; where grave urgency is shown, the appropriate remedy is an expedited direction to the Adjudicating Authority to hear the pending interlocutory application rather than deciding issues prematurely on appeal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of extreme commercial urgency warrants preponement of listing by the Adjudicating Authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The substantive merits cannot be examined in the absence of a reasoned order from the lower bench; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to advance the hearing date and urgently decide the application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 977 of 2020 is disposed of with directions to NCLT Chennai Bench to advance the hearing of I.A. Annexure-11 dated 06.11.2020, and urgently hear and decide it on the merits. Parties directed to appear before NCLT on 18.11.2020.
summary: Liberty Steels SBQ Limited appealed against an oral direction issued on 09.11.2020 by NCLT Chennai scheduling an urgent interlocutory application concerning the liquidation of SBQ Steels Limited to 17.12.2020. The Appellant contended that delay would cause irreparable prejudice. Declining to decide substantive contentions before the Adjudicating Authority had done so, NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the NCLT to take up the application on an expedited basis, ordering both parties to appear before NCLT Chennai on 18.11.2020 for urgent adjudication in accordance with law.

case_title: Narinder Bhushan Aggarwal vs. M/s Little Bee International Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Narinder Bhushan Aggarwal, Liquidator of M/s Little Bee International Private Limited (Appellant) and M/s Little Bee International Private Limited & Anr. (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Fixation and payment of remuneration and liquidation expenses of the Liquidator during the liquidation process of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disputed fee determination: CoC approved liquidator's fee of Rs. 50,000/- per month (or proportion to liquidation estate assets); NCLT overrode this approval, restricting remuneration strictly under default slabs of Regulation 4(2) & (3). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In its 8th meeting held on 25.11.2019, the CoC passed a resolution with a 69.48% voting majority approving estimated expenses into an escrow account and liquidator remuneration; liquidation order passed on 26.02.2019 under Section 33(1)(a). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution passed in the 8th CoC meeting dated 25.11.2019 by 69.48% voting share approving the fee and contribution of liquidation expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh passed a liquidation order directing that the Liquidator's fee be governed strictly under Regulation 4(2) and (3) instead of Regulation 39D, holding that Regulation 39D did not apply to liquidation orders under Section 33(1)(a).
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the power to override the Committee of Creditors' resolution fixing the Liquidator's remuneration under Regulation 39D and enforce the statutory default scale under Regulation 4(2) and (3) on the premise that liquidation was ordered under Section 33(1)(a).
ratio_decidendi: 1.
