ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The determination of the Liquidator's remuneration falls squarely within the statutory commercial prerogative of the Committee of Creditors; where the CoC has fixed such fee by requisite voting majority under Regulation 39D, default statutory fee slabs cannot be substituted by the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39D of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 empowers the CoC to fix the liquidator's fees; this power applies universally irrespective of which specific sub-clause of Section 33(1) triggers the liquidation order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Recourse to the default statutory fee under Regulation 4(2) and (3) of the Liquidation Process Regulations is permissible only if the CoC failed to fix the remuneration under Regulation 39D prior to liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC having duly sanctioned the remuneration with a 69.48% voting majority, the NCLT's direction overriding the fee was unsustainable and contrary to law.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 980 of 2020 is allowed. The impugned order dated 26.02.2019 is set aside to the limited extent of the liquidator's remuneration, and it is directed that the remuneration shall be governed strictly in accordance with the recommendation and approval of the Committee of Creditors.
summary: Liquidator Narinder Bhushan Aggarwal appealed against an order of NCLT Chandigarh which directed that his remuneration be governed by Regulation 4(2) & (3) of the Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016, rather than the fee structure approved by the CoC under Regulation 39D. The CoC had approved a monthly fee of Rs. 50,000/- with a 69.48% voting share. Setting aside the NCLT's direction, NCLAT held that the fee of the liquidator falls within the exclusive domain of the CoC under Regulation 39D regardless of which IBC provision triggered the liquidation order, and default slabs under Regulation 4 only apply when the CoC fails to make such a determination.

case_title: Sudhir Narayanrao Modak & Ors. vs. SMS Paryavaran Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are prospective resolution applicants (Sudhir Narayanrao Modak & Ors.), Respondent No. 1 is the Corporate Debtor (SMS Paryavaran Ltd.), and the Committee of Creditors (CoC) is represented as Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of the Corporate Debtor SMS Paryavaran Ltd. requiring submission of a resolution plan alongside the required Earnest Money Deposit (EMD). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details underlying the original insolvency admission not specified; issue relates to procedural failure to submit resolution plan and EMD within prescribed and extended deadlines. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellants failed to submit the Resolution Plan and EMD within the original timeline and additionally failed to submit within the extended time period granted. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record established that despite being provided opportunities within prescribed and extended timelines, the Appellants omitted both the submission of the Resolution Plan and the deposit of the EMD. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) dismissed the application filed by the Appellants seeking consideration of their resolution plan due to non-compliance with submission and EMD timelines, against which the Appellants appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the application of prospective resolution applicants who failed to submit a Resolution Plan and the requisite Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) within both the prescribed timelines and the extended period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Prospective resolution applicants who fail to adhere to mandatory CIRP timelines and fail to deposit the required Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) even within extended deadlines are not entitled to seek consideration of their resolution plans. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Timelines prescribed for the submission of resolution plans under the CIRP regulations and directions of the CoC/RP are critical; failure to submit both the plan and the mandatory financial commitments (EMD) vitiates any right to participate in the process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict verification of compliance with deadlines and financial deposit prerequisites for plan submission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that no fault could be found with the order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing the application given the Appellants' failure to tender both the plan and the EMD within the extended window.
operative_order: The appeal being devoid of merit is accordingly dismissed.
summary: The Appellants (Sudhir Narayanrao Modak & Ors.) appealed against an order of the Adjudicating Authority which dismissed their application regarding participation in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of SMS Paryavaran Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). The Appellants, despite being granted opportunities, failed to submit their Resolution Plan and the accompanying Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) within both the original prescribed timelines and the extended period. The NCLAT held that because the Appellants had defaulted on these essential procedural and financial prerequisites within the permitted extensions, no error was committed by the lower authority in dismissing their application. Consequently, the appellate tribunal dismissed the appeal as devoid of merit.

case_title: Volkswagen Finance Private Limited vs. Shree Balaji Printopack Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Volkswagen Finance Private Limited is the Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 1 Shree Balaji Printopack Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (under liquidation, represented by Liquidator Nilotpal Shyam); Respondent No. 2 Usaka Electrotech Pvt. Ltd. is an Operational Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor executed a Loan and Hypothecation Agreement on 25.11.2013 for a loan facility of Rs. 36,00,000/- payable in 84 monthly installments of Rs. 61,964/- each (from 15.12.2013 to 15.11.2020) to purchase an AUDI Q3 TDI 2.0 vehicle, with hypothecation endorsed in RTO registration records under Section 51 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant demanded Rs. 21,83,819.18/- following failure to pay scheduled monthly installments. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A demand letter was issued by the Appellant; subsequently, CIRP was initiated, and the Adjudicating Authority ordered liquidation on 03.04.2019. Appellant filed its claim before the Liquidator on 22.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced the unattested loan agreement, hypothecation deed, demand letter, RTO registration certificate reflecting hypothecation, CIBIL records, and vehicle invoices; however, no certificate of charge registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, Information Utility record, or CERSAI registration was produced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On 26.07.2019, the Liquidator rejected Appellant's claim as a secured creditor and treated it as an unsecured financial creditor. Appellant filed an application before NCLT New Delhi (Bench-III) in CP (IB) No. 391/ND/2018, which was dismissed on 08.11.2019 on the ground that failure to register the charge under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 disentitled the Appellant to secured status under Regulation 21 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations.
legal_issues: Whether a creditor holding a hypothecation over a motor vehicle registered solely with the Regional Transport Office under Section 51 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, but not registered under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, can be recognized as a 'secured creditor' entitled to realize security interest under Section 52(1)(b) of the IBC during liquidation proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor claiming security interest over corporate assets cannot be recognized as a secured creditor in liquidation proceedings unless the security interest is duly proved under Section 52(3) of the IBC read with Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, and registered under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 77(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 explicitly bars a liquidator or any other creditor from taking into account an unregistered charge created by a company; registration of an agreement under Section 51 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 operates merely as an administrative entry in transport records and does not substitute or override mandatory charge registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To realize or claim security interest under Section 52 of the IBC, the creditor must conclusively establish existence of the security through the exclusive statutory modes in Regulation 21 of the Liquidation Regulations: Information Utility records, ROC charge registration certificate, or CERSAI registration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the charge was never registered with the ROC, CERSAI, or an Information Utility, the creditor cannot be treated as a secured financial creditor and must rank as an unsecured financial creditor in the waterfall distribution under Section 53 of the IBC.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 02 of 2020 is dismissed. The order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting the secured status of the Appellant and placing it in the queue of unsecured financial creditors under Section 53 of the IBC is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: Volkswagen Finance Pvt. Ltd. financed the purchase of an Audi vehicle for Shree Balaji Printopack Pvt. Ltd. under a loan and hypothecation agreement. During the liquidation of the corporate debtor, the Liquidator rejected the lender's claim as a secured creditor because the charge was not registered with the ROC under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, despite being endorsed on the vehicle's RTO registration under Section 51 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. NCLAT upheld the NCLT and Liquidator's decision, ruling that compliance with Section 52(3) of the IBC and Regulation 21 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations is mandatory, and an RTO entry cannot substitute statutory ROC charge registration.

case_title: Madhusudan Tantia vs. Amit Choraria & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Madhusudan Tantia is the suspended Director/majority shareholder of Corporate Debtor Om Boseco Rail Products Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Amit Choraria (IRP); Respondent No. 2 is Foseco India Limited (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 2 supplied chemicals and allied foundry/steel industry products (resins, coatings, sleeves, fluxes) against unpaid invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 90,00,919.10 (Principal Rs. 78,52,663.00 + interest Rs. 11,48,256.10); dates of default occurred on 11.04.2018, 28.04.2018, and 17.06.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 31.07.2019 and served on 01.08.2019; no reply sent within 10 days; Section 9 petition filed on 05.09.2019; MCA threshold notification issued on 24.03.2020; impugned admission order pronounced on 20.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Respondent No. 2 placed invoices, bank statements under Section 9(3)(c), Section 9(3)(b) affidavit, and an admission letter dated 17.03.2020 from the Corporate Debtor proposing payment of Rs. 60,71,832 in 15 installments; no prior dispute was raised. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Application C.P. (IB) No. 1735/KB/2019 was filed before NCLT Kolkata Bench; Corporate Debtor suffered ex-parte orders, failed to file reply affidavit after recall on terms, and on 20.05.2020 NCLT admitted the petition, holding the MCA notification dated 24.03.2020 increasing threshold to Rs. 1 crore prospective.
legal_issues: Whether the MCA notification dated 24.03.2020 issued under the proviso to Section 4 of the IBC, raising the minimum default threshold for initiating CIRP from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 1 crore, applies retrospectively to applications filed and pending admission prior to the date of the notification.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A delegated statutory notification raising pecuniary jurisdiction thresholds for initiating insolvency proceedings operates purely prospectively unless explicitly or by necessary implication stated to be retroactive, and does not divest tribunals of jurisdiction over applications validly initiated prior to its issuance. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 4 of the IBC does not contain language denoting retrospective effect; applying the notification to applications filed prior to 24.03.2020 would defeat vested accrued statutory rights under Section 9(1) and yield absurd results. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Operational creditor must establish default exceeding the threshold in force at the time of filing, proof of service of demand notice without reply demonstrating a pre-existing dispute, and procedural compliance under Section 9(3). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The notification dated 24.03.2020 is prospective only and does not affect applications pending admission filed before 24.03.2020; the admission of CIRP against the corporate debtor was lawful.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 557 of 2020 is dismissed without costs. All pending interlocutory applications are closed, and Appellant is directed to submit certified copy of impugned order within one week.
summary: Foseco India Limited initiated Section 9 CIRP against Om Boseco Rail Products Ltd. for default of Rs. 90,00,919.10 on 05.09.2019. The suspended director challenged the admission order dated 20.05.2020 on the ground that the MCA notification dated 24.03.2020 raised the default threshold to Rs. 1 crore under Section 4, rendering the pending petition non-maintainable. NCLAT held that the MCA notification is prospective in nature and cannot extinguish accrued rights in applications filed before 24.03.2020, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Ascot Realty Private Limited vs. Ajay Kumar Agarwal, IRP of RDH Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ascot Realty Pvt. Ltd. is a Financial Creditor (admitted on basis of arbitral award); Respondent No. 1 is Ajay Kumar Agarwal (IRP/RP); Respondent No. 2 is Punjab National Bank (formerly Oriental Bank of Commerce / OBC); Respondent No. 3 is Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd.; Respondent No. 14 is RDH Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed direct term loan from OBC and executed bipartite Agreements of Guarantee on 02.09.2014 guaranteeing debts of seven third-party borrower companies; Corporate Debtor was also co-borrower/mortgagor for loan sanctioned by Indiabulls on 31.03.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: OBC claimed total financial debt of Rs. 40.08 Crores (Rs. 7.54 Crores direct borrowing + Rs. 32.54/33 Crores under invoked corporate guarantees); corporate guarantee invoked on 26.09.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantees executed on 02.09.2014; guarantee invocation notice issued on 26.09.2018; Section 7 CIRP application admitted on 28.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement of Guarantee dated 02.09.2014, invocation notice dated 26.09.2018, Indiabulls term loan agreement dated 31.03.2016 showing Corporate Debtor as co-borrower and mortgagor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant challenged OBC's voting share in COC via IA in CP(IB) No. 1671/KB/2019 before NCLT Kolkata, arguing third-party corporate guarantees cannot constitute financial debt under 'Anuj Jain'; NCLT dismissed IA on 09.06.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate guarantee executed to secure credit facilities of third-party borrowers, when invoked prior to CIRP, constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(h) and (i) of the IBC, and whether the Supreme Court's ruling in Anuj Jain excludes such invoked guarantees from financial debt status in the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An invoked corporate guarantee securing a commercial borrowing constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC, as the underlying transaction entails disbursal of debt against time value of money, distinguishing an enforceable personal guarantee from a mere third-party property mortgage. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(i) explicitly covers liability in respect of guarantees for items in sub-clauses (a)-(h); the requirement of disbursal for time value of money is satisfied by disbursal to the principal borrower under Section 127 of the Contract Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between mortgage-only transactions (where no personal monetary obligation or indemnity exists, as in Anuj Jain) versus guarantee agreements binding the guarantor to repay the debt upon invocation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: OBC and Indiabulls were properly admitted as Financial Creditors for their full claim amounts, and the CoC voting shares were lawfully determined.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 658 of 2020 is dismissed. The NCLT Kolkata order dated 09.06.2020 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Ascot Realty Pvt. Ltd., a financial creditor, challenged the admission of Oriental Bank of Commerce's (PNB) claim of Rs. 32.54 Crores arising out of corporate guarantees for third-party loans, relying on the Supreme Court's Anuj Jain judgment. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Anuj Jain was confined to third-party mortgages without personal obligation. Where a corporate guarantee is executed and invoked for debts disbursed against consideration for the time value of money, the liability falls squarely under Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC, making the lender a financial creditor with full CoC voting rights.

case_title: Rajendra Bhai Panchal vs. Jay Manak Steels & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rajendra Bhai Panchal is ex-Director/shareholder of Corporate Debtor Yogi Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is M/s Jay Manak Steels (Operational Creditor/sole proprietorship); Respondent No. 2 is Shalabh Kumar Daga (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of MS Angle steel goods for executing a works contract with Indian Oil Corporation for Gujarat Refinery. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 9,42,841/- out of total supplies of Rs. 27,17,818/- (Corporate Debtor had paid Rs. 17,74,977/-); default date 22.09.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Statutory Demand Notice in Form 3 issued on 06.04.2018 claiming default of Rs. 9,42,841/-; no reply delivered within 10 days; Section 9 petition filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Six tax invoices showing TDS deductions, running account ledger, WhatsApp messages where Corporate Debtor evasively replied 'I will call you later' without raising quality disputes; internal communications with IOCL were uncommunicated to the supplier. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in C.P. (IB) 227/9/NCLT/AHM/2018 admitted the Section 9 petition on 03.06.2020, rejecting the defense of defective goods as moonshine.
legal_issues: Whether a minor clerical discrepancy between the gross debt and defaulted net debt in the Form 3 Demand Notice invalidates Section 9 proceedings, and whether uncommunicated disputes between a Corporate Debtor and third-party client constitute a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An inadvertent error or misstatement of total gross debt in a statutory demand notice does not invalidate insolvency proceedings so long as the defaulted debt indisputably exceeds the statutory threshold and causes no prejudice; a pre-existing dispute must be contemporaneous and communicated to the operational creditor prior to the demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 8 and 9, the existence of an undisputed debt in excess of the threshold requires admission; vague or evasive replies and moonshine defenses cannot defeat CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox standard requires an active, real dispute supported by evidence communicated to the creditor prior to demand; internal third-party correspondence not involving the creditor is inadmissible under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC to show a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Operational creditor established debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 lakh with no pre-existing dispute communicated within 10 days of notice; admission of Section 9 was justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 592 of 2020 is dismissed without costs. Interim stay application is closed, and Appellant is directed to file certified copy within ten days.
summary: Jay Manak Steels supplied MS Angles to Yogi Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd., leaving an unpaid balance of Rs. 9,42,841/-. Following an unreplied Demand Notice, NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the operational creditor's Section 9 petition. The ex-director appealed, alleging discrepancies in the demand notice and quality defects citing third-party communications with IOCL. NCLAT held that clerical errors in demand notices that cause no prejudice do not invalidate proceedings, and third-party correspondence does not prove a pre-existing dispute with the creditor. The admission was upheld.

case_title: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. vs. Yes Bank Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. (GUVNL) is the power purchaser; Respondent No. 1 Yes Bank Limited is the secured Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 Savan Godiawala is the Liquidator of Lanco Infratech Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: 25-year Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) dated 29.04.2010/24.09.2010 for supply of 15 MW solar power from a plant in Bhadrada, Gujarat; loan facility of Rs. 63.50 Crores advanced by Yes Bank on 04.08.2010 secured by exclusive charge/mortgage over the solar plant and receivables. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt obligations to other lenders led to CIRP; default notice issued under Clause 9.3 citing liquidation as default under Clause 9.2.1(e) of PPA. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 07.08.2017; liquidation ordered 27.08.2018; GUVNL default notice issued 23.07.2019; termination notice issued 30.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term Loan Agreement dated 04.08.2010, PPA, termination notice dated 30.08.2019, evidence that power plant maintained continuous, unhindered solar power supply to GUVNL without physical or technical supply default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Yes Bank filed IA No. 809/2019 in CP(IB) No. 111/07/HBD/2017 before NCLT Hyderabad to restrain PPA termination; NCLT set aside termination notice on 06.05.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a power purchaser can terminate a long-term Power Purchase Agreement solely due to the corporate debtor entering liquidation under the IBC, and whether the PPA and physical solar power plant constitute an integrated economic asset protected under the IBC to maximize asset value.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A counterparty cannot invoke ipso facto insolvency termination clauses to terminate an essential operating contract when the corporate debtor continues to perform its substantive obligations, as the contract and underlying assets form an integrated economic asset essential for value maximization in liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits alienation of legal rights or beneficial interests; the IBC overrides contrary contractual terms under Section 238 to prevent destruction of going-concern value. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the power producer has not suspended supply and is able and willing to perform, termination based solely on insolvency default clauses violates the statutory objective of asset maximization and going-concern liquidation under Section 230 of Companies Act/Section 35 IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: PPA and the solar plant constitute an indivisible economic entity; termination was illegal and rightly set aside.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 601 of 2020 is dismissed without costs, upholding NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 06.05.2020 setting aside GUVNL's termination notice.
summary: Lanco Infratech entered liquidation, and its secured creditor Yes Bank sought to realize assets under Section 52. GUVNL issued notices terminating the 25-year solar PPA solely based on the liquidation default clause, despite uninterrupted electricity supply. NCLT Hyderabad set aside the termination, and NCLAT affirmed the ruling. NCLAT held that the solar plant and PPA form an integrated economic asset whose continuation is vital to preserve going-concern status and achieve asset value maximization under the IBC, barring termination where substantive performance is maintained.

case_title: Ashish O. Lalpuria vs. Kumaka Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ashish O. Lalpuria is an individual public equity shareholder; Respondent No. 1 is Kumaka Industries Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Union of India through Regional Director (Western Region, MCA); Respondent No. 3 is BSE Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Scheme of Arrangement under Sections 391-394 (1956 Act) / Sections 230-232 (2013 Act) proposed by Kumaka Industries to ratify prior share capital reduction, cancel deferred public issue shares, and issue bonus shares to meet minimum public shareholding requirements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In 1995 public issue, company illegally retained application money for 10,375 sub-lot shares and in 1997 unilaterally converted 24,13,000 partly paid shares into 6,03,250 fully paid shares without Section 100 confirmation; BSE suspended trading in 2002; SEBI issued severe restraint orders in 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court convened shareholder meetings on 08.02.2016; scheme petition filed 08.03.2016 and transferred to NCLT Mumbai as CP(CAA)190/MB.I/2017; NCLT approved scheme on 06.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BSE rejection letter dated 06.05.1999, SEBI penalty order dated 04.06.2013, Regional Director representation objecting to retroactive ratification of illegal capital reductions and non-compliances. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai sanctioned the scheme on 06.07.2020, treating RD objections as procedural lapses. Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a Scheme of Arrangement under Section 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 can be utilized to post-facto ratify past illegalities, statutory non-compliances, and unauthorized capital reductions to evade regulatory sanctions, and whether the 10% shareholding threshold under Section 230(4) bars scrutiny of public policy violations raised by the Regional Director.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230-232 cannot be used as an umbrella mechanism to ratify past illegal acts, regulatory defaults, or unauthorized capital reductions; companies must have a clean regulatory record without pending enforcement actions before scheme approval. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230(4) shareholding thresholds apply to private objections but do not circumscribe the court's duty under Section 230(5) to uphold public policy and give effect to objections raised by public authorities like the Regional Director. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Schemes cannot violate substantive law or public policy; mandatory statutory compliance forms an integral component of public policy and cannot be bypassed as mere procedural irregularity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The scheme was an illegitimate device to escape SEBI/BSE penalties and ratify illegal acts; NCLT's sanction was invalid and set aside.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 136 of 2020 is allowed; impugned order of NCLT Mumbai dated 06.07.2020 is set aside; Respondent No. 1 is directed to undo all actions taken pursuant to the sanctioned scheme, under supervision of the Regional Director. No costs.
summary: Kumaka Industries Ltd. obtained NCLT Mumbai approval for a Scheme of Arrangement to ratify unauthorized capital reductions dating back to 1997 and avoid SEBI regulatory actions following suspension of trading on BSE. A minority shareholder appealed under Section 421. NCLAT held that Section 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be utilized to sanitize past corporate illegalities or override regulatory enforcement under the guise of an arrangement. The Regional Director's objections on legality and public policy are paramount, irrespective of shareholder voting thresholds. The appeal was allowed and the scheme set aside.

case_title: Sh. B. Prashanth Hegde vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sh. B. Prashanth Hegde is suspended Managing Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Metal Closures Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (lead lender for Consortium); Respondent No. 2 is Abhishek Nagori (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities, working capital cash credit, and letter of credit limits granted by SBI, PNB, Corporation Bank, and UCO Bank under a Consortium arrangement since 2007. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed outstanding default in Form 1 was Rs. 282,02,71,568.08; SBI declared account NPA on 31.01.2010 (restructured then declared NPA on 28.05.2014, and subsequently reverted to 31.01.2010); PNB NPA on 30.06.2014; Corporation Bank and UCO Bank NPA on 31.12.2014. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SBI issued SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice on 12.08.2014 for Rs. 71,27,47,889/- (withdrawn on 07.07.2015); Section 7 petition filed on 23.07.2018; NCLT admitted CIRP on 14.12.2018; matter remanded by Supreme Court on 26.09.2019 in CA No. 8010/2019 to decide limitation under Article 137. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 1 omitted date of default; bank records showed NPA classification dates in 2010 and 2014; SARFAESI notices and possession notices were on record. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru admitted Section 7 application on 14.12.2018; Supreme Court remanded to NCLAT to apply Article 137 of Limitation Act per BK Educational Services and Sagar Sharma.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed more than three years after the date of default / NPA classification is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications under Section 7 and 9 of the IBC are governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, establishing a three-year period running from the date of default; proceedings cannot be used to revive time-barred claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The right to sue accrues on the date default occurs; independent recovery proceedings under SARFAESI or RDDB do not extend limitation for insolvency unless valid Section 18 acknowledgments are shown. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Date of default coincides with NPA declaration date; where default occurred prior to or on 31.12.2014 and petition was filed on 23.07.2018 without condonation under Section 5, claim is time-barred on the face of the record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was barred by limitation under Article 137, warranting dismissal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 68 of 2019 is allowed. NCLT Bengaluru admission order dated 14.12.2018 is set aside, Section 7 application is dismissed, Corporate Debtor is released from moratorium and restored to its Board of Directors.
summary: SBI filed a Section 7 application against Metal Closures Pvt. Ltd. for over Rs. 282 Crores, which NCLT Bengaluru admitted. Following a remand from the Supreme Court to determine limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, NCLAT held that the default accrued when the account became an NPA in 2010/2014. Since the petition was filed on 23.07.2018—well beyond three years from default—the application was time-barred. The admission order was set aside and the corporate debtor was restored to its board.

case_title: Alok Kaushik vs. Mrs. Bhuvaneshwari Ramanathan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Alok Kaushik is a Registered Valuer appointed during CIRP of Kavveri Telecom Infrastructure Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Mrs. Bhuvaneshwari Ramanathan (Resolution Professional); Dena Bank is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP valuation services rendered pursuant to appointment by the Resolution Professional. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Additional/further professional valuation fees claimed by the Registered Valuer over and above Rs. 50,000/- already disbursed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 18.12.2019, NCLAT disposed of Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 207 of 2017 setting aside CIRP admission and directing NCLT to determine CIRP costs/fees payable by Dena Bank. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports, billing statements, and record of prior payment of Rs. 50,000/- made to each of the valuers including the Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed Appellant's application for additional valuer fees citing lack of jurisdiction and absence of merit; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an application for determination and payment of professional fees by a CIRP registered valuer is maintainable before the Adjudicating Authority after CIRP has been set aside, and whether the claim for additional fees lacked merit.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Although the Adjudicating Authority retains jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to adjudicate CIRP costs and fees upon CIRP termination, a claim for additional valuation fees will be dismissed if the professional was already adequately remunerated as per the record. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) encompasses incidental fee adjudication, but appellate intervention is unwarranted where the underlying claim is unmerited. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Payment of Rs. 50,000/- was established on record, and no contractual or evidentiary basis was shown to justify higher fees. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT's jurisdictional reasoning was unsupportable, but its conclusion dismissing the claim on merits was correct.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 857 of 2020 is dismissed without interfering with the NCLT order.
summary: Alok Kaushik, a registered valuer in the CIRP of Kavveri Telecom Infrastructure Ltd., filed an application for additional valuation fees after the CIRP was set aside by NCLAT. NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the application as non-maintainable and lacking merit. NCLAT observed that while the Adjudicating Authority erred in finding it lacked jurisdiction, the valuer had already received Rs. 50,000/- and the claim for additional fees lacked merit, affirming the dismissal.

case_title: Ramesh Kumar Suneja vs. Pawan Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ramesh Kumar Suneja (Corporate Debtor stakeholder); Respondent No. 1 Pawan Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor under liquidation); Sole Financial Creditor constituting 100% voting share of CoC. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unspecified financial debt underlying CIRP where sole financial creditor comprised 100% of CoC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial default resulting in initiation of CIRP and subsequent 100% voting resolution to liquidate. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC meeting resolved to liquidate Corporate Debtor; NCLT New Delhi (Court II) passed liquidation order under Section 33. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of CoC meeting reflecting 100% unanimous vote by sole creditor to liquidate; no procedural irregularity demonstrated. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court II) ordered liquidation under Section 33; Appellant challenged the order before NCLAT alleging bad faith by the sole creditor.
legal_issues: Whether the decision of a Committee of Creditors with 100% voting share to send the Corporate Debtor into liquidation can be challenged on grounds of vindictiveness or lack of bona fides, and whether such commercial wisdom is non-justiciable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in deciding to liquidate the Corporate Debtor is non-justiciable and cannot be interfered with by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal in the absence of material procedural irregularity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 vests supreme commercial autonomy in the CoC; courts cannot review the business merits of a 100% vote for liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of proven procedural violations during the CIRP, allegations of vindictiveness or malafide are legally insufficient. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Liquidation order was valid, but Corporate Debtor retains the right to present a Section 230 Companies Act compromise/settlement scheme during liquidation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 915 of 2020 is dismissed with liberty to the Corporate Debtor to float a scheme of settlement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013.
summary: Ramesh Kumar Suneja appealed against the liquidation order of Pawan Buildwell Pvt. Ltd., alleging that the sole creditor's 100% vote to liquidate was vindictive. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, affirming that the CoC's commercial wisdom is non-justiciable and immune from judicial review absent procedural irregularities, while noting that the debtor remains free to submit a compromise scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 at the liquidation stage.

case_title: Volkswagen Finance Private Limited vs. Shree Balaji Printopack Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Volkswagen Finance Private Limited is the Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 1 Shree Balaji Printopack Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (under liquidation, represented by Liquidator Nilotpal Shyam); Respondent No. 2 Usaka Electrotech Pvt. Ltd. is an Operational Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor executed a Loan and Hypothecation Agreement on 25.11.2013 for a loan facility of Rs. 36,00,000/- payable in 84 monthly installments of Rs. 61,964/- each (from 15.12.2013 to 15.11.2020) to purchase an AUDI Q3 TDI 2.0 vehicle, with hypothecation endorsed in RTO registration records under Section 51 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant demanded Rs. 21,83,819.18/- following failure to pay scheduled monthly installments. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A demand letter was issued by the Appellant; subsequently, CIRP was initiated, and the Adjudicating Authority ordered liquidation on 03.04.2019. Appellant filed its claim before the Liquidator on 22.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant produced the unattested loan agreement, hypothecation deed, demand letter, RTO registration certificate reflecting hypothecation, CIBIL records, and vehicle invoices; however, no certificate of charge registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, Information Utility record, or CERSAI registration was produced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On 26.07.2019, the Liquidator rejected Appellant's claim as a secured creditor and treated it as an unsecured financial creditor. Appellant filed an application before NCLT New Delhi (Bench-III) in CP (IB) No. 391/ND/2018, which was dismissed on 08.11.2019 on the ground that failure to register the charge under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 disentitled the Appellant to secured status under Regulation 21 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations.
legal_issues: Whether a creditor holding a hypothecation over a motor vehicle registered solely with the Regional Transport Office under Section 51 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, but not registered under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, can be recognized as a 'secured creditor' entitled to realize security interest under Section 52(1)(b) of the IBC during liquidation proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor claiming security interest over corporate assets cannot be recognized as a secured creditor in liquidation proceedings unless the security interest is duly proved under Section 52(3) of the IBC read with Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, and registered under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 77(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 explicitly bars a liquidator or any other creditor from taking into account an unregistered charge created by a company; registration of an agreement under Section 51 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 operates merely as an administrative entry in transport records and does not substitute or override mandatory charge registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To realize or claim security interest under Section 52 of the IBC, the creditor must conclusively establish existence of the security through the exclusive statutory modes in Regulation 21 of the Liquidation Regulations: Information Utility records, ROC charge registration certificate, or CERSAI registration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the charge was never registered with the ROC, CERSAI, or an Information Utility, the creditor cannot be treated as a secured financial creditor and must rank as an unsecured financial creditor in the waterfall distribution under Section 53 of the IBC.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 02 of 2020 is dismissed. The order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting the secured status of the Appellant and placing it in the queue of unsecured financial creditors under Section 53 of the IBC is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: Volkswagen Finance Pvt. Ltd. financed the purchase of an Audi vehicle for Shree Balaji Printopack Pvt. Ltd. under a loan and hypothecation agreement. During the liquidation of the corporate debtor, the Liquidator rejected the lender's claim as a secured creditor because the charge was not registered with the ROC under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, despite being endorsed on the vehicle's RTO registration under Section 51 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. NCLAT upheld the NCLT and Liquidator's decision, ruling that compliance with Section 52(3) of the IBC and Regulation 21 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations is mandatory, and an RTO entry cannot substitute statutory ROC charge registration.

case_title: Madhusudan Tantia vs. Amit Choraria & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Madhusudan Tantia is the suspended Director/majority shareholder of Corporate Debtor Om Boseco Rail Products Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Amit Choraria (IRP); Respondent No. 2 is Foseco India Limited (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 2 supplied chemicals and allied foundry/steel industry products (resins, coatings, sleeves, fluxes) against unpaid invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 90,00,919.10 (Principal Rs. 78,52,663.00 + interest Rs. 11,48,256.10); dates of default occurred on 11.04.2018, 28.04.2018, and 17.06.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 31.07.2019 and served on 01.08.2019; no reply sent within 10 days; Section 9 petition filed on 05.09.2019; MCA threshold notification issued on 24.03.2020; impugned admission order pronounced on 20.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Respondent No. 2 placed invoices, bank statements under Section 9(3)(c), Section 9(3)(b) affidavit, and an admission letter dated 17.03.2020 from the Corporate Debtor proposing payment of Rs. 60,71,832 in 15 installments; no prior dispute was raised. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Application C.P. (IB) No. 1735/KB/2019 was filed before NCLT Kolkata Bench; Corporate Debtor suffered ex-parte orders, failed to file reply affidavit after recall on terms, and on 20.05.2020 NCLT admitted the petition, holding the MCA notification dated 24.03.2020 increasing threshold to Rs. 1 crore prospective.
legal_issues: Whether the MCA notification dated 24.03.2020 issued under the proviso to Section 4 of the IBC, raising the minimum default threshold for initiating CIRP from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 1 crore, applies retrospectively to applications filed and pending admission prior to the date of the notification.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A delegated statutory notification raising pecuniary jurisdiction thresholds for initiating insolvency proceedings operates purely prospectively unless explicitly or by necessary implication stated to be retroactive, and does not divest tribunals of jurisdiction over applications validly initiated prior to its issuance. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 4 of the IBC does not contain language denoting retrospective effect; applying the notification to applications filed prior to 24.03.2020 would defeat vested accrued statutory rights under Section 9(1) and yield absurd results. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Operational creditor must establish default exceeding the threshold in force at the time of filing, proof of service of demand notice without reply demonstrating a pre-existing dispute, and procedural compliance under Section 9(3). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The notification dated 24.03.2020 is prospective only and does not affect applications pending admission filed before 24.03.2020; the admission of CIRP against the corporate debtor was lawful.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 557 of 2020 is dismissed without costs. All pending interlocutory applications are closed, and Appellant is directed to submit certified copy of impugned order within one week.
summary: Foseco India Limited initiated Section 9 CIRP against Om Boseco Rail Products Ltd. for default of Rs. 90,00,919.10 on 05.09.2019. The suspended director challenged the admission order dated 20.05.2020 on the ground that the MCA notification dated 24.03.2020 raised the default threshold to Rs. 1 crore under Section 4, rendering the pending petition non-maintainable. NCLAT held that the MCA notification is prospective in nature and cannot extinguish accrued rights in applications filed before 24.03.2020, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Ascot Realty Private Limited vs. Ajay Kumar Agarwal, IRP of RDH Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ascot Realty Pvt. Ltd. is a Financial Creditor (admitted on basis of arbitral award); Respondent No. 1 is Ajay Kumar Agarwal (IRP/RP); Respondent No. 2 is Punjab National Bank (formerly Oriental Bank of Commerce / OBC); Respondent No. 3 is Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd.; Respondent No. 14 is RDH Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed direct term loan from OBC and executed bipartite Agreements of Guarantee on 02.09.2014 guaranteeing debts of seven third-party borrower companies; Corporate Debtor was also co-borrower/mortgagor for loan sanctioned by Indiabulls on 31.03.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: OBC claimed total financial debt of Rs. 40.08 Crores (Rs. 7.54 Crores direct borrowing + Rs. 32.54/33 Crores under invoked corporate guarantees); corporate guarantee invoked on 26.09.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantees executed on 02.09.2014; guarantee invocation notice issued on 26.09.2018; Section 7 CIRP application admitted on 28.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement of Guarantee dated 02.09.2014, invocation notice dated 26.09.2018, Indiabulls term loan agreement dated 31.03.2016 showing Corporate Debtor as co-borrower and mortgagor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant challenged OBC's voting share in COC via IA in CP(IB) No. 1671/KB/2019 before NCLT Kolkata, arguing third-party corporate guarantees cannot constitute financial debt under 'Anuj Jain'; NCLT dismissed IA on 09.06.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate guarantee executed to secure credit facilities of third-party borrowers, when invoked prior to CIRP, constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(h) and (i) of the IBC, and whether the Supreme Court's ruling in Anuj Jain excludes such invoked guarantees from financial debt status in the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An invoked corporate guarantee securing a commercial borrowing constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC, as the underlying transaction entails disbursal of debt against time value of money, distinguishing an enforceable personal guarantee from a mere third-party property mortgage. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(i) explicitly covers liability in respect of guarantees for items in sub-clauses (a)-(h); the requirement of disbursal for time value of money is satisfied by disbursal to the principal borrower under Section 127 of the Contract Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between mortgage-only transactions (where no personal monetary obligation or indemnity exists, as in Anuj Jain) versus guarantee agreements binding the guarantor to repay the debt upon invocation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: OBC and Indiabulls were properly admitted as Financial Creditors for their full claim amounts, and the CoC voting shares were lawfully determined.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 658 of 2020 is dismissed. The NCLT Kolkata order dated 09.06.2020 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Ascot Realty Pvt. Ltd., a financial creditor, challenged the admission of Oriental Bank of Commerce's (PNB) claim of Rs. 32.54 Crores arising out of corporate guarantees for third-party loans, relying on the Supreme Court's Anuj Jain judgment. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Anuj Jain was confined to third-party mortgages without personal obligation. Where a corporate guarantee is executed and invoked for debts disbursed against consideration for the time value of money, the liability falls squarely under Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC, making the lender a financial creditor with full CoC voting rights.

case_title: Rajendra Bhai Panchal vs. Jay Manak Steels & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rajendra Bhai Panchal is ex-Director/shareholder of Corporate Debtor Yogi Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is M/s Jay Manak Steels (Operational Creditor/sole proprietorship); Respondent No. 2 is Shalabh Kumar Daga (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of MS Angle steel goods for executing a works contract with Indian Oil Corporation for Gujarat Refinery. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 9,42,841/- out of total supplies of Rs. 27,17,818/- (Corporate Debtor had paid Rs. 17,74,977/-); default date 22.09.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Statutory Demand Notice in Form 3 issued on 06.04.2018 claiming default of Rs. 9,42,841/-; no reply delivered within 10 days; Section 9 petition filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Six tax invoices showing TDS deductions, running account ledger, WhatsApp messages where Corporate Debtor evasively replied 'I will call you later' without raising quality disputes; internal communications with IOCL were uncommunicated to the supplier. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in C.P. (IB) 227/9/NCLT/AHM/2018 admitted the Section 9 petition on 03.06.2020, rejecting the defense of defective goods as moonshine.
legal_issues: Whether a minor clerical discrepancy between the gross debt and defaulted net debt in the Form 3 Demand Notice invalidates Section 9 proceedings, and whether uncommunicated disputes between a Corporate Debtor and third-party client constitute a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An inadvertent error or misstatement of total gross debt in a statutory demand notice does not invalidate insolvency proceedings so long as the defaulted debt indisputably exceeds the statutory threshold and causes no prejudice; a pre-existing dispute must be contemporaneous and communicated to the operational creditor prior to the demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 8 and 9, the existence of an undisputed debt in excess of the threshold requires admission; vague or evasive replies and moonshine defenses cannot defeat CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox standard requires an active, real dispute supported by evidence communicated to the creditor prior to demand; internal third-party correspondence not involving the creditor is inadmissible under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC to show a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Operational creditor established debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 lakh with no pre-existing dispute communicated within 10 days of notice; admission of Section 9 was justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 592 of 2020 is dismissed without costs. Interim stay application is closed, and Appellant is directed to file certified copy within ten days.
summary: Jay Manak Steels supplied MS Angles to Yogi Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd., leaving an unpaid balance of Rs. 9,42,841/-. Following an unreplied Demand Notice, NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the operational creditor's Section 9 petition. The ex-director appealed, alleging discrepancies in the demand notice and quality defects citing third-party communications with IOCL. NCLAT held that clerical errors in demand notices that cause no prejudice do not invalidate proceedings, and third-party correspondence does not prove a pre-existing dispute with the creditor. The admission was upheld.

case_title: Arenja Enterprises Private Limited vs. Edward Keventer (Successors) Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Arenja Enterprises Private Limited is the purported Financial Creditor; Respondent Edward Keventer (Successors) Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Memorandum of Understanding/collaboration agreements entered into in 1989 for development of land; a Civil Suit CS (OS) No. 1744 of 1992 was settled via Consent Decree dated 10.04.1996 granting Appellant 34,000 sq. ft. built-up area (plus 5,100 sq. ft. delay penalty) in a Group Housing Complex in New Delhi; an earlier security deposit of Rs. 2 Crores had already been fully refunded in January 1995. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on 09.08.2018 (when change of land use occurred) for non-allotment/delivery of 39,100 sq. ft. built-up residential space. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Consent Decree passed on 10.04.1996; execution stayed by Delhi High Court on 06.08.2019 as premature; Section 7 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoUs dated 1989, High Court Consent Decree dated 10.04.1996, High Court order dated 04.01.1995 showing complete refund of Rs. 2 Crores deposit, and order dated 06.08.2019 holding execution premature as construction had not commenced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed Appellant's Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 775 (ND)/2019 on 16.01.2020 holding that the claim was not a financial debt under Section 5(8)(f).
legal_issues: Whether an entitlement to built-up residential area under a court consent decree, entered into in lieu of compensation for past interest-free utilization of a refunded deposit, constitutes a 'financial debt' raised from an 'allottee' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, and whether non-allotment constitutes an actionable default under Section 3(12) while execution is stayed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entitlement to real estate area arising under a consent decree where no funds have been disbursed or raised from an allottee to fund construction does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: To qualify under Section 5(8)(f) read with RERA Section 2(d), an amount must be raised from an allottee having the commercial effect of a borrowing; an arrangement compensating past money utilization where the principal is already refunded does not satisfy the disbursal criteria. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pioneer Urban requires an actual disbursement of money by an allottee against the time value of money for the purpose of financing a real estate project; where no money remains with the developer and execution of the decree is held premature by a civil court, no default exists under Section 3(12). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant is not an allottee, no money was raised having commercial effect of borrowing, and no default occurred; dismissal of Section 7 petition was correct.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 528 of 2020 is dismissed without costs, affirming NCLT New Delhi's order dated 16.01.2020.
summary: Arenja Enterprises entered into development MoUs with Edward Keventer (Successors) Pvt. Ltd. in 1989 and obtained a consent decree in 1996 awarding it 34,000 sq. ft. of built-up area after its initial Rs. 2 Crore deposit was refunded. High Court execution of the decree was stayed as premature. The appellant filed a Section 7 application claiming the decree constituted a financial debt under Section 5(8)(f). NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellant was not an allottee who disbursed money for project construction, no funds were raised having the commercial effect of a borrowing, and no default occurred under the IBC.

case_title: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. vs. Yes Bank Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. (GUVNL) is the power purchaser; Respondent No. 1 Yes Bank Limited is the secured Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 Savan Godiawala is the Liquidator of Lanco Infratech Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: 25-year Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) dated 29.04.2010/24.09.2010 for supply of 15 MW solar power from a plant in Bhadrada, Gujarat; loan facility of Rs. 63.50 Crores advanced by Yes Bank on 04.08.2010 secured by exclusive charge/mortgage over the solar plant and receivables. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt obligations to other lenders led to CIRP; default notice issued under Clause 9.3 citing liquidation as default under Clause 9.2.1(e) of PPA. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 07.08.2017; liquidation ordered 27.08.2018; GUVNL default notice issued 23.07.2019; termination notice issued 30.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term Loan Agreement dated 04.08.2010, PPA, termination notice dated 30.08.2019, evidence that power plant maintained continuous, unhindered solar power supply to GUVNL without physical or technical supply default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Yes Bank filed IA No. 809/2019 in CP(IB) No. 111/07/HBD/2017 before NCLT Hyderabad to restrain PPA termination; NCLT set aside termination notice on 06.05.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a power purchaser can terminate a long-term Power Purchase Agreement solely due to the corporate debtor entering liquidation under the IBC, and whether the PPA and physical solar power plant constitute an integrated economic asset protected under the IBC to maximize asset value.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A counterparty cannot invoke ipso facto insolvency termination clauses to terminate an essential operating contract when the corporate debtor continues to perform its substantive obligations, as the contract and underlying assets form an integrated economic asset essential for value maximization in liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits alienation of legal rights or beneficial interests; the IBC overrides contrary contractual terms under Section 238 to prevent destruction of going-concern value. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the power producer has not suspended supply and is able and willing to perform, termination based solely on insolvency default clauses violates the statutory objective of asset maximization and going-concern liquidation under Section 230 of Companies Act/Section 35 IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: PPA and the solar plant constitute an indivisible economic entity; termination was illegal and rightly set aside.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 601 of 2020 is dismissed without costs, upholding NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 06.05.2020 setting aside GUVNL's termination notice.
summary: Lanco Infratech entered liquidation, and its secured creditor Yes Bank sought to realize assets under Section 52. GUVNL issued notices terminating the 25-year solar PPA solely based on the liquidation default clause, despite uninterrupted electricity supply. NCLT Hyderabad set aside the termination, and NCLAT affirmed the ruling. NCLAT held that the solar plant and PPA form an integrated economic asset whose continuation is vital to preserve going-concern status and achieve asset value maximization under the IBC, barring termination where substantive performance is maintained.

case_title: Mr. Umesh Saraf vs. Tech India Engineers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mr. Umesh Saraf is the suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Triumph Realty Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is Tech India Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 07.06.2016 and Letter of Intent dated 20.05.2016 for executing electrical works at a luxury resort/hotel in Calwaddo, Benaulim, Goa, stipulating completion within 120 days as essence of contract. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default of Rs. 46,64,878/- based on 50 unpaid running account invoices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8(1) issued on 11.04.2019 and received on 16.04.2019; Corporate Debtor sent communication detailing defects on 29.04.2019; Section 9 application (IB) No. 1906(ND)/2019 admitted on 04.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Extensive pre-notice email correspondence: operational creditor admitted delay on 05.12.2017; corporate debtor complained of deficient work on 29.10.2016, 24.02.2017, and 02.04.2018; third-party contractor engaged on 25.08.2018; email dated 04.10.2018 noted exaggerated bills and abandonment of site; independent audit report by IM Cost Management Pvt. Ltd. dated 05.03.2019 recorded qualitative and quantitative deficiencies after joint inspection. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Bench-V) admitted Section 9 CIRP on 04.06.2020 solely on the technical ground that the Corporate Debtor failed to reply to the statutory demand notice within 10 days under Section 8(2).
legal_issues: Whether the failure of a corporate debtor to issue a reply within 10 days of a Section 8 demand notice precludes the Adjudicating Authority from examining contemporaneous pre-notice correspondence and evidence demonstrating a pre-existing dispute under Section 8 and 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The requirement under Section 8(2) of the IBC to bring a dispute to the operational creditor's notice within 10 days of the demand notice is not a fatal procedural bar that precludes an Adjudicating Authority from examining contemporaneous pre-notice records establishing an authentic pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(2)(d) mandates rejection of an application if there is a pre-existing dispute; the core inquiry under Mobilox is whether a dispute truly existed prior to the demand notice, not merely whether a formal reply was filed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Mobilox and Innoventive, courts must examine pre-notice communications; documented complaints regarding delays, unfinished work, engagement of third-party contractors, and third-party technical audit reports establish a plausible, non-illusory pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Abundant pre-notice evidence proved a bona fide dispute regarding execution and quality of electrical works; Section 9 petition was non-maintainable and admission was erroneous.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 548 of 2020 is allowed; NCLT New Delhi order dated 04.06.2020 admitting CIRP is quashed; all consequential steps taken in CIRP are set aside; Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP; IRP/RP directed to restore assets/records to the Board; matter remitted to NCLT to determine CIRP costs payable by the Operational Creditor. No costs.
summary: Tech India Engineers filed a Section 9 petition against Triumph Realty for unpaid electrical contracting dues of Rs. 46,64,878/-. NCLT New Delhi admitted the CIRP solely because the corporate debtor failed to send a reply within 10 days under Section 8(2). NCLAT set aside the admission order, ruling that failure to formally reply within 10 days cannot override contemporaneous pre-notice evidence of a pre-existing dispute. Because extensive pre-notice correspondence and an independent technical audit established genuine disputes concerning delays, defective work, and inflated invoices, the operational creditor was outside the purview of the IBC.

case_title: Ashish O. Lalpuria vs. Kumaka Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ashish O. Lalpuria is an individual public equity shareholder; Respondent No. 1 is Kumaka Industries Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Union of India through Regional Director (Western Region, MCA); Respondent No. 3 is BSE Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Scheme of Arrangement under Sections 391-394 (1956 Act) / Sections 230-232 (2013 Act) proposed by Kumaka Industries to ratify prior share capital reduction, cancel deferred public issue shares, and issue bonus shares to meet minimum public shareholding requirements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In 1995 public issue, company illegally retained application money for 10,375 sub-lot shares and in 1997 unilaterally converted 24,13,000 partly paid shares into 6,03,250 fully paid shares without Section 100 confirmation; BSE suspended trading in 2002; SEBI issued severe restraint orders in 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court convened shareholder meetings on 08.02.2016; scheme petition filed 08.03.2016 and transferred to NCLT Mumbai as CP(CAA)190/MB.I/2017; NCLT approved scheme on 06.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BSE rejection letter dated 06.05.1999, SEBI penalty order dated 04.06.2013, Regional Director representation objecting to retroactive ratification of illegal capital reductions and non-compliances. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai sanctioned the scheme on 06.07.2020, treating RD objections as procedural lapses. Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a Scheme of Arrangement under Section 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 can be utilized to post-facto ratify past illegalities, statutory non-compliances, and unauthorized capital reductions to evade regulatory sanctions, and whether the 10% shareholding threshold under Section 230(4) bars scrutiny of public policy violations raised by the Regional Director.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230-232 cannot be used as an umbrella mechanism to ratify past illegal acts, regulatory defaults, or unauthorized capital reductions; companies must have a clean regulatory record without pending enforcement actions before scheme approval. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230(4) shareholding thresholds apply to private objections but do not circumscribe the court's duty under Section 230(5) to uphold public policy and give effect to objections raised by public authorities like the Regional Director. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Schemes cannot violate substantive law or public policy; mandatory statutory compliance forms an integral component of public policy and cannot be bypassed as mere procedural irregularity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The scheme was an illegitimate device to escape SEBI/BSE penalties and ratify illegal acts; NCLT's sanction was invalid and set aside.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 136 of 2020 is allowed; impugned order of NCLT Mumbai dated 06.07.2020 is set aside; Respondent No. 1 is directed to undo all actions taken pursuant to the sanctioned scheme, under supervision of the Regional Director. No costs.
summary: Kumaka Industries Ltd. obtained NCLT Mumbai approval for a Scheme of Arrangement to ratify unauthorized capital reductions dating back to 1997 and avoid SEBI regulatory actions following suspension of trading on BSE. A minority shareholder appealed under Section 421. NCLAT held that Section 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be utilized to sanitize past corporate illegalities or override regulatory enforcement under the guise of an arrangement. The Regional Director's objections on legality and public policy are paramount, irrespective of shareholder voting thresholds. The appeal was allowed and the scheme set aside.

case_title: Panna Pragati Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Amit Pareek & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Panna Pragati Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. are prospective resolution applicants; Respondent No. 1 is Amit Pareek (RP); Respondent No. 4 is Ngaitlang Dhar (H1 bidder/successful applicant); Meghalaya Infratech Ltd. is Corporate Debtor; Allahabad Bank is Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and negotiation of resolution plans for Meghalaya Infratech Ltd. in Section 7 CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: H1 Bidder submitted plan for Rs. 64.30 Crores plus CIRP costs; Appellants submitted a revised plan offering Rs. 65.65 Crores with higher upfront payment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 5th CoC meeting held on 11.02.2020 and adjourned to 12.02.2020; Appellants submitted revised plan on 14.02.2020 (within original 180 days expiring 24.02.2020); on 26.02.2020 NCLT extended CIRP by 90 days; CoC formally approved H1 plan in 7th meeting on 06.03.2020; NCLT approved plan on 18.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of CoC meetings (11.02.2020, 12.02.2020, 06.03.2020), emails dated 12.02.2020 and 14.02.2020 containing revised resolution plan, and NCLT order dated 26.02.2020 showing CoC had not approved H1 plan on 12.02.2020 but sought 90-day extension. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati in IA No. 27/2020 rejected Appellants' plea to place revised plan before CoC on 18.03.2020 falsely assuming H1 plan was already approved on 12.02.2020; NCLT subsequently approved H1 plan on 18.05.2020.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional committed a material irregularity by refusing to place a revised resolution plan submitted within the statutory CIRP period before the CoC, and whether an approval order based on conflicting findings regarding the date of CoC approval can be sustained.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Resolution Professional is statutorily mandated under Section 25(2)(i) and Section 30(3) of the IBC to place all compliant resolution plans and revisions received within the subsisting CIRP timeline before the CoC to advance asset maximization, and cannot unilaterally exclude applicants for minor delays when extension has been sought. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following Essar Steel, the 330-day timeline is not rigidly mandatory where exclusion of viable bids impairs stakeholder maximization; statutory duties of RP under Section 25(2)(i) and Section 30(3) override administrative convenience. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Material irregularity is established when an adjudicating authority rejects an applicant's plea on an erroneous factual assumption of prior CoC approval contradicted by an extension order on the same record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellants' revised plan was improperly excluded while CIRP was active; orders rejecting consideration and approving H1 plan were flawed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 515 & 516 of 2020 are allowed; impugned orders dated 18.03.2020 and 18.05.2020 are set aside; CIRP resumed from the stage of plan consideration; RP directed to place plans of H1, H2, and Appellants' revised plan before CoC; period of judicial intervention excluded from the 270-day timeline.
summary: During the CIRP of Meghalaya Infratech Ltd., Panna Pragati submitted a revised plan offering higher upfront consideration two days after the CoC meeting and within the 180-day timeline. The RP refused to place it before the CoC, and NCLT Guwahati rejected the applicant's IA on the false factual premise that the CoC had already approved H1's plan on 12.02.2020, subsequently approving H1's plan on 18.05.2020. NCLAT set aside both orders, ruling that the RP committed a material irregularity under Section 25(2)(i) and Section 30(3) by withholding the revised plan from CoC consideration. CIRP was remanded to resume from plan consideration.

case_title: Mr. Bhaskar vs. M/s Sai Precious Traexim Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is M/s Sai Precious Traexim Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Corporate Debtor is Pine View Portfolio Consultants Pvt. Ltd., represented by erstwhile director Mr. Bhaskar (Appellant); Ajay Kumar Kathuria is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged unsecured loan facility purportedly disbursed under instructions from one Rajeev Aggarwal via third-party financial service provider Taj Consultancy Services to the Corporate Debtor, repayable within three months with interest at 24% per annum. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed principal debt of Rs. 25,00,000/- (disbursed as Rs. 15 Lakhs on 30.01.2019 and Rs. 10 Lakhs on 01.02.2019) plus interest of Rs. 4,52,765/-, aggregating to an alleged total default amount of Rs. 29,52,765/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand legal notice issued by Financial Creditor on 05.11.2019; no reply was sent by Corporate Debtor; Section 7 application filed in late 2019 (C.P. No. IB-3228 (ND)/2019). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial Creditor relied solely on bank statements of third party Taj Consultancy Services showing RTGS transfers; Corporate Debtor demonstrated no privity of contract, absence of direct disbursement by Petitioner, and that Rajeev Aggarwal was neither a director nor shareholder. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application was filed before NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI; on 06.12.2019 and 19.12.2019 neither party appeared; NCLT admitted the application ex parte on 31.01.2020 holding overwhelming evidence of default without issuing formal notice to the Corporate Debtor.
legal_issues: Whether service of an advance copy of a Section 7 petition by the petitioner can be treated as valid service of notice under Rule 38 of NCLT Rules, 2016, and whether an Adjudicating Authority can admit a Section 7 application without issuing formal notice to the Corporate Debtor or establishing how a third-party disbursement constitutes a financial debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of an advance copy of an insolvency application by an applicant does not constitute legal service of notice by the tribunal under procedural rules; an ex parte admission order passed without judicial notice and inquiry into privity of debt violates natural justice and is unsustainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 38 and Rule 44 of NCLT Rules, 2016 mandate notice to be issued directly by the Tribunal to the respondent; Section 5(8) read with Section 7 of the IBC requires an express determination of debt disbursement between the creditor and corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must strictly evaluate whether direct privity of contract exists; reliance on third-party bank statements without establishing how the disbursement constitutes a financial debt owed to the applicant is legally defective. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT committed a jurisdictional error in admitting the Section 7 petition ex parte without issuing official notice to the Corporate Debtor and without adjudicating privity of contract regarding the third-party payment, warranting setting aside and remand.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 31.01.2020 set aside; matter remitted to NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI for fresh consideration on merits after issuing due notice under NCLT Rules, 2016; Corporate Debtor released from CIRP rigours; actions of IRP/RP and CoC set aside; IRP directed to hand over records and assets to Corporate Debtor's promoters/directors forthwith; IRP fees and CIRP costs to be determined by NCLT and borne by Respondent No. 1.
summary: An appeal was filed by the suspended director of Pine View Portfolio Consultants Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT New Delhi's ex parte order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Sai Precious Traexim Pvt. Ltd. The appellant contended that NCLT never issued notice of the petition, the debt was paid by an unrelated third party (Taj Consultancy Services), and no privity of contract existed. NCLAT held that serving an advance copy does not equate to service of judicial notice under Rule 38 of NCLT Rules, and NCLT erred by not examining how a third-party payment formed a financial debt. NCLAT set aside the admission order, restored the company, and remanded the matter.

case_title: Switching AVO Electro Power Ltd. vs. Ambient Computronics Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Switching AVO Electro Power Ltd. is the Operational Creditor; Ambient Computronics Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of UPS Power Storage Equipment by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor in the ordinary course of business. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of outstanding invoice balance amounting to Rs. 21,07,916/- out of total cumulative business transactions of Rs. 8,30,45,885/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice sent on 10.04.2018 and received by Corporate Debtor on 24.04.2018; reply to demand notice sent by Corporate Debtor on 30.04.2018 via email on 02.05.2018; Section 9 application filed on 30.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor produced ledger account, bank statements showing regular past payments, invoice dated 21.10.2017 with stamp and acknowledgment of receipt by Varanasi office, and corresponding e-way bill. Corporate Debtor produced ROC complaint dated 31.01.2018 and branch shifting certificate dated 14.12.2017 alleging internal director fraud. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the Section 9 petition (C.P. (IB) No. 993/KB/2019) on 18.11.2019 on grounds that invoices bore Varanasi delivery address instead of Patna registered office, lacking proof of registered office delivery.
legal_issues: Whether internal disputes and allegations of fraud among directors of a corporate debtor or a discrepancy between the delivery address on invoices and the registered office constitute a valid pre-existing dispute under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Internal disputes among the directors of a corporate debtor do not constitute a pre-existing dispute under the IBC, and an adjudicating authority cannot dismiss a complete Section 9 petition by treating summary insolvency proceedings as a formal civil suit or plaint requiring hyper-technical delivery proofs. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 requires admission once the application is complete, unpaid operational debt exists, and no genuine pre-existing dispute was raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Stamped acknowledgment of an invoice by a branch office accompanied by e-way bills and consistent running ledger entries constitutes prima facie proof of supply; vague requests for time to verify transactions do not meet the threshold of a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the Section 9 petition based on internal management disputes and invoice delivery address differences where receipt was duly stamped; the dismissal order was legally unsustainable.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 18.11.2019 set aside; matter remitted to NCLT Kolkata Bench with a direction to admit the Section 9 application and pass consequential orders under the IBC unless the Corporate Debtor settles with the Operational Creditor before the order is passed; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 09.11.2020.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application by NCLT Kolkata Bench regarding an unpaid balance of Rs. 21,07,916/- for UPS equipment.
