NCLT had rejected the petition on the basis that delivery was made to a Varanasi branch rather than the Patna registered office and that the debtor had ongoing internal director disputes. NCLAT set aside the rejection, holding that internal board disputes do not constitute a pre-existing dispute against a creditor, nor should Section 9 summary applications be scrutinized like civil plaints. NCLAT remitted the matter for admission of CIRP failing settlement.

case_title: Mirco Dynamics vs. Cosmos Cooperative Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mirco Dynamics is the Appellant (shareholder of Mirco Dynamics Pvt. Ltd., Respondent No. 2, Corporate Debtor); Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facility extended by Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd. to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date arising out of underlying credit facilities forming the subject of the original Section 7 petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original admission order passed on 23.09.2019; subsequently set aside by NCLAT Five-Member Bench in Comp. App (AT) (Ins) No. 1121 of 2019; consequential NCLT closure order passed on 18.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Applications M.A. Nos. 472/2019 and 479/2019 filed by a Director of Corporate Debtor alleging perjury and fraudulent/malicious initiation under Section 65 of IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 petition on 23.09.2019; NCLAT's Five-Judge Bench reversed the admission holding the petition barred by limitation and directed closure; on 18.03.2020, NCLT closed all consequential pending MAs including M.A. 472/2019 and 479/2019, which the Appellant challenged.
legal_issues: Whether miscellaneous applications alleging perjury and fraudulent initiation under Section 65 survive for independent adjudication by the Adjudicating Authority after the main Section 7 petition has been dismissed as barred by limitation and directed to be closed by an appellate tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the foundational petition initiating CIRP is dismissed on threshold legal grounds (such as limitation) and proceedings are ordered closed, all interlocutory, incidental, and ancillary applications terminate automatically and do not survive for independent enquiry. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 65 proceedings are parasitic upon an active insolvency proceeding; where the basic edifice (Section 7 admission) is erased, continuing an inquiry into alleged fraudulent or malicious initiation is legally preposterous. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Survival test of ancillary motions—ancillary applications require a legally surviving principal proceeding; once the primary jurisdiction is terminated by a limitation bar, collateral proceedings cannot be independently entertained. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of the Section 7 petition due to limitation extinguishes all pending miscellaneous applications concerning perjury and fraudulent initiation; NCLT committed no error in closing M.A. 472/2019 and 479/2019.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Impugned order dated 18th March, 2020 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench closing M.A. Nos. 472/2019 and 479/2019 affirmed without costs.
summary: A shareholder of Mirco Dynamics Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai's closure of miscellaneous applications alleging perjury and fraudulent initiation of Section 7 proceedings by Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd. The closure was ordered following an earlier Five-Judge NCLAT ruling that dismissed the Section 7 application as barred by limitation and directed closure of proceedings. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that once the underlying Section 7 petition is dismissed as time-barred, all ancillary applications, including those under Section 65, collapse and cannot survive for independent inquiry.

case_title: Niyati Chemicals vs. Minepro Minerals Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Niyati Chemicals is the Appellant (purported Financial Creditor/exporter); Minepro Minerals Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent (Corporate Debtor/manufacturer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business dealings during 2016-2017 where Appellant purchased processed Bentonite Powder (360 MTS) for export to Dubai through chain transactions and advanced sums against supplies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Purported unsecured loan/advance of Rs. 20,00,000/- extended on 25.04.2017, from which Rs. 2,88,400/- was adjusted for powder purchase on 21.06.2017; a separate loan of Rs. 2,50,000/- on 23.06.2017 was fully repaid on 28.06.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application under Section 7 of IBC filed by Appellant claiming status of Financial Creditor; dismissed by Adjudicating Authority vide order dated 28.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Ledger accounts in the books of the Respondent demonstrating money flow linked directly to purchase orders, advance payments, and supply of bentonite powder. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Section 7 application on 28.07.2020, holding that the money advanced represented commercial trade advances rather than a financial debt disbursed for the time value of money.
legal_issues: Whether advance payments made by a buyer to a manufacturer during ordinary commercial transactions for the supply of goods can be categorized as a 'Financial Debt' under Section 5(8) to maintain a Section 7 application under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial advances paid in the course of regular business transactions for the procurement/supply of goods do not constitute 'Financial Debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money, and cannot form the basis of a Section 7 application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) defines 'financial debt' strictly as a debt disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money; advance payments made towards commercial purchases are outside this definition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of ledger accounts and contemporaneous transactional records showing mutual debits, credits, and goods movement to establish the true economic nature of the funds as trade advances rather than financial borrowing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transaction was purely a commercial advance for the supply of bentonite powder; hence, Section 7 cannot be invoked, and the dismissal of the petition was legally justified.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed as devoid of merit both on facts and law; liberty granted to the Appellant to pursue recovery of money under applicable civil laws; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Niyati Chemicals challenged an NCLT order dated 28.07.2020 which rejected its Section 7 petition against Minepro Minerals Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant claimed that advances made to the Respondent for purchasing processed Bentonite Powder constituted an unsecured financial debt of Rs. 20 Lakhs (partly adjusted against goods received). NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, ruling that commercial advances made during business dealings for the supply of goods do not constitute 'Financial Debt' disbursed for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC.

case_title: Raman Raheja vs. Prime Air Global Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raman Raheja is the Appellant (Shareholder of the Corporate Debtor); Prime Air Global Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational services/goods provided by Prime Air Global Ltd. to the Corporate Debtor resulting in outstanding operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in unpaid operational debt claimed under Section 9, with partial post-default payment tendered by cheque during informal settlement discussions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notice issued; Corporate Debtor failed to file reply despite an extension of three days granted by NCLT on 24.02.2020 (prior to COVID-19 lockdown); admission order passed after expiry of statutory timelines. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Absence of any pre-existing dispute, reply to demand notice, civil suit, or arbitration proceedings; only evidence tendered was ongoing informal settlement negotiations and part payment by cheque. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Court No. IV) admitted the Section 9 application after the Corporate Debtor failed to file a reply within the granted extension; Appellant appealed claiming lack of opportunity to represent due to impending settlement and lockdown.
legal_issues: Whether ongoing settlement discussions or part payments by cheque can justify delaying the statutory admission of a Section 9 application under Section 9(5) of the IBC in the absence of a pre-existing dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Ongoing settlement negotiations do not constitute a legally tenable defense against the admission of an operational debt petition, and pre-admission proceedings cannot be protracted on the pretext of settlement discussions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5) of the IBC mandates the Adjudicating Authority to admit or reject an application on its merits within the statutory timeline once default is established and no pre-existing dispute or satisfaction of debt is placed on record. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the Corporate Debtor fails to file a reply raising a genuine dispute or proving satisfaction of the operational debt despite opportunity, the statutory requirement for admission is satisfied. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had no substantive defense of a pre-existing dispute or dispute pendency, and the statutory period under Section 9(5) had long elapsed; hence, the admission order had no legal infirmity.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed as being devoid of merit; no order as to costs.
summary: A shareholder of the Corporate Debtor appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed by Prime Air Global Ltd. The Appellant contended that settlement talks were ongoing, part payment had been made by cheque, and adequate opportunity to contest was not given. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that under Section 9(5), NCLT is bound to admit or reject complete petitions within statutory limits and pre-admission proceedings cannot be delayed on the pretext of settlement where no pre-existing dispute is shown.

case_title: Gulshan Gaba vs. Surinder Juneja & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gulshan Gaba is the Appellant (representing the Committee of Creditors/aggrieved party); Surinder Juneja is Respondent No. 1 (Applicant and erstwhile Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Determination and payment of professional remuneration/fees for services rendered by the erstwhile Interim Resolution Professional during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fixed remuneration dispute regarding the direction to pay Rs. 3,50,000/- per month for the period worked by the erstwhile IRP, after excluding earlier payments, within three weeks. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority originally passed an order on 07.01.2019 directing CoC consideration and reference to IBBI upon deadlock; subsequent conflicting impugned order passed on 21.09.2020; appeal heard on 29.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Earlier binding order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 07.01.2019 directing the CoC to convene a meeting to resolve the fee dispute or refer it to IBBI if deadlocked. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT originally directed the CoC to resolve the remuneration deadlock or refer it to IBBI on 07.01.2019; however, on 21.09.2020, NCLT unilaterally fixed the remuneration at Rs. 3,50,000/- per month and ordered the balance paid within three weeks, prompting the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can directly fix and direct the payment of remuneration of an erstwhile Interim Resolution Professional in contradiction to its own prior order directing reference to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) in case of a deadlock within the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot issue an order fixing an insolvency professional's remuneration that contradicts its own earlier binding procedural order directing dispute resolution through the statutory regulator (IBBI) upon CoC deadlock. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Determination of insolvency resolution professional fees amidst deadlock between the Committee of Creditors and the professional is appropriately referred to the IBBI in line with prior binding directions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Conflict of judicial orders test—where an impugned order directly negates an earlier unchallenged order of the same forum establishing a dispute mechanism, the subsequent order is legally untenable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order dated 21.09.2020 is contrary to the earlier order dated 07.01.2019, warranting setting aside with liberty to refer the fee dispute to IBBI.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 21.09.2020 set aside; aggrieved party permitted to refer the quantum of fees payable to the erstwhile IRP to the IBBI in terms of the earlier order dated 07.01.2019; IBBI requested to decide the quantum expeditiously, preferably within three months from reference; no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged an order dated 21.09.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority directing the Committee of Creditors to pay remuneration of Rs. 3,50,000/- per month to the erstwhile IRP. The Appellant contended that this directive contradicted the NCLT's earlier order dated 07.01.2019, which had directed that any unresolved deadlock regarding the IRP's fee should be referred to the IBBI. NCLAT held that the subsequent order ran contrary to the earlier directive, set aside the order dated 21.09.2020, and granted liberty to the parties to approach the IBBI to adjudicate the fee quantum within three months.

case_title: Anurag Chandra vs. Rohit Sehgal, Liquidator of Affinity Beauty Salon Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anurag Chandra is the Appellant (Financial Creditor and member of the Committee of Creditors); Rohit Sehgal is the Respondent (Resolution Professional appointed as Liquidator of Affinity Beauty Salon Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt claims and corporate insolvency resolution proceedings resulting in liquidation of the Corporate Debtor, Affinity Beauty Salon Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics stemming from corporate insolvency resolution proceedings resulting in liquidation and distribution mechanism allocation to the Appellant. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution process concluded and liquidation order passed by the Adjudicating Authority; appeal preferred and heard on 19.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records and minutes of the Committee of Creditors showing that no member ever raised any objection to the Resolution Professional's conduct, found fault with his role, or proposed substituting him with another person as Liquidator. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi passed an order approving liquidation and appointing the Resolution Professional as the Liquidator under the IBC; Appellant challenged the specific appointment of the RP as Liquidator.
legal_issues: Whether an individual Financial Creditor, having been allocated a share under the distribution mechanism, can override the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors regarding the appointment of the Resolution Professional as Liquidator in the absence of any established act of omission or commission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual dissenting creditor cannot override the collective wisdom and decision of the Committee of Creditors appointing the Resolution Professional as Liquidator unless specific acts of omission or commission disentitling the professional are substantiated. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 34 of the IBC contemplates that the Resolution Professional shall act as the Liquidator unless replaced by the Adjudicating Authority on specified grounds or substituted by the Committee of Creditors; individual creditors cannot unilaterally veto this statutory presumption. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold requirement of specific misconduct—the challenger must demonstrate identifiable acts of omission or commission on record; absence of objections or substitution motions during CoC meetings defeats a subsequent collateral challenge. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to establish any disqualifying omission or commission by the Resolution Professional, and the CoC raised no objection; hence, the appeal against the appointment of the Liquidator is devoid of merit.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed at the threshold stage; no order as to costs.
summary: A Financial Creditor appealed against an order of NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi appointing the Resolution Professional as the Liquidator of Affinity Beauty Salon Pvt. Ltd. The challenge was confined to the appointment of the RP as Liquidator. NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the threshold, holding that the Appellant had been allocated a share under the distribution mechanism and that in the absence of any proven acts of omission or commission against the Resolution Professional—or any objection/substitution raised by the Committee of Creditors during proceedings—an individual creditor cannot override the collective wisdom of the CoC.

case_title: Makalu Trading Ltd. & Ors. vs. Rajiv Chakraborty, Resolution Professional for Uttam Value Steels Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Makalu Trading Ltd. & Ors. were Operational Creditors holding an admitted operational debt of Rs. 423.82 Crore (80.88% of total operational debt). Respondent No. 1 Rajiv Chakraborty was the Resolution Professional, Respondent No. 2 was the Committee of Creditors (CoC) represented through State Bank of India, and Respondent No. 3 was CarVal Investors (Consortium of CarVal/Nithia), the Successful Resolution Applicant. The Corporate Debtor was Uttam Value Steels Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under CP (IB) 1830/MB/2018 wherein a Resolution Plan was invited for Uttam Value Steels Limited under the Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditors claimed admitted debt of Rs. 423.82 Crore out of total admitted operational debt of Rs. 524 Crore, alongside total admitted debt of Rs. 3,003 Crore (including Financial Creditor debt of Rs. 2,479 Crore). Under the approved plan, Operational Creditors received 0.18%-0.19% while Financial Creditors received Rs. 1,035 Crore (41.75%). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: E-voting on CarVal's plan scheduled for 19.04.2019 was cancelled; CarVal applied to the CCI on 20.04.2019; CoC approved the revised plan at its 15th meeting on 21.04.2019 by an 81.29% majority; CCI approval was obtained on 04.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Performance Bank Guarantee of Rs. 250 Crores valid till 30.04.2020 was diluted/reduced to Rs. 50 Crores due to COVID-19 pandemic distress under Clause 6.4 of RFRP; Dr. Johannes Sittard resigned as partner of Nithia Capital on 01.04.2018 but retained the designation of Non-Executive Chairman/Director. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi approved the Resolution Plan via orders dated 30.04.2020 and 06.05.2020 in CP (IB) 1830/MB/2018 and MA 1751/2019, which Appellants challenged under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether obtaining prior approval of the Competition Commission of India under the proviso to Section 31(4) of the IBC is mandatory before CoC approval, or directory; whether suppression regarding the status of an expert director (Dr. Johannes Sittard) invalidated the plan under CIRP Regulation 39(1)(c); and whether reduction of the Performance Bank Guarantee from Rs. 250 Crores to Rs. 50 Crores violated RFRP and rendered the plan void.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The requirement under the proviso to Section 31(4) of the IBC to obtain approval from the Competition Commission of India is directory and not mandatory, and it suffices if CCI approval is obtained prior to final approval of the plan by the Adjudicating Authority. Commercial decisions regarding PBG modifications and feasibility/viability fall squarely within the commercial wisdom of the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proviso to Section 31(4) of IBC construed harmoniously with the time-bound objectives of CIRP and the extended timelines under Section 31(11) of the Competition Act, 2002; treating 'shall' as directory prevents pushing viable corporate debtors into liquidation. Differential payment to different classes of creditors is permissible under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53(1) as established in Essar Steel. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantial compliance test; verifying that CCI approval had been procured prior to the Adjudicating Authority's final approval order, and that internal organizational changes of key personnel did not prejudice overall corporate execution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The approval of CarVal's plan was valid; CCI approval obtained on 04.06.2019 cured the procedural timing defect, reduction of PBG fell within the CoC's contractual and commercial remit, and the distribution met statutory minimums under Section 30(2)(b).
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 533 of 2020 is dismissed on merits without costs. All pending Interlocutory Applications stand disposed of and interim orders vacated.
summary: Operational Creditors holding 80.88% of operational debt appealed against NCLT orders approving CarVal Investors' resolution plan for Uttam Value Steels Ltd. Appellants challenged the plan alleging lack of prior CCI approval under Section 31(4) before CoC voting, fraudulent representation of technical director Dr. Johannes Sittard under Regulation 39(1)(c), unilateral reduction of the Performance Bank Guarantee from Rs. 250 Crores to Rs. 50 Crores, and inequitable distribution (0.19% vs 41.75% to Financial Creditors). NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that obtaining CCI approval prior to CoC approval is directory, not mandatory, provided approval is obtained before NCLT approval. The reduction of the PBG was within the CoC's commercial wisdom, and creditor distribution complied with Section 30(2)(b).

case_title: Yogeshkumar Jashwantlal Thakkar vs. Indian Overseas Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Yogeshkumar Jashwantlal Thakkar was the Suspended Director of Jason Dekor Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, Respondent No. 2). Respondent No. 1 was Indian Overseas Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple fund-based credit facilities sanctioned on 07.08.2012 and renewed on 31.03.2015, comprising Term Loans and Letters of Guarantee totaling a sanction limit of Rs. 23.65 Crores (renewed to Rs. 17.73 Crores). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date was recorded as 01.01.2016 (date of NPA classification) for an outstanding financial debt of over Rs. 19.25 Crores (decreed at Rs. 19,25,81,173.31 with 13.20% p.a. interest in OA 470 of 2017 before DRT-II Chennai on 18.02.2019). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default date was 01.01.2016; balance confirmation letters executed periodically on 02.04.2013, 14.10.2013, 15.10.2013, 30.09.2014, 20.05.2015, 05.06.2015, 02.09.2016, and 31.03.2017; Section 7 application filed on 01.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Duly stamped and signed Debit Balance Confirmation letters, revival letters dated 31.03.2015, 30.04.2015, and 31.03.2017, balance sheets for 2015-16, 2016-17, and 2017-18, and an OTS letter dated 12.09.2019 acknowledging subsisting liability. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application CP (IB) 257/7/NCLT/AHM/2019 was admitted by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 19.12.2019 holding the application complete and debt acknowledged; Appellant appealed alleging the claim was time-barred under Article 137.
legal_issues: Whether Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to applications filed under Section 7 of the IBC, 2016 so as to extend the three-year limitation period where written acknowledgments/balance confirmations are executed within the limitation period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is applicable to applications filed under Section 7 of the IBC; a written and signed acknowledgment of liability made prior to the expiration of the prescribed period triggers a fresh period of limitation computed from the date of the acknowledgment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Construed Section 18(1) alongside Article 137 of the Limitation Act; 'application' within Section 18 encompasses Section 7 IBC petitions, interrupting the running of prescription and resetting the limitation clock upon valid written acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that acknowledgment of subsisting debtor-creditor relationship was made in writing and signed/stamped by the authorized representative/director before the expiration of three years from the date of initial default or preceding acknowledgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The balance confirmation dated 31.03.2017 renewed the three-year limitation clock up to 31.03.2020; hence the Section 7 petition filed on 01.04.2019 was well within limitation.
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 236 of 2020 is dismissed. The NCLT order admitting Section 7 application and declaring moratorium is upheld. All connected IAs are closed without costs.
summary: Suspended Director of Jason Dekor Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting Indian Overseas Bank's Section 7 petition, contending that the petition filed on 01.04.2019 was barred by limitation since the date of default/NPA was 01.01.2016. The Bank relied on periodic balance confirmations and revival letters, notably one dated 31.03.2017, along with balance sheets acknowledging the debt. The NCLAT held that Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to applications under Section 7 of the IBC. The written balance confirmation dated 31.03.2017 extended the limitation period up to 31.03.2020, making the application filed on 01.04.2019 legally competent and timely. Appeal dismissed.

case_title: India Power Corporation Ltd. & Anr. vs. Meenakshi Energy Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants India Power Corporation Ltd. (IPCL, 95.2% shareholder/pledgor) and Debasish Som (Independent Ex-Director). Respondent No. 1 Meenakshi Energy Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), Respondent No. 2 State Bank of India (Lead Financial Creditor for consortium of SBI and Associate Banks), Respondent No. 3 PTC India Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan and working capital consortium facilities sanctioned under Common Loan Agreements dated 10.07.2009 (Phase I 300 MW) and 01.10.2010 (Phase II 700 MW) and Working Capital Agreement dated 18.09.2012 for thermal power project at Thamminapatnam, Nellore, secured by pledge of IPCL's shares in Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in servicing principal and interest occurred on 31.07.2017; NPA classified on 28.10.2017; total default amount exceeded Rs. 1,440 Crores across Phase I (Principal Rs. 350.54 Cr + Interest Rs. 86.02 Cr), Phase II (Principal Rs. 1,018.75 Cr + Interest Rs. 58.65 Cr), and Working Capital facilities (Principal Rs. 51.54 Cr + Interest Rs. 12.41 Cr). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Total recall notice issued on 07.08.2018; share pledge invoked on 20.12.2017; Corporate Debtor acknowledged debt on 16.02.2018 and issued settlement proposals on 25.05.2018 and 11.06.2018; Section 7 petition filed on 23.01.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share Pledge Agreement dated 23.09.2016; transfer of 3,91,24,02,331 pledged shares to Demat account of SBICAP Trustee Company Ltd. on 02.05.2018; mala fide issuance of 10,02,34,109 additional shares with differential voting rights by Corporate Debtor reducing SBICAP's voting power from 97.58% to 3.75%. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted SBI's Section 7 petition on 07.11.2019 initiating CIRP; Appellants appealed on grounds that invocation of pledge discharged the debt and petition was triggered under invalid RBI Circular dated 12.02.2018.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition was maintainable as an independent action rather than being instituted pursuant to the invalid RBI circular dated 12.02.2018; and whether the invocation of pledged shares and transfer to the demat account of the Security Trustee (SBICAP Trustee) resulted in discharge of the corporate debt or stripped the Financial Creditors of their locus standi.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The transfer of dematerialized pledged shares to the demat account of a Security Trustee upon invocation does not amount to an absolute transfer of ownership or commercial discharge of underlying debt; the lender remains a Financial Creditor entitled to initiate CIRP until the debt is actually realized through sale or recovery. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 58(8) of the SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996 read subject to Section 176 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and specific covenants of the Share Pledge Agreement; holding demat shares as collateral gives beneficial custody to realize dues upon sale, not outright extinguishment of liability. Section 7 IBC requires only proof of debt exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh and default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substance of subsequent conduct; post-invocation written acknowledgments of debt and settlement proposals submitted by the Corporate Debtor disprove the claim of debt discharge. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was filed independently of the RBI circular after obtaining independent sanction, and invocation of pledged shares by the Security Trustee did not discharge the debt; NCLT rightly admitted the petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1220 of 2019 and No. 1450 of 2019 are dismissed without costs. The NCLT admission order initiating CIRP and imposing moratorium is affirmed.
summary: IPCL and an ex-director appealed the admission of SBI's Section 7 petition against Meenakshi Energy Ltd., arguing the petition was void under the struck-down RBI 12.02.2018 Circular and that debt stood fully discharged because 95.2% pledged shares were transferred to SBICAP Trustee. NCLAT held the petition was independent of the RBI circular as timelines and approvals differed. It further held that transfer of pledged demat shares to the Security Trustee under Regulation 58 of SEBI Regulations and Section 176 of the Contract Act did not extinguish the debt or vest equity ownership in SBI, particularly given the Corporate Debtor's subsequent admissions of debt and settlement letters. Admission upheld.

case_title: Om Parkash Khurana & Ors. vs. Vinod Kumar Mahajan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants in Comp. App. 571/2020 were Shailesh Chawla and Ranjan Sharma (alleged Independent/Non-Executive Directors); Appellants in Comp. App. 572/2020 were Om Parkash Khurana (CMD), Rakesh Khurana, and Rama Khurana (Suspended Directors). Respondent No. 1 was Vinod Kumar Mahajan (RP/Liquidator of Mahabir Techno Ltd., Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated against Mahabir Techno Ltd. under CP (IB) No. 70/Chd/Hry/2018 on 30.10.2018; liquidation ordered on 22.02.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete failure by suspended directors to deliver statutory books, software, financial data, and assets from 01.04.2014 onwards to the RP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 30.10.2018; CoC resolved on 06.12.2018 to file Section 19(2) application; RP issued specific demand notice on 12.10.2019; NCLT issued show cause notice under Section 236 r/w Section 70 on 03.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Suspended directors claimed factory and records were seized by Union Bank of India under SARFAESI on 05.10.2018 and accounting laptop was lost on 03.10.2018 (FIR lodged belatedly on 07.12.2018). Official Panchanama proved premises were completely empty when taken over, exposing the defense as a sham. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed RP's CA No. 3/2019 under Section 19(2) on 23.03.2020, holding respondents non-cooperative and forwarding the order to IBBI for prosecution under Section 70 r/w Section 236.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the power under the IBC to forward/recommend a matter to the IBBI for considering prosecution under Section 70 read with Section 236; and whether 'independent' or alleged 'sleeping' directors are exempt from the statutory duties of co-operation under Section 19.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority has the legal competence to refer non-cooperation and misconduct to the IBBI for considering prosecution under Section 70 read with Section 236. The statutory obligation under Section 19 extends to all personnel and directors; there is no legal protection or concept of 'sleeping director' under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19 read with Section 5(23) applies broadly to all 'personnel' and management; exemptions under Section 149(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 and MCA Circulars are limited to proceedings under company law and do not curtail mandatory compliance duties under IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective evaluation of compliance; failure to establish custody loss through contemporaneous credible evidence (rejecting delayed FIRs and unsupported claims of banking seizure as afterthoughts). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT did not convict or usurp trial powers but merely made a recommendation to IBBI to take an independent assessment, which is well within its jurisdiction.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 571 and 572 of 2020 are dismissed without costs. The NCLT direction referring the matter to IBBI under Section 70 read with Section 236 is confirmed.
summary: Suspended and claimed independent directors of Mahabir Techno Ltd. appealed an NCLT Chandigarh order in a Section 19(2) application referring them to the IBBI for potential prosecution under Section 70 read with Section 236 of IBC for failing to furnish books of accounts and records to the RP. Appellants argued they were non-executive/sleeping directors and records were lost during a SARFAESI takeover by Union Bank. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that Section 19 obligations apply to all personnel without exception for 'sleeping directors', MCA protective circulars do not shield directors from IBC duties, and NCLT possessed full jurisdiction to refer non-compliance to the IBBI to determine whether to initiate prosecution.

case_title: Punjab National Bank vs. Mittal Corp Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Punjab National Bank (erstwhile Oriental Bank of Commerce, Financial Creditor) and Respondent Mittal Corp Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium lending where debt was restructured under a Master Restructuring Agreement dated 30.03.2015; following non-adherence, Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR) was invoked on 16.06.2016 with 18 months to effect a change in management. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Upon failure of SDR, account classified as NPA on 30.06.2016; total default claimed by Appellant Bank was Rs. 2,44,85,29,569.79 out of total consortium debt of approximately Rs. 1,077 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SDR failed on 17.12.2017; Bombay High Court directed time-bound resolution by 06.04.2018 in pending winding-up petitions; JLF met on 26.02.2018 and 13.03.2018; Section 7 application filed on 20.03.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: JLF minutes showing that prospective investor proposals (Trishakti Power) could not be finalized before the High Court deadline of 06.04.2018; decision to file under Section 7 taken independently to protect creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-II dismissed the Section 7 petition on 20.12.2019 holding it non-est on the premise that it was triggered solely under RBI's 12.02.2018 Circular which was declared ultra vires in Dharani Sugars; Financial Creditor appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application filed by the Financial Creditor was instituted pursuant to the RBI Circular dated 12.02.2018 and thereby rendered non-est following the Supreme Court's decision in Dharani Sugars & Chemicals Ltd.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 7 application cannot be dismissed as non-est under Dharani Sugars unless it is conclusively shown that the insolvency proceeding was initiated solely due to the mandatory directions of the RBI Circular dated 12.02.2018. The circular applies only to debts of Rs. 2,000 Crores and above; lenders maintain an independent statutory right to trigger CIRP for defaults below that threshold. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC confers an autonomous statutory remedy upon any financial creditor where default occurs; RBI Circular dated 12.02.2018 applied strictly to accounts with aggregate exposure of Rs. 2,000 Crores or more. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold and causality test; establishing aggregate debt exposure (Rs. 1,077 Crores, well below Rs. 2,000 Crores) and examining contemporaneous minutes to determine if the application was an independent exercise of creditor rights driven by High Court deadlines. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was initiated independently due to high court deadlines and SDR failure, not under the invalid RBI circular; NCLT erred in rejecting the application.
operative_order: Appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 20.12.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-II is set aside, and the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the admission of the Section 7 application on merits expeditiously.
summary: Punjab National Bank appealed the dismissal of its Section 7 petition against Mittal Corp Ltd. for default of Rs. 244.85 Crores. The NCLT had dismissed the petition as non-est, believing it was initiated under the RBI Circular dated 12.02.2018 which was struck down in Dharani Sugars. The NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that the RBI Circular applied only to exposures exceeding Rs. 2,000 Crores, whereas total consortium debt was Rs. 1,077 Crores. JLF minutes revealed the filing was prompted by Bombay High Court directions and failed debt restructuring. The petition was an independent exercise of statutory rights; remanded to NCLT for adjudication on merits.

case_title: QVC Exports Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Cosmic Ferro Alloys Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants QVC Exports Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (minority shareholders holding ~34%-40% post-resolution equity); Respondent No. 1 Cosmic Ferro Alloys Ltd. (company acquired under IBC); Respondent No. 2 United Tradeco FZC (majority shareholder holding 51%-60%); Respondents 3 to 7 and 9 other shareholders/directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Takeover of Cosmic Ferro Alloys Ltd. through a Joint Resolution Plan approved by NCLT Kolkata under Section 31 IBC, wherein Appellants and Respondent No. 2 formed a consortium contributing Rs. 3.40 Crores and Rs. 111.60 Crores respectively. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of financial impropriety and unauthorized related-party transactions exceeding Rs. 18 Crores in FY 2019-20 by nominee director (Neha Singh Chauhan) with Matashree Mercantile Pvt. Ltd., plus embezzlement claims of Rs. 2.51 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Special notice for removal under Section 169 issued on 21.05.2020; Board meeting held on 02.06.2020; notice convening EGM issued on 26.05.2020 for 29.06.2020 (adjourned to and held on 07.07.2020). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan contained no clause ensuring perpetual directorship or proportional management control for minority partner; valid Special Notice under Section 169 served; Appellants abstained from attending the EGM on 07.07.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 1836/KB/2019 alleging oppression/mismanagement under Sections 241-242 and sought interim injunction against removal of nominee director; NCLT Kolkata dismissed interim IA on 11.06.2020; Appellants appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a majority shareholder can lawfully remove a minority consortium member's nominee director under Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013 in the absence of affirmative governance rights or quasi-partnership protections in the approved resolution plan and Articles of Association.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company has an inherent democratic right under Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013 to remove any director by ordinary resolution with requisite notice; principles of quasi-partnership cannot be invoked to restrain director removal unless expressly codified in the Articles of Association, shareholders' agreements, or terms of the approved resolution plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 169(3) mandates that the concerned director must be given a copy of the notice and an opportunity to be heard; where statutory procedures and notices are duly complied with, courts will not grant interim injunctions paralyzing company administration. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of corporate constitutional documents; verifying whether the resolution plan or Articles provide negative covenants against removal or proportional representation under Section 163. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The EGM and removal of the nominee director followed due process of law without any statutory procedural breach; NCLT rightly refused interim injunction.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 92 of 2020 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 93 of 2020 are dismissed without costs. Interim orders vacated. The main Company Petition is left to be decided by NCLT Kolkata on merits.
summary: QVC Exports and its nominee director appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order refusing interim injunction against her removal as director of Cosmic Ferro Alloys Ltd., which was acquired jointly under an IBC resolution plan. The majority shareholder (United Tradeco FZC) issued notice under Section 169 to remove her following breakdown in relations and allegations of siphonage. The Appellants contended the company was a quasi-partnership where nominee directors could not be ousted. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the approved resolution plan and Articles contained no representation guarantees or management rights, statutory requirements under Section 169 were strictly observed, and equitable quasi-partnership principles could not override statutory removal procedures.

case_title: Bank of India & Anr. vs. Coastal Oil Gas Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Bank of India and Central Bank of India (Consortium Financial Creditors) and Respondent Coastal Oil Gas Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan facility of Rs. 641.85 Crores (BOI: Rs. 198.00 Cr; CBI: Rs. 98.85 Cr) sanctioned under Common Loan Agreement dated 01.08.2011 to construct crude oil and product tank farm facilities at Cuddalore refinery for Nagarjuna Oil Corporation Ltd. (NOCL). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under restructured terms where First Repayment Date was fixed as 31.12.2015; total overdue claim exceeded Rs. 750 Crores (OA 478/2018 filed before DRT-II Chennai for Rs. 750,60,91,863.51). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Common Loan Agreement dated 01.08.2011; Second Amendment Agreement executed on 31.03.2015 fixing repayment between Dec 2015 and Sept 2025; Revival Letter executed on 31.01.2017; Recall notice issued on 07.12.2017 giving 15 days; Section 7 petition filed on 19.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Second Amendment Agreement dated 31.03.2015 rescheduling repayment; signed Revival Letter dated 31.01.2017 specifically acknowledging debt under Section 18 of Limitation Act; balance sheets for FY 2016-17 and 2017-18 showing acknowledged liability. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed the Section 7 petition on 30.10.2019 holding it barred by limitation as more than 3 years elapsed from 16.03.2015; Financial Creditors appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether restructuring of a loan facility via an amendment agreement alters the date of default, and whether a revival letter executed under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 together with balance sheet acknowledgments extends the limitation period for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the original loan agreement is restructured by a supplementary or amendment agreement, the original defaults are subsumed, and the fresh date of default is determined strictly in terms of the restructured repayment schedule. Furthermore, a written acknowledgment of debt within three years resets the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act for a Section 7 IBC application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to applications under Section 7 of the IBC. Limitation is a mixed question of fact and law; adjudicating authorities cannot selectively pick an obsolete default date while disregarding executed amendment agreements and revival letters. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Document examination; evaluating restructured repayment schedules and express written balance revival confirmations to determine the precise accrual of the right to sue. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default under the Second Amendment Agreement occurred on 31.12.2015, accelerated on 22.12.2017, and was acknowledged via Revival Letter on 31.01.2017. The Section 7 application filed on 19.09.2018 was well within the three-year limitation period.
operative_order: Appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 30.10.2019 passed by NCLT Hyderabad is set aside. The matter is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority to issue notice and admit the Section 7 application expeditiously within one month. No costs.
summary: Bank of India and Central Bank of India appealed against the NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing their Section 7 application against Coastal Oil Gas Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. as time-barred. The NCLT reckoned limitation from 16.03.2015. The NCLAT set aside the dismissal, holding that the Second Amendment Agreement dated 31.03.2015 restructured the debt and reset the first default to 31.12.2015, subsuming earlier defaults. Moreover, the Corporate Debtor executed a valid revival letter under Section 18 of the Limitation Act on 31.01.2017. Consequently, the application filed on 19.09.2018 was well within the three-year limitation period under Article 137. Remanded for admission.

case_title: M/s. Kuntal Construction Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Bharat Hotels Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s. Kuntal Construction Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) and Respondent M/s. Bharat Hotels Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Execution of civil, structural, and sewage treatment plant (STP) renovation works at Hotel The Lalit, New Delhi under work orders dated 04.10.2011 and 14.10.2013 valued at Rs. 47,50,000/- and Rs. 2,07,00,000/- respectively. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed an unpaid balance of Rs. 14,89,967/- including retention money of Rs. 6,74,247/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mutual full and final settlement letter executed on 07.10.2015 for Rs. 1,21,73,545/-; Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 18,67,489/- in installments post-settlement; Section 8 demand notice issued on 28.11.2018; Section 8(2)(a) notice of dispute replied on 05.12.2018; Section 9 petition filed on 24.12.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email communications dated 23.01.2016 confirming Operational Creditor's knowledge that retention money was adjusted towards defect liability under Clause 4 of the Work Order; full and final settlement letter dated 07.10.2015 showing no reminders or protest raised between 2015 and 2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected the Section 9 petition on 30.01.2020 due to the existence of a pre-existing dispute regarding retention money adjustments; Operational Creditor appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether adjustment of retention money towards defect liability communicated prior to the Section 8 demand notice constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) and Section 9 of the IBC, warranting rejection of the Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The IBC is not a money recovery mechanism. Where contemporaneous correspondence prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice establishes that the corporate debtor raised deductions or adjusted retention money against contractual defect liability, a genuine, plausible, non-spurious pre-existing dispute exists, mandating rejection of a Section 9 application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(6) read with Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC; the scope of 'dispute' is not confined to pending arbitration or litigation, but covers genuine controversies concerning the quality of work, performance, and deductions raised prior to the statutory demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Mobilox Innovations plausibility standard; separating grain from chaff to establish that defense of defect liability adjustment was documented before the statutory demand notice was issued. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Email dated 23.01.2016 proved the Operational Creditor had prior knowledge of retention adjustments; hence a genuine pre-existing dispute existed, barring admission of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 542 of 2020 is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT order dated 30.01.2020. The parties are free to pursue recovery before appropriate civil or arbitral forums.
summary: M/s Kuntal Construction Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order rejecting its Section 9 application against Bharat Hotels Ltd. for alleged dues of Rs. 14.89 Lakhs, which included Rs. 6.74 Lakhs in retention money. The NCLT found a pre-existing dispute existed regarding the adjustment of retention money against defects liability. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal under the Mobilox Innovations doctrine, noting that email correspondence dating back to January 2016 established the Operational Creditor was informed of the adjustment under the contract terms well before the Section 8 demand notice in November 2018. IBC cannot serve as a recovery forum for contentious contractual claims.

case_title: Action Barter Pvt. Ltd. vs. SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant/Appellant Action Barter Pvt. Ltd. (Shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, undergoing CIRP / in provisional liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities availed by Corporate Debtor leading to initiation of CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to Section 7 admission by NCLT Mumbai Bench. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding-up petition admitted by Bombay High Court on 05.10.2016; Provisional Liquidator appointed on 15.11.2017 who took possession of assets on 17.04.2018; Section 7 petition subsequently admitted by NCLT Mumbai; initial NCLAT judgment pronounced on 07.02.2020 dismissing appeal but inadvertently remarking that the Section 7 petition was not maintainable. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Four interlocutory applications (IA Nos. 811, 917, 962, and 1587 of 2020) filed under Rule 11 seeking rectification/clarification of clerical error in paragraph 5 of the 07.02.2020 judgment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In its original judgment dated 07.02.2020, NCLAT relied on the Supreme Court ruling in Forech India Ltd. but accidentally recorded that SREI's Section 7 petition was 'not maintainable' while dismissing the appeal; parties sought rectification under Rule 11.
legal_issues: Whether an error apparent on the face of the record where a Section 7 petition was accidentally recorded as 'not maintainable' instead of 'maintainable' under the Supreme Court doctrine in Forech India Ltd. can be rectified by NCLAT under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 allow the Tribunal to rectify clerical, inadvertent, or apparent errors on the face of the record to ensure the operative decision aligns with the binding legal ratio, provided it does not amount to a merits rehearing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 11 of the IBC bars only a Corporate Debtor from filing an application under Section 10 once a liquidation order is made; it does not bar a Financial Creditor from initiating Section 7 proceedings during the pendency of a winding-up petition, as established in Forech India Ltd. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison between the ratio decidendi applied in the body of the judgment and the conflicting operative recording in the concluding paragraph. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In accordance with Forech India Ltd., the Section 7 application by SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. was fully maintainable, and the word 'not-maintainable' in paragraph 5 was a clerical inadvertence subject to rectification under Rule 11; the shareholder's appeal remained dismissed.
operative_order: I.A. Nos. 811, 917, 962, and 1587 of 2020 are disposed of. Paragraph 5 of the judgment dated 07.02.2020 is rectified to explicitly hold that the Section 7 application filed by SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. is maintainable, while Action Barter's appeal remains dismissed without costs.
summary: Multiple IAs were filed under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules seeking modification/clarification of NCLAT's judgment dated 07.02.2020 in the appeal of Action Barter Pvt. Ltd. against SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. The Tribunal had correctly cited the Supreme Court precedent in Forech India Ltd. holding that pending winding-up petitions before a High Court do not bar a Section 7 IBC application by a financial creditor, yet inadvertently recorded in paragraph 5 that the Section 7 petition was 'not maintainable'. Exercising inherent powers under Rule 11, the NCLAT rectified the typographical/conceptual slip to declare the Section 7 petition maintainable while maintaining the dismissal of the shareholder's appeal.

case_title: Indian Overseas Bank vs. Arvind Kumar, Resolution Professional of M/s Richa Industries Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Indian Overseas Bank (Issuing Bank/Financial Creditor) and Respondent Arvind Kumar (Resolution Professional/Liquidator of M/s. Richa Industries Ltd., Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of an irrevocable Bank Guarantee by Appellant Bank for Rs. 4,01,94,954/- in favour of beneficiary M/s. Tata Steel Processing & Distribution Ltd. against a cash margin money deposit of Rs. 40,50,000/- placed in a Fixed Deposit Receipt (FDR) by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bank Guarantee invoked by beneficiary for Rs. 4,01,94,954/-; margin money held in FDR (principal Rs. 40,50,000/- plus accrued interest Rs. 10,77,591/-) totaled Rs. 51,27,591/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 17.12.2018 with Section 14 moratorium; IRP appointed 21.12.2018; beneficiary invoked Bank Guarantee on 24.12.2018 and 26.12.2018; payment made and margin money adjusted on 27.12.2018; RP filed CA No. 95 of 2019 under Section 60(5) for refund. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Irrevocable bank guarantee agreement; FDR containing margin money specifically earmarked and liened as collateral for honoring the bank guarantee upon invocation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed RP's CA No. 95 of 2019 on 29.04.2020 directing the Bank to release the margin money of Rs. 51,27,591/- to the RP, holding that adjustment during moratorium violated Section 14(1)(c); Bank appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether margin money deposited by a corporate debtor in the form of a fixed deposit to secure an irrevocable bank guarantee constitutes 'security interest' or an asset of the corporate debtor protected by the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, and whether the issuing bank is entitled to appropriate/adjust the margin money towards honoring the guarantee invoked during the moratorium period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Margin money deposited for securing a bank guarantee constitutes an earmarked commercial contribution that is held in trust to honor the guarantee obligation. It does not constitute a 'security interest' under Section 3(31) of the IBC, is exempt from Section 14 moratorium, and does not require registration of a charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(c) read with Section 14(3) and Section 3(31) proviso of IBC; because performance guarantees and invoked bank guarantees are shielded from moratorium restrictions, the earmarked margin money supporting them automatically appropriates towards payment upon invocation, leaving no revertible asset for the Corporate Debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Nature of deposit; verifying whether the margin money is tied to an active, validly invoked irrevocable bank guarantee or remains an unencumbered free balance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bank guarantee was lawfully invoked on 27.12.2018 under Section 14(3), and the margin money was properly adjusted towards payment; the RP had no legal right to seek release of the consumed funds.
operative_order: Appeal is partly allowed. The impugned direction of the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh) in CA No. 95 of 2019 ordering the release of Rs. 51,27,591/- margin money to the Resolution Professional is set aside. No order as to costs.
summary: Indian Overseas Bank appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order directing it to release Rs. 51,27,591/- in margin money held in an FDR of the Corporate Debtor (Richa Industries Ltd.). The Bank had adjusted this margin money to satisfy an irrevocable bank guarantee invoked by Tata Steel Processing & Distribution Ltd. during the Section 14 moratorium. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order, holding that margin money is an earmarked contribution that does not constitute a 'security interest' under Section 3(31) of the IBC nor requires registration of a charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act. Under Section 14(3), bank guarantee invocation cannot be stayed, and upon invocation, the margin money is lawfully appropriated towards payment, leaving no asset for the RP to reclaim.

case_title: Kridhan Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. Venkatesan Sankaranarayan & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Kridhan Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (now Krish Steel And Trading Pvt. Ltd.) and anr. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 Venkatesan Sankaranarayan (erstwhile RP of Corporate Debtor Tecpro Systems Ltd.); Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (lead Financial Creditor holding ~85% voting share); Ramachandran Subramanian (appointed Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Tecpro Systems Ltd. initiated under Section 7 IBC by Edelweiss; Resolution Plan submitted by Kridhan Infrastructure approved by CoC on 08.03.2019 (89.92% majority) and confirmed by NCLT under Section 31 on 15.05.2019, proposing a total plan value of Rs. 470 Crores with incorporation of SPV Kridhan Projects Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete failure by Resolution Applicant to infuse upfront equity of Rs. 15 Crores within 7 days and make upfront payment of Rs. 50 Crores within 3 months post-approval; five extensions granted up to 15.11.2019; Rs. 5 Crore PBG forfeited. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 07.08.2017; Plan approved by NCLT 15.05.2019; 5th extension expired 15.11.2019; CoC voted 99.28% for liquidation on 11.11.2019; RP filed liquidation application under Section 33(3) in late November 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Over 8 months elapsed post-plan approval without equity infusion; RA's guarantor Candid Wealth Management reported annual revenue of only Rs. 3.38 Lakhs; RA's foreign subsidiaries defaulted to Union Bank of India (Hong Kong) for ~Rs. 750 Crores triggering compulsory winding up in Singapore; RA suffered net loss of Rs. 12.11 Crores on Rs. 21.17 Crore turnover as of 31.03.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi allowed CA No. 2683(PB)/2019 on 16.01.2020 ordering liquidation of Tecpro Systems Ltd. under Section 33(3) and forfeiting Rs. 5 Crore PBG; Resolution Applicant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in ordering liquidation under Section 33(3) of the IBC upon failure of the Successful Resolution Applicant to implement the approved resolution plan and infuse upfront funds despite multiple extensions, and whether NCLAT should exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 to grant further time for revival over liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 33(3) of the IBC, where an approved resolution plan is contravened by failure to adhere to mandatory financial timelines and commitments, liquidation must follow; inherent powers under Rule 11 cannot be invoked to subvert statutory timeframes or compel endless indulgences to a defaulting resolution applicant at the cost of asset value destruction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(3) read with Section 12 mandates strict adherence to statutory timelines; timely liquidation is preferred over indefinite resolution to preserve the economic value of assets. Section 61(4) restricts grounds of appeal against a liquidation order to material irregularity or fraud. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective appraisal of financial capacity; assessing whether the resolution applicant possessed demonstrable solvency and verified means (rejecting subjective asset-sale models and shell guarantors) to implement the plan within statutory time limits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Applicant utterly failed to infuse funds for over eight months post-approval; no material irregularity or fraud was demonstrated, making the liquidation order passed under Section 33(3) unimpeachable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 202 of 2020 is dismissed without costs. The liquidation order dated 16.01.2020 is affirmed. RA is permitted to withdraw the Rs. 15 Crores deposited in the escrow account pursuant to interim directions.
summary: Kridhan Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., whose resolution plan for Tecpro Systems Ltd. was approved under Section 31 in May 2019, appealed an NCLT order ordering liquidation under Section 33(3) and forfeiting its Rs. 5 Crore PBG due to failure to infuse Rs. 15 Crores equity and Rs. 50 Crores upfront payments over eight months. RA sought relief under Rule 11 to implement the plan. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that speed is the essence of IBC, timely liquidation is statutorily preferred over endless resolution delays, inherent powers cannot override express provisions of Section 33(3), and RA demonstrated severe financial incapacity and Section 29A disabilities.

case_title: Saurabh Bharatbhushan Jain vs. Excel Tubes & Cones & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Saurabh Bharatbhushan Jain (Shareholder & Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Sysco Industries Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 Excel Tubes & Cones (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 Kailash T. Shah (Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of paper tubes by Operational Creditor to Corporate Debtor for use in manufacturing finished LDPE products. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed in Section 9 application with alleged undisputed settlement amount of Rs. 21 Lakhs; Corporate Debtor counter-claimed damages of Rs. 32,00,000/- due to defective supplies. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Defective supplies raised internally and forwarded to OC on 06.07.2017; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 10.03.2018; Corporate Debtor replied on 13.03.2018 raising disputes on quality and plant rejection; settlement proposal sent on 05.07.2018 during proceedings. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 06.07.2017 from Head of Production to directors forwarded to OC detailing collapsed paper tube cores; reply dated 13.03.2018 requesting OC's QC personnel to inspect rejections; settlement proposal dated 05.07.2018 made without prejudice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitted the Section 9 petition CP (IB) 241/9/NCLT/AHM/2018 on 19.02.2020 relying on the settlement proposal as an admission of debt; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether contemporaneous emails complaining of defective goods and timely reply to a Section 8 demand notice constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, and whether a 'without prejudice' settlement proposal submitted during proceedings can be treated as an admission of debt to initiate CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC, an application must be rejected if there is a bona fide pre-existing dispute raised prior to or in reply to the statutory demand notice. A settlement proposal submitted without prejudice during litigation cannot be construed as an admission of liability or used to extinguish a genuine pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandates dismissal where notice of dispute has been received; 'dispute' under Section 5(6) is not limited to pending suits or arbitrations but encompasses bona fide assertions of breach of warranty, defective goods, and damages under Sections 13 and 59 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Mobilox Innovations plausibility standard; ascertaining whether the dispute regarding inferior quality was contemporaneous (July 2017 email) and not a spurious afterthought, bluster, or patently feeble legal argument. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The record proved a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding defective paper tubes dating back to June/July 2017; NCLT erred in admitting the petition based on a settlement offer. CIRP initiation was illegal.
operative_order: Appeal is allowed. The impugned admission order dated 19.02.2020 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad is set aside; appointment of IRP, moratorium, and all consequential actions are quashed. Corporate Debtor is restored to independent board management; Corporate Debtor to bear CIRP costs in first instance and recover same from Operational Creditor. No costs.
summary: Director of Sysco Industries Ltd. appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Excel Tubes & Cones for unpaid paper tube supplies. The NCLT had admitted the petition based on a settlement proposal dated 05.07.2018 as an undisputed debt acknowledgment. The NCLAT reversed the order, holding that contemporaneous emails dated 06.07.2017 and a prompt reply to the Section 8 demand notice proved a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods causing Rs. 32 Lakhs in damages under the Sale of Goods Act. In accordance with Mobilox Innovations, IBC cannot be used as a recovery forum, and without-prejudice settlement talks cannot override an existing dispute. CIRP quashed.

case_title: Kodeboyina Srinivas Krishna vs. PVM Innvensys Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kodeboyina Srinivas Krishna (Director of Corporate Debtor M/s C-Tel Infosystems Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 M/s PVM Innvensys Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 C-Tel Infosystems Pvt. Ltd. through IRP Shyam Arora. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Master Service Agreement dated 02.05.2014 and Managed Services Agreement dated 01.09.2014 for supply, installation, and management of GPS vehicle trackers for Hedonic Path Finder System (HPFS) projects for Telangana Excise Department. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed debt of Rs. 53,99,228/- consisting of Rs. 50,32,028/- for 804 trackers and Rs. 3,67,200/- for 30 Hippo trackers; default of Rs. 3,67,200/- (exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh threshold) admitted and unpaid at the time of petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purchase order for 30 trackers dated 11.12.2015/12.12.2015; Demand notice in Form 3 issued on 20.11.2018; Reply to demand notice dated 03.12.2018 admitting 30 trackers; Section 9 application filed on 08.12.2018 / 12.12.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase order dated 12.12.2015 and Tax Invoice No. 1122 dated 14.12.2015 for 30 Hippo GPS vehicle trackers; Axis Bank certificate confirming non-payment; Corporate Debtor's reply dated 03.12.2018 explicitly admitting receipt of 30 trackers without making payment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench V admitted the Section 9 application on 23.01.2020 based on the admitted, unpaid, and in-limitation debt of Rs. 3,67,200/-; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable and within limitation where the corporate debtor disputes a larger component of the claim (804 trackers) but admits receipt of and non-payment for a distinct smaller tranche (30 trackers) exceeding the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is only required to satisfy itself that an operational debt exceeding the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh is due, payable, and in default within the period of limitation, and is free from any pre-existing dispute; disputes regarding other independent invoice components do not bar CIRP initiation for the admitted default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 8 and 9 read with Section 5(21) of IBC; admission of supply and non-payment in the debtor's reply to the demand notice constitutes an indisputable operational debt and default under the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Corroboration of default; bank certificate and written admission of purchase and supply without contemporaneous proof of payment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor admitted receipt and non-payment of 30 GPS trackers worth Rs. 3,67,200/-, which fell within the three-year limitation period from 12.12.2015; NCLT correctly admitted the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 205 of 2020 is dismissed without costs. Interim stay on CoC constitution vacated; IRP directed to proceed with CIRP.
summary: Director of C-Tel Infosystems Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Delhi Bench V order admitting PVM Innvensys Pvt. Ltd.'s Section 9 petition. The Operational Creditor claimed Rs. 53,99,228/- covering 804 GPS trackers (Rs. 50.32 Lakhs) and 30 Hippo trackers (Rs. 3.67 Lakhs). While the Corporate Debtor disputed the 804 trackers, it expressly admitted receiving the 30 trackers under a December 2015 purchase order without making payment. The NCLAT affirmed the admission, holding that admission of an unpaid operational debt exceeding the Rs. 1 Lakh threshold within three years of default satisfies Section 9 requirements, notwithstanding disputes over other unproven claims. Appeal dismissed.

case_title: Jaideep Halwasiya vs. A. A. Infraproperties Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Jaideep Halwasiya (minority shareholder holding 12.5% equity and erstwhile Director); Respondent No. 1 AA Infraproperties Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 South City Projects (Kolkata) Ltd. (majority shareholder holding 87.5%); Respondent No. 3 Man Mohan Bagree (Director); Respondents 4 to 6 (newly appointed Directors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint corporate governance in AA Infraproperties Pvt. Ltd., holding 100% equity in Sri Lankan subsidiary Indocean Developers Pvt. Ltd. developing the 'ALTAIR' project in Colombo. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of mutual oppression and breach of trust; Respondent group allegedly altered Board control without quorum, while Appellant allegedly diluted R-1's equity in IDPL from 100% to 13.84%. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purported Board Meeting held 22.06.2019; alleged AGM held 24.09.2019 appointing Respondents 4-6 as Directors; EoGM notice issued 12.12.2019; EoGM held 04.01.2020 removing Appellant as Director. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lack of minutes or board resolutions under Section 118 for the 22.06.2019 meeting; unverified notice dated 05.08.2019 lacking proof of dispatch/service; passport and travel records demonstrating Respondent No. 3 was outside India on the AGM date (24.09.2019), negating valid quorum under Section 103(1)(b); shifting stands by Respondents asserting an unauthorized non-director employee chaired the meeting. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 264/KB/2020 alleging oppression and mismanagement under Section 241/242 along with IA No. 131/KB/2020 seeking interim stay of director appointments and removal; NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the IA on 21.02.2020; Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing interim relief under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 by relying on questioned meeting notices where a prima facie case of fabricated corporate meetings, lack of quorum, and illegal director removal was established.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal is empowered to grant interim relief regulating company affairs pending probe into oppression and mismanagement where a petitioner demonstrates a strong prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury. The Tribunal cannot base a prima facie refusal on disputed notices whose service, authenticity, and quorum are the subject of serious challenge. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) read with Sections 103, 118, and 241 of the Companies Act, 2013; where serious questions exist regarding statutory compliance and fraudulent ouster of a minority director without quorum, interim status quo must be maintained to prevent irreversible prejudice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prima facie evaluation and balance of convenience test; assessing whether the petitioner raised fair, substantial questions requiring trial rather than accepting contested documents at face value. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant established a strong prima facie case of non-service of notices and absence of statutory quorum for the AGM and EoGM; NCLT's approach was fundamentally flawed.
operative_order: Appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 21.02.2020 is set aside. The appointment of Respondents 4 to 6 as Directors and the removal of the Appellant as Director are stayed pending final decision of CP No. 264/KB/2020 by NCLT Kolkata. No costs.
summary: A 12.5% minority shareholder and director appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order rejecting interim relief under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013. The Appellant alleged that the majority shareholder fabricated an AGM on 24.09.2019 to induct three new directors and an EoGM on 04.01.2020 to oust him, without serving statutory notices or meeting quorum rules under Section 103 (the sole other director being abroad). NCLAT allowed the appeal and reversed the NCLT order, holding that the Appellant raised substantial, credible questions of fraud and non-service that warranted interim protection. The appointment of the new directors and the removal of the Appellant were stayed pending trial.

case_title: Mrs. Rita Kapur vs. Invest Care Real Estate LLP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mrs. Rita Kapur (Investor/Partner); Respondent No. 1 Invest Care Real Estate LLP (Corporate Debtor); Respondents 2 to 4 (Promoting and Designated Partners). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant initially advanced Rs. 40 Lakhs as a loan under a Loan Agreement dated 09.07.2013 to Respondent No. 1 LLP to be repaid in four installments; late husband had also invested Rs. 1 Crore. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default in repayment of Rs. 40 Lakhs principal plus interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan advanced July 2013; Amended Agreement executed 01.12.2013 admitting 40 investors as partners; Supplementary Agreement executed on 25.03.2014 converting loans into partner capital; Section 7 application filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Amended Agreement dated 01.12.2013 signed by Appellant at S.No. 29; Supplementary Agreement dated 25.03.2014 registered with ROC converting debt to equity/capital contribution; Auditor certificates confirming investment as capital contribution. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench VI rejected the Section 7 petition CP (IB) 987 of 2019 on 26.11.2019 under Section 7(5), holding that the investment had been converted into capital/equity and therefore did not constitute financial debt; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an advance originally disbursed as a loan retains the character of 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC after it has been converted into equity/partner's capital contribution in an LLP, and whether the investor can maintain an application as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 7.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a loan or debt is converted into equity or partner's capital contribution, it loses the commercial character of a debt disbursed against consideration for the time value of money; the contributor assumes the status of a partner/equity holder and cannot initiate CIRP as a Financial Creditor under Section 7 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict interpretation of Section 5(7) ('Financial Creditor') and Section 5(8) ('Financial Debt'); conversion of debt into capital contribution is antithetical to a subsisting debtor-creditor relationship required to maintain a Section 7 petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of registered statutory filings and partnership deeds confirming conversion of debt to capital contribution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Appellant's loan was converted into capital contribution under agreements executed in 2013 and 2014, there existed no subsisting financial debt or debtor-creditor relationship; the Section 7 application was rightly rejected.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 111 of 2020 is dismissed without costs. Interim orders vacated. Liberty is granted to the Appellant to approach appropriate civil/company forums for redressal.
summary: Rita Kapur appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting her Section 7 application against Invest Care Real Estate LLP. The Appellant claimed she advanced a loan of Rs. 40 Lakhs in 2013 which was never repaid. The Respondent demonstrated that under subsequent Amended and Supplementary Agreements executed in 2013 and 2014 and registered with ROC, all 40 investors, including the Appellant, became partners and their loans were converted into capital contributions. The NCLAT affirmed the rejection, holding that once a debt is converted into capital, it ceases to be a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8), and the contributor is not a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(7). Remedies lie before other civil forums, not the IBC.

case_title: Prakash Kalash vs. Apeejay Surrendra Park Hotels Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Prakash Kalash (Shareholder & Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Gurusukh Vintrade Service Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 M/s Apeejay Surrendra Park Hotels Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 Teena Saraswat Pandey (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and Technical Services Agreement (MTSA) for pre-operation consultancy, staff training, and operation/management of Corporate Debtor's hotel at Raipur, Chhattisgarh. 3.
