DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed unpaid operational debt of Rs. 1,45,99,236/- (Principal Rs. 1,25,63,786/- + Interest Rs. 20,35,450/- @ 24% p.a.) for the period from 01.01.2018 to 20.05.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MTSA executed; operational disputes raised in emails dated 14.07.2018, 17.10.2018, 17.01.2019, and 14.03.2019; Section 8 demand notices issued 22.03.2019 and 21.05.2019; Section 9 petition filed June/July 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 14.07.2018 objecting to false entries on barter ledgers; email dated 17.10.2018 protesting issuance of unauthorized post-dated cheques of Rs. 73 Lakhs to itself; email dated 17.01.2019 complaining of poor service quality; email dated 14.03.2019 terminating management for non-performance; unserved postal notice returned for insufficient address followed immediately by newspaper publication without attempting email service. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack proceeded ex-parte based on newspaper publication and admitted the Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 62/CTB/2019 on 14.11.2019; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an ex-parte order of CIRP admission based on substituted service by newspaper publication without attempting service via email is legally sustainable under Order V Rule 20 CPC and Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules; and whether contemporaneous pre-demand notice emails raising complaints of non-performance and unauthorized ledger entries establish a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot resort to substituted service by newspaper publication without first exhausting ordinary and electronic modes of service like email, or satisfying itself that the respondent is deliberately evading service. Furthermore, where genuine disputes regarding deficient services and financial irregularities are raised in writing prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice, a pre-existing dispute exists, mandating dismissal of a Section 9 application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) read with Section 5(6); a 'dispute' includes assertions of breach of representation, quality deficiencies, or unauthorized financial acts communicated prior to the statutory notice. Order V Rule 20 CPC applies to service procedures before NCLT. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of pre-notice correspondence under the Mobilox Innovations standard to distinguish between genuine, contemporaneous controversy and spurious afterthoughts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ex-parte order was vitiated by improper substituted service, and the emails dated July 2018 through March 2019 established a real pre-existing dispute; NCLT erred in admitting the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: Appeal is allowed. The impugned admission order dated 14.11.2019 passed by NCLT Cuttack is set aside; appointment of IRP, moratorium, and all consequential actions are declared illegal and quashed. The Section 9 application is dismissed, and NCLT is directed to close proceedings and fix the IRP's fee. No costs.
summary: Director of Gurusukh Vintrade Service Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an ex-parte NCLT Cuttack order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Apeejay Surrendra Park Hotels Ltd. for alleged hotel management dues of Rs. 1.45 Crores. The NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission, holding that substituted service by newspaper publication was invalidly ordered without attempting service via email, violating Order V Rule 20 CPC. Furthermore, emails sent between July 2018 and March 2019 proved a serious pre-existing dispute concerning improper barter ledger entries, substandard service, and unauthorized issuance of post-dated cheques of Rs. 73 Lakhs well before the Section 8 demand notice. Under Mobilox Innovations, the Section 9 petition was unmaintainable.

case_title: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. vs. Kotak Mahindra Prime Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. (Trustee of Phoenix Trust FY 16-18, Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 1 Kotak Mahindra Prime Ltd. (Lender/Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 Jitendra Lohia (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Sunitti Papers Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Vehicle/equipment loan facility availed by Corporate Debtor from Respondent No. 1 repayable by automated Electronic Clearance Service (ECS) monthly debits from ICICI Bank account. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Deduction of 4 ECS instalments totaling Rs. 2,24,792/- by ICICI Bank and credited to Respondent No. 1 between 05.12.2019 and 05.03.2020 during the CIRP moratorium period. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 06.11.2019 imposing Section 14 moratorium; RP instructed ICICI Bank to freeze ECS debits on 04.12.2019; Respondent No. 1 submitted its belated financial claim on 01.05.2020; NCLT passed impugned order on 06.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Automated loan agreements and ECS mandates entered into prior to CIRP; automated debits occurred post-moratorium due to banking execution delay; NCLT directed RP to adjust Rs. 2,24,792/- against admitted claim and admit balance. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench directed RP on 06.07.2020 to verify Respondent No. 1's claim and treat ECS deductions received during moratorium as adjusted against the claim; Appellant challenged this under Section 61 alleging preferential treatment violating Section 14.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority committed an error in directing the Resolution Professional to adjust routine loan EMIs deducted via automated ECS mandates during the moratorium period against the creditor's overall admitted financial claim, or whether such deductions constitute impermissible preferential transactions requiring refund.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging routine procedural directions issued to a Resolution Professional to verify a financial claim and adjust automated post-commencement EMI deductions against the total claim is premature. If an automated debit represents an avoidable preference, the statutory remedy is an application under Section 43 of the IBC, not a summary challenge under Section 14. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 read with Section 43 of the IBC; mere routine automated deduction of pre-existing loan EMIs does not automatically invite appellate interference where the Adjudicating Authority directs equitable adjustment against the verified claim balance. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ripeness and prejudice test; examining whether an order directing claim verification and net calculation causes actionable legal injury warranting appellate intervention. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Directions to verify claims and reconcile adjusted EMIs do not constitute a final determination of preferential transfer; the appeal was premature and rightly dismissed by the majority.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 749 of 2020 is dismissed at the threshold by majority decision without costs.
summary: Phoenix ARC appealed against an NCLT Kolkata Bench order directing the RP of Sunitti Papers Pvt. Ltd. to reconsider Kotak Mahindra Prime Ltd.'s claim and treat Rs. 2,24,792/- deducted through automated ECS mandates during the moratorium as adjusted against its claim. The Appellant argued this violated Section 14 and constituted preferential treatment. The NCLAT (majority) dismissed the appeal as premature, holding that routine directions to verify and net off claims do not warrant appellate interference. If the deductions constituted an invalid preference, the appropriate statutory recourse for the RP was an avoidance application under Section 43 of the IBC.

case_title: Deepakk Kumar vs. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Review Application No. 09 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 848 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Review Applicant/Appellant Deepakk Kumar (Director of Sovereign Infrastructure & Developers Ltd., Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 M/s Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. (Assignee of Karnataka Bank, Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 Sovereign Infrastructure & Developers Ltd. through RP Goutham Shivshankar. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility originally sanctioned by Karnataka Bank, assigned to Phoenix ARC, and subsequently augmented with an 'Acceptance of Loan Assignment Agreement' and a fresh financing agreement of Rs. 5 Crores executed on 09.06.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in the original facility occurred in November 2012; balance outstanding on fresh loan facility was Rs. 2.5 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Initial default November 2012; assignment acceptance agreement executed on 09.06.2016; Section 7 petition filed on 05.09.2018 / 06.09.2018 before NCLT Bengaluru; NCLAT dismissed main appeal on 05.03.2020; Review application filed under Section 420(2). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Executed Acceptance of Loan Assignment Agreement dated 09.06.2016 signed by Corporate Debtor and directors; fresh loan documentation and partial repayments made towards the restructured debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 848 of 2019 on 05.03.2020 holding the Section 7 petition within limitation due to acknowledgment; Appellant filed Review Application No. 09 of 2020 alleging error apparent on face of record under Section 420(2) of Companies Act read with Rule 11.
legal_issues: Whether NCLAT possesses statutory jurisdiction under the IBC, 2016, Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, or Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules to review and rehear its own final judgment on questions of law regarding limitation and acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The power of review is not an inherent power but a creation of statute; neither the IBC, 2016 nor the NCLAT Rules, 2016 confer power on the Appellate Tribunal to review its own final judgments. Inherent powers under Rule 11 cannot be invoked to exercise a review jurisdiction or rehear a matter on merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 is limited to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for rectifying mistakes apparent from the record and cannot be imported into the IBC to enable NCLAT to exercise substantive review. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Patent error vs. debatable issue; an error apparent on the face of the record must be self-evident without elaborate argument; re-examining the legal effect of an acknowledgment constitutes an appellate exercise, not a reviewable slip. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Re-hearing a decided appeal on the legal correctness of applying Section 18 of the Limitation Act is impermissible in the absence of express statutory review jurisdiction. The review application is incompetent.
operative_order: Review Application No. 09 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 848 of 2019 is dismissed without costs.
summary: Director of Sovereign Infrastructure & Developers Ltd. filed a review application under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act read with Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules seeking to review NCLAT's final judgment dated 05.03.2020, which held Phoenix ARC's Section 7 application within limitation based on an assignment and acknowledgment agreement dated 09.06.2016. Applicant contended that an acknowledgment made more than three years after the initial 2012 default was an error apparent on the face of the record. NCLAT dismissed the review application, holding that review is a creature of statute not provided for under the IBC or NCLAT Rules, Rule 11 cannot create review powers, and Section 420(2) applies only to NCLT. The applicant's remedy lay solely before the Supreme Court.

case_title: Kundan Care Products Ltd. vs. Amit Gupta & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kundan Care Products Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 Amit Gupta (Resolution Professional of Astonfield Solar (Gujarat) Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 Export Import Bank of India (CoC Member); Respondent No. 3 Power Finance Corporation Ltd.; Respondent No. 4 Astonfield Renewables Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Astonfield Solar (Gujarat) Pvt. Ltd. under CP No. (IB) - 940(ND)/2018 where Appellant submitted a Resolution Plan which was approved by the CoC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unilateral attempt by the Successful Resolution Applicant to withdraw its approved Resolution Plan and seek cancellation and refund of its Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under IBC; Appellant emerged as highest bidder (H1) and its Resolution Plan was approved by CoC by requisite majority; application under Section 31 filed before NCLT; Appellant filed IA No. 1679/2019 seeking withdrawal of plan due to commercial unviability and CIRP delays. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan containing binding commitments; absence of any clause treating the plan as a contract of personal service or permitting unilateral withdrawal; PBG submitted under CIRP Regulations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Special Bench Court-II rejected IA 1679/2019 on 03.07.2020 holding that it had no jurisdiction to permit withdrawal of a CoC-approved plan and that the issue was sub-judice before the Supreme Court; Resolution Applicant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a Successful Resolution Applicant has a legal right under the IBC to withdraw its Resolution Plan after it has been approved by the Committee of Creditors and is pending before the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the power or jurisdiction to permit such withdrawal on grounds of delay or commercial unviability.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Successful Resolution Applicant whose plan has been approved by the Committee of Creditors cannot be permitted to withdraw its Resolution Plan or resile from its obligations. The IBC does not confer any power or jurisdiction on the Adjudicating Authority to allow withdrawal of a CoC-approved resolution plan, as doing so would defeat the time-bound objectives of CIRP and push corporate debtors into liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 30 and 31 read with Section 25(2)(h) and Section 61(3) of the IBC; once approved by the CoC, the resolution plan becomes a binding commitment from which the applicant is estopped by conduct from wriggling out. The business decision of the CoC is not open to judicial review. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Estoppel and finality test; once rival bidders are eliminated and the CoC approves the plan, the applicant cannot plead commercial unviability or passage of time to walk away with impunity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to permit withdrawal of an approved plan. The principles laid down in Educomp Solutions apply squarely, making the appeal meritless.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 653 of 2020 is dismissed without costs. The NCLT order rejecting the withdrawal application and prayer for PBG refund is affirmed.
summary: Kundan Care Products Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant for Astonfield Solar (Gujarat) Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application to withdraw its resolution plan and obtain a refund of its PBG. The Appellant contended that inordinate CIRP delays had rendered the plan commercially unviable. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that there is no provision under the IBC permitting a successful resolution applicant to make a U-turn and withdraw an approved plan. Under the precedent in Educomp Solutions, the resolution plan approved by the CoC is binding, the applicant is estopped by conduct from withdrawing after eliminating competing bidders, and the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to permit withdrawal.

case_title: Siva Rama Krishna Prasad vs. S. Rajendran, Official Liquidator of M/s Krishna Industrial Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Dr. Siva Rama Krishna Prasad (Erstwhile Promoter/Director of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 S. Rajendran (RP/Liquidator of M/s Krishna Industrial Corporation Ltd., Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 Maximus Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated against Krishna Industrial Corporation Ltd. by Financial Creditor Maximus ARC under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt obligations leading to Section 7 admission; operations of the Corporate Debtor were completely defunct. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted; CIRP period expired; Expression of Interest (EoI) floated by RP evoked no viable bids even within extended timelines; CoC unanimously voted to liquidate; RP filed MA/376/2020 under Section 33(2) for liquidation; Promoter filed application under Section 60(5)(c) to stay liquidation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: No Expression of Interest or Resolution Plan was received by CoC during the entire CIRP; Promoter presented vague settlement discussions without concrete proof of investor capability, funding source, or viable terms. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai rejected the Promoter's application to defer liquidation and allowed RP's MA/376/2020 on 27.07.2020 ordering liquidation under Section 33(2); Promoter filed Company Appeal Nos. 751 and 752 of 2020 under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is bound to order liquidation under Section 33(2) of the IBC when the CoC unanimously resolves to liquidate the Corporate Debtor in the absence of any resolution plan, notwithstanding an informal settlement proposal submitted by the erstwhile promoter.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where no resolution plan is received during the CIRP period and the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom resolves to liquidate the corporate debtor under Section 33(2), the Adjudicating Authority has no option but to order liquidation. A vague or unverified settlement proposal from an erstwhile promoter cannot be thrust upon the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) explanation (as inserted by Act 26 of 2019); primacy lies entirely with the CoC, which is empowered to liquidate the corporate debtor at any stage prior to confirmation of a resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom test; determining whether an actionable, concrete, and funded resolution plan exists, or whether the proposal is an unsubstantiated offer dependent on subsequent asset liquidations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: With zero resolution plans before the CoC and a unanimous vote for liquidation, the NCLT had no legal alternative but to pass an order of liquidation under Section 33(2).
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 751 of 2020 and 752 of 2020 are dismissed without costs. The liquidation order dated 27.07.2020 passed by NCLT Chennai is affirmed.
summary: Erstwhile promoter of Krishna Industrial Corporation Ltd. appealed against NCLT Chennai orders rejecting his plea to defer liquidation and ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor under Section 33(2) of the IBC. Appellant contended he had proposed a settlement and the debt-to-asset ratio was favourable. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that because no Expression of Interest or resolution plan was received during CIRP, and the CoC unanimously resolved to liquidate, the Adjudicating Authority had no option but to order liquidation. Settlement proposals cannot be forced upon the CoC against its commercial wisdom. The promoter remains at liberty to submit a scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act during liquidation if eligible.

case_title: Anshul Vashistha vs. Jayhind Steel Traders & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Anshul Vashistha is a shareholder and suspended director of Corporate Debtor M/s Saturn Prefab India Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); Respondent No. 1 M/s Jayhind Steel Traders is the Operational Creditor; Dr. Shri G.K. Saraswat is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Running account business transactions for the supply of Angles, Channels, TMP, and GP/CR/GC Sheets by Respondent No. 1 to the Corporate Debtor for site fabrication and roofing projects under various purchase orders containing different credit terms (30 to 60 days) and arbitration clauses. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed a total defaulted amount of Rs. 1,81,61,422 (including principal and interest across invoices dated April 2016 to March 2018), while Demand Notice Form 3 claimed Rs. 1,56,25,154; date of first default was alleged as 2016-11-30. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Operational Creditor issued a demand notice under Section 8(1) in Form 3 on 2018-06-13, served on 2018-06-20; original petition CP (IB) No. 374/9/NCLT/AHM/2018 was filed on 2018-07-11. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor sent an email on 2018-02-05 demanding payment, to which Corporate Debtor replied on 2018-02-29/2018-03-29 disputing ledger mismatch, missing purchase order numbers on invoices, lack of test certificates, and rejected materials lying at the site following ultrasonic testing; 27 invoices totaling Rs. 1,04,19,944 were disputed as fabricated/false. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad) admitted the Section 9 petition on 2020-03-13 holding that debt above Rs. 1 lakh was due, default occurred on 2016-11-30, and no pre-existing dispute existed prior to demand notice.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when the parties maintain a running account requiring reconciliation of conflicting invoice claims and the Corporate Debtor raised issues regarding defective/rejected goods and ledger mismatches prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An undisputed debt that is due and payable is a sine qua non for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9; the IBC is not a recovery forum, and an application must be rejected where there is a genuine pre-existing dispute or where unsettled running accounts require extensive reconciliation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandates rejection of an application if a notice of dispute has been received; communication highlighting mismatched accounts, missing purchase orders, and rejected materials constitutes a valid pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the standard laid down in Mobilox Innovations, the dispute must be real and substantiated by pre-demand correspondence rather than a spurious or illusory defense; an Adjudicating Authority cannot sit to adjudicate, settle, or reconcile running accounts to determine the debt due. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because an email disputing invoices and citing rejected materials was issued prior to the Section 8 demand notice, a plausible pre-existing dispute existed, rendering admission of the Section 9 petition unsustainable.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; the impugned order dated 2020-03-13 passed by NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad admitting CIRP, appointing IRP, declaring moratorium, and constituting the CoC is set aside and declared illegal; Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP rigours to function independently through its Board; Corporate Debtor shall initially bear CIRP costs incurred by IRP/RP with liberty to recover the same from the Operational Creditor; no order as to costs.
summary: Anshul Vashistha, suspended director of Saturn Prefab India Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by operational creditor Jayhind Steel Traders for alleged unpaid steel supplies amounting to Rs. 1.81 crores. The appellant demonstrated that prior to the Section 8 demand notice, the corporate debtor had sent an email flagging ledger discrepancies, lack of test certificates, and rejected materials lying at the site. The NCLAT held that the IBC cannot serve as a recovery mechanism to reconcile disputed running accounts. Setting aside the admission order, the Appellate Tribunal held that the pre-existing dispute barred initiation of CIRP.

case_title: Rajesh Mahajan vs. Park Network Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rajesh Mahajan is the suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s PP Telecell Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); Respondent No. 1 M/s Park Network Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 3 Mr. Ajay Goyal is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was the authorized distributor of Gionee mobile phones (manufactured by Syntech HK Technology Ltd.) and appointed Respondent No. 1 as sub-distributor vide Sub-Distribution Agreement dated 2015-04-15; distributor was contractually obligated to bear costs of price drops, sales schemes, unsaleable inventory, and sales returns. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 20,02,872 (comprising Rs. 13,49,770 pending claim amount under schemes and Rs. 6,53,102 pending claim in ledger) plus interest @ 8% p.a.; date of default was recorded as 2019-01-05. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 in Form 4 was issued on 2019-05-02; reply to demand notice disputing liability was sent by Corporate Debtor on 2019-05-21; Section 9 application was filed on 2019-07-18. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Emails dated 2019-01-03, 2019-01-05, and 2019-01-07 sent by Corporate Debtor attaching claim summary and ledger account acknowledging dues of Rs. 20,02,872, alongside an unaccepted settlement offer by the manufacturer to settle at 50% via billing of handsets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench V admitted the Section 9 application vide order dated 2020-05-27 in CP No. (IB) 1717 (ND)/2019.
legal_issues: Whether outstanding monetary claims arising out of price protection, sales return of unactivated stock, and promotional schemes under a sub-distribution contract constitute an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC, and whether the distributor's post-demand disclaimer of liability amounts to a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Liabilities arising under a bilateral commercial distribution agreement—including adjustments for price drops, incentive schemes, and sales returns—fall within the scope of claims in respect of the provision of goods and services, constituting an operational debt under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) encompasses claims arising from the operational matrix of supplying and distributing goods, including credits for unactivated stock returns; an evasive defense in reply to a Section 8 notice contrary to admitted ledger entries does not satisfy Section 8(2)(a). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, a defense disputing privity of contract or liability is illusory and moonshine when contradicted by clear written admissions and ledger statements issued by the Corporate Debtor itself. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt of Rs. 20,02,872 was an operational debt exceeding the statutory threshold, default occurred upon failure to discharge admitted ledger dues, and the dispute raised was illusory, justifying CIRP admission.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order dated 2020-05-27 passed by NCLT Delhi Bench V admitting the Section 9 application affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Rajesh Mahajan, suspended director of PP Telecell Marketing Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT order admitting a Section 9 application filed by sub-distributor Park Network Pvt. Ltd. The Corporate Debtor had acknowledged outstanding dues of Rs. 20,02,872 towards promotional schemes, price protection, and sales returns in its ledger and email correspondence following the cessation of Gionee operations. The Corporate Debtor subsequently resisted the claim, arguing that sub-distribution adjustments do not qualify as operational debt and that manufacturer liability precluded privity. The NCLAT held that claims under a distribution agreement constitute operational debt and dismissed the appeal, characterizing the defense as imaginary.

case_title: Naresh Kumar Sharma & Ors. vs. Shekhar Resorts Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Naresh Kumar Sharma, Chandra Shekar Sharma, and K.K. Sharma are ex-promoters/suspended management of Corporate Debtor Shekhar Resorts Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Respondent No. 2 M/s NCJ Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant; Vikram Kumar is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities from Financial Creditor Oriental Bank of Commerce, secured against assets including the 5-star Hotel Orient Taj in Agra and land parcels in Mauja Basai Mustakil and Greater Noida. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial default of Rs. 19,67,64,134 including interest owed to Oriental Bank of Commerce. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition CP No. 22/ND/2018 admitted on 2018-09-11; Committee of Creditors approved Respondent No. 2's Resolution Plan with 100% voting share in its 15th meeting on 2019-06-04; Plan approved by Adjudicating Authority on 2020-07-24 in CA-441/ND/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants challenged the resolution plan value of Rs. 143.50 Crores, asserting circle rate valuation of Rs. 410-490 Crores against RP-ascertained fair value of Rs. 157.12 Crores and liquidation value of Rs. 125.92 Crores; prior 2016 SARFAESI auction failed to elicit bidders even at a reserve price of Rs. 110 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Delhi Bench III approved the Resolution Plan under Section 31(1); Appellants challenged the approval under Section 61(3) alleging single-member reconstitution during COVID-19 and undervaluation.
legal_issues: Whether an approved Resolution Plan can be challenged by suspended management on grounds that the offer is lower than fair value or circle rates, and whether the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a plan satisfying all claims is subject to judicial review under Section 61(3) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating business viability and approving a resolution plan is non-justiciable; the IBC does not mandate that the resolution offer match or exceed the fair value or liquidation value of the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial review under Section 31(1) read with Section 61(3) is confined strictly to the grounds enumerated under Section 30(2), and the Adjudicating or Appellate Authority lacks jurisdiction to test the quantitative adequacy of financial bids. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Maharashtra Seamless and K. Shashidhar, absent any demonstrated material irregularity or violation of law, CoC decisions taken with requisite statutory majorities cannot be disturbed on equitable claims of undervaluation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan satisfied all statutory criteria under Section 30(2), provided 100% recovery to all creditors, and was approved by 100% CoC voting share, rendering the promoters' appeal non-maintainable and devoid of merit.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed at the threshold stage as non-maintainable and lacking merit; approval of the Resolution Plan affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Suspended directors of Shekhar Resorts Ltd. challenged the NCLT Delhi order approving a Rs. 143.50 crore Resolution Plan submitted by NCJ Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., alleging that the Corporate Debtor's hotel and real estate assets were worth over Rs. 410 crores. The Appellants also contested the hearing by a reconstituted single-member Special Bench. Relying on Supreme Court precedents in Maharashtra Seamless and K. Shashidhar, the NCLAT affirmed that the commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving a viable resolution plan with 100% voting share is non-justiciable and does not require matching fair or liquidation value, thereby dismissing the appeal.

case_title: S. Uma Devi vs. Sir M Visvesvaraya Co-operative Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant S. Uma Devi is a shareholder and director/guarantor of Corporate Debtor M/s Ind-lab Equipments Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 Sir M. Visvesvaraya Co-operative Bank Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 Addanki Haresh is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two term loans sanctioned to Corporate Debtor: first loan of Rs. 2,27,00,000 on 2014-09-25 (agreement dated 2014-10-01 at 15.50% interest) for industrial land purchase and factory construction; second loan of Rs. 48,00,000 on 2016-11-16 (agreement dated 2016-11-23), against which Rs. 33,46,000 was disbursed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 3,03,82,953 as on 2019-06-30 (comprising principal Rs. 2,40,06,843 and interest Rs. 63,76,110); date of default recorded as 2018-07-31. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor issued demand recall notice on 2018-08-20; Corporate Debtor replied on 2018-09-15 seeking time; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 319/BB/2019 was filed on 2019-09-11. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term loan agreements, personal guarantee bonds, and financial statements showing short-term borrowings rising to Rs. 3,79,28,638 and net operating loss of Rs. 89,97,077 for year ended 2019-03-31; out of Rs. 2.60 crores disbursed, only Rs. 1,08,11,399 was repaid. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Bengaluru Bench) admitted the Section 7 petition on 2020-02-19, rejecting debtor's unaccepted settlement proposals and technical objections regarding Form 1 defects.
legal_issues: Whether hyper-technical defects in Form 1 computation workings or absence of Banker's Books Evidence Act certification can defeat the admission of a Section 7 IBC application where debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold are manifest from the record, and whether rejected settlement proposals constitute a valid defense.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a financial debt due exceeds the statutory minimum threshold and that a default has occurred, initiation of CIRP under Section 7 is mandatory, irrespective of hyper-technical procedural omissions in the petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires proof of financial debt and default; minor defects in tabular workings in Form 1 are curable procedural technicalities that do not invalidate the application if essential loan documents and default records substantiate the claim. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantive loan agreements, guarantee bonds, ledger records showing substantial unserviced disbursements, and audited balance sheets reflecting operational distress establish default beyond dispute; unaccepted one-time settlement (OTS) offers corroborate rather than refute the existence of debt and default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Financial debt and default well above Rs. 1 lakh were incontrovertibly established on the record, justifying the admission of the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order dated 2020-02-19 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: S. Uma Devi, director and shareholder of Ind-lab Equipments Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Bengaluru Bench's admission of a Section 7 petition filed by Sir M. Visvesvaraya Co-operative Bank Ltd. for default in repayment of two term loans amounting to over Rs. 3.03 crores. The appellant raised procedural challenges, arguing that Form 1 lacked itemized computation tables, non-compliance with the Banker's Books Evidence Act, and that settlement proposals were disregarded. The NCLAT rejected these contentions, holding that admitted loan disbursals of over Rs. 2.60 crores against repayments of merely Rs. 1.08 crores conclusively established debt and default above the statutory threshold, affirming the admission order.

case_title: Arul Muthu Kumaara Samy vs. Registrar of Companies
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Arul Muthu Kumaara Samy is an ex-shareholder of M/s Chikara Eco Ventures Ltd.; Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (RoC), Chennai. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Administrative statutory striking off of the company name from the Register of Companies by RoC Chennai under Section 248 of the Companies Act, 2013, and subsequent restoration proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; appeal concerned condonation of an inordinate delay of 338 days in refiling the appeal paper book. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned restoration order was passed by NCLT Chennai on 2019-05-27; certified copy delivered on 2019-07-10; statutory 45-day limitation expired on 2019-08-24; appeal originally filed on 2019-08-28 (4 days late); defect memo issued on 2019-10-01 requiring cure within 7 days (by 2019-10-08); appeal refiled after 338 days on 2020-07-28 via IA No. 1774 of 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant cited translation of documents, obtaining records, and the nationwide COVID-19 lockdown from 2020-03-24 as reasons for the 338-day refiling delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant appealed the NCLT Chennai Bench order dated 2019-05-27 restoring the company name upon RoC/third-party appeal in CA No. 399(252) of 2019; Registry placed the matter before the Bench due to non-curation of defects within 7 days.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT possesses jurisdiction under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to condone a 338-day delay in refiling an appeal where defects were not cured within the mandatory 7-day period and the total delay exceeded the statutory outer limit of 45 days.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When procedural defects notified by the Registry are not cured within the prescribed 7-day period under Rule 26, subsequent refiling is treated as a fresh appeal; the Appellate Tribunal has no statutory power or jurisdiction to condone any delay exceeding the outer limit of 45 days provided under Section 421(3). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421(3) allows an extension of up to 45 days beyond the initial 45-day limitation period but not thereafter; this special limitation constitutes an express exclusion under Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, completely barring Section 5 condonation beyond the 90th day. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict statutory compliance standard as laid down in Union of India v. Popular Construction Company and Jitendra Virmani v. MRO Tek Realty Ltd.; inherent powers cannot override unambiguous statutory prohibitions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction to condone a 338-day delay in refiling, rendering the application and the appeal barred by limitation.
operative_order: IA No. 1774 of 2020 for condonation of 338 days delay is dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) No. 122 of 2020 is dismissed as barred by limitation; no order as to costs.
summary: Arul Muthu Kumaara Samy, ex-shareholder of Chikara Eco Ventures Ltd., filed an appeal challenging an NCLT Chennai order that restored the struck-off company to the register. The appeal was initially filed with a 4-day delay and returned by the Registry for defects, which the appellant failed to cure within 7 days as mandated by Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules, ultimately refiling after an unexplained delay of 338 days. The NCLAT held that failure to cure defects within 7 days causes the filing to be treated as a fresh appeal. Because Section 421(3) of the Companies Act bars condonation beyond the maximum 45-day grace period, the appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation.

case_title: Pankaj Kumar Mishra vs. Registrar of Companies, Mumbai & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Pankaj Kumar Mishra is the Ex-Director, majority shareholder, and Power of Attorney Holder of Viking Ship Managers Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Registrar of Companies, Mumbai; Respondent No. 2 is Principal Commissioner of Income Tax-15, Mumbai. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: RoC Mumbai struck off Viking Ship Managers Pvt. Ltd. from the Register of Companies under Section 248; Respondent No. 2 initiated reopening of assessment under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2011-12 regarding financial transactions where no tax returns were filed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Reassessment proceedings initiated under Section 148 for undisclosed income; striking off threatened Government revenue recovery. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 148 notice issued for AY 2011-12; Respondent No. 2 filed restoration petition under Section 252 before NCLT Mumbai in 2019; NCLT Mumbai allowed the petition on 2019-11-11 in CP No. 364/252/(MB)/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT record revealed that although Viking Ship Managers Pvt. Ltd. was arrayed as a respondent, no notice or show cause was ever served upon the company, its directors, or shareholders before passing the restoration order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai allowed the Income Tax Department's petition and ordered restoration of the company without issuing notice to the affected company; Ex-Director appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether an order passed by the NCLT under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 restoring the name of a struck-off company on an application by the Income Tax Department without issuing statutory show cause notice to the company or its directors violates natural justice and Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order restoring the name of a struck-off company under Section 252 without issuing notice and affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the company and concerned persons is void ab initio for violating principles of natural justice and mandatory statutory procedure. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 252(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 explicitly mandates that the Tribunal shall give a reasonable opportunity of making representations and being heard to the Registrar, the company, and all persons concerned prior to making an order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 requires the issuance of a show-cause notice accompanied by the petition copy to the respondent; absence of proof of service on record vitiates the adjudicatory order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's ex-parte restoration order without notice was unsustainable in law and liable to be set aside, requiring remand for a de novo hearing.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 2019-11-11 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench set aside; matter remitted back to NCLT Mumbai Bench to decide the Section 252 appeal afresh on merits after affording hearing to all parties; Appellant directed to appear before NCLT Mumbai on 2020-11-02; copy of order transmitted forthwith; no order as to costs.
summary: Pankaj Kumar Mishra, ex-director and majority shareholder of Viking Ship Managers Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order that restored the company's name to the register upon an application filed by the Income Tax Department under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013. The Income Tax Department sought revival to complete reassessment proceedings for AY 2011-12 under Section 148. The Appellate Tribunal found that NCLT passed the restoration order without serving notice on the company or its directors, directly violating the proviso to Section 252(1) and Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules. Setting aside the impugned order, the NCLAT remitted the matter for fresh adjudication.

case_title: Yajur Commodities Ltd. vs. Nanda Energy Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Yajur Commodities Ltd. is the Operational Creditor; Respondent Nanda Energy Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational supply transaction between the parties leading to an alleged unpaid operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified operational debt default forming the basis of the Section 9 petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petition was pending at pre-admission stage; pre-emptory appearance order passed on 2019-11-20 directing appearance on 2019-12-04; Section 9 petition dismissed for default on 2019-12-04; restoration application IA No. 142/IB/2020 dismissed on 2020-03-03. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: In IA No. 142/IB/2020, Appellant falsely asserted that Advocate V. Dinesh Raja appeared on 2019-12-04, filed a one-page written submission, and requested an adjournment, directly contradicting the judicial minutes of 2019-12-04 recording complete non-appearance despite pre-emptory directions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench-II Chennai dismissed the Section 9 petition for default on 2019-12-04, and dismissed IA No. 142/IB/2020 on 2020-03-03 due to contradictory and false averments; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an applicant seeking restoration of a petition dismissed for default under Rule 48(2) and Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 is barred by the doctrine of estoppel by record when pleading facts that directly contradict the tribunal's judicial record.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the doctrine of estoppel by record, a litigant is legally precluded from asserting facts in an application that contradict or belie the formal judicial proceedings and recorded minutes of the court. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Restoration under Rule 48(2) and Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules requires showing sufficient and bona fide cause; raising false assertions to explain a default does not constitute valid cause. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Minutes of court proceedings recorded in judicial orders are conclusive evidence of what transpired; any contrary self-serving assertion is barred by estoppel by record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Operational Creditor defaulted on pre-emptory directions and advanced false pleas contrary to the recorded record, no cogent ground for restoration was made out, warranting dismissal.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed for lack of merit; the order of NCLT Special Bench-II Chennai dated 2020-03-03 refusing restoration affirmed.
summary: Yajur Commodities Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Chennai refusing to restore its Section 9 IBC petition, which had been dismissed for default on 2019-12-04 after the appellant failed to appear despite peremptory orders. In its restoration application under Rules 48(2) and 11 of the NCLT Rules, the appellant claimed its counsel had appeared and filed written submissions. The NCLAT held that this claim was belied by the record, invoking the doctrine of estoppel by record to bar the appellant from falsifying judicial minutes. Finding that the creditor played hide-and-seek with the court, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Committee of Creditors Represented by IDBI Bank Ltd. vs. V. Venkata Sivakumar & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Committee of Creditors of the Corporate Debtor represented by IDBI Bank Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is V. Venkata Sivakumar (Resolution Professional confirmed as Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by IDBI Bank and CoC lenders to the Corporate Debtor, culminating in CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial defaults triggering CIRP; the statutory outer time limit of 330 days expired without an approved resolution plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP exceeded the maximum period of 330 days (inclusive of judicial intervention); CoC supported RP's extension application, which was rejected by NCLT Special Bench Chennai, ordering liquidation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: No exceptional circumstances were substantiated by the CoC to warrant an extension beyond 330 days under the Essar Steel framework; CoC challenged the appointment of the Liquidator alleging he lacked a valid Authorization for Assignment (AFA) under Regulation 7-A. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench Chennai rejected further CIRP extension beyond 330 days, ordered liquidation, and appointed the existing RP as Liquidator; CoC appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the expiration of the 330-day CIRP timeline without exceptional circumstances warrants an order of liquidation, and whether an alleged lack of Authorization for Assignment under Regulation 7-A renders the liquidation order invalid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Following the expiry of the maximum statutory period of 330 days for CIRP, liquidation of the corporate debtor is the mandated consequence unless extraordinary circumstances justifying extension are demonstrated; any procedural irregularity in the liquidator's authorization does not vitiate the liquidation order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 mandates strict adherence to the 330-day outer ceiling, and non-compliance with IBBI Regulation 7-A affects only the individual assignment of the IP, not the jurisdiction or validity of an order passed under Section 33. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Essar Steel, an extension beyond 330 days is an exceptional exception requiring proof that the delay was entirely attributable to judicial delay and that resolution was imminent; failure to substantiate this test makes liquidation inescapable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidation order was legally sound; any challenge to the Liquidator's Regulation 7-A authorization could be addressed via a separate application before the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of; order of liquidation upheld; liberty granted to the Appellant to bring any irregularity regarding Respondent No. 1's authorization under Regulation 7-A to the notice of the Adjudicating Authority to have a re-look at the appointment of the Liquidator.
summary: The Committee of Creditors led by IDBI Bank appealed an order of NCLT Chennai ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor after refusing to extend the CIRP beyond the maximum prescribed period of 330 days. The CoC also challenged the appointment of the Resolution Professional as Liquidator on the ground that he lacked a valid Authorization for Assignment under Regulation 7-A of the IBBI Regulations. The NCLAT held that absent exceptional circumstances under the Essar Steel doctrine, the liquidation order was valid. It further ruled that any irregularity concerning the Liquidator's AFA did not invalidate the liquidation order, granting liberty to approach the NCLT for substitution.

case_title: JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. Samay Electronics Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Respondent Samay Electronics Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial assistance/credit facilities extended to the Corporate Debtor, subsequently assigned to the Appellant asset reconstruction company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial debt exceeding the statutory threshold under Section 7. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor filed Section 7 application; division bench of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court I pronounced split orders on 2020-02-26. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Split verdict delivered by two-member bench: Technical Member ordered admission of the Section 7 petition, while Judicial Member delivered a dissenting order rejecting the petition as barred by limitation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Instead of referring the split verdict to the President of NCLT under Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, conflicting orders were issued; Financial Creditor appealed under Section 61 seeking a reference to a third Member.
legal_issues: Whether a division bench of the NCLT delivering an evenly split verdict on admission versus limitation dismissal must refer the points of difference to the President of NCLT under Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 for decision by a third member.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the members of an Adjudicating Authority bench are equally divided in opinion on any point, they cannot dispose of the matter with conflicting orders; they are statutorily required to state the points of difference and refer them to the President for hearing by a third member. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 is mandatory; when a split verdict occurs, the final decision must follow the opinion of the majority of the members who heard the case, including the third member nominated by the President. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct examination of the two contradictory orders dated 2020-02-26 establishing a 1:1 judicial stalemate without a majority operative determination. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench erred in terminating proceedings with conflicting orders without complying with Section 419(5), warranting an order directing reference to the President of NCLT.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with directions to the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-I to make a reference to the Hon'ble President, NCLT, under Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, to place the matter before a third Member so that the petition can be decided in accordance with majority opinion; copy of the order directed to be transmitted forthwith to the bench and the President, NCLT.
summary: JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. appealed after a division bench of NCLT Ahmedabad delivered a split verdict on its Section 7 petition against Samay Electronics Pvt. Ltd., where the Technical Member allowed admission while the Judicial Member dismissed the petition on limitation grounds. The bench failed to refer the disagreement to a third member. The NCLAT held that under Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, an equally divided bench cannot issue conflicting final orders and must refer the points of difference to the President of NCLT. The Appellate Tribunal remitted the matter for reference to a third member for a majority determination.

case_title: Akbar Kothawala vs. Megamet Steels Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Akbar Kothawala is the erstwhile Promoter and Managing Director of Corporate Debtor Supreme Startech Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); Respondent No. 1 Megamet Steels Private Limited is the Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 3 Pawan Kumar Ramdhan Agarwal is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business relations since 2017 involving marketing of industrial goods and supplying Road Bitumen; timely payments made for bitumen purchases with no bills pending. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default of Rs. 14,78,496 as principal and Rs. 5,83,297 as interest aggregating to Rs. 20,61,793 as of date of default 2017-09-01 based on 5 invoices dated 2017-08-14. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice in Form 3 issued on 2018-04-13; Section 9 application filed before NCLT Mumbai. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor sent emails on 2017-09-09 and 2017-09-13 stating that no material was received against three of the invoices (Nos. 306, 307, and 309) and requesting dispatch details or threatening bill reversal, to which Operational Creditor did not reply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV) admitted the Section 9 application ex parte on 2019-10-25 in CP (IB) 1689/MB/C-IV/2019 due to non-appearance of the Corporate Debtor.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when there is a pre-existing dispute regarding non-delivery of goods raised by the Corporate Debtor prior to the issuance of the demand notice under Section 8.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9 of the IBC, if there is an existence of a dispute between the parties prior to the receipt of the demand notice of unpaid operational debt, the application must be rejected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Section 9 mandate that undisputed operational debt and delivery of goods/services are prerequisites; unrefuted emails questioning non-supply establish a bona fide dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-demand emails sent by the debtor challenging specific invoices for non-receipt of goods constitute clear evidence of a pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox Innovations framework. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Adjudicating Authority failed to consider pre-existing dispute emails sent prior to the Section 8 demand notice, the admission order could not be sustained.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 2019-10-25 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV is set aside and Section 9 application dismissed; Corporate Debtor released from CIRP rigor; IRP/RP and CoC actions set aside; IRP/RP directed to handover records and assets to the Director of Corporate Debtor immediately; matter remitted to Adjudicating Authority to determine CIRP fees and costs payable to IRP/RP, which shall be borne by Operational Creditor / Respondent No. 1.
summary: Akbar Kothawala, erstwhile promoter of Supreme Startech Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Megamet Steels Pvt. Ltd. for default on bitumen supply invoices. The appellant contended that emails sent on September 9 and 13, 2017—prior to the Section 8 demand notice—disputed three invoices due to non-receipt of goods, which the operational creditor ignored. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority failed to consider this pre-existing dispute. Consequently, the appellate tribunal set aside the admission order, dismissed the Section 9 petition, and released the corporate debtor from CIRP.

case_title: Kind Special Steels (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Amtek Auto Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kind Special Steels (India) Pvt. Ltd. is an Operational Creditor; Respondent Amtek Auto Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/materials under commercial invoices raised by the Operational Creditor on the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default were not admitted by the Resolution Professional due to lack of substantiating proof; claim was submitted on 04-08-2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No Section 8 notice dates were specified; claim was originally submitted on 04-08-2017, and subsequent Application CA-293/2018 was filed on 27-07-2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor failed to attach acceptable proof of delivery corresponding to the disputed unadmitted invoices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CA-293/2018 in CP(IB)/42/CHD/HRY/2017 was filed before NCLT Chandigarh Bench to direct the RP to revise and ascertain liquidation value and admit its 04-08-2017 claim; NCLT dismissed it on 09-07-2020 because it was filed post-approval of the LHG resolution plan, the Supreme Court had only ordered inviting fresh offers without reopening the entire CIRP de novo, and delivery proofs were lacking.
legal_issues: Whether an order of the Supreme Court directing the invitation of fresh offers due to the non-implementability of an approved resolution plan reopens the entire CIRP de novo to permit filing and adjudication of rejected/unadmitted operational creditor claims under Section 60(5) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate direction ordering the invitation of fresh resolution offers upon the failure of an approved resolution plan opens a limited window solely for rebidding and does not recommence the CIRP de novo, thereby precluding belated filing or reconsideration of claims post-moratorium timelines. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) cannot be invoked to reopen settled claim stages or invite claims afresh after the resolution plan stage has matured, as doing so contradicts the strict mandatory timelines of the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An operational creditor must produce verifiable contemporaneous evidence establishing delivery of goods (proof of delivery) to validate and compel the admission of disputed invoices. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that CIRP was not reopened from the stage of public announcement and that unproved claims cannot be entertained at the stage of inviting fresh offers.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the threshold stage along with I.A. Nos. 2094/2020, 2095/2020, and 2096/2020.
summary: Operational Creditor Kind Special Steels appealed NCLT Chandigarh's dismissal of its application under Section 60(5) seeking admission of its claims and redetermination of liquidation value after the resolution plan of LHG failed. Appellant argued that the Supreme Court's order directing fresh offers reopened the CIRP, permitting reconsideration of its unadmitted claim. NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the threshold, holding that the Supreme Court provided only a limited window to invite fresh bids rather than recommencing the CIRP de novo from the stage of public announcement and claim verification, particularly when the appellant failed to produce delivery proof for the invoices.

case_title: M/s. Mohindera Chemicals Private Limited vs. Registrar of Companies NCT of Delhi & Haryana & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s. Mohindera Chemicals Private Limited is the struck-off company; Respondent No. 1 is the Registrar of Companies (ROC) NCT of Delhi & Haryana; Respondent No. 2 is the Income Tax Department. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Running corporate entity holding immovable property, commercial receivables, and ongoing business operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory non-filing of balance sheets and annual returns after financial year 2013-2014; Income Tax assessment for FY 2011-2012 completed on 29-12-2018 with an outstanding demand of Rs. 7,79,74,290 pending recovery. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Public notice STK-5 issued by ROC on 18-06-2018; striking off order STK-7 notified with effect from 08-08-2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prepared Balance Sheets from 2014-2015 to 2018-2019 showing existing immovable property and substantial outstanding trade receivables from willing debtors; Income Tax assessment order showing active tax recovery of Rs. 7,79,74,290. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant's appeal/petition under Section 252 for restoration was dismissed by NCLT on the ground that past returns were filed as mere formalities without demonstrating active business operation.
legal_issues: Whether the name of a company struck off under Section 248 for failure to file annual returns should be restored under Section 252 when evidence demonstrates active operations, immovable properties, uncollected debts, and substantial pending income tax recovery liabilities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a struck-off company demonstrates ongoing commercial existence, holds tangible property, has outstanding debts to collect, and faces active statutory tax assessment liabilities, it is just and equitable to restore its name to the register under Section 252 subject to compliance costs and filing statutory defaults. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252 mandates restoration if the company was carrying on business or in operation, or if it is otherwise 'just' that the name be restored, ensuring administrative non-filing does not extinguish corporate recovery and statutory dues. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Existence of prepared audited balance sheets, asset schedules, recoverable trade debts, and tax assessment orders showing pending recovery constitute sufficient proof of operation and justification for restoration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal concluded that the company was functional and the striking off caused severe prejudice to creditors, debtors, and revenue recovery, warranting reversal of the NCLT order.
operative_order: The impugned order is set aside, and ROC is directed to restore the Appellant Company's name to the Register of Companies subject to payment of Rs. 1 Lakh costs to Respondent No. 1 and filing of all outstanding documents, balance sheets, and returns within two months along with statutory late fees and penalties.
summary: M/s Mohindera Chemicals appealed against the NCLT order refusing to restore its corporate name after it was struck off by the ROC under Section 248 on 08-08-2018 for failing to file balance sheets after 2013-2014. The Appellant produced balance sheets for 2014-2015 to 2018-2019 showing immovable properties, outstanding debts due from debtors, and an outstanding Income Tax recovery liability of Rs. 7.79 Crore. NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT order, and directed restoration of the company's name subject to Rs. 1 Lakh costs and filing of all overdue returns within two months.

case_title: Economy Hotels India Services Private Limited vs. Registrar of Companies & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Economy Hotels India Services Private Limited is a closely held private company limited by shares and a wholly owned subsidiary of AAPC Singapore Pte. Ltd.; Respondents are Registrar of Companies NCT of Delhi & Haryana and the Regional Director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate capital restructuring involving reduction of issued, subscribed, and paid-up share capital from Rs. 67,47,90,000 divided into 6,74,79,000 equity shares of Rs. 10 each to Rs. 4,90,00,000 divided into 49,00,000 equity shares of Rs. 10 each pursuant to Article 9 of its Articles of Association. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; no monetary default or debt liability, as the matter pertains strictly to non-infringing internal share capital reduction. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board resolution passed on 29-07-2019; Annual General Meeting held on 19-08-2019; statutory e-form MGT-14 filed with the MCA21 registry following the AGM. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unanimous vote by 100% of the equity shareholders attending the AGM on 19-08-2019 in favor of capital reduction; approved e-form MGT-14 reflecting the registration of the Special Resolution; Registrar of Companies report confirming statutory compliance; clerical typographical error on page 124 of the AGM minutes mischaracterizing the unanimously approved special resolution as an 'ordinary resolution'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed C.P. No. 149/66/ND/2019 under Section 66(1)(b) before NCLT New Delhi Bench V; NCLT rejected the petition on 27-05-2020 solely on the ground that the AGM minutes recorded the approval as an ordinary resolution rather than a special resolution as mandated by Section 66 and Article 9.
legal_issues: Whether a unanimous resolution passed by 100% voting shareholders satisfies the substantive statutory mandate of a special resolution under Section 114(2) read with Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013, despite a typographical clerical error in the recorded minutes labelling it an ordinary resolution.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Reduction of share capital is an internal domestic affair of a company governed by the will of its majority shareholders, and a resolution passed unanimously by the entire voting membership meets the substantive legal threshold of a special resolution irrespective of inadvertent clerical misdescriptions in the recorded minutes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 114(2) defines a special resolution based on whether votes cast in favor are not less than three times the votes cast against; where 100% of shareholders vote in favor, the mandatory threshold of a three-fourths majority under Section 114(2) is fully satisfied for the purpose of confirming capital reduction under Section 66. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantive statutory compliance evidenced by unanimous shareholder voting records and regulatory MCA filings (Form MGT-14) takes precedence over typographical inadvertence appearing in the extract of the minutes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the statutory requirements of Section 66 and Section 114(2) were satisfied, and the NCLT erred in rejecting the petition based merely on a typographical error in the minutes.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 27.05.2020 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench V is set aside, the reduction of share capital resolved at the AGM on 19.08.2019 is confirmed, the form of minutes under Section 66(5) is approved for registration with the Registrar of Companies, and pending interlocutory applications are closed with no order as to costs.
summary: Economy Hotels India Services appealed against the NCLT order rejecting its petition under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 for reduction of share capital from Rs. 67.47 Crore to Rs. 4.90 Crore. The NCLT rejected the application because the AGM minutes inadvertently recorded the decision as an ordinary resolution instead of a special resolution. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that capital reduction is an internal domestic affair and that because 100% of the shareholders voted in favor, the substantive requirements of a special resolution under Section 114(2) were met. The clerical error in the minutes did not invalidate the resolution, and the reduction was accordingly confirmed.

case_title: Invent Assets Securitization and Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Xylon Electrotechnic Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Invent Assets Securitization and Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. is the Assignee/Financial Creditor; Respondent Xylon Electrotechnic Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Union Bank of India is the original Assignor Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Cash-credit financial facilities sanctioned on 03-01-2008 by Union Bank of India and subsequently restructured on 12-06-2009, later assigned to the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount was Rs. 54,49,40,510.35, with the date of default fixed as 20-02-2010 when the Corporate Debtor's loan account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Assignor filed recovery proceedings before DRT Mumbai on 08-02-2011; DRT allowed the claim on 17-01-2014; DRAT appeal remained pending; Section 7 application was filed well beyond three years from the NPA declaration. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial debt was reflected in the audited balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor for financial years 2010 through 2016; Appellant showed no separate written acknowledgement of debt executed within three years of the NPA date. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed by Appellant was dismissed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 28-05-2020 as barred by limitation under Article 137 because no continuous written acknowledgement of debt was furnished within the initial three-year limitation period.
legal_issues: Whether entry of a financial debt in the mandatory statutory annual balance sheet of a corporate debtor constitutes an acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and whether money decrees or recovery proceedings before the DRT shift forward or extend the limitation period for filing a Section 7 IBC petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Filing of annual financial statements is a mandatory penal statutory duty under company law and does not constitute a voluntary acknowledgement of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, nor do parallel recovery proceedings or decrees by a Debt Recovery Tribunal shift or exclude the limitation period for an insolvency application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications are governed strictly by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, with the three-year clock commencing on the date of NPA/default; SARFAESI notices and DRT actions do not qualify as proceedings before a court without jurisdiction under Section 14(2) to permit exclusion of time. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To invoke Section 18 of the Limitation Act, an unequivocal, voluntary acknowledgement in writing must be executed prior to the expiry of the three-year limitation period running from the date of default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Relying on its larger bench rulings in Ishrat Ali and V. Padmakumar, the Tribunal held that the debt became barred on 20-02-2013 and could not be revived via annual return filings or DRT litigation.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the pre-admission stage, upholding the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order dated 28.05.2020 holding the Section 7 petition time-barred.
summary: Invent Assets Securitization appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing its Section 7 petition against Xylon Electrotechnic for recovery of Rs. 54.49 Crore as barred by limitation. The Corporate Debtor's account was declared NPA on 20-02-2010, but the Appellant contended that limitation was extended by balance sheet entries from 2010 to 2016 under Section 18 and parallel DRT recovery proceedings. Following its larger bench precedents in Ishrat Ali and V. Padmakumar, NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that mandatory statutory balance sheet filings do not amount to acknowledgement under Section 18, and DRT recovery proceedings do not shift forward the original date of default.

case_title: Jagdish Prasad Sarada vs. Allahabad Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Jagdish Prasad Sarada is the suspended Managing Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Sarda Agro Oils Limited; Respondent Allahabad Bank is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-credit banking facilities comprising Cash Credit facility of Rs. 20 Crores, Term Loan of Rs. 14 Crores, and Letter of Credit of Rs. 65 Crores sanctioned via Common Sanction Letter dated 31-05-2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account became irregular and was declared a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30-09-2015; subsequent part payment of Rs. 49,50,000 was deposited into the account on 19-02-2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30-09-2015; Section 13(2) and Section 13(4) SARFAESI notices issued; Section 7 petition filed before NCLT on 31-12-2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank ledger statement reflecting a cash credit payment of Rs. 49,50,000 made on 19-02-2016; Corporate Debtor's balance sheet for FY 2014-15; High Court Writ Petition No. 2214 of 2016 and DRT Hyderabad order in S.A. No. 10/2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent Bank filed CP(IB) No. 102/07/HDB/2019 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench under Section 7; NCLT admitted the petition ex-parte on 27-08-2019, holding that the part payment of Rs. 49,50,000 on 19-02-2016 extended the limitation period under Section 19 of the Limitation Act.
legal_issues: Whether a part payment made by a corporate debtor after loan classification as an NPA extends the three-year limitation period under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for filing a corporate insolvency application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 is three years from the date of default/NPA pursuant to Article 137, and that statutory trigger date remains fixed and cannot be shifted forward by interim part payments under Section 19. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: By virtue of Section 238A of the IBC read with Article 137 of the Limitation Act, an application must be brought within three years of default; extension is strictly permissible only under Section 5 for sufficient cause and not by importing Section 19 part-payment resets into CIRP filings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ledger entries proving deposit of funds into a loan account post-NPA classification do not regularize the account or alter the crystallised date of default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the account was declared NPA on 30-09-2015, the Section 7 application filed on 31-12-2018 was barred by limitation notwithstanding the interim payment of 19-02-2016.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 27.08.2019 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench admitting the Section 7 petition is set aside; appointment of the IRP/RP, moratorium, account freezing, and all consequential CIRP actions are declared illegal and vacated; NCLT directed to close CIRP and fix RP fees payable by Corporate Debtor.
summary: Allahabad Bank initiated CIRP against Sarda Agro Oils Limited under Section 7 on 31-12-2018, claiming that an interim payment of Rs. 49.50 Lakhs made on 19-02-2016 renewed limitation under Section 19 of the Limitation Act beyond the NPA date of 30-09-2015. NCLT Hyderabad admitted the petition. On appeal, NCLAT reversed the admission order, holding that under Article 137 read with Section 238A, the limitation period of three years begins strictly from the date of NPA/default and does not shift forward due to part-payment under Section 19. The application was held time-barred, and the entire CIRP was quashed.

case_title: Pioneer Rubchem Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vivek Raheja, Resolution Professional, Trading Engineers (International) Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Pioneer Rubchem Pvt. Ltd. is a prospective resolution applicant; Respondent No. 1 is Vivek Raheja, Resolution Professional of Trading Engineers (International) Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Participation in the competitive Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor to submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) and a Resolution Plan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; matter concerns statutory procedural deadlines for CIRP completion and resolution plan submissions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 04-07-2019; initial EOI deadline was 05-03-2020 and plan submission deadline was 05-04-2020; RP subsequently extended EOI deadline to 30-06-2020 and plan submission to 30-07-2020; maximum 330-day CIRP period was set to expire on 29-08-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant submitted a request for extension of time to submit an EOI belatedly on 13-07-2020, thirteen days after the extended 30-06-2020 deadline; two competing resolution plans had already been received by the RP; CoC formally rejected Appellant's belated request on 16-07-2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following CoC's rejection on 16-07-2020, Appellant approached the Appellate Tribunal seeking extension of time to file its EOI and plan on the grounds of asset value maximization.
legal_issues: Whether a prospective resolution applicant is entitled to an extension of time to submit an Expression of Interest after the expiry of extended deadlines and when the outer CIRP statutory deadline under Section 12 is about to expire, despite competitive plans having already been received.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory timelines prescribed for CIRP under Section 12 must be strictly respected, and belated requests to submit expressions of interest past formal cut-off dates cannot be entertained where competitive bids have already been validly received, as doing so would derail the CIRP process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 mandates resolution within 180 days, extendable to 270 days, with 330 days serving as an outer benchmark accommodating judicial timelines; practically, all efforts must be made to finish CIRP within statutory parameters rather than indefinitely extending bidding cycles. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the RP and CoC establish that multiple conforming resolution plans have been submitted within the extended deadline, the statutory objective of competitive bidding is deemed met. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Permitting belated applicants to tender EOIs at the tail end of the CIRP would open floodgates and subvert the time-bound scheme of the Code.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of any merit.
