summary: Prospective resolution applicant Pioneer Rubchem appealed against the decision of the RP and CoC of Trading Engineers (International) Limited refusing to extend the deadline for submitting an Expression of Interest. Appellant submitted its request on 13-07-2020, well past the extended deadline of 30-06-2020, arguing that its participation would maximize the asset value of the Corporate Debtor. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that two resolution plans had already been received, satisfying competitive bidding requirements, and that granting an extension with the 330-day CIRP deadline expiring on 29-08-2020 would derail the process and defeat the core time-bound objectives of Section 12 of the IBC.

case_title: Kotak Investment Advisors Limited vs. Krishna Chamadia (Resolution Professional in the matter of Ricoh India Limited) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kotak Investment Advisors Limited (KIAL) is an unsuccessful Resolution Applicant; Respondent No. 1 Krishna Chamadia is Resolution Professional of Ricoh India Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondents No. 2 & 3 Kalpraj Dharamshi & Rekha Jhunjhunwala are Successful Resolution Applicants. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and consideration of Resolution Plans in the CIRP of Corporate Debtor Ricoh India Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory CIRP process milestone dispute; deadline for submission of Resolution Plans expired on 08-01-2019 at 6:00 pm. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-G invitations published on 24-08-2018, 09-11-2018, and 11-12-2018 (fixing deadline of 08-01-2019); KIAL plan opened on 10-01-2019 and discussed on 15-01-2019; belated EOI received from Respondents No. 2 & 3 on 27-01-2019 and plan on 28-01-2019; CoC approved belated plan on 13-02-2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Virtual data room was closed to all applicants on 07-01-2019 but subsequently made accessible to Respondents No. 2 & 3 post-deadline without fresh Form-G publication; KIAL's plan financials had already been opened and disclosed to competitors; NCLT Single Member Bench heard MA 1039/2019 on 03-07-2019 but final order was signed by a reconstituted Division Bench. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: KIAL filed MA 1039/2019 challenging acceptance of belated bids; RP filed MA 691/2019 for plan approval; NCLT Mumbai rejected MA 1039/2019 and approved the plan on 28-11-2019 holding CoC's commercial wisdom non-justiciable under K. Sashidhar.
legal_issues: Whether the CoC and RP have the authority under the guise of commercial wisdom and value maximization to accept an Expression of Interest and Resolution Plan submitted long after the published Form-G deadline without issuing a fresh public notice, and whether an order signed by a Technical Member who did not hear oral arguments violates natural justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors cannot validate or shield material procedural illegalities committed during the CIRP; any extension or reopening of the resolution application process requires issuance of a fresh public notice in Form-G rather than clandestine acceptance of belated bids after competing plans have been unsealed. Furthermore, under the doctrine of natural justice and Rule 150(2) of the NCLT Rules, an order cannot be pronounced by a member who did not hear the oral arguments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) and Section 61(3)(ii) empower the appellate tribunal to set aside plan approvals tainted by material irregularity in the exercise of powers by the RP, even if approved by the statutory voting majority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where contemporaneous record demonstrates that the bid submission deadline lapsed, existing bids were unsealed, and the data room was selectively reopened for an entity that did not submit an EOI within statutory timelines, the process is tainted with material irregularity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The acceptance of the belated plan of Respondents No. 2 & 3 without publishing a fresh Form-G was illegal and vitiated the CIRP, requiring the orders approving the plan and rejecting the objections to be set aside.
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 28.11.2019 passed in MA No. 1039/2019 and MA No. 691/2019 are set aside. CoC is directed to take a fresh decision within ten days on the conforming resolution plans submitted within the stipulated deadline; failing which, NCLT is directed to order liquidation.
summary: Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant KIAL challenged NCLT Mumbai's approval of a resolution plan submitted by a consortium of Kalpraj Dharamshi and Rekha Jhunjhunwala for Ricoh India Limited. The successful bidders submitted their EOI and plan weeks after the final Form-G deadline had expired and after KIAL's plan had been opened and deliberated upon by the CoC. NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the approval, holding that commercial wisdom cannot cure material illegalities and deviations from mandatory CIRP regulations, such as accepting late bids without issuing a fresh Form-G public notice. The order was additionally vitiated as it was signed by a Technical Member who had not heard the oral arguments.

case_title: Sushil Ansal vs. Ashok Tripathi & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sushil Ansal is former Director/Shareholder of M/s Ansal Properties and Infrastructure Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondents No. 1 & 2 Ashok Tripathi and Saurabh Tripathi are RERA Recovery Certificate holders; Respondent No. 3 is the IRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking of two residential units in the real estate project 'Sushant Golf City', Lucknow via Builder Buyer Agreements dated 12-09-2014 and 29-09-2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 73,35,686.43 pursuant to UP RERA Recovery Certificate dated 10-08-2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: UP RERA refund orders passed on 16-11-2017 and 13-12-2018; Section 40 RERA Recovery Certificate issued on 10-08-2019; Section 7 petition filed post-recovery certificate; admission order passed on 17-03-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: UP RERA Recovery Certificate forwarded to District Collector to recover dues as arrears of land revenue; lack of requisite numerical threshold of 100 or 10% allottees under Section 7 proviso; post-admission bilateral settlement deed dated 01-06-2020 entered between parties while over 280 third-party claims were pending before the IRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-II admitted Respondents No. 1 & 2's Section 7 application on 17-03-2020 holding that as decree-holders seeking recovery of an adjudicated debt, the allottee numerical threshold under the 2019/2020 IBC Amendments did not apply to them.
legal_issues: Whether an allottee of a real estate project holding a RERA recovery certificate qualifies as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether an application under Section 7 can be maintained purely to execute an adjudicated recovery certificate.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a decree-holder falls within the general definition of a 'creditor' under Section 3(10), a decree-holder is not a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(7) because an adjudicated recovery debt does not constitute a debt disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8); hence, a Section 7 petition cannot be used as an execution tool for a money decree. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An allottee who obtains a final recovery certificate from RERA ceases to initiate CIRP in the capacity of an allottee under Section 5(8)(f) explanation; Section 7 cannot be utilized as an execution forum under the guise of an adjudicated debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The character of the debt must be judged at the time of approaching the Adjudicating Authority; petitioning solely on the strength of an unexecuted RERA recovery certificate proves an intent to execute a money recovery rather than seek corporate resolution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application filed by the decree-holders was not maintainable, and NCLT erred in admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned admission order dated 17.03.2020 is set aside, appointment of IRP, moratorium, and all consequential actions are declared illegal and quashed, and the Section 7 petition is dismissed with the Corporate Debtor released to its Board of Directors.
summary: Former Director Sushil Ansal challenged NCLT New Delhi's admission of a Section 7 IBC application filed by two homebuyers who had procured a UP RERA recovery certificate for Rs. 73.35 Lakhs against Ansal Properties and Infrastructure Ltd. The allottees claimed status as Financial Creditors in their capacity as decree-holders to bypass the minimum threshold requirements of 100 allottees or 10%. NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the admission order, ruling that a decree-holder or RERA recovery certificate holder does not qualify as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8), as an adjudicated decree is not a debt disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and Section 7 cannot be leveraged as an execution mechanism.

case_title: Park Energy Pvt. Ltd. vs. Syndicate Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Park Energy Pvt. Ltd. is a shareholder of Bhadreshwar Vidyut Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 Syndicate Bank (merged with Canara Bank) is a Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional; Punjab National Bank is the Lead Bank of the consortium. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working Capital Consortium Agreement dated 17-12-2015, Inter-se Credit Agreement, and Trust and Retention Account (TRA) Agreement dated 26-07-2016 for financing a 2 x 150 MW Thermal Power Plant in Gujarat. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Syndicate Bank claimed an outstanding default amount of Rs. 32,22,50,660.16 as on 29-07-2019; account declared NPA retrospectively from 30-06-2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30-06-2018; demand letter issued on 05-12-2018; Section 7 application filed on 30-07-2019; admitted by NCLT on 27-01-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor deposited total revenues of Rs. 962.92 Crores into the Lead Bank (PNB) TRA account between 01-07-2018 and 30-06-2019 as certified by Chartered Accountants; PNB restricted disbursals to Syndicate Bank because Syndicate Bank unilaterally froze and refused to open/renew agreed Letter of Credit limits of Rs. 46.50 Crores for coal procurement; Syndicate Bank held only 1.64% stake of total consortium debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Syndicate Bank filed IBA/967/2019 under Section 7 against Corporate Debtor; NCLT Chennai admitted the application on 27-01-2020 holding that default in non-payment of dues was established.
legal_issues: Whether non-receipt of payment by a consortium member holding a minority debt stake constitutes a 'default' by the corporate debtor under Section 3(12) of the IBC when the corporate debtor has deposited its entire revenue collections into the mandated Trust and Retention Account (TRA) regulated by the lead bank.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mere existence of a debt due and payable is insufficient to trigger Section 7; the applicant financial creditor must strictly establish that a default occurred due to a failure on the part of the corporate debtor. Where an obligor fully complies with contractual debt restructuring and deposits all revenues into a designated escrow/TRA account, non-disbursal resulting from inter se consortium lender disputes does not constitute a default attributable to the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Default' under Section 3(12) requires non-payment arising out of a debtor's failure to discharge its liability; it does not extend to payment blockages arising solely from inter-creditor arrangements or lead bank withholding. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted audited financial certificates establishing adequate cash flows deposited into the TRA pool, coupled with minutes showing lead bank instructions, rebut any prima facie assertion of debtor default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had fully honored its contractual obligations by depositing all funds into the TRA, and the refusal of PNB to release funds to Syndicate Bank was an inter-creditor dispute, negating the existence of default under Section 7.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 27.01.2020 admitting the Section 7 application is set aside; all actions taken by the IRP/RP, moratorium, and freezing of accounts are declared illegal and vacated; Corporate Debtor is restored to its Board; matter remitted to NCLT solely for fixing IRP/RP fees.
summary: Park Energy appealed NCLT Chennai's admission of a Section 7 petition initiated by Syndicate Bank against Bhadreshwar Vidyut Pvt. Ltd. for an alleged default of Rs. 32.22 Crores. Syndicate Bank held a 1.64% share in a consortium governed by a Trust Retention Account (TRA) Agreement. Corporate Debtor deposited Rs. 962.92 Crores into the TRA, but the lead bank (PNB) withheld payouts to Syndicate Bank because Syndicate Bank unilaterally refused to open letters of credit for fuel procurement. NCLAT allowed the appeal and quashed the CIRP, holding that non-payment arose from inter-creditor consortium disputes and not a failure or default by the Corporate Debtor, thereby rendering Section 7 inapplicable.

case_title: M/s. Vipul Limited vs. M/s. Solitaire Buildmart Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Vipul Limited and Respondent M/s Solitaire Buildmart Pvt. Ltd. are co-developers / joint venture partners. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint Development Agreement (JDA) dated 25-01-2006 and Master Development Agreement (MDA) dated 12-04-2011 (with Addendum dated 13-04-2011) to develop an Integrated Township in Ludhiana with a 75:25 project sharing ratio. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed principal default of Rs. 1,11,24,693 representing Solitaire's unpaid share of project costs incurred by Vipul, plus 18% p.a. interest as stipulated under Clause 6.7 of the MDA. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Costs incurred by 16-01-2010; payment obligations matured 45 days post-MDA execution; Respondent demanded conveyance of components on 09-04-2018; Appellant issued Section 8 demand notice on 17-04-2018; Section 7 petition filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clause 3.1 of MDA acknowledging receipt of Rs. 17,51,10,000 paid by Solitaire to Vipul for allocated project components; reciprocal obligations requiring conveyance of plots/units within 30 days against cost reimbursements within 90 days; Section 8 notice issued by Vipul describing the debt as an 'Operational Debt'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Vipul Limited filed IB-1017/ND/2018 under Section 7 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-II; NCLT dismissed the petition on 16-01-2020 holding the dispute arose out of breach of reciprocal contract obligations and lacked the essential elements of a financial debt under Section 5(8).
legal_issues: Whether outstanding cost reimbursements between collaborating partners in a joint real estate development agreement constitute a 'Financial Debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8), clothing the claiming partner with the status of a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unpaid cost-sharing contributions or contractual cross-claims between business collaborators in a joint venture/joint development agreement do not constitute financial debts disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and one joint partner cannot trigger Section 7 against another over reciprocal contractual breaches. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) requires an underlying disbursal of loan capital against the time value of money having the commercial effect of a borrowing; profit/cost sharing allocations in an integrated township do not qualify. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual construction of mutual obligations: where covenants reveal reciprocal, dependent promises of land transfer against cost allocation, and where the claimant initially served a Section 8 operational debt notice, the transaction represents a commercial works partnership, not a financial creditor-debtor relationship. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant was a co-venturer rather than a financial lender; the petition did not meet the requirements of Section 5(8) and was properly rejected.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT New Delhi Bench-II order dated 16.01.2020 rejecting the Section 7 application.
summary: Vipul Limited appealed against the dismissal of its Section 7 petition against Solitaire Buildmart Pvt. Ltd. seeking recovery of Rs. 1.11 Crores representing Solitaire's unpaid share of infrastructure and development costs under a Master Development Agreement for an integrated township in Ludhiana. The Appellant argued that contractual interest of 18% gave the transaction the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8). NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the relationship between the parties was that of collaborating joint venture partners sharing costs and profits governed by reciprocal promises under the Indian Contract Act. The claim did not involve a disbursal of financial debt against the time value of money, disentitling Vipul from petitioning as a Financial Creditor under Section 7.

case_title: Rajendra Kumar Tekriwal vs. Bank of Baroda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rajendra Kumar Tekriwal is Ex-Director of Pithampur Poly Products Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent Bank of Baroda (amalgamated Dena Bank) is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial credit and loan facilities extended by Dena Bank to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor's loan account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 01-05-2000, which was recorded as the crystallised date of default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 01-05-2000; Dena Bank filed recovery suit before DRT Jabalpur on 30-06-2004; DRT decreed the claim on 27-07-2011; High Court writ stayed decree until dismissal in 2018; Section 7 petition C.P. (IB) No. 421/7/NCLT/AHM/2018 filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial Creditor relied on balance confirmations/letters of acknowledgment executed on 31-03-1999, 31-03-2001, and 12-04-2004, the DRT money decree dated 27-07-2011, and High Court writ proceedings to argue continuation of limitation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Dena Bank filed Section 7 petition before NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad in 2018; NCLT admitted the petition on 03-01-2020 holding the debt legally subsisting and enforceable pursuant to the DRT decree and acknowledgments.
legal_issues: Whether the obtaining of a DRT money decree, pendency of writ proceedings, or acknowledgments of debt executed more than three years prior to the enactment of the IBC can extend or reset the three-year limitation period under Article 137 for initiating CIRP under Section 7.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, where the right to sue accrues strictly on the date of default/NPA; subsequent DRT recovery proceedings, civil decrees, or time-barred acknowledgments cannot shift forward the date of default or extend the statutory three-year limitation window. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act requires an acknowledgment to be executed before the expiration of the prescribed limitation period; an acknowledgment cannot revive a time-barred debt for an insolvency petition, nor do decrees grant a fresh three-year trigger under Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since Section 7 was brought into force on 01-12-2016, defaults occurring prior to 01-12-2013 are prima facie time-barred unless a valid, continuous chain of timely Section 18 acknowledgments extending up to the date of filing is established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The date of default being 01-05-2000, and the last acknowledgment being in 2004, the Section 7 petition filed in 2018 was hopelessly barred by limitation.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 03.01.2020 admitting the Section 7 application is set aside; the appointment of IRP, moratorium, and freezing orders are quashed; the Section 7 petition is dismissed; and the Corporate Debtor is released to its Board of Directors.
summary: Ex-Director Rajendra Kumar Tekriwal appealed NCLT Indore's admission of a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Bank of Baroda (formerly Dena Bank) against Pithampur Poly Products Limited. The loan had been declared an NPA on 01-05-2000, and the bank obtained a DRT decree in 2011, relying on acknowledgments executed up to 2004 and the stay of writ proceedings until 2018 to bridge limitation. NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the admission order, reiterating that under Article 137, the three-year limitation period commences from the date of NPA/default. Recovery proceedings or decrees before the DRT do not shift the date of default, and defaults that occurred prior to 01-12-2013 cannot be resuscitated under Section 7 without valid, continuous, timely acknowledgments.

case_title: Smt. Andal Bonumalla vs. Tomato Trading LLP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Tomato Trading LLP (Respondent No. 1, engaged in commodity import/export); Corporate Debtor is Smart Login Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); Appellant is Smt. Andal Bonumalla (Promoter and Ex-Executive Director of Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and Purchase Agreement dated 04.01.2017 executed between the parties wherein the Corporate Debtor agreed to supply 130 Metric Tons of Sugar to the Operational Creditor. Operational Creditor paid an advance of Rs. 3,58,020 on 07.01.2017 and Rs. 31,32,160 on 08.02.2017 (total advance Rs. 34,90,180), for which a proforma invoice dated 08.02.2017 was issued. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor failed to supply the sugar and refunded only Rs. 9,00,000, leaving a balance principal debt of Rs. 25,90,180 along with Rs. 4,92,634 interest, totaling Rs. 30,82,814 in default as on 07.03.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice was issued by the Operational Creditor on 07.03.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sale and Purchase Agreement dated 04.01.2017, proforma invoice dated 08.02.2017, bank statements showing advance payments and partial refund, particulars of claim under Annexure-D, and email correspondence regarding sugar supply and refund demands. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition filed as CP(IB)-334/09/HDB/2019 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench, which admitted the application and initiated CIRP on 03.06.2019 holding that the debt arose from an agreement for sale of goods.
legal_issues: Whether an advance amount paid by a purchaser for the supply of goods constitutes an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC, thereby entitling the purchaser to initiate CIRP as an 'operational creditor' under Section 5(20) and Section 9 upon failure to supply goods; and whether non-compliance with the prescribed demand notice format under Section 8(1) invalidates a Section 9 application when raised for the first time on appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance payment made by an entity for the procurement of goods or services does not constitute an operational debt under the IBC if that entity is the purchaser/recipient and has not itself supplied any goods or rendered any services to the counterparty; consequently, a buyer seeking refund of an advance cannot maintain a Section 9 petition as an operational creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) read with Section 5(20) requires that an operational debt must represent a claim in respect of the provision of goods or services; the claimant must be the provider/supplier. Advance consideration paid by a purchaser does not fall within the definition of operational debt owed by the defaulting supplier. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal examines the underlying commercial relationship to determine whether the claimant was a supplier of goods/services or merely an advance payer/buyer. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Tomato Trading LLP only advanced funds to buy sugar and did not supply goods or services, it is not an operational creditor and the advance refund claim is not an operational debt; the Section 9 admission order was illegal and without jurisdiction.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned admission order dated 03.06.2019 set aside; Corporate Debtor released from CIRP rigours; actions taken by IRP/RP and CoC set aside; IRP/RP directed to restore management and records to promoters/directors; matter remitted to Adjudicating Authority to determine IRP/RP fees and costs to be borne exclusively by Respondent No. 1 (Tomato Trading LLP); no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, promoter of Corporate Debtor Smart Login Solutions Pvt. Ltd., challenged NCLT Hyderabad's admission of a Section 9 IBC application filed by Tomato Trading LLP. Tomato Trading LLP had advanced Rs. 34,90,180 to the Corporate Debtor for purchasing 130 Metric Tons of Sugar, but the Corporate Debtor neither delivered the goods nor refunded the full sum, returning only Rs. 9 Lakhs. NCLAT held that an advance payment made for the supply of goods does not constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) because the purchaser did not provide any goods or services. Consequently, the purchaser is not an operational creditor under Section 5(20), and Section 9 proceedings are not maintainable for recovery. The admission order was set aside and CIRP was quashed.

case_title: M/s. Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. & Ors. vs. Mr. Dinkar Venkatasubramanian & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are M/s. Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. & Ors. (claiming status of secured financial creditors); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Dinkar Venkatasubramanian (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s. Amtek Auto Limited); Respondent No. 2 is Committee of Creditors of Amtek Auto Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants lent money to third-party entities WLD and BRASSCO; the Corporate Debtor created a pledge of shares in favour of Appellant No. 1 as security for the loans advanced to those third parties. Corporate Debtor did not borrow funds directly. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified debt default by third-party borrowers (WLD and BRASSCO); claim was filed to enforce/protect the share pledge against the Corporate Debtor in CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claim submitted by Appellants was formally rejected by the Resolution Professional in 2017; Appellants did not challenge the rejection until filing I.A. No. 62 of 2020 on 11.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pledge of shares created by Corporate Debtor for loans advanced to WLD and BRASSCO; rejection communications by RP in 2017; approved resolution plans of Liberty House Group (2017) and Deccan Value Investors (DVI) (2020); absence of direct loan agreements or disbursal records between Appellants and Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was in CIRP in CP (IB) No. 42/Chd./Hry./2017. Appellants filed I.A. 62 of 2020 under Section 60(5) seeking inclusion as secured financial creditors in the CoC. NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed I.A. 62 of 2020 while approving DVI's resolution plan, holding Appellants never lent money to the Corporate Debtor and had not timely challenged the 2017 rejection.
legal_issues: Whether a third-party security holder holding a pledge of shares created by the Corporate Debtor (to secure loans advanced to third-party entities) qualifies as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) of the IBC; and whether a belated application under Section 60(5) challenging the Resolution Professional's rejection after a three-year delay is maintainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A pledge of shares executed by a corporate debtor to secure third-party borrowings does not constitute a financial debt under the IBC in the absence of direct disbursement against the consideration for time value of money or an express contract of guarantee/indemnity, precluding the pledgee from claiming financial creditor status or CoC membership. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) requires a disbursement of debt against time value of money. A mere pledge of shares does not equate to a contract of guarantee or indemnity and cannot be subsumed within the definition of financial debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct disbursement test and timeliness standard; an unexplained multi-year delay in challenging an RP's rejection cannot be excused on an alleged subjective belief that subsequent resolution plans would protect the claimant's security interest. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants never disbursed money to Amtek Auto Limited, and the share pledge did not create an indemnity or guarantee liability; thus, Appellants are not financial creditors and the belated challenge fails on merits and laches.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed at the threshold stage; NCLT Chandigarh Bench order dismissing I.A. No. 62 of 2020 affirmed; no costs.
summary: Appellants appealed against an order of NCLT Chandigarh dismissing their Section 60(5) application (I.A. 62 of 2020) in the CIRP of Amtek Auto Limited. The Appellants sought inclusion in the CoC as secured financial creditors based on a pledge of shares executed by the Corporate Debtor to secure loans advanced by the Appellants to third-party entities (WLD and BRASSCO). The RP had rejected this claim in 2017, which went un-assailed for three years. NCLAT held that the creation of a share pledge for third-party debts does not amount to a guarantee, indemnity, or financial debt under Section 5(8) without direct disbursement for the time value of money, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Suman Kukrety & Ors. vs. Manish Kumar Gupta, RP of Three C Projects Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (with Manish Kumar Gupta vs. New Okhla Industrial Development Authority & Ors.)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants in Comp. App. 603/2020 are 100 homebuyer allottees of the residential project 'Lotus Zing'; Appellant in Comp. App. 659/2020 is Manish Kumar Gupta (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Three C Projects Pvt. Ltd.); Respondents include New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) and original land-owning farmers. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NOIDA Authority executed a lease and conveyance deed dated 01.09.2010 granting 69,998.73 sq. meters of land (Plot GH-01/A) to the Corporate Debtor to construct 2,454 residential flats under the 'Lotus Zing' project with promised possession by 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in project delivery; claim for damages of Rs. 500 Crores sought against NOIDA Authority due to deficient leased title. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Conveyance deed executed 01.09.2010; Allahabad High Court judgment in CWP No. 73850 of 2010; NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench order passed on 05.02.2020 in CA-207(PB)/2020 and CA-187(PB)/2020 in CP (IB)-1718(PB)/2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Conveyance Deed dated 01.09.2010; sanctioned building plans 2010-11; Allahabad High Court judgment in CWP No. 73850 of 2010 holding that NOIDA had acquired only 0.4873 hectares out of 0.847 hectares of Khasra No. 87 and declaring the unacquired 0.3597 hectares to remain the lawful property of the farmers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CIRP of Three C Projects Pvt. Ltd., the RP filed CA-207(PB)/2020 seeking directions compelling NOIDA to settle disputes with farmers and hand over unencumbered possession of the full 0.847 hectares, plus Rs. 500 Crores in damages. NCLT New Delhi dismissed CA-207(PB)/2020 holding it could not override the High Court's decree or determine damages.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority exercising jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC can issue directions compelling a statutory development authority (NOIDA) to settle disputes and transfer possession of land whose title has been conclusively adjudicated in favor of third-party land owners by a Constitutional Court; and whether NCLT possesses jurisdiction to adjudicate and award unliquidated tortious/contractual damages against a statutory authority within insolvency proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority under the IBC lacks statutory jurisdiction to adjudicate unliquidated contractual or tortious damages and cannot grant reliefs under Section 60(5) that run contrary to or undermine a binding final title decree issued by a Constitutional Court regarding property rights. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) confers power to adjudicate questions of priorities, law, or facts arising out of or in relation to insolvency resolution, but it cannot be invoked as a substitute for regular civil remedies or writ proceedings to enforce disputed third-party proprietary rights or assess damages. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Res judicata and binding judicial precedence; where a High Court conclusively determines title in favor of land owners, neither the Corporate Debtor nor the RP holds lawful leasehold rights over unacquired property. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because NOIDA acquired only 0.4873 hectares, it possessed no legal title or interest in the remaining 0.3597 hectares to transfer to the Corporate Debtor; the RP's application under Section 60(5) was fundamentally unmaintainable, and NCLT rightly refused to award damages.
operative_order: Appeals dismissed; NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench order dated 05.02.2020 dismissing CA-207(PB)/2020 affirmed; no costs.
summary: Resolution Professional and 100 homebuyers of Three C Projects Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of CA-207(PB)/2020. The RP had sought directions directing NOIDA Authority to settle disputes with farmers and hand over possession of 0.847 hectares of land allotted for the 'Lotus Zing' housing project, alongside Rs. 500 Crores in damages. The Allahabad High Court had previously ruled that NOIDA only acquired 0.4873 hectares, leaving the remaining 0.3597 hectares with the original farmers. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to assess unliquidated damages or issue orders conflicting with High Court title determinations. The appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Shaji Purushothaman vs. S. Rajendran, RP of M/s Empee Distilleries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shaji Purushothaman is the Promoter/Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Empee Distilleries Limited (Appellant); S. Rajendran is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Union Bank of India is the lead Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 2); SNJ Distilleries Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 8). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities from a consortium of financial creditors led by Union Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default led to initiation of CIRP under Section 7; Appellant submitted a subsequent settlement offer of Rs. 513 Crores against the Resolution Applicant's approved plan of Rs. 475 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 01.11.2018; Supreme Court granted two weeks on 18.10.2019 to present a Section 12A settlement; Appellant submitted settlement proposal to Union Bank on 30.10.2019; CoC rejected settlement on 04.11.2019; NCLT Chennai approved SNJ Distilleries' plan and dismissed Appellant's MA/1250/2019 on 20.01.2020; appeal filed on 12.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Manager's cheque dated 23.07.2019 for Rs. 12.65 Crores tendered to Union Bank; absence of Form FA and Bank Guarantee of Rs. 10.79 Crores for CIRP costs; lack of disclosed source of funds and ambiguous 12-instalment schedule for Rs. 124 Crores tax liabilities in the settlement plan; RP comparative evaluation note dated 31.10.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted Section 7 petition on 01.11.2018. On 20.01.2020, NCLT Chennai allowed MA/780/2019 approving SNJ Distilleries' resolution plan and dismissed MA/1250/2019 holding that Appellant failed to comply with statutory and judicial directions for withdrawal.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal was barred by limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC; and whether the CoC arbitrarily rejected the promoter's Section 12A settlement proposal in favor of the resolution plan submitted by SNJ Distilleries Ltd., rendering approval under Section 31 legally infirm.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating the feasibility, viability, and financial matrix of a resolution plan as against a Section 12A settlement proposal is non-justiciable, and the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal cannot substitute its own business judgment for that of the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A read with Section 60(5) and Section 31(1) does not confer plenary equity powers on adjudicating authorities to impose a settlement proposal on unwilling creditors when the proposal lacks a credible source of funds, omits mandatory bank guarantees, or contains impermissible conditional waivers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of commercial decisions is strictly confined to the statutory grounds in Section 30(2) and Section 61(3); judicial intervention requires proof of patent illegality or material irregularity, not merely an assertion that the settlement offer is numerically higher on paper. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC substantively evaluated and rejected the promoter's structurally deficient and non-compliant settlement proposal on its merits and unanimously approved the resolution plan; hence, the approval order suffers from no legal infirmity.
operative_order: Delay of 14 days in filing the appeal condoned under Section 61(2) proviso; Appeal dismissed on merits; approval of SNJ Distilleries Limited's resolution plan affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: The promoter of Empee Distilleries Ltd. appealed an NCLT Chennai order approving the Rs. 475 Crore resolution plan of SNJ Distilleries Pvt. Ltd. and dismissing his application for Section 12A withdrawal based on an alleged Rs. 513 Crore settlement offer. The Appellant argued his settlement offer was superior and arbitrarily rejected without comparison. NCLAT held that the CoC had substantively evaluated both proposals and rejected the settlement due to lack of verified funding sources, ambiguous tax repayment schedules, absence of Form FA, and failure to provide the CIRP bank guarantee. Reaffirming that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is non-justiciable under Sections 31 and 61(3), the Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mr. Karan Gambhir vs. Mr. Sajeve Bhushan Deora & Ors. (with DD Real Estate Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mr. Sajeve Bhushan Deora & Ors.)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Karan Gambhir is the Erstwhile Director and D.D. Real Estate Pvt. Ltd. is the 99% holding company of Corporate Debtor M/s Forgings Pvt. Ltd. (Appellants); Mr. Sajeve Bhushan Deora is the Liquidator (Respondent No. 1); Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. is the sole Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 2); Mars Infraengineering Pvt. Ltd. and Davinder Kumar are successful auction purchasers (Respondents Nos. 3 and 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by Corporate Debtor from Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd., secured by mortgage of its sole asset, a piece of land and building admeasuring approximately 42,447 sq. yards at Main Mathura Road, Faridabad, Haryana. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on outstanding debt of approximately Rs. 25.80 Crores principal (with total claims around Rs. 40 Crores); land auctioned and sold for Rs. 52.83 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation order passed on 26.10.2018; first sale notice issued on 28.02.2019; fresh sale notice issued on 15.05.2019; NCLT Principal Bench dismissed CA No. 1079(PB)/2019 with Rs. 50,000 costs on 04.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered valuation reports by Anil Kumar Saxena and Sunil Dhingra; District Town Planner communication dated 02.05.2019 confirming no Change of Land Use (CLU) was ever granted; Municipal Corporation Faridabad letter dated 16.12.2002 demanding unpaid external development charges of Rs. 1,21,80,505; prior representations under SARFAESI by CD admissions acknowledging the land was agricultural. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CA No. 1079(PB)/2019 challenging the reserve price of Rs. 52.58 Crores and the valuation methodology under Regulation 35 of the Liquidation Regulations, alleging the land was industrial rather than agricultural. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the application on 04.12.2019, holding the valuation and auction were proper, and imposed Rs. 50,000 punitive costs for delaying liquidation.
legal_issues: Whether the reserve price and valuation of the Corporate Debtor's immovable asset conducted by registered valuers under Regulation 35 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 were vitiated by treating the land as agricultural rather than industrial; and whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction in upholding the valuation and imposing punitive costs on the promoter.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Valuation of liquidation assets conducted by registered valuers under the Liquidation Regulations cannot be set aside on the mere ipse dixit of suspended management where the debtor failed to satisfy statutory land-conversion conditions, and a base reserve price fixed on 'as is where is' terms does not restrict competitive price discovery. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 35 requires registered valuers to determine realizable value in accordance with lawful status; non-payment of mandatory external development charges precludes formal legal conversion of agricultural land into industrial land, irrespective of historic physical use. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Estoppel by prior admission and documentary verification; an erstwhile management that previously pleaded the agricultural nature of land to resist SARFAESI proceedings cannot contradict that stance without evidence of statutory conversion or producing higher competing bidders. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The valuers properly evaluated the property in accordance with law, the sale notice was unambiguous, and the application was an abuse of process aimed at thwarting liquidation.
operative_order: Appeals dismissed; NCLT Principal Bench order dated 04.12.2019 dismissing CA No. 1079(PB)/2019 and imposing Rs. 50,000 costs affirmed; no order as to costs in appeal.
summary: The erstwhile management of Forgings Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order dismissing their challenge to the liquidation valuation and sale notice of its Faridabad property, where a reserve price of Rs. 52.58 Crores had been fixed and the asset sold for Rs. 52.83 Crores. Appellants claimed the property was industrial and worth over Rs. 100 Crores. NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor had never paid statutory external development charges to obtain a valid change of land use from agricultural to industrial, and had itself previously admitted the agricultural status under SARFAESI proceedings. Finding the valuation compliant with Regulation 35 and the litigation a dilatory tactic, NCLAT affirmed the dismissal and the Rs. 50,000 cost.

case_title: Sunil S. Kakkad vs. Atrium Infocom Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sunil S. Kakkad is the Promoter and Shareholder of Corporate Debtor Atrium Infocom Private Limited (Appellant); Atrium Infocom Private Limited through Liquidator Sunil Kumar Aggarwal (Respondent No. 1); Manish Kumar Bhagat is the Erstwhile IRP (Respondent No. 2); State Bank of India is Lead Bank of Consortium/CoC (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor from the State Bank of India consortium. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to initiation of CIRP; Corporate Debtor was non-operational and had ceased business operations for over five years. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 10.07.2019; CoC 2nd meeting deferred EOI; CoC 3rd meeting held on 21.09.2019 (minuted 01.10.2019) resolved to liquidate; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench passed liquidation order on 05.12.2019 in IA No. 758 of 2019 in CP No. 181/NCLT/AHM/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 2nd and 3rd CoC meetings recording that the company had no business operations for five years and had zero prospect of resolution, resulting in a 100% vote share resolution to liquidate under Section 33(2). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench initiated CIRP on 10.07.2019. On 05.12.2019, NCLT allowed the IRP's application under Section 33(2) and ordered liquidation based on the 100% unanimous CoC vote without issuing Form G.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors, acting with the requisite voting share, possesses statutory authority under Section 33(2) read with the Explanation thereto to recommend direct liquidation of a Corporate Debtor without issuing Form-G or inviting Expressions of Interest; and whether such a decision falls within the unreviewable commercial wisdom of the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the Explanation to Section 33(2) of the IBC, the Committee of Creditors is statutorily empowered to resolve to liquidate a corporate debtor at any stage of the CIRP following its constitution, including prior to the preparation of an information memorandum or publication of an Expression of Interest, and such a commercial decision is non-justiciable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Explanation inserted into Section 33(2) by Act 26 of 2019 explicitly clarifies that CoC may decide to liquidate at any time between Section 21(1) constitution and plan confirmation; resolution steps like Form-G and EOI are not mandatory statutory prerequisites if the CoC concludes resolution is unviable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom doctrine established in K. Sashidhar; the subjective assessment by a 100% CoC vote that a company defunct for five years has no prospects of revival cannot be reviewed by judicial authorities under Section 61(3). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC acted fully within its statutory rights under Section 33(2) in liquidating the Corporate Debtor without issuing an EOI, and the liquidation order is lawful.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench liquidation order dated 05.12.2019 affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: The promoter of Atrium Infocom Private Limited appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order directing liquidation of the Corporate Debtor under Section 33(2) of the IBC. The Appellant argued that liquidation is an exceptional measure and the IRP/CoC erred by liquidating the company after only three meetings without issuing Form-G or inviting Expressions of Interest. NCLAT held that pursuant to the 2019 amendment adding the Explanation to Section 33(2), the CoC is explicitly authorized to resolve to liquidate the Corporate Debtor at any time after its constitution, including prior to the preparation of an Information Memorandum or EOI. Because the CoC unanimously decided with 100% voting share that revival was unviable for a company non-functional for five years, its commercial wisdom is non-justiciable. Appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Girish Baduni vs. Punjab National Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Girish Baduni is the Ex-Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Atlas Alloy (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant); Punjab National Bank is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Satyendra Prasad Khorania is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities consisting of Cash Credit, Bills Discounting, and Term Loan sanctioned by PNB to the Corporate Debtor in 2005 and renewed/enhanced periodically, secured by a hypothecation agreement dated 09.11.2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account classified as NPA on 30.09.2017; recall notice issued on 03.10.2017 demanding outstanding default amount of Rs. 11,25,09,298.94. Corporate Debtor subsequently submitted a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal admitting debt and default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition filed before NCLT Jaipur; admission order passed ex-parte on 20.09.2019; statutory public announcement made on 01.11.2019; appeal filed after an alleged delay of 110 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Speed post receipts and tracking reports dated 26.08.2019; emails sent to gbincoeatlas@rediffmail.com (printed on company letterheads) and cs.shubham@gmail.com; physical notices pasted at premises of related entity Grand Batteries Pvt. Ltd.; SARFAESI notices served at common registered office; Statutory Auditor audit report emails dated 04.11.2019; minutes of CoC meetings attended by Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PNB filed Section 7 petition CP No. (IB)-205/7/JPR/2019 before NCLT Jaipur. Due to non-appearance despite service, NCLT proceeded ex-parte and admitted the Corporate Debtor into CIRP on 20.09.2019.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 CIRP admission order was passed in violation of principles of natural justice due to defective service of notice on the Corporate Debtor; and whether the appeal was barred by limitation under Section 61(2) in light of effective service and statutory public announcement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of petition notice upon the corporate email address printed on the official letterhead of a corporate debtor and via physical affixation at its operational premises constitutes valid service, and former management cannot evade service by claiming that the official email was neglected or managed solely by former employees. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 admission requires satisfaction of debt and default; where existence of financial debt and default are admitted via an OTS proposal, technical objections regarding service will not vitiate admission, especially when the statutory public announcement fixes constructive notice on all stakeholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Constructive notice and active participation; where suspended directors attend multiple CoC meetings and statutory auditors engage with the IRP, a belated claim of ignorance of the CIRP order is untruthful and barred by limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Service of notice was fully effected in compliance with natural justice; debt and default stood proved by the OTS; and the appeal was a delayed abuse of process.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed on both merits and limitation; NCLT Jaipur admission order dated 20.09.2019 affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: The ex-director of Atlas Alloy (India) Pvt. Ltd. challenged an ex-parte order of NCLT Jaipur admitting a Section 7 petition filed by Punjab National Bank for a default of Rs. 11.25 Crores, alleging breach of natural justice due to lack of notice service. NCLAT rejected the challenge, observing that notice was served on the corporate debtor's official letterhead email, pasted at its premises, and sent to related director emails. Furthermore, the debt and default were admitted via an OTS proposal, the corporate debtor's auditor was actively liaising with the IRP since November 2019, and the director had attended multiple CoC meetings before belatedly filing the appeal after a 110-day delay. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Shree Sidhivinayak Cotspin Private Limited & Anr. vs. Resolution Professional of Maruti Cotex Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shree Sidhivinayak Cotspin Private Limited & Anr. are the Successful Resolution Applicants (Appellants); Resolution Professional of Maruti Cotex Limited is Respondent No. 1; Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of a resolution plan in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Corporate Debtor Maruti Cotex Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Insolvency arising in CP (IB) No. 241/30(6)/MB/2018; resolution plan provided specific payouts to creditors and contained extensive blanket liability waiver clauses under para 6.4 (running from pages 48 to 67 of the plan). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the resolution plan with observations on 02.07.2020 in MA No. 422 of 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan containing clauses seeking blanket waivers, extinguishment, and concessions regarding past statutory dues, taxes, and penalties; paragraphs 23, 24, and 25 of the NCLT approval order directing the applicant to approach relevant regulatory authorities for such concessions under applicable laws. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan under Section 31 on 02.07.2020, but declined to grant blanket general exemptions, directing the SRA to approach statutory authorities for concessions and ensure compliance with applicable laws. The SRA appealed under Section 61(3) contending that withholding these reliefs altered the plan and made it commercially unviable.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed by a Successful Resolution Applicant challenging an Adjudicating Authority's refusal to grant blanket statutory reliefs and concessions—directing it instead to approach relevant statutory authorities—falls within the grounds specified under Section 61(3) of the IBC; and whether declining blanket waivers amounts to an impermissible modification of the resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against an order approving a resolution plan is strictly maintainable only on the exhaustive statutory grounds enumerated in Section 61(3) of the IBC, which do not permit a successful resolution applicant to challenge the approval order on the ground that the adjudicating authority refused to grant blanket concessions or waivers of statutory liabilities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) renders an approved plan binding on all stakeholders and allows the resolution applicant to start on a clean slate regarding claims dealt with therein, but the Adjudicating Authority is not obligated to grant blanket prospective immunities and acts within law by directing the applicant to apply to competent regulatory bodies for statutory concessions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Jurisdictional threshold under Section 61(3); appellate scrutiny is circumscribed to contravention of law, material irregularity by RP, or non-compliance with Section 30(2) priority distributions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's direction to comply with prevailing laws and seek concessions from competent authorities does not modify the terms of the resolution plan, and the appeal is outside the maintainable scope of Section 61(3).
operative_order: Appeal dismissed as not maintainable under Section 61(3) of the IBC; NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 02.07.2020 affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: The Successful Resolution Applicant of Maruti Cotex Limited appealed against the approval order of NCLT Mumbai Bench under Section 61(3) of the IBC. The Appellant contended that NCLT modified the approved plan by refusing to grant blanket waivers and reliefs for past statutory dues and penalties, instead directing the applicant to approach relevant regulatory authorities under applicable laws. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority did not modify the plan, but correctly declined general statutory exemptions while reiterating compliance with law. Further, challenging the refusal of concessions does not fall within any of the limited grounds in Section 61(3) for appealing an approval order. The appeal was dismissed as non-maintainable.

case_title: Adish Jain vs. Sumit Bansal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Adish Jain is the Shareholder of Corporate Debtor M/s J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant); Sumit Bansal is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Worldwide Metals Private Limited is the Operational Creditor (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was a regular purchaser of Aluminium Ingots and Wire Rods maintainable under an open running account with the Operational Creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed for the period 06.12.2017 to 16.04.2018 amounting to Rs. 16,18,18,265 in principal default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Prior notice issued on 17.08.2018; replied on 28.08.2018; statutory Section 8 demand notice issued on 27.10.2018; notice of dispute replied on 05.11.2018; Section 9 admission order passed by NCLT New Delhi on 26.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor relied on unilateral journal adjustment entries and confirmatory letters involving sister concerns Olympus Metal, Simla Holdings, and Oyster Steel; letter dated 30.04.2018 allegedly signed by Vikas Gandhi who had already resigned on 22.01.2018; RTGS transfers of Rs. 1,95,34,823 and Rs. 1,95,79,294 made directly to the Operational Creditor and omitted from debt computation; confirmation of accounts dated 01.04.2019 created post-demand notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application CP (IB) No. 1048/ND/2019 before NCLT New Delhi Court-II, which admitted the application on 26.02.2020 finding the alleged adjustment disputes moonshine and illusionary.
legal_issues: Whether unilateral ledger journal entries and disputed adjustments with third-party sister concerns constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9 of the IBC to warrant rejection of CIRP initiation under the Mobilox Innovations standard.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A defense of account reconciliation or debt extinguishment through tripartite adjustment entries across corporate group entities must be founded on genuine, contemporaneous, and authorized agreements, failing which the defense is moonshine and does not constitute a valid pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5), a pre-existing dispute must be substantiated by real, plausible controversy regarding the quality, quantity, price, or subsistence of the debt existing prior to the demand notice, rather than fabricated post-facto assertions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Plausible contention test under Mobilox Innovations; documents featuring patent discrepancies, signatures of former employees post-resignation, and contradictory pleas of debt denial and simultaneous discharge fail to establish a bona fide dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to prove any authorized tripartite adjustment agreement, and the alleged ledger entries were spurious; the unpaid operational debt exceeding statutory thresholds was due and payable, justifying admission.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; NCLT New Delhi admission order dated 26.02.2020 affirmed; I.A. No. 1509 of 2020 disposed of granting liberty to the IRP to pursue Section 19(2) non-cooperation proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority; no order as to costs.
summary: A shareholder of Corporate Debtor J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Worldwide Metals Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 16.18 Crores arising from the supply of Aluminium Ingots and Wire Rods. The Appellant claimed the debt stood discharged via journal entries and adjustments among sister concerns, creating a pre-existing dispute. NCLAT held that the adjustment documents were uncorroborated, contained forged signatures of resigned personnel, lacked tripartite board authorization, and were contradicted by direct RTGS records. Applying the Mobilox Innovations doctrine, NCLAT found the dispute spurious and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mr. Mahendra Govindlal Agarwal vs. Taranjot Resources Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Mahendra Govindlal Agarwal is a Director and Shareholder of Corporate Debtor Dhanurdhar Processors Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant); Taranjot Resources Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Dhanurdhar Processors Pvt. Ltd. through IRP Rajeev Saxena is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply and delivery of coal by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor pursuant to sales invoices requiring payment within 10 days of delivery. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal operational debt of Rs. 87,25,069.90 claimed by the Operational Creditor; disputed portion alleged by Corporate Debtor was approximately Rs. 20 Lakhs, leaving debt above the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued under Section 8 on 20.04.2018; no notice of dispute or reply received within 10 days; Section 9 petition filed in July 2018; admission order passed by NCLT Ahmedabad on 05.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Government-approved third-party lab sampling and analysis certificates confirming coal quality; invoices and delivery challans; continued coal supplies accepted after 18.12.2017 without objection; alleged defect acknowledgment letter dated 01.01.2018 bearing disputed and unauthorized signatures; returned cheques explained by bank account closure. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition CP(IB) No. 357/9/NCLT/AHM/2018 was admitted by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 05.06.2020 after finding that default exceeded statutory limits and no valid dispute had been raised within the statutory period.
legal_issues: Whether an omission to mention a specific board meeting in a corporate annual return invalidates an application under Section 9 of the IBC; and whether an unsubstantiated quality dispute raised after receipt of a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor body corporate's application under Section 9 is valid if duly authorized by board resolution attested by affidavit, notwithstanding typographical or formatting omissions in its regulatory annual returns; furthermore, belated quality defenses unsupported by contemporaneous objections do not constitute a pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii) provides exhaustive grounds for rejecting a petition; minor statutory filing disclosures do not render an application incomplete under Section 9(2) where competent corporate authority is established on record. Under Section 8(2)(a), the debtor must bring existence of dispute to notice within 10 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous conduct and documentation standard; continued acceptance of goods without complaint together with third-party testing certificates negates post-default claims of inferior quality. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to reply to the statutory demand notice or prove a bona fide pre-existing dispute, while the admitted debt far exceeded the threshold; the admission order was fully justified.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admission order dated 05.06.2020 initiating CIRP against Dhanurdhar Processors Pvt. Ltd. affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: The promoter of Corporate Debtor Dhanurdhar Processors Pvt. Ltd. challenged NCLT Ahmedabad's order admitting a Section 9 application filed by coal supplier Taranjot Resources Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid dues of Rs. 87.25 Lakhs. The Appellant contended that the petition lacked a valid Board Resolution due to an omission in annual returns, that coal quality was deficient, and that cheques were returned. NCLAT held that the Board authorization was adequately substantiated by affidavit, government-approved lab reports proved coal quality, and the debtor continued accepting supplies without issuing a Section 8(2)(a) dispute notice. Finding no genuine pre-existing dispute, NCLAT affirmed the admission order and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Sarabjit Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Gopal Singh & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sarabjit Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. & majority shareholders holding 77.8% equity (Appellants); Gopal Singh & 7 other minority shareholders/removed directors (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate internal governance dispute regarding convening of an Extra Ordinary General Meeting (EOGM) on 27.06.2020, resulting in the removal of Respondents Nos. 1 and 2 from the directorship, which removal was registered with ROC Jharkhand on 29.06.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute pertains to management and control under oppression and mismanagement provisions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EOGM notice issued 03.06.2020; EOGM held 27.06.2020; ROC intimation 29.06.2020; unnumbered Company Petition heard and interim injunction granted on 08.07.2020 (later numbered 762/KB/2020). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: EOGM notices dated 03.06.2020; written Defence Note (Annexure-A8) and List of Dates and Events submitted by the Appellants; ROC Jharkhand filing receipts; absence of formal reply affidavits due to lack of time afforded. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed an unnumbered petition under Sections 241, 242, and 244 before NCLT Kolkata Bench via email; on the first date of consideration, NCLT granted ex-parte interim relief staying the operation of the EOGM resolutions and directorship removals without permitting the Appellants to file a reply affidavit or evidentiary documents.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority violated the fundamental principles of natural justice by granting substantive, open-ended interim injunctions staying corporate resolutions on the initial hearing of an unnumbered company petition without providing the contesting majority shareholders an opportunity to file a reply affidavit and evidentiary rebuttal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The grant of interim relief in company petitions under Sections 241 and 242 without affording the contesting respondents a reasonable opportunity to file a formal reply affidavit and supporting evidence amounts to a denial of natural justice and renders the interim order unsustainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The exercise of discretionary powers to grant interim orders under Section 242 must adhere to basic procedural fairness; an interim stay that effectively grants the primary relief on a prima facie basis cannot operate indefinitely without affording the respondents an opportunity to be heard on a formal pleading. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Breach of natural justice test; disposing of urgent interim applications by rejecting written defense summaries without permitting formal counter-affidavits violates due process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT bypassed natural justice in issuing the interim injunction; the order must be quashed and the matter remitted for de novo consideration after completion of pleadings.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned interim order dated 08.07.2020 set aside without expressing opinions on merits; matter remitted to NCLT Kolkata Bench; Appellants directed to file Reply Affidavit within one week and Respondents to file Rejoinder within three days thereafter; NCLT directed to hear both parties afresh on interim relief and decide within one month; no costs.
summary: Appellants, holding 77.8% shares in Sarabjit Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd., appealed an interim order passed by NCLT Kolkata in an unnumbered petition under Sections 241-244 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLT had stayed EOGM resolutions that removed Respondents Nos. 1 and 2 from directorships on the first day of hearing, without allowing the Appellants to file a reply affidavit or produce evidence. NCLAT held that granting indefinite interim relief without affording the respondents an opportunity to place their pleadings and evidence on record violated principles of natural justice. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the interim order and remitted the matter for expeditious hearing after exchange of affidavits.

case_title: K.V. Brahmaji Rao vs. Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant K.V. Brahmaji Rao was the Executive Director of Punjab National Bank (PNB), Head Office, New Delhi; Respondent is the Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs through the Regional Director (Western Region). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Investigation and oppression proceedings initiated by the Central Government concerning the massive financial banking fraud orchestrated by the Nirav Modi and Gitanjali Groups against PNB. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Multi-crore financial fraud perpetrated against PNB through unauthorized letters of undertaking and credit instruments. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CBI FIRs registered on 31.01.2018 and 15.02.2018; MCA initiated CP No. 277 of 2018; NCLT Mumbai Bench passed asset-freezing and impleadment order on 31.01.2019 in M.A. Nos. 406 & 407 of 2019; Supreme Court judgment in companion case rendered on 12.02.2020; appeal decided on 17.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CBI charge-sheets in Nirav Modi and Gitanjali Group cases naming 19 bank officials alleging dishonest omissions; absence of any corporate directorship, employment, or management link between Appellant and the accused companies. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: MCA filed M.A. Nos. 406 and 407 of 2019 in CP No. 277 of 2018 seeking to implead 19 PNB officials and freeze their personal assets. NCLT Mumbai allowed the applications on 31.01.2019, impleading the Appellant as Respondent No. 83 and freezing his assets.
legal_issues: Whether statutory powers under Section 241(2) read with Sections 337 and 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 can be invoked to implead and freeze the personal assets of an executive officer of a third-party lending institution (PNB) in an oppression and mismanagement petition concerning external debtor companies.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory provisions governing oppression, mismanagement, and fraudulent conduct under Sections 241, 242, 337, and 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 apply exclusively to officers, directors, and entities involved in the affairs and management of the company under investigation, and cannot be invoked against officers or heads of third-party external organizations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 339(1) refers to persons who were knowingly parties to the carrying on of the business of the mismanaged corporate entity with intent to defraud; it does not extend to officers or employees of independent lending organizations who are not connected with the management of that corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct nexus test; external bank employees cannot be roped into company mismanagement petitions without proof of direct participation in the corporate governance of the fraudulent enterprise. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Following the Supreme Court precedent in Usha Ananthasubramanian vs. Union of India, the Appellant, as an officer of PNB, could not be impleaded or subjected to asset restraint under Section 339 in a petition concerning Nirav Modi/Gitanjali companies.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 31.01.2019 impleading Appellant as Respondent No. 83 and freezing his personal movable and immovable assets set aside; clarification made that this order does not affect independent criminal investigations by CBI or SFIO; no costs.
summary: Appellant, the former Executive Director of Punjab National Bank, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order impleading him as a respondent and freezing his personal assets in CP No. 277 of 2018, an oppression and fraud petition filed by the Union of India regarding the Nirav Modi and Gitanjali group banking scam. NCLAT applied the Supreme Court ruling in Usha Ananthasubramanian vs. Union of India, holding that powers under Sections 241, 242, 337, and 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 are restricted to persons involved in the management of the mismanaged company and cannot be used against employees or heads of external organizations such as lending banks. The impleadment and asset-freezing orders were quashed.

case_title: LCL Logistix (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Waaree Energies Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: LCL Logistix (India) Pvt. Ltd. is the freight forwarding and logistics service provider (Operational Creditor/Appellant); Waaree Energies Ltd. is a solar photovoltaic module manufacturer and trader (Corporate Debtor/Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Freight forwarding, cargo stuffing, customs clearance, and container logistics agreement requiring Corporate Debtor to de-stuff import cargo and return containers within agreed free periods or incur container detention and demurrage charges. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Demurrage and detention claim of Rs. 1,50,97,439 principal plus 24% interest amounting to Rs. 25,94,012.65, totaling Rs. 1,76,91,452.70. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor sent dispute email on 09.03.2018; Section 8 demand notice issued on 05.09.2018; notice of dispute issued on 14.09.2018; Section 9 petition rejected by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 29.06.2020 in CP No. 4603(IB)/MB/2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email communication dated 09.03.2018 from the Corporate Debtor questioning and disputing demurrage charges and detention invoice calculations across project sites (Bhiwandi, SEZ Sachin, and Akola); reply notice dated 14.09.2018 denying liability; disputed detention period computations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application before NCLT Mumbai Bench, which rejected the petition on 29.06.2020 holding that the Corporate Debtor had raised a genuine, non-frivolous dispute regarding detention charges prior to the demand notice.
legal_issues: Whether pre-demand notice email correspondence disputing the basis, computation, and crystallization of container detention and demurrage charges constitutes a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Section 8 and Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC, requiring dismissal under the summary jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt claim based on uncrystallized, contentious demurrage and detention charges that requires extensive evidentiary appraisal cannot be enforced under the summary jurisdiction of the IBC where the corporate debtor raised contemporaneous disputes prior to the delivery of the statutory demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9(5)(2)(d), the Adjudicating Authority must reject a Section 9 petition if a valid notice of pre-existing dispute exists; the authority is not empowered in summary proceedings to adjudicate unliquidated claims requiring extensive evidence on contractual defaults. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox Innovations plausible contention test; the court must determine only whether a plausible contention exists requiring further trial and whether the defense is not patently frivolous, spurious, or mere bluster, without evaluating the ultimate likelihood of success. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor's email of 09.03.2018 established a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding demurrage claims before the 05.09.2018 demand notice, rendering the Section 9 petition unmaintainable.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed at threshold; NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 29.06.2020 rejecting Section 9 application CP No. 4603(IB)/MB/2018 affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: LCL Logistix (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its Section 9 application against Waaree Energies Ltd. for unpaid demurrage and container detention charges of Rs. 1.76 Crores. The NCLT rejected the petition on grounds of a pre-existing dispute. NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor had expressly disputed the demurrage calculations via email on 09.03.2018, nearly six months prior to the Section 8 demand notice dated 05.09.2018. Holding that uncrystallized demurrage charges requiring extensive evidence cannot be decided in summary IBC proceedings and applying the Mobilox test, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. vs. Anil Goel, Liquidator of Visa Power Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL, Operational Creditor claiming secured status); Respondent No. 1 is Anil Goel (Liquidator of Visa Power Limited); Respondent No. 2 is Agrawal Structure Mills Pvt. Ltd. (Auction Purchaser). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Notice Inviting Tender and Letter of Award dated 28.06.2010 awarded by Visa Power Ltd. to BHEL for design, engineering, supply, erection, and commissioning of a 2 x 600 MW Coal-based Thermal Power Plant in Raigarh, Chhattisgarh; BHEL supplied ~26,000 MT and erected ~9,500 MT of material before work was suspended due to non-payment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: BHEL claimed monetary default of Rs. 664,98,37,221, of which Liquidator admitted Rs. 572,19,46,434 under Section 53(1)(f); auction Block 'B' was sold to Respondent No. 2 for Rs. 27.61 Crores (including GST) against a reserve price of Rs. 23.30 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 22.12.2017; Liquidation ordered on 11.10.2018; Form C submitted on 09.11.2018; NCLT remitted security interest adjudication to Liquidator on 10.05.2019; Liquidator issued Sale Certificate on 20.05.2019 prior to deciding BHEL's claim on 03.06.2019; NCLT Kolkata passed impugned order on 13.12.2019 in C.A. (IB) Nos. 684 & 792/KB/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Discrepancies between newspaper Sale Notice dated 10.04.2019 (46 items) and internal E-Auction Document (57 items shifting Turbine Generator, Boiler Tower, and ESP from Block 'A' Building to Block 'B' Plant/Machinery without changing reserve price); balance sheets of sole competing dummy bidder Pavani Construction; police complaints dated 06.08.2019 and 19.12.2019 for theft of Rs. 20 Crores worth of transmission towers and pipelines. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: BHEL challenged the auction sale and rejection of its secured claim before NCLT Kolkata; NCLT found valuation flaws and irregularities but upheld the sale to Respondent No. 2 as a bona fide purchaser and rejected BHEL's statutory lien.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory unpaid seller's lien under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 or statutory charge under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 constitutes a 'security interest' under Section 3(31) making the claimant a 'Secured Creditor' under Section 3(30) of the IBC without a transaction/contractual creation; and whether an auction sale is vitiated where the liquidator shifts major embedded structures from building to machinery blocks without adjusting reserve prices, fails to prescribe pre-bid qualifications under Schedule 1 of the Liquidation Regulations, and issues a sale certificate before determining pending security interests.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Sections 3(30) and 3(31) read with Section 238 of the IBC, a security interest must be consciously created by the parties through a consensual transaction or contractual agreement, and statutory liens or charges arising purely by operation of general statutes do not confer secured creditor status under the Code; however, an auction sale conducted with fundamental variances between public notices and bidding documents, lacking pre-bid qualifications and marred by unauthorized removal of unauctioned assets, is void ab initio. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'created' in Section 3(30) and Section 3(31) requires deliberate, bilateral acts of the parties; Schedule 1 Sub-Clause (3) of the Liquidation Process Regulations mandates prescribing pre-bid qualifications to ensure competitive, genuine auctions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Material variance and procedural legality standard; substantial deviations between public tender descriptions and private bidding sheets, coupled with absence of genuine competitive bidding and theft of unvalued assets, invalidate the defense of being a bona fide auction purchaser. 4.
