DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: BHEL is an unsecured operational creditor under Section 53(1)(f); however, the auction sale was tainted by fundamental illegalities and is quashed, directing full restitution of assets.
operative_order: Appeal allowed in part; NCLT directions in paras 91-101 quashed; rejection of BHEL's claim as a Secured Creditor affirmed; auction sale dated 01.05.2019, Sale Notice dated 10.04.2019, and Certificate of Sale dated 20.05.2019 set aside; Respondent No. 2 directed to return all removed material to the project site at its own cost within 15 days; Liquidator directed to pursue police complaints, inventory assets, obtain fresh valuations from two new valuers, and conduct re-auction; matter remitted to NCLT Kolkata; copy of judgment forwarded to IBBI for potential Section 218 inquiry; Respondent No. 2 ordered to pay Rs. 5 Lakhs costs to Appellant.
summary: BHEL appealed an NCLT Kolkata order rejecting its claim as a secured creditor holding an unpaid vendor's lien over plant and machinery supplied to Visa Power Ltd., while upholding the liquidation sale of the assets to Agrawal Structure Mills Pvt. Ltd. despite finding grave valuation errors. NCLAT held that a 'security interest' under Section 3(31) of the IBC requires consensual creation through a transaction, meaning general statutory liens under the Sale of Goods Act do not make an operational creditor a secured creditor. However, NCLAT quashed the auction sale as illegal due to fundamental discrepancies between the advertised notice and the assets transferred, absence of pre-bid qualifications, a non-genuine bidding process, and unauthorized removal of Rs. 20 Crores of unauctioned assets, ordering full restitution.

case_title: M/s Allied Silica Limited vs. M/s Tata Chemicals Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Allied Silica Limited is the Operational Creditor/Transferor (Appellant); M/s Tata Chemicals Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Transferee (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business Transfer Agreement (BTA) dated 07.04.2018 for the acquisition and transfer of Appellant's precipitated silica manufacturing plant undertaking at Cuddalore, Tamil Nadu on a slump sale basis under Section 2(42C) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 as a going concern on 'as is where is' basis for a total consideration of Rs. 123 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor paid Closing Balance Consideration of Rs. 65.19 Crores on 18.06.2018, Tranche-I of Rs. 35 Crores, and Tranche-II of Rs. 17 Crores; Appellant claimed an outstanding operational debt of Rs. 58 Crores (including interest of Rs. 10.44 Crores, total claim Rs. 68.44 Crores), whereas Corporate Debtor adjusted Tranche-III of Rs. 6 Crores against improvement costs due to unfulfilled Conditions Precedent. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Slump sale consummated on 18.06.2018; interim dispute letters/emails exchanged on 13.10.2018, 08.01.2019, 11.02.2019, 06.03.2019, 08.04.2019, and 13.05.2019; Form 3 Demand Notice issued on 03.06.2019; Reply to Demand Notice delivered on 14.06.2019; Section 9 application filed on 02.08.2019; NCLT Mumbai rejected application on 15.11.2019 in CP (IB) No. 2953/NCLT/MB/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bilateral letter agreement dated 08.01.2019 recording non-completion of Tranche-II Conditions Precedent and adjusting Tranche-III payments; Corporate Debtor's demand letter dated 06.03.2019 demanding refund of Rs. 15.01 Crores; emails alleging BTA drafting coercion and EGM resolution tampering; invoice dated 18.06.2018; timely reply dated 14.06.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 petition before NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT dismissed the petition on 15.11.2019 on grounds of pre-existing dispute and failure to establish an undisputed operational debt.
legal_issues: Whether a dispute regarding compliance with contractual Conditions Precedent, set-off of milestone tranches under a Business Transfer Agreement, and allegations of contractual duress raised prior to the statutory demand notice constitutes a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected where the corporate debtor establishes a bona fide, plausible pre-existing dispute regarding contractual non-performance and milestone tranche entitlement raised prior to the service of the Section 8 demand notice, as summary insolvency proceedings cannot determine contested claims of contractual breach and set-off. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9(5)(2)(d), the receipt of a notice of dispute documenting pre-existing controversies bars admission; the Adjudicating Authority does not assess the ultimate likelihood of success on the merits but merely verifies whether the dispute is plausible, substantiated by contemporaneous record, and not mere bluster. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox Innovations plausible contention standard; extensive pre-notice correspondence demonstrating bilateral negotiations, adjustments, and demands for refund precludes summary CIRP initiation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The mutual letter dated 08.01.2019 and correspondence dated 06.03.2019 established a real, contemporaneous pre-existing dispute regarding completion of conditions precedent and set-offs prior to the demand notice of 03.06.2019, justifying rejection of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 15.11.2019 rejecting Section 9 application affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Allied Silica Limited appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its Section 9 application against Tata Chemicals Limited for an alleged balance operational debt of Rs. 58 Crores arising from a slump sale of its silica plant under a Business Transfer Agreement valued at Rs. 123 Crores. The Corporate Debtor had disbursed over Rs. 117 Crores across initial consideration and milestone tranches but withheld Tranche-III pursuant to a signed agreement dated 08.01.2019 due to unfulfilled Conditions Precedent and incurred rectification costs. NCLAT held that extensive correspondence prior to the Section 8 notice—including allegations of contract modification and demands for refund—demonstrated a genuine pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox doctrine, affirming dismissal of the petition.

case_title: M/s Jitendra Impex Private Limited vs. Compack Enterprise India Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Jitendra Impex Private Limited is the Operational Creditor/wholesale paper trader (Appellant); Compack Enterprise India Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/paper purchaser (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regular commercial supply of paper and paper board products by Appellant to Corporate Debtor on a 30-day credit period maintainable under an open running account with FIFO invoice adjustment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default of Rs. 1,81,45,943 arising from sales of Rs. 7,89,06,382 in FY 2017-18 and Rs. 2,03,52,062 in FY 2018-19 against payments received; Corporate Debtor admitted an outstanding payable debt of Rs. 22,56,833 and tendered a cheque before NCLT, which Appellant declined. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Ledger confirmation emails exchanged on 08.10.2016 and 17.05.2018; Section 8 demand notice issued on 28.12.2018; reply to demand notice sent on 11.01.2019; NCLT New Delhi Bench-II dismissed Section 9 petition on 23.08.2019 in CP (IB)-183/ND/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's email dated 08.10.2016 confirming balance from official MCA email ID compackindia@gmail.com; email dated 17.05.2018 admitting outstanding liability of Rs. 2,34,10,945 as on 30.04.2018; running ledger statements; unverified credit notes and CENVAT dispute letters dated 13.09.2018 and 14.09.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II dismissed the Section 9 petition on 23.08.2019 holding that discrepancies in opening/closing ledger balances amounted to inconsistent conduct, failing to prove default.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can dismiss a Section 9 application on grounds of ledger reconciliation discrepancies when the Corporate Debtor has explicitly admitted an operational debt exceeding the statutory threshold (Rs. 1 Lakh) via email confirmations and an admitted balance of Rs. 22,56,833 tendered in open court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC, the applicant is not required to establish the indisputable precision of the entire claimed quantum; rather, establishing the occurrence of a default of an operational debt exceeding the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh, in the absence of a genuine pre-existing dispute, mandates admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Macquarie Bank and Mobilox Innovations under Section 9(5), the core inquiry is whether there is an unpaid operational debt exceeding the statutory minimum and whether default has occurred; reconciliation variances regarding the larger claim do not justify dismissal if an admitted debt above the statutory minimum is established. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admission of liability standard; unambiguous written admissions via corporate emails and in-court tender of payment for sums exceeding the threshold constitute conclusive proof of debt and default, rendering post-notice defenses spurious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Corporate Debtor conceded an unpaid liability of Rs. 22,56,833 (well above Rs. 1 Lakh) and confirmed balances via email, NCLT committed an error of record in dismissing the petition for lack of exact accounting reconciliation.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT New Delhi Bench-II order dated 23.08.2019 set aside; matter remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the Section 9 application after notice to both parties and granting the Corporate Debtor an opportunity to settle prior to formal admission; parties directed to appear on 15.09.2020; no costs.
summary: Jitendra Impex Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 application against Compack Enterprise India Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 1.81 Crores arising from paper supplies. The NCLT had dismissed the petition citing irreconcilable discrepancies between the parties' respective ledger accounts. NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that under Macquarie Bank and Mobilox principles, an operational creditor is not required to prove the totality of the claimed amount, but merely that an undisputed debt exceeding the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh is due and in default. Because the Corporate Debtor admitted owing Rs. 22,56,833 in its reply and tendered a cheque before the tribunal, the occurrence of default stood established, warranting admission.

case_title: Nirmal K. Dhiran, Proprietor of NKV Home Depot vs. Landmark Housing Projects Chennai Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Nirmal K. Dhiran, Proprietor of NKV Home Depot, is the Operational Creditor (Appellant); Landmark Housing Projects Chennai Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of NKV Gypsum bags and fine plaster materials by Operational Creditor to Corporate Debtor from 29.05.2017 onwards for construction project works pursuant to purchase orders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total invoices raised amounted to Rs. 50,16,306; Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 35,58,130; claimed outstanding operational debt was Rs. 14,58,176 principal plus Rs. 1,46,776.85 interest; two dishonored cheques of Rs. 4,00,000 and Rs. 2,00,000 had been replaced and paid via RTGS. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Quality dispute meetings held on 16.11.2018; dispute emails exchanged on 21.11.2018, 29.11.2018, 15.12.2018, and 17.12.2018; Section 8 Form-3 demand notice issued on 29.03.2019; NCLT Chennai Bench-I dismissed Section 9 application IBA/834/2019 on 05.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase orders dated 15.07.2017 and 28.08.2017 for 1,200 and 4,400 bags; delivery challans showing expired Gypsum bags manufactured in September 2017 delivered in November 2018 (exceeding one-year shelf warranty); minutes of meeting dated 16.11.2018 and termination emails dated 15.12.2018 and 17.12.2018 asserting over Rs. 25 Lakhs in losses due to excessive consumption and uncompleted plastering works. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application IBA/834/2019 before NCLT Chennai Bench-I; NCLT dismissed the application on 05.05.2020 on grounds of a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding defective and expired materials raised prior to the demand notice.
legal_issues: Whether contemporaneous documentary evidence of defective, expired supplies, delayed delivery, and contractual termination communicated prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where contemporaneous communications establish a real, substantiated dispute regarding product quality, shelf life expiry, and consequential losses prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice, the claim cannot be resolved under the summary jurisdiction of the IBC and the Section 9 petition must be rejected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(2)(a) read with Section 9(5)(2)(d) and the principles in Mobilox Innovations, the Adjudicating Authority must only examine whether a plausible contention exists that is not a patently feeble legal argument or mere bluster, without inquiring into whether the defense will ultimately succeed at trial. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Plausible contention standard; internal memos, minutes of meeting, and emails documenting delivery of expired goods and termination of orders prior to the demand notice satisfy the threshold of an existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because extensive emails and minutes from November and December 2018 demonstrated a substantive dispute concerning defective gypsum prior to the demand notice of 29.03.2019, NCLT rightly dismissed the application.
operative_order: Delay in filing appeal condoned; Appeal dismissed at the admission stage; NCLT Chennai Bench-I order dated 05.05.2020 affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Nirmal K. Dhiran, proprietor of NKV Home Depot, appealed an NCLT Chennai order dismissing his Section 9 application against Landmark Housing Projects Chennai Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid dues of Rs. 14.58 Lakhs regarding gypsum supplies. The NCLT dismissed the petition finding a pre-existing dispute. NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, noting that emails and minutes of meetings from November and December 2018—well before the Section 8 demand notice of 29.03.2019—established that the Corporate Debtor had raised specific grievances concerning the supply of expired materials, defective plaster coverage, and losses exceeding Rs. 25 Lakhs. Applying the Mobilox Innovations rule that summary IBC proceedings cannot resolve bona fide quality disputes, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Darode Jog Homes Pvt. Ltd. vs. IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Darode Jog Homes Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor, and Respondent IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. is the Creditor seeking insolvency resolution. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter pertains to insolvency proceedings under CP (IB) 1346/MB of 2019 and an interim asset protection order concerning the transfer/sale of Transferable Development Rights (TDR) assets of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact loan quantum and default date are not explicitly detailed in the interlocutory order; however, the Adjudicating Authority directed deposit of Rs. 2 Crores or the consideration amount of the TDR, whichever is higher. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 6th June 2019, an undertaking was formulated before the Adjudicating Authority; the impugned order in I.A. No. 1011 of 2020 was subsequently passed on 9th July 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's solemn undertaking recorded on 6th June 2019 not to alienate any assets, juxtaposed against evidence that the Corporate Debtor alienated and sold TDR assets without court modification or disclosure, alleging an unnotified private settlement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed I.A. No. 1011 of 2020 in CP (IB) 1346/MB of 2019 before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court No. II; NCLT directed the Corporate Debtor to deposit Rs. 2 Crores or TDR sale consideration and maintain status quo as on the sale date, which the Corporate Debtor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Debtor can alienate its assets in violation of an undertaking given before the Adjudicating Authority under the guise of an unnotified subsequent settlement, and whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses the power under the IBC to restrain asset alienation and direct deposit of sale consideration to protect creditor interests during insolvency proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party bound by an undertaking before a judicial tribunal cannot unilaterally alienate assets or breach the undertaking under the pretext of an out-of-court settlement without formally seeking vacation or modification of the undertaking order; such equitable misconduct precludes appellate relief. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Adjudicating Authority under the IBC possesses inherent and statutory authority to slap restrictions on the transfer or disposal of the Corporate Debtor's assets to safeguard the res and protect creditors' interests pending insolvency resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance test; an undertaking given to a court has the force of an injunction/order, and breach thereof constitutes inequitable conduct disentitling the defaulter from equitable remedies. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the Corporate Debtor brazenly breached its undertaking by disposing of TDR assets without tribunal leave, validating the Adjudicating Authority's protective directions to deposit Rs. 2 Crores or sale consideration.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed finding no legal infirmity in the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 9th July 2020.
summary: Darode Jog Homes Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing it to deposit Rs. 2 Crores or TDR sale consideration and maintain status quo for selling TDR assets in breach of an undertaking given on 6th June 2019. The Appellant claimed the sale occurred post-settlement with Creditor IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. The NCLAT held that alienating assets without tribunal permission or modification of its undertaking constitutes inequitable conduct and a breach of court orders. Affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction under the IBC to restrict asset transfers, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Dhananjay Krishnanath Gaikwad vs. ICICI Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mr. Dhananjay Krishnanath Gaikwad is the Director of the Corporate Debtor, Respondent No. 1 is ICICI Bank Ltd. (Financial Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is Tuljabhavani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor represented by IRP Mr. Gaurav Adikia). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan and credit facilities extended by ICICI Bank Ltd. to Tuljabhavani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaulted outstanding dues claimed by the Financial Creditor exceeding Rs. 900 lakhs (Rs. 9 Crores); debt and default were undisputed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor filed Section 7 petition, which was admitted by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 24.02.2020; CoC was subsequently constituted. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Undisputed record of debt and default, admission of inability to repay due to severe financial difficulty by the Corporate Debtor, and absence of any executed settlement agreement or concrete proposal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed by ICICI Bank Ltd. was admitted by NCLT Court-III Mumbai Bench on 24.02.2020; Appellant appealed on the sole ground that the Adjudicating Authority should have granted time to raise funds for repayment instead of admitting CIRP.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is obligated to postpone admission of a Section 7 application to grant the Corporate Debtor time to raise funds or negotiate a settlement when debt and default are undisputed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 7 of the IBC, once debt and default are established and undisputed, the Adjudicating Authority is duty-bound to admit the application and cannot drag proceedings endlessly to facilitate debt refinancing or speculative settlements. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory scheme of Section 7 mandates prompt admission upon proof of default; post-admission settlement must follow the prescribed mechanism under Section 12-A of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective satisfaction of existence of financial debt and occurrence of default without room for equitable postponement based on financial hardship. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since debt and default were undisputed and no actual settlement existed, the Adjudicating Authority rightly admitted the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the initiation of CIRP, while granting the Appellant liberty to resort to Section 12-A IBC settlement proceedings in accordance with law.
summary: Dhananjay Krishnanath Gaikwad, Director of Tuljabhavani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Mumbai order admitting ICICI Bank's Section 7 petition for unpaid dues exceeding Rs. 900 lakhs. The Appellant contended that the tribunal should have granted time to raise funds to settle the dues given financial difficulties. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that where financial debt and default are undisputed and no settlement has materialized, insolvency proceedings cannot be dragged endlessly. The admission of CIRP was upheld, leaving the Appellant liberty to seek settlement under Section 12-A IBC.

case_title: Samay Impex Pvt. Ltd. vs. Gujarat Ambuja Exports Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Samay Impex Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor, and Respondent Gujarat Ambuja Exports Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of 1500 MT steam coal pursuant to Purchase Order No. 4500191669 dated 18.07.2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed as Rs. 9,39,730.14 against 6 pending invoices for 200 MT of coal; Respondent asserted accounts were reconciled and settled in full. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: PO issued 18.07.2018; Debit note issued 17.08.2018; Credit note and cheque payment advice dated 27.10.2018; Demand emails sent on 13.11.2018, 29.11.2018, and 17.01.2019; followed by statutory Demand Notice and reply under Section 8. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor issued debit note dated 17.08.2018 for Rs. 11,12,721, subsequent credit note dated 27.10.2018 adjusting debit to Rs. 9,12,721 regarding GCV, final reconciled payment of Rs. 23,69,023 paid via Bank of India cheque dated 27.10.2018, and weight discrepancy (1499.050 MT received vs. 1504.730 MT billed). No criminal complaint was filed by the creditor regarding alleged debit note fabrication. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed by Appellant was dismissed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court II on 17.02.2020 due to pre-existing dispute regarding goods and reconciliation.
legal_issues: Whether a dispute concerning price adjustments via pre-notice debit/credit notes, quantity discrepancies, and full-and-final payment reconciliation constitutes a plausible pre-existing dispute under Section 8 and 9 of the IBC sufficient to reject an insolvency application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt claim cannot be sustained under Section 9 where the debtor establishes a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding quality/quantity and reconciliation of accounts supported by debit and credit notes issued prior to the demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A pre-existing dispute under Section 8/9 must be real, substantiated by contemporaneous pre-notice documentation, and not illusory, spurious, or moonshine; CIRP cannot be invoked for disputed account reconciliations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Plausibility standard established under Mobilox Innovations; contemporaneous debit notes and cheques issued prior to the demand notice satisfy the threshold of a genuine pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the operational debt stood satisfied after reconciliation and rebate, and the dispute raised in the reply to the demand notice was genuinely pre-existing, barring initiation of CIRP.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the pre-admission stage with no legal infirmity found in the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 17th February 2020.
summary: Samay Impex Pvt. Ltd. appealed the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench's dismissal of its Section 9 application against Gujarat Ambuja Exports Ltd. for an alleged operational debt of Rs. 9,39,730.14 for steam coal supply. The Corporate Debtor proved that prior to the statutory demand notice, it had issued debit and credit notes for GCV and weight variances, and made a reconciled full-and-final payment of Rs. 23,69,023 via cheque. The NCLAT affirmed that contemporaneous pre-notice debit notes and reconciled account disputes constitute a genuine, non-spurious pre-existing dispute under the IBC, making CIRP inappropriate and justifying dismissal.

case_title: Harish Amilineni vs. Rajkumar Brothers and Production Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Harish Amilineni is the Shareholder and erstwhile Director of Amilionn Technologies Private Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Rajkumar Brothers and Production Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods and services from July 2016 till the first week of November 2016 under a Master Services Agreement executed between Revenue, Registration and Land Records Department, Government of Jharkhand and Jharkhand Agency, pursuant to which Work/Purchase Orders were issued by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed as defaulted was Rs. 2,30,62,247.90/-; no specific date of default was detailed by the creditor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on 14.01.2019; statutory reply raising disputes was sent by the Corporate Debtor via Annexure A-8. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor sent an email terminating the Work Order on 17.11.2016 citing delay beyond the 08.10.2016 deadline, failure to complete even one location (Khunti), and non-furnishing of Bank Guarantee; accompanied by pre-notice email trails dated 27.09.2016, 29.09.2016, 30.09.2016, 04.10.2016, 14.10.2016, 19.10.2016, 23.10.2016, 26.10.2016, and 09.11.2016 evidencing contemporaneous disputes regarding workmanship and delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed an application under Section 9 before NCLT Hyderabad; the Adjudicating Authority proceeded ex parte on deemed service and admitted the application holding the operational debt was undisputed, which the Appellant challenged.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can admit a Section 9 application where pre-notice correspondence, contractual termination emails, and Section 8 reply notices demonstrate a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding defective service and project delay.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC is not maintainable and must be dismissed if the record demonstrates a genuine, contemporaneous pre-existing dispute regarding deficiency of service, delay, or contractual termination prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 mandates an objective inquiry into the existence of a pre-existing dispute; even in an ex parte proceeding, the Adjudicating Authority has a duty to examine the operational creditor's own annexures and pleadings to determine if a dispute exists. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Plausible defense standard under Mobilox Innovations; pre-notice termination letters and emails highlighting substandard workmanship and breach of contractual milestones preclude summary admission under Section 9. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that pre-existing disputes regarding workmanship and timelines were fully established, rendering admission of the Section 9 petition improper, requiring the insolvency order to be quashed.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned admission order is quashed and set aside; the Section 9 application is dismissed; actions taken by the IRP/RP are quashed; Corporate Debtor's management is restored to its Board of Directors; and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to fix CIRP costs and fees to be paid by Respondent No. 1.
summary: Harish Amilineni, shareholder of Amilionn Technologies Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Hyderabad order admitting Rajkumar Brothers and Production Pvt. Ltd.'s Section 9 petition for Rs. 2,30,62,247.90. The NCLT had admitted the petition ex parte. The NCLAT observed that the operational creditor's own documents and email trail showed that the Corporate Debtor had terminated the work order on 17.11.2016 for project delays, failure to complete sites, and non-furnishing of a bank guarantee, which was reiterated in the Section 8 reply. Setting aside the admission, the NCLAT held that a genuine pre-existing dispute barred Section 9 proceedings and restored company management to the Board.

case_title: Sunil Amarlal Chawla vs. Union Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sunil Amarlal Chawla is the Ex-Promoter of Spark Green Energy (Satara) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2, represented by IRP Anil Rajkotia); Respondent No. 1 is Union Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two term loan facilities totaling Rs. 30 Crores sanctioned on 23.08.2011 and disbursed on 26.07.2013 under a consortium arrangement involving Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, and Union Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaulted long-term borrowings from Union Bank of India reflected in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets as Rs. 37,22,33,333/- (as of 30.03.2015) and Rs. 48,18,73,388/- (as of 31.03.2016); projected Date of Commercial Operations (COD) was 30.11.2016 (extended from 31.07.2016), which was missed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall notice issued by Bank on 05.12.2016; confirmation reply sent by Corporate Debtor; Section 7 application CP No. 4260/IB/NCLT/MB/MAH/2018 filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Acknowledgment of debt in Corporate Debtor's reply to recall notice dated 05.12.2016; balance sheets reflecting long-term borrowings for FY 2013-14, FY 2014-15, and FY 2015-16; and failure to achieve agreed COD milestone of 30.11.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application was admitted by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 28.11.2019 relying on Innoventive Industries, rejecting the defense that project delays by third parties (MSETCL transmission lines and villager resistance) negated default.
legal_issues: Whether non-commencement of commercial operations due to external infrastructure delays and land acquisition resistance negates the occurrence of default under Section 7 of the IBC when repayment terms and debt acknowledgments are established.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: External project execution delays, failure to achieve commercial operations, or blame assigned to consortium lenders or state authorities do not negate default under Section 7 of the IBC where financial debt is established and repayment conditions are breached. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following Innoventive Industries, the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction under Section 7 is confined strictly to ascertaining the existence of debt and default; entries in balance sheets constitute unequivocal acknowledgment of debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted ledger and balance sheet entries coupled with failure to meet milestone completion dates satisfy the conclusive evidentiary threshold for default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that default had occurred because the corporate debtor failed to meet the agreed commercial operation deadline and did not service the loan, justifying the initiation of CIRP.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any orders as to costs, affirming the admission order of the NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 28.11.2019.
summary: Sunil Amarlal Chawla, ex-promoter of Spark Green Energy (Satara) Ltd., appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order admitting Union Bank of India's Section 7 petition for long-term borrowings exceeding Rs. 48 Crores. The Appellant argued that default had not arisen because commercial operations had not begun due to land acquisition resistance and delays by MSETCL in constructing transmission lines. The NCLAT affirmed the admission, holding under the Innoventive Industries doctrine that external operational hurdles and blaming third parties do not excuse default. Because balance sheets acknowledged the debt and projected commercial deadlines were breached, Section 7 was rightly invoked.

case_title: Dr. Vandana Parvez vs. IVRCL Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Dr. Vandana Parvez is an individual purchaser/third-party claimant; Respondent No. 1 is IVRCL Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation represented by Liquidator/RP Sutanu Sinha); other respondents include associate entities and SPV IVR Hotels and Resorts Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contract entered into by the Appellant to buy a plot of land from IVR Hotels and Resorts Ltd. (a separate SPV subsidiary of the Corporate Debtor IVRCL Ltd. with shareholding held by Kotak Group Companies). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary metrics of the underlying insolvency are not at issue; Appellant alleged fraud and an unauthorized loan of Rs. 169 Crores allegedly made in favor of the Corporate Debtor by Indravathi Investments Pvt. Ltd. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order of Liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC had already been passed against the Corporate Debtor IVRCL Ltd. prior to the disposal of the applications. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Mortgages and charges on the subject lands were documented and legally registered by the landowners in favor of Central Bank of India and Kotak Investment Advisors Ltd.; property belonged entirely to the subsidiary SPV and not IVRCL Ltd.; Appellant had approached other regulatory and police forums (SFIO, IBBI, TNRERA). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. Nos. 523, 524, and 672/2018 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench seeking exclusion of lands, investigation of fraud, and appointment of a forensic auditor; NCLT dismissed the IAs for want of jurisdiction and locus standi on 04.08.2020, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a third-party purchaser contracting with an SPV subsidiary of a Corporate Debtor has locus standi under the IBC to demand a forensic audit or investigation into alleged inter-company fraud, and whether such summary adjudication is permissible during liquidation proceedings of the parent Corporate Debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Third-party buyers contracting with a subsidiary entity lack locus standi under the IBC to challenge transactions or seek forensic investigations against a parent corporate debtor undergoing liquidation proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proceedings under the IBC are summary in nature and cannot be expanded to investigate complex allegations of corporate fraud concerning independent non-debtor subsidiaries, as doing so would render the time-bound liquidation process under Section 33 unworkable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Locus standi and privity test; an applicant must establish direct legal privity and statutory standing under the IBC to invoke the adjudicatory powers of the NCLT regarding corporate transactions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the subject properties belonged to an independent SPV and that fraud allegations regarding third-party loans cannot be adjudicated in summary IBC liquidation proceedings, upholding the dismissal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the admission stage, with liberty reserved to the Appellant to pursue appropriate civil or criminal remedies before competent forums.
summary: Dr. Vandana Parvez appealed the NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing three Interlocutory Applications filed against IVRCL Ltd. (in liquidation). The Appellant, who had contracted to purchase land from IVRCL's subsidiary SPV (IVR Hotels and Resorts Ltd.), sought to exclude assets, investigate alleged asset-stripping, and appoint a forensic auditor to examine a Rs. 169 Crore loan. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal at the admission stage, holding that the Appellant lacked locus standi because the assets belonged to a separate legal subsidiary entity. Furthermore, IBC liquidation proceedings are summary and time-bound and cannot be derailed to litigate allegations of fraud.

case_title: Kanakabha Ray vs. Narayan Chandra Saha & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kanakabha Ray is the appointed Resolution Professional; Respondent Narayan Chandra Saha & Ors. are representatives/stakeholders of the Corporate Debtor; Union Bank of India is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying CIRP administration of the Corporate Debtor initiated by the Financial Creditor Union Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default figures in the CIRP are not detailed; the issue centers entirely on the eligibility, neutrality, and replacement of the RP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 03.07.2020, the Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned replacement order; appeal argued and decided on 18.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Undisputed evidence that the RP had been in gainful employment of the Financial Creditor (Union Bank of India) for 34 years, had actively dealt with the Corporate Debtor's accounts during employment (facts not previously disclosed to the Corporate Debtor), and an admitted procedural mistake/deviation in his discharge of duties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench by order dated 03.07.2020 directed the Committee of Creditors to replace the Appellant RP with a new IRP within one week on grounds of reasonable apprehension of bias; the RP appealed asserting that removal required prior concurrence of the CoC.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has independent jurisdiction to order the replacement of an Interim Resolution Professional/Resolution Professional on grounds of reasonable apprehension of bias arising from past employment with the Financial Creditor, without the prior concurrence or recommendation of the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent power to replace an IRP or RP independent of a CoC resolution if there is a reasonable apprehension of bias arising from prolonged past employment with the initiating financial creditor or previous handling of the debtor's accounts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Although Section 18 outlines the statutory collation functions of the IRP, the IRP/RP must function as an independent and neutral umpire; bias must be evaluated from the perspective and reasonable apprehension of the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The objective reasonable apprehension of bias test laid down in Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India; the court looks not to whether bias actually exists, but whether a reasonable stakeholder would harbor a justifiable apprehension of lack of impartiality. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that 34 years of employment with the Financial Creditor and handling the debtor's accounts created justifiable apprehension of bias, validating the Adjudicating Authority's suo motu order directing replacement.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, finding no legal infirmity in the NCLT Kolkata order dated 03.07.2020 directing replacement of the Resolution Professional.
summary: Kanakabha Ray appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order directing the Committee of Creditors to replace him as Resolution Professional within one week due to potential bias. The Corporate Debtor discovered that the Appellant had been employed by the Financial Creditor (Union Bank of India) for 34 years and had handled the Corporate Debtor's accounts. The Appellant argued that an RP cannot be removed without the CoC's concurrence. Applying the Supreme Court's Ranjit Thakur test and its own ruling in SBI v. Metenere Ltd., the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that an RP must act as an independent umpire and that the Adjudicating Authority can replace an RP where a reasonable apprehension of bias exists.

case_title: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II vs. Bijay Murmuria & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II, EPFO, Tinsukia (Assam); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Bijay Murmuria (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is M/s SREI Multiple Asset Investment Trust (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approval of a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Plan under I.A. No. 73 of 2018 in C.P. No. (IB) 02/GB/2018 concerning statutory provident fund claims. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default quantum is unstated in the order; the dispute involved provident fund dues sought to be addressed in the approved resolution plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned resolution plan approval order passed by NCLT Guwahati on 07.12.2018; Corporate Debtor's Company Secretary informed Appellant of the order on 11.12.2018; Appellant alleged becoming aware via RP on 02.07.2019; applied for certified copy on 24.01.2020 (issued same day); appeal presented before NCLAT on 18.03.2020; I.A. No. 1386 of 2020 filed seeking condonation of 22 days (with an effective delay of 436 days from order date). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Written communication dated 11.12.2018 sent by the Corporate Debtor to the Appellant establishing knowledge of the approval order as of 11.12.2018, contradicting assertions of knowledge only in July 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati approved the Resolution Plan on 07.12.2018; Appellant filed an appeal alongside an application for condonation of delay (I.A. No. 1386 of 2020) claiming sufficient cause for delay beyond 30 days.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT has the statutory jurisdiction or discretion under Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone a delay in filing an appeal beyond the maximum statutory grace period of 15 days following the expiration of the initial 30-day limitation window.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The appellate tribunal has no legal jurisdiction or power to condone delay in preferring an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC beyond the outer limit of 15 days following the expiry of the initial 30-day limitation period, regardless of the perceived merits of the appellant's claim. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) proviso contains an express negative mandate ('such period shall not exceed fifteen days'), which completely bars the extension or condonation of time beyond 45 total days from the date of the impugned order or receipt of certified copy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict statutory limitation threshold; once documentary proof establishes receipt of order communication beyond 45 days prior to filing, the tribunal is stripped of adjudicatory jurisdiction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that because the appeal was presented with an impermissible delay well beyond the statutory 15-day grace period, it was strictly time-barred and must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as time-barred for lack of jurisdiction along with the dismissal of I.A. No. 1386 of 2020.
summary: The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II appealed an NCLT Guwahati order dated 07.12.2018 that approved a Resolution Plan submitted by SREI Multiple Asset Investment Trust, accompanied by an application to condone delay. Although the Appellant argued that delay should be computed from certified copy receipt, the record demonstrated actual knowledge of the approval order since 11.12.2018, resulting in a 436-day delay. The NCLAT held that under the mandatory proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC, its power to condone delay is strictly limited to 15 days beyond the initial 30 days. Finding the delay completely outside statutory limits, the tribunal dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

case_title: Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. Manoj Garg (Resolution Professional, Sunar Jewels Pvt. Ltd.) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (lawful assignee of financial debt); Respondent No. 1 is Manoj Garg, Resolution Professional of Sunar Jewels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); assignor bank is Karnataka Bank Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities and temporary overdraft limits originally sanctioned by Karnataka Bank Limited to the Corporate Debtor Sunar Jewels Pvt. Ltd., which were subsequently assigned to the Appellant asset reconstruction company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim admitted by the Resolution Professional was Rs. 65,81,74,830/-; the disputed default component comprised penal interest charged at 3% per annum on excess drawings/temporary overdrafts, additional expenses incurred, and payment difference amounts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench) passed the impugned order upholding partial claim rejection on 04.03.2020; appeal decided on 26.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of the original bank sanction letter providing for penal interest at 3% on excess drawings leviable before debt assignment; the underlying Deed of Assignment; and RP's claim collation records showing admission of Rs. 65,81,74,830/- and disallowance of uncrystallized post-assignment penal interest and unverified expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application before NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench challenging the RP's partial rejection of its claim; NCLT upheld the RP's rejection on 04.03.2020, which the assignee appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an assignee of a financial debt is legally entitled to claim penal interest at 3% against the Corporate Debtor for periods post-assignment when such penal interest was leviable prior to the assignment and not covered as a crystallized debt within the deed of assignment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assignee of a debt cannot assert a claim against a corporate debtor in insolvency proceedings for penal interest or levies that are not expressly transferred and crystallized in the assignee's hands under the assignment agreement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For a financial claim to be admitted under the IBC framework, the liability must represent a legally enforceable, crystallized debt; components of penal interest leviable prior to assignment but claimed post-assignment without express contractual coverage under the assignment instrument cannot form part of the admitted debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict construction of the assignment instrument and crystallization standard; an asset reconstruction company must demonstrate that the specific monetary liability claimed was validly assigned and constitutes a crystallized debt rather than an arbitrary post-assignment levy. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that penal interest at 3% on excess drawings was not covered by the assignment and did not represent a crystallized debt in the hands of the assignee, thereby justifying the RP's rejection and dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the threshold stage, affirming the order dated 4th March 2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench).
summary: Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench order upholding the Resolution Professional's partial rejection of its financial claim against Sunar Jewels Pvt. Ltd. While the RP admitted the claim to the extent of Rs. 65,81,74,830/-, he rejected additional claims concerning 3% penal interest on excess drawings, expenses, and differential payments. The Appellant argued that the sanction letter from the assignor (Karnataka Bank Limited) permitted penal interest. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the threshold, holding that the post-assignment levy was not covered under the assignment deed and did not constitute a crystallized debt in the assignee's hands, making the RP's rejection legally sound.

case_title: Dr. Vivek Agarwal vs. Kanak Resources Management Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Dr. Vivek Agarwal; Respondent No. 1 is Kanak Resources Management Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, an IL&FS Group subsidiary); Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated against the Corporate Debtor in CP (IB) No. 89(PB)/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default quantum and date are not specified in the order; the dispute centers on the maintainability of CIRP and appointment of an Administrator in light of an appellate stay. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 25.09.2017; NCLAT stayed proceedings against IL&FS subsidiaries on 15.10.2018; NCLAT declined to clarify moratorium impacts in I.A. No. 2566 of 2019 on 02.09.2019; NCLT dismissed CP (IB) No. 89(PB)/2017 on 21.10.2019; NCLT rejected review on 12.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellate Tribunal's stay order dated 15.10.2018 halting suits and proceedings against IL&FS group companies; admission dated 25.10.2018 that the Corporate Debtor is an IL&FS subsidiary; absence of any subsequent material change in circumstances. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed CA No. 2222(PB)/2019 seeking clarification; NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench dismissed the main petition on 21.10.2019 with liberty to revive; Appellant filed CA Nos. 2872/2019 and 1330(PB)/2020 seeking appointment of an Administrator and RP, which NCLT rejected on 12.05.2020 as functus officio.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority becomes functus officio upon dismissing a Company Petition in compliance with an overarching appellate stay against group companies, and whether it can revisit its dismissal order absent any change of circumstances in the resolution of the group entities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority that dismisses an insolvency petition in compliance with a superior tribunal's blanket stay order against a group conglomerate cannot revisit or revive proceedings to appoint insolvency personnel absent a demonstrated material change in circumstances or modification of the superior stay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The doctrine of functus officio applies strictly where the main insolvency petition has been closed/dismissed with liberty; until the trigger condition of the liberty arises, the tribunal lacks jurisdiction to entertain collateral applications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold burden of proving a changed circumstance; an applicant seeking to revive dismissed proceedings must affirmatively prove a subsequent legal or factual development lifting the judicial stay. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the overarching stay on IL&FS subsidiaries remained intact without changed circumstances, the NCLT correctly held itself functus officio and rightly declined to revisit its order.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merit, affirming the order dated 12.05.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi).
summary: Dr. Vivek Agarwal appealed an NCLT Principal Bench order refusing to revisit its previous dismissal of CP (IB) No. 89(PB)/2017 against Kanak Resources Management Ltd., an IL&FS subsidiary. The NCLT had dismissed the main petition on 21.10.2019 due to the NCLAT's blanket stay on proceedings against IL&FS group companies, granting liberty to apply if circumstances changed. The Appellant sought the appointment of an Administrator and Resolution Professional. The NCLAT held that absent any change of circumstances or vacation of the stay, the Adjudicating Authority was functus officio, and upheld the dismissal of the appeal.

case_title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. vs. Shri Shyam Sundar Rathi & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Shri Shyam Sundar Rathi (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor, which was not a going concern and failed to elicit any resolution plans. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details not recorded in the order; the dispute centers on the mandatory statutory obligation to liquidate when the Committee of Creditors votes unanimously for liquidation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Professional filed an application under Section 33 in September 2019 pursuant to unanimous CoC approval; NCLT passed the impugned order on 01.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unanimous CoC resolution approving liquidation of the Corporate Debtor; absence of any resolution plan; non-operational status of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 01.07.2020 deferred the Section 33 liquidation application and directed the RP to produce asset details and valuation reports from two valuers within four weeks, which the Financial Creditor challenged.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to postpone the liquidation of a Corporate Debtor and demand fresh valuation reports and asset details when the Committee of Creditors has unanimously resolved to liquidate under Section 33(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the Committee of Creditors resolves by statutory majority to liquidate the Corporate Debtor in the absence of a viable resolution plan, the Adjudicating Authority has no statutory discretion or option but to order liquidation under Section 33(2) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) of the IBC leaves no room for judicial interference with the commercial wisdom of the CoC; seeking collateral valuation reports or asset information is extraneous and not germane to adjudicating a Section 33 liquidation application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom and statutory compliance test; verifying that the CoC approved liquidation with the requisite statutory majority without delving into valuation inquiries. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that collecting valuation reports is legally impermissible when deciding a Section 33 application backed by a unanimous CoC resolution, setting aside the impugned order.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 01.07.2020 is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) is directed to dispose of the Section 33 liquidation application within one week.
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad order directing the Resolution Professional to procure fresh valuation reports and asset details in a Section 33 liquidation proceeding pending since September 2019. The Corporate Debtor was defunct and the Committee of Creditors had voted unanimously to liquidate. The NCLAT set aside the order, ruling that under Section 33(2) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority has no option but to order liquidation once the CoC unanimously resolves to do so. Collecting additional asset valuations is extraneous to the mandate of Section 33.

case_title: Anil Goel & Anr. vs. Amit Agrawal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Anil Goel & Anr.; Respondent is Amit Agrawal (Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process withdrawal and settlement mechanism formulated under Section 12A of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amounts not specified; the dispute concerns the terms of the settlement withdrawal and revival mechanism. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Seventh meeting of the CoC held on 10.06.2020; original NCLT order passed on 15.06.2020; rectification order passed under Rule 154(1) on 13.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 7th CoC meeting dated 10.06.2020 (Clause 5) resolving that Financial Creditors retain the right to reinstate and revive CIRP from the stage of Form-G issuance if the settlement agreement is breached; original order dated 15.06.2020 containing typographical/clerical errors stating 'petitioner' shall have 'liability' to apply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench invoked Rule 154(1) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to rectify clerical errors in its order dated 15.06.2020 by substituting 'Petitioner' with 'Financial Creditors' and 'liability' with 'liberty' to align with CoC minutes, which the Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the legal authority under Rule 154(1) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to rectify clerical and accidental slips in an order to align it strictly with the approved Section 12A withdrawal minutes of the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority is fully empowered under its slip rule powers to rectify accidental clerical errors in an order to accurately reflect the true intent and terms of an approved creditor settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 154(1) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 permits correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes arising from accidental slips or omissions, which includes correcting typographical terminology ('liability' to 'liberty', and 'petitioner' to 'financial creditors') to reflect the consensus in Section 12A CoC resolutions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict conformity test between the court's transcribed order and the underlying contractual/CoC resolution records. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the rectification strictly conformed to Clause 5 of the CoC minutes and was properly exercised under Rule 154, warranting no appellate interference.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, finding no infirmity in the rectification order passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Allahabad Bench).
summary: Anil Goel & Anr. appealed against an NCLT Allahabad Bench order rectifying a previous order under Rule 154(1) of the NCLT Rules, 2016. In the original order closing CIRP pursuant to a Section 12A settlement, the NCLT had inadvertently stated that the 'petitioner' had the 'liability' to apply upon breach. The NCLT rectified the wording to state that 'Financial Creditors' had the 'liberty' to seek revival from the Form-G stage, conforming strictly to Clause 5 of the 7th CoC meeting minutes. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Rule 154 was properly invoked to correct clerical errors.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Educomp Solutions Ltd. vs. Ebix Singapore Pte. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Committee of Creditors of Educomp Solutions Ltd. (through State Bank of India); Respondent No. 1 is Ebix Singapore Pte. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional of Educomp Solutions Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of a Resolution Plan dated 19.02.2018 (with financial proposal/addendum dated 21.02.2018) by Ebix pursuant to the Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP) issued under Section 25(2)(h) of the IBC during the CIRP of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor; specific default amount for admission was not directly in issue, but the plan involved an earnest money deposit of Rs. 2,00,000,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 30.05.2017; 180 days expired on 30.11.2017; extended 90 days ended on 24.02.2018; RFRP issued on 05.12.2017; Plan approved by CoC with 75.36% voting share; RP filed approval application CA No. 195/2018 on 07.03.2018; Ebix issued letter seeking withdrawal on 02.07.2018; first revision application CA No. 1252/2019 dismissed on 10.07.2019; CA No. 1310/2019 dismissed with liberty on 05.09.2019; third application CA No. 1816/2019 filed and allowed by NCLT on 02.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RFRP clauses 1.8.4, 1.10(1), and 1.13.5 stipulating that the plan is irrevocable and no supplemental modifications are permissible after submission date; BDO transaction audit dated 06.12.2016 and RP affidavit dated 08.10.2018 confirming no avoidance/fraudulent transactions; ongoing SFIO and CBI investigations against the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 30.05.2017 under Section 9 IBC; NCLT Principal Bench allowed Ebix's CA No. 1816/2019 on 02.01.2020 permitting withdrawal of the approved Resolution Plan with Rs. 1 lakh costs on grounds of commercial unviability, delay beyond statutory timelines, and reluctance of the applicant.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to permit a Successful Resolution Applicant to unilaterally withdraw or modify an approved Resolution Plan pending confirmation under Section 31 of the IBC; and whether the subsequent withdrawal application was barred by the principles of res judicata and constructive res judicata.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a Resolution Plan is approved by the requisite majority of the Committee of Creditors, it becomes a binding statutory arrangement that cannot be unilaterally withdrawn, modified, or resiled from by the Successful Resolution Applicant pending its approval before the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31 is confined strictly to the limited judicial review parameters under Section 30(2) of the Code; it cannot sit in appeal over or encroach upon the commercial wisdom of the CoC, nor does it possess inherent jurisdiction to sanction the withdrawal of an approved plan. Delay caused by judicial proceedings falls under the maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit and confers no legal ground for withdrawal, nor do investigations by agencies warrant an exit in light of the statutory immunity provided under Section 32A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict application of constructive res judicata (Explanation IV to Section 11 CPC); where a party omits or fails to secure a relief claimed or capable of being claimed in an earlier application that attained finality, the Adjudicating Authority has no power to grant reservation or liberty to re-agitate the same cause of action in successive proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The withdrawal application was barred by res judicata and constructive res judicata, and the Adjudicating Authority acted without jurisdiction in permitting the Successful Resolution Applicant to withdraw its CoC-approved Resolution Plan.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 203 of 2020 is allowed with no costs. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 02.01.2020 in CA No. 1816(PB)/2019 in C.P. (IB) No. 101(PB)/2017 is set aside, and CA No. 1816(PB)/2019 stands dismissed.
summary: The NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by the Committee of Creditors of Educomp Solutions Ltd. against the NCLT's order permitting the successful resolution applicant, Ebix Singapore Pte. Ltd., to withdraw its CoC-approved resolution plan on grounds of delays and pending investigations. The Appellate Tribunal held that after a resolution plan receives CoC approval with the requisite statutory majority, the Adjudicating Authority possesses no jurisdiction to allow the applicant to resile from or withdraw the plan. The Tribunal also ruled that Ebix's withdrawal application was barred by res judicata following the dismissal of its previous application. The impugned order of the NCLT was accordingly set aside.

case_title: Archer Power System Pvt. Ltd. vs. Cascade Energy Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 213 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 296 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Archer Power System Pvt. Ltd. (initial 49% shareholder of R-2); Respondent No. 1 is Cascade Energy Pvt. Ltd. (registered 51% shareholder of R-2, nominee of Kohli Ventures); Respondent No. 2 is Zynergy Solar Projects and Services Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 3 is Rohit Rabindranath (Managing Director and promoter of R-2); Respondents 4 and 5 are subsidiary entities (Greatshine Holdings Pvt. Ltd. and Alectrona Energy Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Strategic Investment Agreement and Shareholder Agreement dated 27.07.2015 along with OFCD Subscription Agreement dated 11.08.2015, under which Kohli Ventures invested Rs. 30 Crores into R-2 and 67,46,998 equity shares of Rs. 10/- each (51% equity stake) were allotted to R-1. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an insolvency debt default; disputes pertained to alleged siphoning of funds, failure to file financial statements for FY 2015-16 and 2016-17, illicit loans to subsidiaries, unauthorized board meetings on 07.06.2017 and 09.06.2017, and EGM on 08.06.2017 altering share capital to dilute R-1. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: C.P. No. 13 of 2017 filed by Archer on 16.03.2017; C.P. No. 19 of 2017 filed by Cascade in April 2017; NCLT passed interim order for forensic audit on 14.06.2017; status quo order passed on 18.07.2017; Benami provisional attachment dated 19.05.2017 stayed by Madras High Court in WP 14625 of 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Shareholder agreements, bank KYC cautionary letters from KEB Hana Bank regarding loan of USD 4 Million, communications regarding unfiled balance sheets, and non-declaration under Section 89 forms MGT-4/MGT-5. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: R-1 filed C.P. No. 19/2017 under Section 241/242; NCLT Chennai passed interim orders appointing an independent CA and CS to conduct a comprehensive forensic audit (14.06.2017) and directing maintenance of status quo ante as of 27.04.2017 regarding board composition, shareholding, and Articles of Association (18.07.2017).
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has jurisdiction under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, 2016 to pass interim orders directing a forensic audit and status quo ante on shareholding prior to deciding an application challenging maintainability under Section 89(8) read with Section 244.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Maintainability of a petition under Section 241 is a mixed question of fact and law that can be adjudicated alongside the main petition, and the Tribunal possesses statutory and inherent powers to issue interim regulatory orders or direct an independent forensic audit to ascertain material facts and preserve the company's substratum pending final hearing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, the Tribunal has wide discretion to make any interim order it deems fit for regulating the conduct of the company's affairs on just and equitable grounds. The beneficial ownership restrictions under Section 89(8) cannot extinguish a registered shareholder's statutory right to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition where no competent authority or court has declared the registered holding invalid as on the date of filing. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prima facie evaluation of grave allegations involving fund siphoning, financial non-filing, and unauthorized alteration of shareholding patterns; forensic audit functions as an independent fact-finding mechanism for the court rather than an impermissible pre-judgment of final relief under Section 213. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no jurisdictional error or perversity in ordering a forensic audit and preserving status quo ante as of the date of the petition prior to the final determination of the preliminary objections on maintainability.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 213 of 2017 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 296 of 2017 are dismissed. The interim orders dated 14.06.2017 and 18.07.2017 passed by NCLT Chennai in C.P. No. 19 of 2017 are affirmed with no order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed the appeals preferred by Archer Power System Pvt. Ltd. challenging two interim orders of NCLT Chennai in an oppression and mismanagement petition filed by Cascade Energy Pvt. Ltd. The appellant argued that the petition was not maintainable under Section 89(8) of the Companies Act, 2013 and that interim reliefs directing a forensic audit and status quo ante on shareholding could not precede the maintainability ruling. The Appellate Tribunal held that maintainability is a mixed question of law and fact to be determined at final hearing, and the NCLT possesses ample power under Section 242(4) and Rule 11 to pass interim regulatory orders and commission a forensic audit to protect the company's affairs.

case_title: Monotrone Leasing Private Limited vs. PM Cold Storage Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Monotrone Leasing Private Limited (Financial Creditor / Non-Banking Financial Company); Respondent is PM Cold Storage Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disbursement of an inter-corporate loan/deposit of Rs. 25,00,000/- for a period of 90 days carrying interest at the rate of 15% per annum, remitted via RTGS through HDFC Bank on 14.06.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on financial debt of Rs. 27,19,110/- (principal sum of Rs. 25,00,000/- along with accrued interest); replacement post-dated cheque No. 242294 dated 09.10.2018 for Rs. 25,00,000/- drawn on SBI was dishonoured upon presentation for insufficient funds. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan disbursed on 14.06.2017; initial post-dated security cheque No. 242228 dated 12.09.2017 issued; tenure mutually extended for one year; fresh cheque dated 09.10.2018 dishonoured; Section 138 NI Act legal demand notice served on the Corporate Debtor on 01.11.2018; Section 7 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank transaction statement dated 14.06.2017 confirming RTGS transfer of Rs. 25,00,000/-; signed loan receipt confirming inter-corporate deposit at 15% interest; balance confirmation letter executed by the Corporate Debtor acknowledging the Rs. 25,00,000/- debt; ledger showing interest credits; and Form 26AS establishing interest payment of Rs. 72,945/- with TDS deduction of Rs. 7,295/- for FY 2018-19. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed Company Petition (IB) No. 142(KB)/2019 under Section 7 IBC; NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected the petition on 11.12.2019 holding that the tribunal was not a recovery forum, Corporate Debtor was solvent with over Rs. 25 lakhs bank balance, an interim prohibitory civil court order existed, and NBFC loan application documents/IU certificates were missing.
legal_issues: Whether the commercial solvency of a Corporate Debtor, the pendency of a civil suit with an interim prohibitory order, or the absence of NBFC loan appraisal paperwork/IU certificates can justify the rejection of an otherwise complete Section 7 application where the existence of a financial debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold is established.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an application under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is strictly confined to verifying the existence of a financial debt and an occurrence of default; neither the commercial solvency of the Corporate Debtor nor the pendency of a parallel civil proceeding can serve as a lawful defense to avoid admission into CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the IBC, legislative policy has fundamentally shifted from the concept of 'inability to pay debts' to 'determination of default'. Section 238 accords overriding effect to the Code over any conflicting municipal civil court order or suit. Furthermore, Section 65 applies strictly to instances where fraudulent or malicious initiation is affirmatively proven by evidence, which cannot be invoked summarily merely by characterizing Section 7 proceedings as a recovery mechanism. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The evidentiary test under Section 7(5) requires clear proof of disbursement for the time value of money and failure to repay when due; balance confirmation letters, bank statements, and tax deducted at source (Form 26AS) constitute conclusive documentary evidence of financial debt and default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default exceeded the threshold of Rs. 1 lakh, the application was complete, and the Adjudicating Authority was statutorily mandated to admit the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 99 of 2020 is allowed. The impugned order dated 11.12.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order of admission within 7 days from the date of the order.
summary: The NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by Monotrone Leasing Private Limited against the NCLT Kolkata's rejection of its Section 7 IBC petition against PM Cold Storage Private Limited. The NCLT had dismissed the petition holding that the corporate debtor was solvent, an interpleader civil suit was pending, and the tribunal was not a recovery forum. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the order, holding that under the IBC, solvency has no relevance and determination of default is the sole criterion. Relying on bank statements, balance confirmations, and Form 26AS showing TDS deductions on interest, the Tribunal held default was established and directed NCLT to admit the petition within 7 days.

case_title: Mr. Vishal Vijay Kalantri vs. Mr. Shailen Shah (Resolution Professional of Dighi Port Limited) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vishal Vijay Kalantri (former Director and shareholder of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Shailen Shah (Resolution Professional of Dighi Port Limited); Respondent No. 2 is Dighi Port Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 4 is Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited (APSEZ, Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approval of APSEZ's Resolution Plan offering an upfront cash payment of Rs. 650 Crores, payment of CIRP costs, and dues to Maharashtra Maritime Board in priority, against admitted financial creditor claims exceeding Rs. 3,000 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from CIRP initiated by operational creditor DBM Geotechnics and Constructions Ltd.; total claims admitted against the Corporate Debtor exceeded Rs. 3,000 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Admission order passed on 25.03.2018; JNPT plan approved by CoC on 31.01.2019 but rejected modifications on 08.05.2019; appellate directions granted two weeks to promoters on 24.07.2019 to submit Section 12A settlement; promoter deadline to deposit 20% EMD expired on 12.09.2019; CoC rejected promoter settlement offer by 99.68% votes on 17.09.2019; CoC approved APSEZ plan with 99.68% votes on 19.09.2019; NCLT approved plan on 05.03.2020 in MA 3270/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 17th to 22nd CoC meetings showing BIPL/promoter failed to deposit required EMD and failed to disclose the source of funds of funding partner SPGP Holdings (HK Ltd.); registered valuation reports determining fair value and liquidation value; and absence of breach under Section 5 Competition Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai Bench) approved APSEZ's Resolution Plan vide order dated 05.03.2020 in MA 3270/2019 in C.P. (IB) 1382/MB/2017; Appellant appealed challenging approval and non-disposal of MA 3298/2019.
legal_issues: Whether the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in rejecting a promoter's Section 12A settlement proposal and approving a Resolution Plan is justiciable; and whether obtaining prior approval from the Competition Commission of India under the proviso to Section 31(4) of the IBC is mandatory prior to CoC approval.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating the feasibility, viability, and financial matrix of competing proposals is non-justiciable and immune from judicial review, and the requirement under the proviso to Section 31(4) to obtain prior approval from the Competition Commission of India for a combination is directory rather than mandatory. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) read with Section 30(2) circumscribes judicial review solely to ensuring compliance with statutory requirements, asset maximization, and balancing stakeholder interests; neither the NCLT nor NCLAT can sit in appeal over the business decision of the CoC. Proviso to Section 31(4) is directory, permitting approval by the CoC subject to obtaining CCI approval prior to final approval by the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Record evidence demonstrating compliance with Section 30(2) parameters; absence of any legal infraction; and default by the promoter to furnish EMD or verify fund sources justified the CoC's business evaluation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC approved the APSEZ plan by an overwhelming 99.68% majority after rejecting the unviable promoter offer, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no illegality in approving the Resolution Plan.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 466 of 2020 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Vishal Vijay Kalantri, promoter of Dighi Port Limited, challenging the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order approving the resolution plan of Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited (APSEZ). The appellant contended that the promoter's Section 12A settlement proposal was superior, an interlocutory application was left undecided, and prior CCI approval was absent under Section 31(4). The Appellate Tribunal held that the CoC's commercial decision to approve APSEZ's plan and reject the promoter's proposal (due to lack of EMD and funding clarity) is non-justiciable. It also reiterated that the requirement of prior CCI approval under the proviso to Section 31(4) is directory, not mandatory.

case_title: Office of the Specified Officer, Special Economic Zone, Warora vs. Mr. V. Venkatachalam (Resolution Professional of Sai Wardha Power Generation Limited)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Office of the Specified Officer, Special Economic Zone, Warora; Respondent is Mr. V. Venkatachalam, Resolution Professional of Sai Wardha Power Generation Limited (Corporate Debtor); Resolution Applicants are Consortium of Sri City Private Limited and KCR Enterprise LLP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approval of a Resolution Plan under Section 31 IBC proposing total capital infusion of Rs. 495 Crores (comprising equity, CCDs, and Rs. 325 Crores working capital), including an estimated allocation of Rs. 45 Crores for de-notification/exit duties to the Customs Department under Rule 74 of SEZ Rules, 2006. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP initiated by financial creditors (India Opportunities III Pte. Ltd. & Anr.); claims admitted included 15 financial creditors, 133 operational creditors, and employees; Appellant's operational claim of Rs. 36,21,42,252/- had been rejected during the CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 09.11.2018; plan approved by CoC with 75.91% voting shares; NCLT approval order passed on 17.10.2019; communicated to Appellant via RP letter on 29.11.2019 and acknowledged on 10.12.2019; appeal filed before NCLAT on 04.02.2020 (75 days from communication). 5.
