FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clause 3(j) & (r) of the approved plan providing Rs. 45 Crores based on internal assessment for de-notification under the Customs Act/SEZ Rules, waiving interest/penalties; letter dated 29.11.2019 proving communication of the order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench approved the Resolution Plan on 17.10.2019 in I.A. No. 703 of 2019 in C.P. (IB) No. 275/7/HDB/2018; Appellant filed appeal challenging concessions on SEZ exit duties and waiver of penalties.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed under Section 61 of the IBC beyond the maximum condonable period of 45 days (30 days plus 15 days) from the date of knowledge is maintainable; and whether an estimated allocation in an approved Resolution Plan for de-notification duties under Rule 74 of the SEZ Rules encroaches upon the statutory jurisdiction of the Development Commissioner.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation scheme under Section 61(2) of the IBC constitutes a special law where the outer timeline of 45 days (30 days statutory period plus a discretionary 15-day condonation window) cannot be extended under the Limitation Act, 1963, depriving the Appellate Tribunal of jurisdiction to entertain an appeal preferred after 45 days from the date of knowledge; furthermore, incorporating an estimated budgetary provision in a resolution plan for statutory exit duties does not usurp statutory assessment powers. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(1) and (2) contains a non-obstante clause overriding the Companies Act and Limitation Act. On merits, Section 31 mandates approval of a CoC-approved plan that conforms to Section 30(2); setting apart an estimated sum of Rs. 45 Crores for de-notification subject to final assessment under Rule 74 of the SEZ Rules, 2006 does not violate the SEZ Act or constitute an illegal judicial encroachment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Date of knowledge must be reckoned from actual written receipt and acknowledgment of the order, not a subsequent secondary correspondence; documentary proof showed receipt on 29.11.2019. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was hopelessly barred by limitation having been filed 75 days after communication; additionally, on merits, the plan's estimated duty provision for SEZ exit did not violate any statutory provisions.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 268 of 2020 is dismissed as barred by limitation and devoid of merit. No order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by the Office of the Specified Officer, SEZ Warora, against the NCLT Hyderabad Bench's order approving the resolution plan for Sai Wardha Power Generation Limited. The Appellant challenged the concessions and estimated allocation of Rs. 45 Crores towards SEZ de-notification duties under Rule 74 of the SEZ Rules. The Appellate Tribunal held that the appeal was filed 75 days after the communication of the order, which was well beyond the mandatory outer limit of 45 days under Section 61(2) of the IBC, rendering it unmaintainable. On merits, it held that allocating an estimated sum for statutory de-bonding duties does not encroach upon the Development Commissioner's authority.

case_title: Mr V Nagarajan Resolution Professional in respect of M/s Cethar Limited (under Liquidation) vs. SKS Ispat and Power Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. V. Nagarajan, Resolution Professional of M/s Cethar Limited (Corporate Debtor, under liquidation); Respondents include SKS Ispat and Power Ltd. (Respondent No. 1), SKS Power Generation Chattishgarh Ltd. (Respondent No. 10), ICICI Bank Limited (Respondent No. 14, issuing bank), and several other commercial entities/promoters. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of bank performance guarantees by ICICI Bank on behalf of the Corporate Debtor in respect of external commercial contracts executed with the respondents. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated against Cethar Limited under CP No. 511/(IB)/2017; interim relief was sought to stay the invocation and set-off of performance guarantees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order pronounced by NCLT Chennai on 31.12.2019; unsigned order uploaded on 12.03.2020; appeal presented before the NCLAT on 08.06.2020 without an application for condonation of delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Defect query raised by the NCLAT Registry pointing out delay beyond the statutory limitation period; reply by Appellant claiming non-issuance of certified/free copy and relying on Supreme Court suo motu extension from 15.03.2020; failure of the Appellant to annex a certified copy in terms of Rule 22 or produce supporting affidavits. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed M.A. No. 908 of 2019 in I.A. No. 38/2018 in C.P. No. 511/(IB)/2017 before NCLT Chennai seeking to interdict guarantee invocation; NCLT Chennai dismissed the application on 31.12.2019 holding that performance guarantees relating to external contracts cannot be restrained under Section 14.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed under Section 61 of the IBC beyond the 30-day statutory period without a formal condonation application or certified copy is maintainable; and whether the moratorium under Section 14(1) extends to the invocation of performance bank guarantees issued on behalf of the Corporate Debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 61 of the IBC must be preferred strictly within 30 days, extendable by no more than 15 days upon demonstration of sufficient cause via a formal application, failing which the appellate tribunal lacks jurisdiction to entertain it; furthermore, the statutory moratorium under Section 14 does not prohibit the invocation of performance bank guarantees. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) proviso sets an immovable outer ceiling of 45 days (30 + 15 days) that cannot be enlarged automatically or via general limitation extensions without a condonation application. Substantively, the definition of 'security interest' in Section 3(31) expressly excludes performance guarantees, and Section 14(3)(b) explicitly exempts contracts of guarantee/sureties from the moratorium imposed under Section 14(1). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Self-serving statements regarding non-receipt of certified copies cannot be accepted without documentary evidence or an affidavit supporting the delay, and non-compliance with Rule 22 of NCLAT Rules renders an appeal defective and barred by time. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was barred by limitation, and on merits, the Adjudicating Authority committed no illegality in refusing to interfere with the invocation of the performance bank guarantee.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 561 of 2020 is dismissed both on grounds of limitation and lack of merit. No order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by the Resolution Professional of M/s Cethar Limited challenging the NCLT Chennai's refusal to restrain the invocation of a performance bank guarantee issued by ICICI Bank. The Appellate Tribunal held that the appeal, filed on 08.06.2020 against an order dated 31.12.2019 without a condonation application or certified copy, was unmaintainable and barred by limitation beyond the non-extendable 45-day outer limit under Section 61(2) of the IBC. On merits, it held that under the proviso to Section 3(31) and Section 14(3)(b), the CIRP moratorium does not bar the invocation of performance bank guarantees.

case_title: Mr. Devarajan Raman, Resolution Professional (Poonam Drum & Containers Pvt. Ltd.) vs. Bank of India Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. Devarajan Raman, Resolution Professional of Poonam Drum & Containers Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is Bank of India Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Determination and payment of fees and insolvency resolution process costs incurred by the Resolution Professional during the CIRP of the Corporate Debtor, directed to be borne by Bank of India Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fixation of professional fee and CIRP costs; NCLT allowed all out-of-pocket expenses and sanctioned a consolidated professional fee of Rs. 5 Lakhs plus GST for the RP's tenure. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In terms of earlier directions in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1092 of 2019, NCLT Mumbai passed the fee determination order on 07.02.2020; the RP worked for a duration of approximately three months. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions showing full actual operational CIRP expenses were reimbursed; billing records and time spent by the RP during the three-month period of CIRP administration. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following appellate directions to fix fees and CIRP expenses payable by Bank of India, NCLT Mumbai Bench passed an order on 07.02.2020 reimbursing all actual expenses and awarding a consolidated fee of Rs. 5 Lakhs plus GST; Appellant appealed seeking enhancement.
legal_issues: Whether the determination and fixation of a Resolution Professional's fee is exclusively governed by the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors; and whether a consolidated fee of Rs. 5 Lakhs plus GST for three months of work is inadequate or unreasonable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The fixation and determination of fees payable to an Insolvency Resolution Professional is an administrative and adjudicatory determination rather than a business decision falling within the sacrosanct commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While CoC commercial wisdom reigns supreme on matters of viability, feasibility, and financial debt distribution, the assessment of reasonable professional remuneration and CIRP costs is subject to judicial scrutiny and equitable evaluation by the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Rationality and proportionality test based on the actual duration of CIRP administration (three months) weighed against the full reimbursement of actual incurred out-of-pocket expenses. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Awarding a consolidated professional fee of Rs. 5 Lakhs plus GST in addition to 100% expense reimbursement for three months of work is just and reasonable, warranting no appellate interference.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 646 of 2020 is dismissed for lack of merit. No order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by Mr. Devarajan Raman, Resolution Professional of Poonam Drum & Containers Pvt. Ltd., against an order of NCLT Mumbai fixing his professional fees at a consolidated Rs. 5 Lakhs plus GST payable by Bank of India Ltd. The appellant argued that the fee was inadequate and fell under the commercial wisdom of the CoC. The Appellate Tribunal held that the fixation of an RP's fees is not a business decision governed by the commercial wisdom of the CoC, and that granting Rs. 5 Lakhs plus GST alongside full reimbursement of all incurred CIRP expenses for three months of work was just, reasonable, and valid.

case_title: Wayne-Burt Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Chain Tools & Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 181 of 2019 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 183 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Wayne-Burt Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. (Company) and its Director Triplicani Gowrishankar Mahesh; Respondents 1 and 2 are Chain Tools & Products Pvt. Ltd. and R. Vashudevan (Petitioners before NCLT); Respondents 3 to 14 are other directors/connected entities. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant Company allotted 87,972 shares to R-2 on 30.03.2015 for Rs. 4,83,84,600/- and 2,32,937 shares to R-1 on 21.05.2017 for Rs. 12,81,15,350/-, totaling 19.38% of paid-up capital; dispute involved alleged cross-dealings regarding transfer of Cetex Petro Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. shares under an MOU. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement dispute alleging fund siphoning, fraud, and non-compliances; Appellants asserted non-payment of share consideration exceeding Rs. 90 Lakhs, while Respondents claimed payment of Rs. 35.26 Crores across transactions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice issued on 28.09.2018; reply to notice issued on 08.10.2018; Company Petition filed in 2019; NCLT Chennai dismissed maintainability objections on 01.04.2019; call money notice issued by Appellants on 01.07.2019; NCLT stayed call notice on 04.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Return of Allotment in Form PAS-3 filed with ROC, audited balance sheets for FY 2014-15 and 2015-16, list of shareholders as of 31.03.2016 reflecting R-1 and R-2 as fully paid-up shareholders of 19.38% capital, and Appellants' preliminary counter admitting receipt of Rs. 17.65 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents 1 and 2 filed CP No. 110 of 2019 under Sections 241/242 before NCLT Chennai; NCLT held the petition maintainable under Section 244(1)(a) on 01.04.2019 and stayed Appellants' subsequent call notice on 04.07.2019.
legal_issues: Whether a petition under Section 241 is maintainable under Section 244(1)(a) when company filings and allotment records show petitioners hold more than 10% of paid-up share capital, and whether a respondent can challenge maintainability at a preliminary stage by raising disputed factual defenses of unpaid call money or accounting error.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An objection to the maintainability of a petition under Section 241 raised at the threshold is analogous to Order 7 Rule 11 of the CPC and must be determined demurrer-style exclusively from the petition averments and annexed documents, without evaluating defenses or conflicting claims on merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 244(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013, members holding not less than one-tenth of the issued share capital are qualified to apply so long as all calls and other sums due on their shares have been paid; when official company statutory filings show the shares as fully paid up and not cancelled, qualification is satisfied prima facie. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory returns of allotment (Form PAS-3), financial statements, and register of members filed before the ROC establish prima facie eligibility to file an oppression petition, and retrospective assertions of bookkeeping mistake cannot be accepted to oust jurisdiction at an interlocutory stage. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly held the petition maintainable at the preliminary stage and acted within jurisdiction in staying the subsequent call money notice intended to bypass judicial findings.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 181 of 2019 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 183 of 2019 are dismissed without costs. Interim orders vacated, and parties directed to appear before NCLT Chennai on 17th August, 2020.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed the appeals preferred by Wayne-Burt Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. and its director against NCLT Chennai's orders holding an oppression and mismanagement petition maintainable and staying a subsequent call money notice. The Appellants contended that the respondents had not paid share consideration and lacked locus under Section 244(1)(a). The Appellate Tribunal held that preliminary objections on maintainability must be decided solely based on the petition averments and annexed statutory filings like Form PAS-3 and audited financial statements, which showed the respondents holding 19.38% fully paid-up shares. As qualifications were met on record, the petition was maintainable.

case_title: Pradeep M.R vs. Ravindra Beleyur & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 306 of 2019 with Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 307 of 2019, 315 of 2019, 554 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Pradeep M.R (ex-employee), Merchem (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Grove Ltd. (licensors/landlords), P.E. Thomas (Promoter/Director), and Industrial Engineering Co. (Operational Creditor); Respondents are Ravindra Beleyur (RP of Merchem Ltd.), State Bank of India (Lead CoC Banker), and Acme Chem Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approval and implementation of Acme Chem Ltd.'s Resolution Plan valued at Rs. 115.25 Crores (liquidation value Rs. 86.27 Crores) for Merchem Limited, which included restructuring, continuing operations as a going concern, and taking over leased factory premises. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Various claims including admitted workmen/financial debts exceeding plan value, unpaid CIRP occupation license fee dues claimed at Rs. 82,65,000/- plus Rs. 5 Lakhs/month, promoter salary and unsecured loans over Rs. 18.65 Crores, and operational contractor claim of Rs. 84,30,487/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 15.01.2018; NCLT approved Resolution Plan on 23.01.2019 in MA/515/2018; plan implemented by Resolution Applicant on 18.03.2019; NCLAT interim order passed on 29.03.2019; appeals disposed on 29.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: License agreement dated 01.10.2011 for factory premises, premises handover record dated 17.06.2019, balance sheet as of 31.03.2018 reflecting accumulated losses over Rs. 121 Crores, and tax filings showing disputed license rental income figures. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench approved the Resolution Plan of Acme Chem Ltd. on 23.01.2019; multiple appeals were preferred by ex-employees, operational creditors, licensors, and the suspended promoter alleging discrimination, non-payment of CIRP cost for premise license fees, and impermissible statutory tax exemptions.
legal_issues: Whether license fees for the use and occupation of factory premises during the CIRP constitute CIRP costs payable in full; and whether the Resolution Applicant must provide an affidavit undertaking completion of the Resolution Plan irrespective of statutory approvals for carrying forward and setting off accumulated income tax losses.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: License fees and rental dues incurred for running the corporate debtor's business as a going concern during the CIRP constitute mandatory CIRP costs that must be paid in full to the asset owner, and conditional tax benefits embedded in a plan cannot relieve an applicant of its absolute obligation to implement the approved plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 14(1) read with the CIRP Regulations, the use and occupation of third-party property by the Resolution Professional for operating the corporate debtor requires treating corresponding rental/license obligations as part of insolvency resolution costs; however, such claims are restricted to figures reflected in verified income tax returns. Furthermore, Section 61(3) requires strict conformity with extant statutes, meaning tax loss set-offs remain subject to revenue scrutiny. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of audited financial statements, lease/license deeds, and income tax declarations filed by the claimant to verify quantum and genuineness of CIRP expenses. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Resolution applicant must file an undertaking affidavit committing to complete the plan irrespective of Income Tax Department approval on loss carry-forwards, and accrued factory license fees for the CIRP period must be computed and discharged as CIRP costs.
operative_order: Appeals CA (AT) (Ins) Nos. 306/2019 and 554/2019 are dismissed. Appeals CA (AT) (Ins) Nos. 307/2019 and 315/2019 are partly allowed. Adjudicating Authority is directed to ensure compliance of directions regarding CIRP cost payments and filing of undertaking affidavit within four weeks. No costs.
summary: The NCLAT disposed of four connected appeals challenging NCLT Chennai's approval of Acme Chem Limited's resolution plan for Merchem Limited. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals filed by an ex-employee and an operational contractor challenging distribution priorities. However, it partly allowed the appeals filed by the factory licensor and the promoter, holding that license fees for occupying factory premises to run the debtor as a going concern during CIRP must be included and paid as CIRP costs, restricted to figures in Income Tax returns. The Tribunal also directed the resolution applicant to submit an affidavit undertaking full plan completion regardless of Income Tax Department approval on tax loss set-offs.

case_title: Vijay Kumar V Iyer (RP for Dishnet Wireless Ltd. & Aircel Ltd.) vs. Bharti Airtel Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vijay Kumar V. Iyer, Resolution Professional for Dishnet Wireless Limited and Aircel Limited (Corporate Debtors); Respondents 1 and 2 are Bharti Airtel Ltd. and Bharti Hexacom Ltd. (Operational Creditors); Respondents 3 and 4 are State Bank of India representing the Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Spectrum Trade Agreement executed in April 2016 between Aircel entities and Airtel entities for sale/transfer of spectrum assets for a total consideration of Rs. 453 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Airtel was directed to return Rs. 453 Crores retained consideration; it paid Rs. 341.80 Crores and unilaterally set off Rs. 112 Crores against past operational claims owed by Aircel entities under separate, unrelated telecommunication interconnect transactions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Dishnet Wireless CIRP commenced on 19.03.2018; Aircel Ltd. CIRP commenced on 12.03.2018; Supreme Court order directing refund passed on 08.01.2019; Airtel issued set-off letters on 10.01.2019 and 11.01.2019; RP rejected set-off on 12.01.2019; NCLT allowed set-off on 01.05.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Spectrum Trade Agreement dated April 2016, Supreme Court order dated 08.01.2019 in Contempt Petition No. 271/2018, letters dated 10.01.2019 and 11.01.2019 reflecting adjustment of Rs. 112 Crores against pre-CIRP mutual debits, and charges registered in favor of secured lenders (SBI) on spectrum proceeds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench passed an order on 01.05.2019 in MA 230/2019 and MA 219/2019 permitting Bharti Airtel and Bharti Hexacom to set off Rs. 112 Crores from spectrum sale consideration payable to the Corporate Debtors; RP appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor can claim accounting set-off against dues payable to a Corporate Debtor during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process when a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC is in force.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: General accounting conventions and statutory principles of set-off are barred during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, as permitting a creditor to adjust pre-insolvency claims against dues payable to the corporate debtor violates the statutory moratorium and creates an impermissible preference over other creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 imposes an absolute statutory moratorium prohibiting recovery or appropriation of any amount from the corporate debtor; this provision, when read with the non-obstante clause in Section 238 of the IBC, overrides accounting customs, common law principles, and other procedural enactments like Order 8 Rule 6 CPC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Temporal verification of whether debts sought to be adjusted arose prior to the CIRP admission date; pre-CIRP claims cannot be adjusted against assets or considerations receivable by the corporate debtor during the moratorium. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The set-off of Rs. 112 Crores executed by Airtel entities was impermissible under Section 14, and the full consideration must be remitted to the Corporate Debtors.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 530 & 700 of 2019 are allowed. The impugned order dated 01.05.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside, and Respondents 1 and 2 are directed to pay the set-off amount to the Aircel Entities. Interim orders vacated. No costs.
summary: The NCLAT allowed the appeals filed by the Resolution Professional of Aircel Ltd. and Dishnet Wireless Ltd. challenging NCLT Mumbai's order permitting Bharti Airtel Ltd. to set off approximately Rs. 112 Crores from spectrum purchase consideration against its past operational dues. The Appellate Tribunal held that accounting conventions or common law set-off cannot override express statutory provisions of the IBC. Under Section 14, a complete moratorium applies, prohibiting any creditor from recovering or appropriating debts of the corporate debtor, with Section 238 overriding all contrary laws. Bharti Airtel was directed to refund the entire set-off amount to the Aircel entities.

case_title: M. P. Agarwal vs. Shri Lakshmi Cotsyn Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M. P. Agarwal (Promoter and Member of the suspended Board of Directors); Respondent No. 1 is Shri Lakshmi Cotsyn Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, through Liquidator); Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rejection of the promoter's One-Time Settlement (OTS)/settlement offer under Section 12A of Rs. 650 Crores and the subsequent passing of a resolution for liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Insolvency default under CP (IB) No. 142(ALD)/2018; liquidation value fixed at Rs. 500 Crores against CoC's settlement benchmark of Rs. 1,000 Crores; OTS offered Rs. 650 Crores without upfront deposit. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in 2018; three EOIs received but zero plans submitted by cutoff dates; CoC in 9th meeting on 18.02.2019 resolved to liquidate the Corporate Debtor upon expiry of statutory timelines; five subsequent CoC meetings considered Section 12A proposal; NCLT liquidation order passed on 01.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of CoC meetings recording that prospective resolution applicants failed to submit plans; promoter repeatedly changed funding partners, withheld identities of backer entities in two proposals, and failed to deposit upfront funds upon introducing a foreign investor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed an application under Section 33(1)(a) read with Section 33(2) before NCLT Allahabad Bench; Adjudicating Authority ordered liquidation on 01.07.2020; Appellant appealed on grounds of arbitrary rejection of OTS and reliance on stale valuations.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can interfere with the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in rejecting a promoter's Section 12A settlement proposal and resolving to liquidate the Corporate Debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving or rejecting a settlement proposal or resolving to liquidate the corporate debtor is non-justiciable and immune from judicial review absent proven material procedural irregularity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 33(1)(a) and 33(2) of the IBC, where no resolution plan is received within the statutory CIRP period or where the CoC resolves by the requisite vote to liquidate, the Adjudicating Authority is bound to pass an order of liquidation; Section 12A acceptance is entirely subject to the commercial evaluation of the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The CoC's subjective dissatisfaction with a promoter's financial mobilization capacity and failure to deposit upfront earnest money constitutes a valid commercial determination. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC acted within its commercial authority in rejecting the promoter's proposal and opting for liquidation, warranting no appellate interference.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 620 of 2020 is dismissed. Impugned liquidation order dated 01.07.2020 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by M. P. Agarwal, suspended promoter of Shri Lakshmi Cotsyn Ltd., against the NCLT Allahabad's order initiating liquidation of the corporate debtor. The appellant argued that the CoC arbitrarily rejected his Rs. 650 Crore settlement proposal despite it exceeding the Rs. 500 Crore liquidation value. The Appellate Tribunal held that the CoC enjoys supreme commercial wisdom in approving or rejecting Section 12A proposals and deciding to liquidate. Since no compliant resolution plans were received within statutory timelines and the promoter failed to deposit upfront money or substantiate funding sources, the liquidation order was fully justified.

case_title: Rajeswary Ramakrishnan vs. V. Venkata Sivakumar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rajeswary Ramakrishnan; Respondent No. 1 is V. Venkata Sivakumar (IRP/RP); Respondent No. 2 is an answering creditor; sole prospective Resolution Applicant was Mr. Jayaram Chowdary. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor wherein the sole resolution plan received was submitted by an ineligible applicant whose account had been classified as NPA. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under CIRP; sole prospective applicant Jayaram Chowdary owed Rs. 192 Crores to State Bank of India, which declared his account as an NPA in 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Total CIRP timeline spanning the maximum outer threshold of 330 days had expired without any eligible resolution plan being submitted; NCLT Chennai declined extension and passed a liquidation order; appeal disposed on 27.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Self-confessed disqualification under Section 29A by prospective resolution applicant Jayaram Chowdary regarding an outstanding default of Rs. 192 Crores owed to SBI and its NPA classification since 2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench Chennai refused to grant an extension beyond the outer limit of 330 days under Section 12 IBC on the ground that no exceptional circumstances existed and ordered liquidation; Appellant appealed against refusal of extension.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is required to order liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC upon the expiry of 330 days where no viable, legally compliant resolution plan exists and the sole applicant is disqualified under Section 29A.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of exceptional circumstances or a valid, legally compliant resolution plan, CIRP cannot be extended beyond the statutory outer limit of 330 days, and the Adjudicating Authority is legally mandated to order the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 mandates completion of CIRP within 330 days; an applicant disqualified under Section 29A cannot submit a resolution plan, rendering the process void of any eligible plan and triggering compulsory liquidation under Section 33. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted and admitted disqualification under Section 29A precludes any judicial extension of CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly declined to grant an extension beyond 330 days and had no statutory option but to order liquidation, with liberty remaining to explore a scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act during liquidation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 622 of 2020 is dismissed. Liquidation order upheld with clarification that eligible persons may pursue a scheme of arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed an appeal challenging NCLT Chennai's refusal to extend the CIRP period beyond the 330-day statutory timeline and the consequent order of liquidation. The Appellate Tribunal held that the only resolution plan received was from an applicant who was admittedly ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC due to an unresolved NPA debt of Rs. 192 Crores owed to SBI. As no valid resolution plan was available and no exceptional circumstances existed, the Adjudicating Authority had no option but to order liquidation, while keeping open the possibility of a scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act.

case_title: Sh V.J. Paul Joseph & Ors. vs. Alexander Correya & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 338 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 349 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants in CA 338/2018 are V.J. Paul Joseph (former Managing Director) and four other erstwhile directors/trustees; Appellants in CA 349/2018 are Kathrikutty Augusthy, Ullas Shankar Purohit, and Deepa Simon (third-party purchasers); Respondents 1 to 3 are Alexander Correya, Henry Peter, and V.R. Jude Jose (original petitioners/members); Respondent No. 7 is M/s Bhagyodayam Company (Company licensed under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 / Section 25 of 1956 Act). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported sale deeds executed on 03.05.2017 by the Managing Director and two Trustees conveying 2 acres and 36 cents of prime company immovable property for Rs. 35 Lakhs to Kathrikutty Augusthy, and 2.60 acres for Rs. 39 Lakhs to her son and daughter-in-law, purportedly authorized under Board resolutions dated 13.01.2017 and 18.06.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate governance and fiduciary default involving unauthorized alienation of charitable company land, diversion of corporate funds to purchase computers with internet totaling Rs. 13,50,000/- for select members, expenditure on a pleasure trip to Goa during financial losses of Rs. 23,70,483/-, and unlawful expulsion of protesting members. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Historic Travancore-Cochin High Court decree in AS 47 of 1125 passed on 10.11.1952; Munsiff Court injunction order passed on 18.06.2015 restraining policy decisions; illegal EGM altering Articles 31 and 41 convened on 04.07.2015; sale deeds executed on 03.05.2017; illegal member expulsions on 18.05.2017; Company Petition No. 29/2017 filed in 2017; NCLT final order passed on 28.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Articles of Association (clauses 26, 29, 31, 40, and 41); ROC declaration holding amendments to AOA void for lack of Central Government approval; civil court injunction orders in OS No. 6 of 2015; Administrator's compliance reports dated 10.05.2019 noting willful suppression and non-cooperation by the management. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Original petitioners filed CP No. 29/2017 under Sections 241 and 242 before NCLT Chennai; NCLT allowed the petition on 28.08.2018, declaring the sale deeds null and void, invalidating the expulsions, and appointing an independent Administrator to investigate and oversee operations.
legal_issues: Whether an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable in respect of a charitable company governed by Section 8; and whether the alienation of company real estate executed in violation of civil court injunctions, charter documents, and statutory limits can be protected under the doctrine of indoor management.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 8 charitable companies are fully amenable to the oppression and mismanagement jurisdiction of the NCLT under Sections 241 and 242, with management subject to higher fiduciary standards of probity and public trust; transfers of immovable property executed in direct contravention of judicial injunctions and fundamental charter provisions are ultra vires, null, and void ab initio, depriving third-party purchasers of the defense of indoor management. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory remedies provided under Sections 241 and 242 are expansive and cannot be ousted by technicalities or circumscribed to commercial companies; Section 179 and 180 powers of the board are subordinate to explicit charter limitations, prior binding judicial decrees, and the general body's approval on core policy dispositions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict scrutiny of corporate minutes, compliance with court injunctions, and execution formalities under the Articles of Association; failure by purchasers to establish lack of notice or adherence to fundamental constitutional mandates defeats a plea of bona fide purchase. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The management committed blatant illegalities, financial diversion, and unauthorized property transfers in violation of judicial injunctions, justifying the setting aside of the sale transactions, nullification of member removals, appointment of an independent Administrator, and imposition of exemplary costs.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 338 of 2018 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 349 of 2018 are dismissed with costs. Shri V.J. Paul Joseph is directed to pay a cost of Rs. 10 Lakhs to the Registrar, NCLT Chennai within 30 days.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed two appeals challenging an order of NCLT Chennai which allowed an oppression and mismanagement petition against the management of M/s Bhagyodayam Company, a Section 8 charitable company. The appellants challenged maintainability and defended the sale of company land under the doctrine of indoor management. The Appellate Tribunal held that Section 8 companies are subject to scrutiny under Sections 241 and 242, demanding higher fiduciary probity. The unauthorized sale of valuable land in defiance of civil court injunctions and charter provisions was declared ultra vires and void. The appointment of an Administrator was upheld, and exemplary costs of Rs. 10 Lakhs were imposed on the erstwhile Managing Director.

case_title: GRIDCO Limited vs. Surya Kanta Satapathy & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is GRIDCO Limited (bulk power supply distribution licensee owned by the State of Odisha); Respondent No. 1 is Surya Kanta Satapathy (Resolution Professional of Alex Green Energy Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Hemant Khaitan (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 3 is M/s Alex Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 4 is Fortis Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) dated 26.05.2012 executed pursuant to a tariff bidding process through OREDA for supply of 5 MW solar power by the Corporate Debtor to GRIDCO for a duration of 25 years at a fixed tariff of Rs. 7/- per kWh. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Insolvency default under Section 9 IBC; solar power plant suffered extensive storm damage on 24.05.2018, leading to an involuntary suspension of power supplies to GRIDCO from June 2018; GRIDCO issued termination notice on 08.07.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: PPA signed on 26.05.2012; storm event occurred on 24.05.2018; Section 9 petition admitted and moratorium imposed on 18.02.2019; RP intimated moratorium to GRIDCO on 25.02.2019; GRIDCO issued PPA termination notice on 08.07.2019; NCLT restored PPA on 14.10.2019; CoC approved Fortis Chemicals' Resolution Plan on 11.11.2019; NCLT approved plan on 25.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of PPA Clauses 7 (fixed tariff of Rs. 7/kWh without downward escalation clause), 14 (Force Majeure relieving non-performance liability caused by natural storm damages), and 17.4-17.5 (mandatory default notice requiring cure within one month and automatic revival within six months); GRIDCO's tariff filings before OERC for FY 2019-20 and 2020-21 accounting for procurement from Corporate Debtor at Rs. 7/- per kWh. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed CA(IB) No. 1184/KB/2019 before NCLT Kolkata Bench challenging GRIDCO's unilateral contract cancellation; NCLT set aside the termination on 14.10.2019 as violative of Section 14(1) moratorium and ordered restoration of the PPA; GRIDCO appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the unilateral termination of a long-term Power Purchase Agreement during the currency of a Section 14 moratorium violates the IBC; and whether the approval of a Resolution Plan predicated upon a restored contract is binding in rem on a statutory power purchaser under Section 31(1).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The termination of a corporate debtor's critical operational contracts during the subsistence of an insolvency moratorium is prohibited under Section 14(1) of the IBC, and upon approval by the Adjudicating Authority, a Resolution Plan predicated upon such contracts becomes conclusively binding in rem upon all contracting parties and statutory utilities under Section 31(1). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1) is enacted to preserve the operational existence of the corporate debtor as a going concern, barring actions that alienate or suspend contractual rights; contractual termination effected without issuing mandatory default cure notices under force majeure clauses is unlawful. Further, under Section 31(1), once a resolution plan is confirmed and remains unappealed, it operates on a 'fresh slate' binding all stakeholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of force majeure events versus voluntary non-performance, coupled with regulatory filings demonstrating that the utility budgeted for and treated the power procurement contract as subsisting. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The termination of the PPA was void for violating the moratorium under Section 14(1) and the contractual notice terms, and GRIDCO is legally bound to honour the restored PPA under the confirmed Resolution Plan.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1271 of 2019 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by GRIDCO Limited challenging the NCLT Kolkata Bench's order which set aside GRIDCO's unilateral termination of a 25-year Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with the Corporate Debtor, Alex Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. GRIDCO had terminated the PPA during the CIRP moratorium because the debtor's storm-damaged plant had suspended supplies. The Appellate Tribunal held that the termination violated the moratorium under Section 14(1) of the IBC and breached contractual cure procedures. Furthermore, as the Resolution Plan submitted by Fortis Chemicals was approved based on the subsisting PPA and that approval had attained finality, it was binding in rem on GRIDCO under Section 31(1).

case_title: Jayprakash Vyas vs. Prabhat Steel Traders Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jayprakash Vyas (shareholder/director of Shree Sai Industries India Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Prabhat Steel Traders Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Bhaskar Gopal Shetty (Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale, supply, and delivery of steel materials under tax invoice dated 13.12.2011 providing a 60-day credit window, after which interest at 21% per annum was chargeable on delayed payment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed at Rs. 5,97,09,566/-, comprising principal of Rs. 2,05,28,636.05 and interest of Rs. 3,91,80,930/- calculated up to 30.11.2018; default fell due upon expiry of credit period on 12.01.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoice raised on 13.12.2011; default occurred on 12.01.2012; statutory 3-year limitation expired on 12.01.2015; alleged part payment made on 30.05.2015; balance confirmation executed on 01.04.2017; Section 8 demand notice issued on 09.06.2018; Section 9 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tax invoice dated 13.12.2011, ledger accounts showing last payment receipt on 30.05.2015, balance confirmation letter signed by the Corporate Debtor on 01.04.2017 acknowledging outstanding dues of Rs. 2,05,28,636.05 as on 01.04.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP No. 343/I&BC/NCLT/MB/MAH/2019 under Section 9 IBC; NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application on 26.09.2019 holding that goods were supplied and acknowledged in ledger statements; Appellant appealed on limitation grounds.
legal_issues: Whether a balance confirmation or part-payment executed after the statutory three-year limitation period has already expired can revive a time-barred debt under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for initiating CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of liability or part-payment under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 must be executed prior to the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation to trigger a fresh limitation period; any acknowledgment or payment made after limitation has run cannot revive a stale claim to trigger CIRP under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3 of the Limitation Act mandates that courts and tribunals examine limitation sua sponte and dismiss time-barred actions even if not raised in defense; the term 'debt due' under Sections 3(11) and 3(12) strictly signifies debts that are legally enforceable and not barred by limitation under Article 137. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Chronological timeline calculation determining the initial date of default; balance confirmations executed after the lapse of the initial 3-year window fail the statutory test of Section 18. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt fell into default on 12.01.2012, rendering the 3-year limitation period exhausted on 12.01.2015, such that the part-payment on 30.05.2015 and confirmation on 01.04.2017 were invalid to resurrect the claim under the IBC.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1238 of 2019 is allowed. The impugned admission order dated 26.09.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside, and the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP to be governed by its Board of Directors.
summary: The NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by Jayprakash Vyas against the NCLT Mumbai's order admitting a Section 9 petition against Shree Sai Industries India Pvt. Ltd. The Appellate Tribunal held that the underlying debt arose from an invoice dated 13.12.2011 where default occurred on 12.01.2012. The three-year limitation period expired on 12.01.2015. Consequently, the subsequent part-payment made on 30.05.2015 and the balance confirmation executed on 01.04.2017 were made after the expiration of limitation and could not revive the debt under Section 18 or 19 of the Limitation Act. Under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, admitting a time-barred claim was illegal.

case_title: C R Badrinath vs. Eight Capital India (M) Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is C R Badrinath (suspended director of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Eight Capital India (M) Limited (Financial Creditor / Debenture Holder); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Wellknit Apparels Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Master Facility Agreement and Debenture Subscription Agreement dated 21.05.2007 under which R-1 disbursed Rs. 15 Crores to R-2 by subscribing to two series of fully convertible debentures for a tenure of 84 months, carrying quarterly interest at 12% per annum plus 6% default interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 15 Crores principal plus accrued interest; Corporate Debtor paid interest only once for the quarter ending September 2007 and defaulted continuously thereafter; Form-1 recorded the initial date of default as 31.12.2007. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed on 21.05.2007; initial default on interest occurred on 31.12.2007; 84-month tenure expired on 20.05.2014; subsequent Memorandum of Agreement executed on 18.04.2017; Section 7 application filed on 26.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture subscription agreements dated 21.05.2007, statutory Form-1 declaring default date as 31.12.2007, balance sheet of R-2 for FY 2016-17 classifying R-1 as debenture holder under long-term borrowings, and Memorandum of Agreement dated 18.04.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed IBA/312/2019 under Section 7 IBC before NCLT Chennai; Adjudicating Authority admitted the application on 11.12.2019 on finding debentures constitute financial debt without adjudicating limitation; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed more than eleven years after the initial date of default is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963; and whether a Memorandum of Agreement executed long after the initial three-year limitation period has expired can revive the claim under Section 18.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications under Section 7 of the IBC are governed strictly by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requiring the petition to be presented within three years from the date of default; an acknowledgment of debt executed after the expiration of the prescribed three-year period cannot extend limitation under Section 18. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3 of the Limitation Act imposes a mandatory statutory duty on the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal to dismiss time-barred petitions even if the defense was not raised below; the term 'debt due' under Section 3(11) of the IBC contemplates only debts that are legally recoverable and not extinguished by limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict adherence to the default date specified in statutory Form-1; when default occurs and accelerates repayment, the three-year clock starts immediately, and an agreement executed 11 years later fails Section 18 scrutiny. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default occurred on 31.12.2007, and the right to sue expired in December 2010; the Section 7 application filed in February 2019 was time-barred, rendering the admission order unsustainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 132 of 2020 is allowed. The impugned admission order dated 11.12.2019 passed by NCLT Chennai Division Bench-I is set aside, and the Corporate Debtor is restored to its Board of Directors.
summary: The NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by C R Badrinath against the NCLT Chennai's order admitting Eight Capital India (M) Limited's Section 7 petition against M/s Wellknit Apparels Private Limited. The Financial Creditor had subscribed to debentures in 2007, and the Corporate Debtor defaulted on interest from 31.12.2007. The Appellate Tribunal held that the right to apply under Section 7 is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act and expired three years from the initial default. The subsequent Memorandum of Agreement executed in 2017 was signed years after limitation had already expired and could not extend the time under Section 18. The application filed after 11 years was barred by limitation.

case_title: M/s MTS Logistics Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Brijesh Uppal & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 402 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 407 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are M/s MTS Logistics Pvt. Ltd. and Parvesh Kumar Jain (50% shareholder and director in Tryambakam Logistics Pvt. Ltd., and director in MTS Logistics); Respondent No. 1 is Brijesh Uppal (50% shareholder and director in Tryambakam Logistics Pvt. Ltd.); Tryambakam Logistics Pvt. Ltd. (TL Company) was the operating joint venture. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Vehicle Hiring and Transportation Agreement dated 25.06.2016 whereby five trucks purchased by TL Company with ICICI Bank financing (supported by MTS corporate guarantee) were leased exclusively to MTS Logistics for logistics operations against an advance of Rs. 2 Lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Mismanagement and non-accounting of commercial revenues; Parvesh Kumar Jain failed to deposit or account for truck revenues generated between 20.08.2016 and 05.01.2017 (four and a half months), resulting in EMI defaults to ICICI Bank and subsequent repossession/auction of the trucks; Brijesh claimed Rs. 50 Lakhs damages, while NCLT awarded Rs. 20 Lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: TL Company incorporated on 01.05.2016; trucks acquired in June 2016; Vehicle Hiring Agreement executed on 25.06.2016; operations commenced on 08.07.2016; revenues deposited till 15.08.2016; legal notice issued by Brijesh on 12.09.2016; trucks repossessed by lender on 05.01.2017; NCLT judgment dated 31.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Vehicle Hiring Agreement dated 25.06.2016; legal notice dated 12.09.2016 issued by Brijesh acknowledging mutual operation of trucks under MTS Logistics; absence of bank statements or accounts submitted by Parvesh for 20.08.2016 to 05.01.2017; unaccounted withdrawals of Rs. 3,71,500/- by Brijesh. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Brijesh Uppal filed a company petition under Sections 241 and 242 before NCLT New Delhi; NCLT held Parvesh and MTS Logistics jointly and severally liable to pay Rs. 20 Lakhs compensation to Brijesh and directed the ROC to initiate prosecution under Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013; Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can award arbitrary damages without calculable proof of actual losses in a petition under Section 241/242; and whether a director can be held liable for entering into an unauthorized related-party transaction under Section 188 when the transaction was executed with the knowledge and implied consent of the complaining shareholder.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Compensation or damages awarded by the Tribunal under Section 242 for acts of oppression and mismanagement must be grounded in calculable, rational financial evidence rather than conjecture, and an order directing prosecution under Section 188 cannot stand where the commercial transaction had the consent and participation of the complaining shareholder. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reliefs under Section 242 are tailored to rectify corporate wrongdoing; awarding speculative profits on an initial capital investment without examining actual operational tenure, counter-withdrawals, or finance defaults is legally unsustainable. A transaction made with consent cannot be treated as a clandestine related-party transaction under Section 188. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of reasonable monthly returns on invested capital (fixed at 10% per month) for the proven un-accounted four-and-a-half-month operational duration, rather than speculative multiplication of initial equity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The finding of an unauthorized related-party transaction under Section 188 was erroneous, and the arbitrary compensation of Rs. 20 Lakhs lacked evidentiary foundation, requiring modification to Rs. 7.25 Lakhs (initial capital of Rs. 5 Lakhs plus reasonable earnings of Rs. 2.25 Lakhs).
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 402 and 407 of 2018 are allowed with modification. Compensation awarded to Brijesh Uppal is reduced to Rs. 7.25 Lakhs payable jointly and severally by Parvesh Kumar Jain and MTS Logistics Pvt. Ltd. within one month (failing which 8% p.a. interest applies), and NCLT directions directing ROC prosecution under Section 188 are quashed. No costs.
summary: The NCLAT modified an order passed by NCLT New Delhi in an oppression and mismanagement petition between two 50% shareholders of Tryambakam Logistics Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had directed the director Parvesh Jain and MTS Logistics to pay Rs. 20 Lakhs compensation to Brijesh Uppal and directed ROC prosecution under Section 188 for unauthorized related-party truck leases. The Appellate Tribunal held that the lease had the knowledge and consent of Brijesh, thereby setting aside the Section 188 prosecution. Furthermore, finding the Rs. 20 Lakhs award speculative for a 4.5-month dispute on a Rs. 5 Lakh investment, the Tribunal reduced the compensation to Rs. 7.25 Lakhs.

case_title: A.K. Alloys vs. Emrise Engineering Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant A.K. Alloys (through sole proprietor Prakash Doshi) is the Operational Creditor; Respondent Emrise Engineering Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Operational Creditor manufactured and supplied Valve Casting products to the Corporate Debtor, a supplier of Gate Valves and Globe Valves. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on unpaid invoices dated August 4, 2016 to December 9, 2017 amounting to Rs. 15,57,708/- principal, totaling Rs. 18,58,101/- including interest @ 18% p.a. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 in Form 3/Form 4 issued on 22.08.2018; replied to by the Corporate Debtor on 19.09.2018 offering early repayment due to cash-flow slowdown, followed by an email dated 27.09.2018 proposing an installment plan; Section 9 petition filed on 14.11.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor produced email correspondence dated 12.11.2016 showing a tripartite understanding among Operational Creditor, Corporate Debtor, and Flovel Valves Pvt. Ltd., wherein Rs. 22-25 Lakh was paid/held as an advance subject to recovery from Flovel Valves; appellant ledger dated 23.01.2017 showing receipt of Rs. 25,00,000/- on 02.09.2016; letter dated 10.03.2017 (marked 'X') regarding adjustment of Flovel dues not produced before the NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench (CP (IB) No. 2/9/NCLT/AHM/2019) was dismissed on 23.09.2019 due to the existence of a prior arrangement and pre-existing dispute regarding advance payments and adjustments.
legal_issues: Whether a valid pre-existing dispute existed between the parties prior to the service of the Section 8 Demand Notice concerning mutual financial adjustments and third-party liabilities, thereby barring admission under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC cannot be admitted when the record demonstrates a pre-existing arrangement or dispute regarding the adjustment of accounts and third-party liabilities dating prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandates rejection where notice of dispute is established, and mutual tripartite understanding regarding fund adjustments and conditional advances subsisting before the Section 8 demand notice constitutes a legitimate pre-existing dispute rather than an undisputed operational debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must ascertain whether the dispute raised by the Corporate Debtor is supported by pre-dated contemporaneous correspondence and ledger adjustments showing that the underlying liability is not clear and unequivocal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because email communications dating back to November 2016 evidenced a tripartite arrangement concerning an advance of Rs. 25,00,000/- and pending account reconciliations prior to the August 2018 demand notice, the lower authority properly dismissed the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1171 of 2019 is dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, A.K. Alloys, filed an appeal against the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench's order dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Emrise Engineering Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid invoices of Rs. 15,57,708/- (totaling Rs. 18,58,101/- with interest). Although the Corporate Debtor had sent emails acknowledging financial difficulty and proposing payment plans, it proved the existence of an earlier tripartite arrangement dating to November 2016 involving an advance payment of Rs. 25,00,000/- tied to recoveries from a third party (Flovel Valves). The NCLAT held that these contemporaneous records established a genuine pre-existing dispute prior to the Section 8 notice, dismissing the appeal without costs.

case_title: Rakesh Wadhawan vs. Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rakesh Wadhawan is a shareholder/promoter of Housing Development & Infrastructure Ltd. (HDIL, Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 Bank of India is the Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 Abhay Narayan Manudhane is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of India subscribed to Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) issued by HDIL to the extent of Rs. 248.63 Crores (out of a total issue of Rs. 1,150 Crores plus Green Shoe options) secured by a Debenture Trust Deed dated 22.03.2010, and disbursed a Term Loan facility of Rs. 20.66 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 04.12.2018 for non-repayment of facilities aggregating to Rs. 522,29,06,768/- (inclusive of interest); account had previously been classified as NPA. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IDBI Trusteeship issued demand notice on 08.07.2015 for Rs. 616,91,40,462.26; earlier Section 7 petition (CP No. 1788 of 2018) withdrawn on 25.09.2018 pursuant to an OTS dated 31.08.2018; post-dated cheques issued under OTS dishonoured; OTS revoked on 04.12.2018; fresh Section 7 petition filed as CP No. 27 of 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Dishonoured post-dated cheques, revocation letter dated 04.12.2018, letters and multiple orders dated 01.02.2019, 28.02.2019, 08.04.2019, and corporate debtor extension request letters dated 26.07.2019 demonstrating repeated adjournments granted for settlement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted Bank of India's Section 7 petition on 20.08.2019, declared moratorium, and appointed the IRP; Appellant appealed alleging denial of natural justice to file a written reply.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority violated the principles of natural justice by admitting a Section 7 application without granting further time to file a formal reply, when multiple adjournments had been sought and granted to enable settlement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Repeated opportunities granted to a corporate debtor to settle an admitted debt satisfy the requirements of natural justice; the debtor cannot subsequently claim denial of due process for lack of formal reply if it continually sought adjournments and defaulted on settlement terms. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires the Adjudicating Authority to ascertain the existence of default from records within strict statutory timelines; the Code does not contemplate endless adjournments for settlement, and once debt and default exceeding the threshold are established, admission is mandatory. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where debt and default are admitted on the record (including through failed OTS proposals and dishonored settlement cheques), the formal completeness of the application under Form-1 and absence of a written rebuttal are sufficient to justify admission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had ample opportunity between February and August 2019 to contest the debt but chose to pursue settlements and reneged on undertakings; hence, natural justice was not violated, and admission was valid.
operative_order: The appeal fails and is dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: Shareholder Rakesh Wadhawan challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting Bank of India's Section 7 petition against HDIL for a default of Rs. 522.29 Crores under NCD and Term Loan facilities. The Appellant claimed natural justice was breached as HDIL was not allowed to file a written reply. The NCLAT rejected this plea, observing that after an earlier Section 7 petition was withdrawn on an OTS that failed due to dishonored cheques, the NCLT granted repeated extensions between February and August 2019 for settlement. The Appellate Tribunal held that statutory debt and default were conclusively established and dismissed the appeal without costs.

case_title: Bank of Baroda On behalf of Committee of Creditors of Veda Biofuel Ltd. vs. Mr. Sisir Kumar Appikatla, Resolution Professional for Veda Biofuel Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bank of Baroda on behalf of the Committee of Creditors of Corporate Debtor Veda Biofuel Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Sisir Kumar Appikatla, Resolution Professional (replacing Gonugunta Murali); other parties include ex-promoter P. Vijay Kumar, resolution applicant Madhusudhan Raju Chintalapati, and operational creditor Priya Trading Company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying CIRP triggered under Section 9 by Priya Trading Company against Veda Biofuel Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Veda Biofuel Ltd. under operational liabilities leading to CIRP initiation, with substantial financial debt owed to member banks of the CoC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application admitted on 12.02.2019; statutory 180-day period extended; I.A. 15 of 2020 filed on 27.01.2020 to place restructuring plan; settlement agreement between promoters and Priya Trading dated 06.02.2020; I.A. 64 of 2020 under Section 31 filed on 12.03.2020; subsequent I.A.s 66, 67, and 68 of 2020 filed in May 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement between applicant Madhusudhan Raju Chintalapati and ex-promoter P. Vijay Kumar allocating 50% shares to Madhusudhan and 30.81% to P. Vijay Kumar (formerly holding 45.32%); settlement agreement dated 06.02.2020 with the Section 9 operational creditor; CoC approved restructuring plan with 96.39% voting share while ignoring Section 12A withdrawal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Amaravati Bench rejected I.A. 64/2020 and passed an order of liquidation under Section 33(1)(b) on grounds that the restructuring plan circumvented Section 29A by facilitating backdoor entry for the former promoter.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan approved by a 96.39% majority of the Committee of Creditors under its commercial wisdom can be rejected by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 30(2) read with Section 29A if it allows the defaulting erstwhile promoter to retain substantial shareholding and backdoor management control.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors cannot validate a resolution plan that violates statutory ineligibility provisions under Section 29A; plans that facilitate backdoor management entry or retain substantial control for persons who contributed to the corporate debtor's default are unlawful and cannot be approved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 30(2) and Section 29A (read with 'connected person' provisions), a restructuring scheme masquerading as a resolution plan where an ineligible erstwhile promoter retains a significant equity stake (over 30%) and managerial continuity fails to satisfy the mandatory criteria of a resolution plan under Section 30. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must look behind the corporate structure of the proposal to determine whether the formal resolution applicant is an instrument or ploy for the ineligible promoter to regain operational or substantial ownership control. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The approval of a restructuring plan by the CoC that retains the defaulting ex-promoter's substantial equity shareholding without properly considering a Section 12A withdrawal justified the Adjudicating Authority's refusal to approve under Section 31 and its subsequent liquidation order under Section 33(1)(b).
operative_order: The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting the resolution plan and ordering liquidation is upheld; the appeal is dismissed in limine.
summary: Bank of Baroda, representing the Committee of Creditors of Veda Biofuel Ltd., appealed the NCLT Amaravati Bench's rejection of a Resolution Plan submitted by Madhusudhan Raju Chintalapati and the consequent order of liquidation under Section 33(1)(b). The CoC had approved the plan by 96.39% voting share. However, under an underlying agreement, the defaulting ex-promoter P. Vijay Kumar retained 30.81% equity, and a concurrent Section 12A settlement was bypassed. The NCLAT held that commercial wisdom cannot supersede the strict prohibitions of Section 29A and Section 30(2) against backdoor entry of defaulting promoters, upholding the liquidation order and dismissing the appeal in limine.

case_title: Kashi Viswanathan Sivaraman, Resolution Professional, Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd. vs. New Okhla Industrial Development Authority
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kashi Viswanathan Sivaraman, Resolution Professional of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment and statutory lease of project development land by NOIDA Authority to Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd. for construction and delivery of flats to home buyers/allottees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor in payment of lease rent and allotment charges leading to lease cancellation, alongside financial insolvency triggering CIRP under CP No. IB-470(ND)/2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NOIDA cancelled the land lease vide letter dated 31.03.2015 (reiterated as 13.08.2015); Corporate Debtor sought revival on 14.06.2016; I.A. 1592/2019 filed by NOIDA; RP filed I.A. 1664/2019 under Section 30(6) for plan approval; NCLT passed interim directions on 20.02.2020 directing police complaint and adjourning approval; RP filed police complaint on 20.05.2020; appeal decided on 27.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter of lease cancellation dated 31.03.2015; RTI response showing outstanding dues but silent on lease subsistence; pending representation for restoration dated 14.06.2016; Resolution Plan approved by CoC assuming land belonged to Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court II) declined to approve the plan in I.A. 1592/2019 and I.A. 1664/2019 on 20.02.2020 because the project land lease was cancelled in 2015, directed the RP to file an EOW complaint, and adjourned the application for further consideration.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal lies under the IBC against an interlocutory order of the Adjudicating Authority that defers approval of a Resolution Plan pending factual determination of the subsistence or cancellation of the project land lease.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal before the Appellate Tribunal is premature and not maintainable when the Adjudicating Authority has not rendered a conclusive adjudication or final decision on the approval or rejection of a resolution plan and has merely adjourned the proceedings for factual determination. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(6) applications for resolution plan approval necessitate a clear threshold finding on the subsistence of the corporate debtor's title or leasehold rights in the project substratum before final statutory approval can be accorded. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ambiguous secondary evidence (such as RTI letters merely showing rent arrears) is insufficient to establish that a lease remains legally subsisting in the face of an explicit cancellation notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no final order approving or rejecting the resolution plan had been entered, the appeal was non-maintainable and was disposed of with directions to the Adjudicating Authority to record an express finding on lease cancellation and decide the matter expeditiously.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as not maintainable, directing the Adjudicating Authority to prioritize the matter, hear all parties, record a clear finding regarding the subsistence or cancellation of the lease, and decide the Section 30(6) application on its merits.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Kindle Developers Pvt. Ltd. appealed an interim order of the NCLT New Delhi Bench in CP No. IB-470(ND)/2017 deferring consideration of an approved Resolution Plan. NOIDA had pointed out that the lease of the underlying project land had been cancelled in 2015 for non-payment of lease rent. The NCLT had directed the RP to lodge a complaint with the Delhi Police EOW and adjourned the matter. The NCLAT held that the appeal was not maintainable since the Adjudicating Authority had not taken a final decision on the approval or rejection of the Resolution Plan, and disposed of the appeal directing the NCLT to decide the lease subsistence issue and the plan expeditiously.

case_title: SNS Starch Ltd. vs. Vasavi & Company
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is SNS Starch Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Vasavi & Company (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/materials under various commercial invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt default including specific disputed sums such as Rs. 2,28,500/- under Invoice No. 180 (Sl. No. 16) and variations in amounts under Sl. Nos. 15 and 160. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Main petition CP (IB) No. 441/9/HDB/2019 was heard and orders reserved in February 2020; Corporate Debtor filed I.A. No. 308 of 2020 at a belated stage; dismissed by NCLT on 13.05.2020; appeal dismissed on 28.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor alleged discrepancies in material papers at pages 85-223 and 241-380 compared to petition pages 5-7, illegibility of invoice copies, and omitted documents for Invoice No. 180. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed I.A. No. 308 of 2020 on 13.05.2020 holding it was filed at a highly belated stage purely to prolong the proceedings after the main Section 9 case had been reserved for orders; Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing to re-open a Section 9 petition after orders were reserved, where an application to place additional documents and contest illegible invoices was filed belatedly.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications seeking to re-open heard and reserved proceedings under the IBC filed at an advanced, belated stage without sufficient cause are dilatory tactics and may be rightfully dismissed without constituting a procedural or legal infirmity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The summary procedure under Section 9 of the IBC requires strict adherence to timelines and does not allow endless opportunities to introduce piecemeal objections or re-argue facts once a case is ripe for judgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Allegations of illegibility or discrepancies in invoices must be timely raised during oral hearings or prior written replies, not through reopening applications after judgment has been reserved. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no legal error in dismissing the reopening petition; however, to ensure substantial justice, limited liberty to file written submissions within a set deadline was granted.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed; connected I.A. Nos. 1623/2020, 1624/2020, and 1625/2020 are closed. Corporate Debtor is granted liberty to submit Written Submissions before NCLT Hyderabad Bench by 13.08.2020 to be considered on merits, and directed to file a certified copy of the impugned order within two weeks.
summary: Corporate Debtor SNS Starch Ltd. challenged an order of the NCLT Hyderabad Bench dated 13.05.2020 dismissing its application (I.A. No. 308 of 2020) to re-open CP (IB) No. 441/9/HDB/2019 and direct the Operational Creditor, Vasavi & Company, to submit legible documents and clarify invoice discrepancies. The NCLT had reserved orders in February 2020 and dismissed the application as a belated attempt to delay judgment. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, finding no legal infirmity, but granted the Appellant liberty to file its written submissions before the NCLT by 13.08.2020 for consideration on the merits before final orders are pronounced.

case_title: Mr. Samant Sekhri vs. HBD Financial Services Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. Samant Sekhri, suspended director of Corporate Debtor M/s Hint Publication Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is HBD Financial Services Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Gautam Singhal (Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities availed by M/s Hint Publication Pvt. Ltd. from HBD Financial Services Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed in repayment of financial debt giving rise to Section 7 proceedings in CP No. (IB) 515/ALD/2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Hearing concluded and orders reserved by NCLT Allahabad on 26.02.2020; Section 7 admission order with moratorium and IRP appointment pronounced on 27.02.2020; appeal decided on 21.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record established that the Adjudicating Authority had heard both counsels at length and closed the matter for orders, followed the very next day by a formal admission order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor's suspended director filed an appeal challenging only the reserving order dated 26.02.2020 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench, omitting to appeal the subsequent final admission order dated 27.02.2020.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal lies under the IBC against a purely interlocutory order reserving judgment after a full hearing, when a subsequent substantive order of admission has been pronounced but left unassailed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order merely reserving judgment after a full hearing does not cause prejudice or legal grievance to any party, and an appeal preferred against such an order while leaving the substantive final order of admission unassailed is non-maintainable, frivolous, and an abuse of process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory appellate remedy under the IBC requires an aggrieved party to challenge substantive determinations affecting rights (such as an order under Section 7); procedural docket entries reserving judgment cannot be treated as appealable grievances. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the record reveals an intentional failure to challenge an effective admission order alongside an appeal against a harmless reserving order, the court may infer an intent to mislead the tribunal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal against the reserving order is frivolous and designed to mislead, warranting outright dismissal with costs.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as frivolous with costs of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh Only) imposed on the Appellant.
summary: Suspended Director Samant Sekhri appealed an order dated 26.02.2020 of the NCLT Allahabad Bench which had merely reserved orders in a Section 7 petition filed by HBD Financial Services Ltd. against M/s Hint Publication Pvt. Ltd. On 27.02.2020, the NCLT formally admitted the petition, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP. The Appellant chose not to challenge the admission order, instead appealing only the reserving order. The NCLAT held that a party cannot be aggrieved by an order reserving judgment and condemned the appeal as a frivolous attempt to mislead the tribunal, dismissing it with Rs. 1 Lakh costs.

case_title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. Nishiland Park Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent is Nishiland Park Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt and credit facilities assigned to/held by Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial debt giving rise to Section 7 application in C.P. (IB)-897/(MB)/2019 before NCLT Mumbai Bench. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was heard and reserved for orders on 22.01.2020; tribunal operations were disrupted by the nationwide COVID-19 lockdown; appeal disposed of on 31.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showed the matter remained reserved without pronouncement of orders from 22.01.2020 to July 2020 due to suspension of regular tribunal work during the pandemic. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by the prolonged delay in pronouncement of orders after reservation, the Financial Creditor approached the NCLAT seeking directions for expeditious disposal.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT should issue directions for time-bound pronouncement of orders or reconstitution of a bench when a Section 7 application has remained reserved for an extended period due to pandemic-related lockdown and administrative disruption.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Following the lifting of pandemic lockdowns, tribunals face no legal impediment to pronouncing orders in matters heard and reserved; prolonged pendency post-reservation warrants peremptory directions to pronounce orders within a rigid timeline or reconstitute the bench. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The summary nature and time-bound architecture of Section 7 require expeditious determination of default, precluding indefinite withholding of reserved judgments despite intervening administrative disruptions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of tribunal order sheets showing a lapse of over six months post-hearing establishes an administrative delay remediable by appellate supervisory directions. 4.
