DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority must dispose of the reserved matter within one week, or reconstitute the bench within one week to hear and decide it within two weeks, with a compliance report to the NCLAT.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with directions that the Adjudicating Authority dispose of the matter within one week, or, if the bench is unavailable due to member transfers, reconstitute the bench within one week to hear and dispose of the matter within two weeks from reconstitution. Registry of NCLT directed to submit a compliance report.
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. appealed regarding its Section 7 petition against Nishiland Park Ltd. in C.P. (IB)-897/(MB)/2019, which had been reserved for orders by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 22.01.2020 but remained unpronounced due to the COVID-19 lockdown and regular hearing suspensions. The NCLAT observed that with unlocking in effect, no impediment remained to pronouncing orders in reserved cases. The Appellate Tribunal disposed of the appeal by directing the NCLT to dispose of the matter within one week, or reconstitute the bench within one week to hear and conclude the matter within two weeks, subject to filing a compliance report.

case_title: Mr. Shivang Prakashchandra Patel & Anr. vs. Mr. Bhavesh Devidas Narumalani
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mr. Shivang Prakashchandra Patel & Anr.; Respondent is Mr. Bhavesh Devidas Narumalani. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company proceedings under the Companies Act concerning corporate disputes between the parties. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disputed aspects and alleged omissions in the initial orders of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench passed an order on 15.03.2017 read with order dated 26.04.2017; said decision was appealed before NCLAT and decided; NCLAT judgment was affirmed by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 2425 of 2018 on 23.03.2018; rectification IA filed belatedly before NCLT was rejected. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records showed the initial NCLT order merged into the appellate order of NCLAT and the subsequent Supreme Court dismissal dated 23.03.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed an IA before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench seeking rectification of alleged missing elements in its 2017 orders; NCLT dismissed the IA on the doctrine of merger; Appellants appealed this dismissal to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has jurisdiction under Section 420 of the Companies Act, 2013 to rectify its own original order after that order has been appealed, adjudicated by the NCLAT, and affirmed by the Supreme Court under the doctrine of merger.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the doctrine of merger, once an order of an original adjudicating authority has been challenged and decided in appeal by an appellate tribunal, the original order merges with the appellate decision, depriving the original authority of jurisdiction to entertain rectification applications. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420 of the Companies Act, 2013 permits rectification of mistakes apparent from the record by the NCLT only in relation to its operative, unmerged orders; it does not confer power to amend an order that has merged into higher appellate judgments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented history showing final disposal by NCLAT and affirmation by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal conclusively bars subordinate tribunal review or rectification. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rightly refused to entertain the rectification application under Section 420, and the appeal against such refusal is without merit.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, upholding the NCLT order declining rectification, while observing that any appropriate rectification must be pursued before the higher forum in accordance with law and limitation.
summary: Appellants Shivang Prakashchandra Patel & Anr. appealed against an order of the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissing their rectification application concerning orders dated 15.03.2017 and 26.04.2017. The original NCLT order had already been appealed before the NCLAT and subsequently affirmed by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 2425 of 2018 on 23.03.2018. The NCLAT held that under Section 420 of the Companies Act, 2013, once an order merges into an appellate decision, the subordinate tribunal cannot entertain an application for rectification. The appeal was accordingly disposed of without interfering with the NCLT's decision.

case_title: Mrs. Manasi Indrajit Wadkar vs. UCO Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mrs. Manasi Indrajit Wadkar (representing the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is UCO Bank (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit/loan facilities extended by UCO Bank to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of the financial loan occurred initially in the year 2013; balance liability carried forward and debt subsequently acknowledged. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Initial default occurred in 2013; Corporate Debtor acknowledged debt in balance sheet of FY 2016-17; submitted Resolution/Restructuring Plans on 10.03.2018 and 29.03.2018; Section 7 petition admitted by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench; appeal decided on 20.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheet for FY 2016-17 reflecting the financial debt; written proposals for Resolution Plan/Restructuring Plan dated 10.03.2018 and 29.03.2018 submitted to UCO Bank. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitted UCO Bank's Section 7 application, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP; Appellant appealed on the sole ground that the debt was time-barred since default occurred in 2013.
legal_issues: Whether reflection of debt in the corporate debtor's balance sheet followed by the submission of written restructuring/resolution plans constitutes a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, thereby extending limitation for initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entry acknowledging a financial liability in a corporate debtor's balance sheet, coupled with subsequent written settlement or restructuring proposals to the creditor, constitutes a clear acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, resetting the three-year limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For the purpose of Section 7 of the IBC, limitation is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act read with Section 18; written restructuring plans submitted by a borrower are unequivocal admissions of liability preventing claims from becoming time-barred. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous reflection of outstanding debt in corporate balance sheets along with signed settlement correspondence completely refutes an uncorroborated plea of limitation expiration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the corporate debtor acknowledged the debt in its 2016-17 balance sheet and submitted restructuring plans in March 2018, the Section 7 petition was well within limitation despite an initial 2013 default.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed in limine. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Manasi Indrajit Wadkar challenged the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order admitting UCO Bank's Section 7 IBC application, contending that the debt was barred by limitation as default originated in 2013. The NCLAT rejected the plea, finding that the Corporate Debtor had reflected the debt in its FY 2016-17 balance sheet and subsequently submitted written Resolution/Restructuring Plans on 10.03.2018 and 29.03.2018. Holding that these written instruments constituted clear acknowledgments of debt resetting the period of limitation, the Appellate Tribunal found no infirmity in the admission order and dismissed the appeal in limine.

case_title: Neeraj Kumar Sharma vs. Bee Kay Precision (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Neeraj Kumar Sharma; Respondent No. 1 is Bee Kay Precision (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); other respondents include the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Bee Kay Precision (India) Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Insolvency default resulting in CIRP wherein the statutory period was extended up to the maximum permissible threshold of 270 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Public announcement issued inviting Expressions of Interest (EoI); 270 days expired without submission of any resolution plan; NCLT passed liquidation order; appeal dismissed on 21.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP records indicated that only two Expressions of Interest were received in response to the public announcement, but none of the prospective applicants submitted a formal resolution plan; no record of a resolution plan submitted by the Appellant within the CIRP window. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed an order under Section 33 sending the Corporate Debtor into liquidation upon expiration of 270 days; Appellant appealed claiming his resolution plan was improperly excluded from consideration.
legal_issues: Whether an order of liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC is valid when the extended 270-day CIRP timeline expires without receipt of any compliant resolution plan, and whether an applicant whose plan was not formally received during the process can challenge liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the statutory CIRP period (including extensions) expires without any prospective resolution applicant submitting a resolution plan, the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily obligated to order liquidation of the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 leaves no discretion to the Adjudicating Authority to continue CIRP once statutory timelines lapse without an approved resolution plan; unsubmitted or unsubstantiated plans cannot halt mandatory liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where contemporaneous CIRP records demonstrate that prospective bidders submitted EoIs but failed to turn up with formal resolution plans, unsubstantiated assertions of non-consideration are factually meritless. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly ordered liquidation upon the expiry of 270 days without a plan, though the dismissal does not preclude submission of a Section 230 scheme during liquidation if eligible.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, clarifying that dismissal does not preclude the Appellant from floating a Scheme of Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, if found eligible.
summary: Appellant Neeraj Kumar Sharma appealed against the liquidation order of Bee Kay Precision (India) Pvt. Ltd. passed by the NCLT, alleging that his resolution plan was not considered by the Resolution Professional. The NCLAT observed that while two Expressions of Interest had been received, prospective applicants never submitted actual resolution plans, and the extended statutory CIRP period of 270 days had expired. Holding that liquidation was mandatory under Section 33 when no resolution plan is received within the statutory period, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, noting that the Appellant could still propose a scheme of arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, if eligible.

case_title: Bank of Baroda On behalf of Committee of Creditors of Veda Biofuel Ltd. vs. Madhusudhan Raju Chintalapati
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bank of Baroda representing the Committee of Creditors of Veda Biofuel Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Madhusudhan Raju Chintalapati, the unsuccessful Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Veda Biofuel Ltd. wherein Respondent submitted a Resolution/Restructuring Plan accompanied by a Performance Bank Guarantee. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory CIRP default metrics under CP (IB) No. 423/9/HDB/2018 leading to consideration and ultimate rejection of Respondent's Resolution Plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The connected Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 579 of 2020 challenging the rejection of the resolution plan was dismissed on 20.07.2020; NCLT passed the impugned PBG release order on 08.06.2020; appeal decided on 20.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT Amaravati Bench order dated 08.06.2020 directing the release of the Performance Bank Guarantee to Respondent following rejection of his Resolution Plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following rejection of the Resolution Plan and dismissal of the CoC's appeal in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 579 of 2020, Bank of Baroda appealed the NCLT order directing release of the Performance Bank Guarantee.
legal_issues: Whether a Performance Bank Guarantee furnished by a Resolution Applicant must be released upon the final rejection of the Resolution Plan and confirmation of liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon final rejection of a resolution plan by the adjudicating authorities and the subsequent upholding of liquidation, the resolution applicant is legally entitled to the refund or release of its Performance Bank Guarantee in the absence of valid forfeiture grounds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 and CIRP regulatory provisions governing performance security do not permit retention or forfeiture of a performance guarantee once a resolution plan is conclusively rejected as non-compliant and corporate debtor is sent into liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Upholding of the underlying rejection of the resolution plan confirms the absence of a subsisting contractual or statutory entitlement by the CoC to hold the applicant's bank guarantee. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 579 of 2020 rendered the release of the PBG lawful, leaving no infirmity in the Adjudicating Authority's order.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 8th June, 2020 releasing the Performance Bank Guarantee is upheld, and the appeal is dismissed.
summary: Bank of Baroda, representing the Committee of Creditors of Veda Biofuel Ltd., challenged an order of the NCLT dated 08.06.2020 directing the release of the Performance Bank Guarantee to unsuccessful resolution applicant Madhusudhan Raju Chintalapati. The NCLAT noted that the companion appeal challenging the rejection of the underlying Resolution Plan (Company Appeal No. 579 of 2020) had been dismissed on the same day. Holding that rejection of the plan removed any legal basis to withhold the guarantee, the Appellate Tribunal upheld the release and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Smt. Sushilabai & Anr. vs. Rai Homes Universal Pvt. Ltd. Through its IRP & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Smt. Sushilabai & Anr.; Respondents are Rai Homes Universal Pvt. Ltd. through its Interim Resolution Professional and Anr. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying insolvency proceedings involving the Corporate Debtor, Rai Homes Universal Pvt. Ltd.. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics and claims arising within the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: An inordinate delay of 338 days occurred in filing the appeal against the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority; appeal and condonation application decided on 28.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Limitation calculation on the record evidencing 338 days delay, substantially exceeding the 30-day statutory limitation period plus the 15-day maximum condonable window. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants preferred an appeal accompanied by an application for condonation of a 338-day delay before the NCLAT against an order of the NCLT.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT possesses statutory jurisdiction or discretion under Section 61 of the IBC to condone a delay in filing an appeal exceeding the maximum condonable limit of 15 days (a total of 45 days).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory time limits for filing appeals under the IBC are rigid and absolute; the Appellate Tribunal lacks subject-matter jurisdiction to condone any delay beyond the 15-day period provided in the proviso to Section 61(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 prescribes an appeal period of 30 days, extendable by a maximum of 15 days upon sufficient cause; the tribunal has no jurisdiction to extend limitation beyond this outer cap of 45 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Arithmetical computation of elapsed days from the date of the impugned order demonstrating that the delay exceeds 45 days mandates dismissal without inquiry into underlying substantive merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A delay of 338 days cannot be condoned under Section 61; hence, both the condonation application and the appeal are barred and non-maintainable.
operative_order: The application for condonation of delay is dismissed; consequently, the appeal is dismissed.
summary: Appellants Smt. Sushilabai & Anr. filed an appeal before the NCLAT against Rai Homes Universal Pvt. Ltd. through its IRP with an application seeking condonation of a 338-day delay. The NCLAT held that under Section 61 of the IBC, the statutory period for filing an appeal is 30 days, with the tribunal's condonation jurisdiction strictly restricted to a further maximum of 15 days (total 45 days). Finding that it had no jurisdiction to condone delays beyond 45 days, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the condonation application and the appeal as time-barred.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vs. ARSS Infrastructure Projects Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent is ARSS Infrastructure Projects Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities extended by Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. to ARSS Infrastructure Projects Ltd.. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed in repayment of financial obligations resulting in the filing of a Company Petition under the IBC before NCLT Cuttack Bench. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority adjourned the Company Petition for the limited purpose of allowing the respondent to file a counter; appeal decided on 28.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showing that the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority was merely a procedural order granting an adjournment for the filing of a counter affidavit. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Dissatisfied with procedural delay and adjournment granted to the Corporate Debtor, the Financial Creditor appealed to the NCLAT requesting adherence to statutory timelines.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal lies under the IBC against a routine procedural adjournment granted by the Adjudicating Authority for filing a counter-affidavit.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A purely procedural order of adjournment granted by the Adjudicating Authority to file a reply or counter-affidavit does not decide substantive rights and cannot form the basis of a maintainable appeal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While tribunals are expected to adhere to statutory timelines under the IBC, interlocutory scheduling decisions do not constitute appealable orders determining liability or default under the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An order sheet demonstrating a simple adjournment for pleadings without any adverse substantive disposition precludes appellate intervention. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is non-maintainable, but the Adjudicating Authority should be requested to expedite proceedings to uphold the time-bound framework of the IBC.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as not maintainable, with a request to the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Cuttack Bench) to take steps to deal with the company petition expeditiously.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. appealed against an interlocutory order of the NCLT Cuttack Bench which adjourned its insolvency petition against ARSS Infrastructure Projects Ltd. for the filing of a counter-affidavit. The Appellant sought adherence to statutory CIRP timelines. The NCLAT held that the appeal was not maintainable against a mere procedural adjournment, but took note of the need for speedy disposal under the IBC and requested the NCLT to expedite the proceedings.

case_title: Mr. Vijay Kumar V. Iyer, Erstwhile Resolution Professional of S.P.S. Steels Rolling Mills Ltd. vs. Bipin Kumar Vohra & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. Vijay Kumar V. Iyer, the erstwhile Resolution Professional of S.P.S. Steels Rolling Mills Ltd.; Respondents are Bipin Kumar Vohra & Ors. (former promoters/directors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Discharge of statutory duties by the Resolution Professional in identifying and determining preferential transactions during the CIRP of S.P.S. Steels Rolling Mills Ltd. under CP (IB) No. 595/KB/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Preferential transactions and related voidable clawback metrics under C.A. (IB) No. 937/KB/2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Kolkata Bench passed the impugned order in C.A. (IB) No. 937/KB/2018 on 26.02.2020; appeal decided on 22.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Adverse judicial strictures in Paragraph 14 of the NCLT order recording that the Resolution Professional non-complied with and violated Section 43 of the IBC read with Regulation 35A of the CIRP Regulations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an appeal seeking expungement/modification of the adverse remarks on the ground that they prejudiced his professional career, to which Respondents gave no objection.
legal_issues: Whether adverse remarks and findings attributing statutory non-compliance and violations under Section 43 read with Regulation 35A against a Resolution Professional should be modified to prevent harm to professional standing.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adverse remarks in a judicial order attributing non-compliance and violation of statutory obligations against a resolution professional should be toned down or expunged if they unfairly prejudice the professional's reputation and standing, particularly where opposing parties do not object. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Failure to meet the strict criteria of Section 43 read with Regulation 35A is more appropriately characterized as statutory non-satisfaction of conditions rather than a contumacious statutory violation by the Resolution Professional. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consent and absence of objection from contesting respondents concerning the modification of judicial strictures justify appellate correction to secure fairness. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The stricture that Section 43 read with Regulation 35A stood 'non-complied and violated' is expunged and substituted with 'stand not satisfied', leaving the remainder of the order intact.
operative_order: The sentences stating 'provisions of Section 43 of the IBC, 2016 read with Regulation 35A of IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016 stand non-complied and violated' in Para 14 of the impugned order are deleted and replaced with 'stand not satisfied'; remaining parts of the impugned order stand as they are; appeal disposed of and I.A. No. 1594 of 2020 closed.
summary: Mr. Vijay Kumar V. Iyer, erstwhile RP of S.P.S. Steels Rolling Mills Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated 26.02.2020 seeking expungement of adverse observations in Para 14 stating that Section 43 of the IBC read with Regulation 35A stood 'non-complied and violated', which harmed his career. The Respondents did not object to the modification. The NCLAT deleted the offending sentences and substituted them with 'stand not satisfied', disposing of the appeal while keeping the rest of the order intact.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Shailen Shah, Resolution Professional for Wind World India Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor); Respondent is Shailen Shah, Resolution Professional for Wind World India Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Wind World India Ltd. arising from credit facilities extended by State Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial default leading to CIRP initiation under CP (I.B.) No. 14/NCLT/AHM/2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency resolution commenced on 20.02.2018; on 16.03.2020, NCLT Ahmedabad adjourned I.A. 476 of 2018 to 21.04.2020 due to COVID-19 lockdown; listed for virtual hearing on 27.07.2020; appeal disposed of on 21.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order sheets and listing schedules establishing prolonged pendency of the CIRP from February 2018 and subsequent disruption caused by pandemic-related lockdowns. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI approached the NCLAT aggrieved by delays and adjournments in hearing pending interlocutory applications in the protracted CIRP.
legal_issues: Whether appellate intervention is warranted to direct expedited hearing of pending interlocutory applications in an insolvency process that commenced in 2018 and was interrupted by COVID-19.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the resolution process has experienced extraordinary delays, the Appellate Tribunal may issue supervisory directions mandating the Adjudicating Authority to prioritize and decide pending applications with utmost expedition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Timelines under the IBC are essential to its objective of value maximization; procedural suspensions caused by external disruptions must be swiftly resolved once virtual or regular hearings resume. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A documented chronology demonstrating that a CIRP initiated in early 2018 remains unresolved justifies urgent appellate supervisory directives. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority must prioritize and hear the matter and all pending interlocutory applications expeditiously, regardless of the hearing mode.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with directions to the Adjudicating Authority to hear the matter and all pending IAs expeditiously, according priority to the matter without further loss of time.
summary: State Bank of India appealed against the adjournment order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in I.A. 476 of 2018 arising from the CIRP of Wind World India Ltd., which commenced on 20.02.2018. The NCLT had adjourned the matter on 16.03.2020 due to COVID-19 lockdown advisories. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the NCLT to hear the case along with all pending interlocutory applications with utmost expedition and priority, irrespective of whether conducted physically or virtually.

case_title: M/s Sai Abacus Education System Pvt. Ltd. vs. Registrar of Companies, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Sai Abacus Education System Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is Registrar of Companies, New Delhi. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regulatory corporate compliance involving the statutory filing of financial statements and annual returns under the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in filing annual returns for financial years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017 resulting in the company's name being struck off. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RoC initiated striking off for non-filing for FY 2015-16 and 2016-17; NCLT granted restoration subject to costs; appeal decided on 27.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Proof of filing subsequent returns with only one balance sheet pending; evidence that the company is engaged in educational activities and suffering business losses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT restored the struck-off company on condition of paying Rs. 25,000/- to the PM Relief Fund and Rs. 50,000/- to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs; Appellant appealed solely challenging the quantum of costs.
legal_issues: Whether the quantum of costs imposed by the NCLT as a condition for restoring a struck-off company under Section 252 was disproportionate given the nature of default and financial hardship of the company.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Costs imposed as a condition precedent for restoring a company's name to the register must be proportionate to the gravity of statutory default, considering the entity's commercial standing and bona fide efforts to comply. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252 empowers tribunals to restore companies upon 'just' terms; excessive or punitive financial conditions that undermine the rehabilitation of a loss-making educational enterprise violate the principle of proportionality. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantial compliance coupled with documented educational operations and operational losses warrants judicial mitigation of revival costs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The condition directing payment of Rs. 50,000/- to the MCA is set aside, and the costs are reduced to Rs. 25,000/- payable to the Prime Minister Relief Fund.
operative_order: The impugned order is modified by reducing the costs to Rs. 25,000/- payable to the Prime Minister Relief Fund, and the direction to pay Rs. 50,000/- to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs is set aside; appeal disposed of.
summary: Sai Abacus Education System Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT order which restored its struck-off name on condition of paying Rs. 25,000/- to the PM Relief Fund and Rs. 50,000/- to the MCA. The company had failed to file annual returns for 2015-16 and 2016-17. The Appellant argued that it was an educational enterprise suffering financial losses. Applying the principle of proportionality, the NCLAT modified the order by reducing the total costs to Rs. 25,000/- to the PM Relief Fund and setting aside the Rs. 50,000/- MCA penalty.

case_title: Euro Pratik Ispat (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ramesh Shetty, Resolution Professional of The 4Mann Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Euro Pratik Ispat (India) Pvt. Ltd.; Respondents are Ramesh Shetty (Resolution Professional of The 4Mann Industries Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor) & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying insolvency proceedings and withdrawal of the company petition relating to The 4Mann Industries Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics underlying the original insolvency application triggering CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order of withdrawal passed by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 12A; appeal against withdrawal decided on 29.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant alleged fraud was practiced upon the Adjudicating Authority in obtaining the withdrawal order under Section 12A. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor's petition was withdrawn under Section 12A before the NCLT; Appellant directly filed an appeal before the NCLAT alleging that the withdrawal was procured by fraud.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal lies directly to the Appellate Tribunal against an order allowing withdrawal of a company petition on allegations of fraud, or whether such allegations must first be raised before the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal is not maintainable before the Appellate Tribunal to adjudicate allegations of fraud practiced upon the Adjudicating Authority in securing a withdrawal order; such factual grievances must first be raised before the forum where the alleged fraud was committed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An order granting withdrawal under Section 12A is a valid exercise of statutory power; allegations that it was procured by misrepresentation or fraud cannot be determined de novo in appellate proceedings under Section 61. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where fraud is alleged without a prior factual determination or finding by the original forum, the appellate body must decline maintainability and grant liberty to move the original authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal against the withdrawal order is not maintainable, reserving liberty to the appellant to approach the Adjudicating Authority directly.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as not maintainable, granting liberty to the Appellant to raise the issue of alleged fraud before the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: Euro Pratik Ispat (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order permitting the withdrawal of the insolvency petition against The 4Mann Industries Pvt. Ltd. under Section 12A of the IBC, alleging that the order was procured through fraud. The NCLAT held that the appeal against the withdrawal order was not maintainable on grounds of fraud and that any grievance regarding fraud played upon the lower tribunal must be raised before that authority. The appeal was accordingly disposed of with liberty to approach the Adjudicating Authority.

case_title: Mr. R.R. Gopaljee vs. Indian Overseas Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Indian Overseas Bank; Corporate Debtor is Malar Energy & Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.; Appellant is Mr. R.R. Gopaljee, promoter and shareholder of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 4 is Shriram City Union Finance Limited (an intervening financial creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Indian Overseas Bank granted financial assistance by way of term loan facilities of different amounts disbursed to the Corporate Debtor at various dates between 13.06.2011 and 29.05.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred when Corporate Debtor failed to repay, leading to its declaration as an NPA on 30.06.2015 (or 01.04.2015 per bank affidavit); total default claimed was Rs. 29,96,10,603.01 as of 28.02.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor issued a SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice on 09.07.2015 and a legal demand notice on 15.03.2017 demanding Rs. 21,86,26,661 plus interest; Corporate Debtor replied on 27.03.2017; OTS proposal submitted by Corporate Debtor on 13.04.2017, accepted by Bank on 03.07.2017 for Rs. 17 Crores payable in 30 days, extended on 28.08.2017 to 13.09.2017 upon request dated 05.08.2017, and cancelled by Bank on 22.11.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Reply letter dated 27.03.2017 signed by Director admitting liability and stating ongoing settlement efforts; OTS proposal dated 13.04.2017; bank sanction and extension letters dated 03.07.2017 and 28.08.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition was filed by Indian Overseas Bank on 15.03.2019 before NCLT Special Bench, Chennai; NCLT admitted the petition on 05.07.2019 holding that debt was acknowledged within limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition filed on 15.03.2019 was barred by limitation considering the default/NPA date of 30.06.2015, or whether the Corporate Debtor's reply dated 27.03.2017 and subsequent OTS proposals constituted a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, renewing the limitation period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 renews the limitation period before its expiry if there is an admission of a subsisting jural relationship of debtor and creditor, even without specifying the exact amount due or containing an express promise to pay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1) is satisfied where a written communication affirms a continuing jural relationship and subsisting liability; an offer to settle or a reply indicating steps to clear dues qualifies as an acknowledgment of liability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Document must be in writing signed by the party or authorized agent admitting subsisting liability; oral evidence is excluded, but surrounding circumstances and tenor of documents are evaluated to discern the clear intention to admit the jural relationship. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor's signed reply dated 27.03.2017 and OTS proposal dated 13.04.2017 consciously admitted liability within three years of default (30.06.2015), effectively resetting limitation under Section 18 and rendering the Section 7 application filed on 15.03.2019 timely.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 748 of 2019 is dismissed; interim order vacated; no order as to costs; Respondent No. 4 permitted to lodge its claim before the Interim Resolution Professional.
summary: The promoter of Malar Energy & Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Chennai order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Indian Overseas Bank, contending the debt was barred by limitation since default/NPA occurred in 2015 while the application was filed in March 2019. NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor's reply dated 27.03.2017 to the bank's demand notice and its subsequent OTS proposal constituted a valid written acknowledgment of a subsisting jural relationship under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Consequently, limitation was extended, making the application timely, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: State of Haryana vs. Uttam Strips Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is State of Haryana through Excise & Taxation Officer-cum-Assessing Authority Mewat; Corporate Debtor is Uttam Strips Ltd.; Resolution Professional is Mr. Sanjay Gupta; Successful Resolution Applicant is M/s Jyoti Strips Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory sales tax/VAT assessments conducted by the State of Haryana against the Corporate Debtor under state taxation laws for Assessment Years 2013-14 to 2016-17. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory tax dues totaling Rs. 1,95,62,231 across assessment years (AY 2013-14: Rs. 8,13,708; AY 2014-15: Rs. 53,15,274; AY 2015-16: Rs. 9,03,665; AY 2016-17: Rs. 1,25,29,584). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9 on 09.04.2018 (filed 26.12.2018/admitted 09.04.2018/2019); CoC approved resolution plan with 100% voting share and NCLT approved it on 06.06.2019; Appellant learned of CIRP via email on 04.06.2019; submitted belated proof of claim on 11.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assessment orders dated 27.03.2017, 26.03.2018, 29.03.2019, and 12.07.2019; Form B claim dated 11.11.2019; approved resolution plan assigning NIL value to unfiled operational claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA-1552/(ND)/2019 under Section 60(5) before NCLT Delhi seeking inclusion of statutory claims; NCLT dismissed it on 18.12.2019 as highly belated since the resolution plan had already been approved and implemented.
legal_issues: Whether statutory tax authorities can enforce unpaid pre-CIRP tax dues against a Successful Resolution Applicant after approval and implementation of the Resolution Plan under Section 31 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory operational creditors cannot assert belated or unsubmitted claims against a successful resolution applicant once a resolution plan has been approved and implemented, as the applicant acquires the corporate debtor on a fresh slate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Statutory dues constitute 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC; upon approval under Section 31, the resolution plan binds all stakeholders, including government and statutory authorities, extinguishing past untreated liabilities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict adherence to the CIRP claims process; claims must be filed before the Resolution Professional within prescribed timelines to be accounted for, and unfiled claims accorded nil value under an approved plan cannot be revived. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Relying on Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel, prospective resolution applicants cannot be burdened with undecided hydra-headed claims post-approval; the dismissal of the Appellant's Section 60(5) application was fully justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 319 of 2020 is dismissed; impugned order dated 18.12.2019 upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: The State of Haryana appealed an NCLT Delhi order rejecting its application to recover VAT dues of Rs. 1,95,62,231 from Uttam Strips Ltd. after the approval and implementation of a resolution plan submitted by Jyoti Strips Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT held that statutory dues qualify as operational debts under Section 5(21) of the IBC and must be submitted within the CIRP timelines. Relying on the Supreme Court's clean-slate principle in Essar Steel, the Appellate Tribunal held that a successful resolution applicant cannot be burdened with belated past claims, affirming the dismissal of the application.

case_title: Bank of India vs. M/s. Nithin Nutritions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bank of India (sole Financial Creditor with 100% voting share in CoC); Respondents are Corporate Debtors (including M/s Nithin Nutritions Pvt. Ltd., M/s Nithin Proteins Pvt. Ltd., Ramanasri Logistics Pvt. Ltd., Ramanasri Consumer Products Pvt. Ltd., and M/s Nithin Grains and Mills Pvt. Ltd.) represented by IRP Mr. Pavan Kankani. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/banking facilities extended by Bank of India to the Corporate Debtors, leading to insolvency proceedings initiated by the debtors themselves under Section 10 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtors on loan facilities prompting admissions under Section 10 on 15.11.2019, where Mr. Pavan Kankani was appointed as IRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 15.11.2019; CoC held its 3rd meeting on 08.02.2020, wherein 100% voting share resolved to replace IRP Pavan Kankani with Mr. B. Naga Bhushan as RP; I.A. 34/2020 filed promptly thereafter before NCLT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution passed in 3rd CoC meeting on 08.02.2020 with 100% vote share; written consent of proposed RP Mr. B. Naga Bhushan in Form AA under Regulation 3(1A). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank of India filed I.A. No. 34/2020 in CP (IB) No. 160/10/AMR/2019 under Section 22 before NCLT Amaravati; NCLT rejected the application on 20.02.2020 holding CoC failed to replace IRP in the first meeting and cannot do so in subsequent meetings without assigned reasons.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors is legally barred from resolving to replace the Interim Resolution Professional with a new Resolution Professional in meetings subsequent to its first meeting, and whether the CoC is required to record reasons for such replacement under Sections 22 and 27 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Committee of Creditors possesses absolute statutory authority to replace an Interim Resolution Professional/Resolution Professional with a 66% majority vote at any stage, including meetings subsequent to the first meeting, and is not required to record or substantiate reasons for such replacement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(2) read with Section 27 and Section 16(5) establishes that an IRP continues until an RP is appointed; there is no statutory prohibition restricting the replacement decision strictly to the first CoC meeting. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The relationship between the CoC and the RP is purely based on mutual confidence; neither the IBC nor its regulations require CoC to demonstrate misconduct, assign reasons, or satisfy the Adjudicating Authority on the sufficiency of grounds. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in law by restricting the replacement power exclusively to the first CoC meeting; CoC validly resolved to appoint Mr. B. Naga Bhushan with 100% majority, requiring the replacement to be allowed.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins) Nos. 497, 498, 499, 500, and 501 of 2020 are allowed; impugned orders dated 20.02.2020 are set aside; CoC is permitted to engage Shri B. Naga Bhushan as RP; outgoing IRP Pavan Kankani directed to hand over charge and submit fee/cost claims for CoC approval; no order as to costs.
summary: Bank of India, holding 100% voting share in the CoC of five Corporate Debtors, appealed the NCLT Amaravati's rejection of its applications to replace the IRP with a new RP during the 3rd CoC meeting. The NCLT had held that replacement must strictly occur in the first meeting. The NCLAT set aside the orders, holding that under Section 22 read with Section 27 and Section 16(5) of the IBC, the CoC has the statutory power to replace the IRP/RP at any subsequent meeting with the requisite 66% majority without assigning reasons, given the relationship of confidence between the CoC and the professional.

case_title: IMR Metallurgical Resources AG vs. Ferro Alloys Corporation Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is IMR Metallurgical Resources AG (unsuccessful resolution applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Ferro Alloys Corporation Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is Rural Electrification Corporation (Financial Creditor/CoC member); Respondent No. 3 is Bhuwan Madan (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 4 is M/s Sterlite Power Transmission Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Ferro Alloys Corporation Limited under the IBC, involving invitation and submission of resolution plans. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor on financial liabilities owed to secured financial creditors including Rural Electrification Corporation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan submission deadline expired on 30.10.2019 with only STPL submitting on time; Appellant submitted late expression of interest on 07.11.2019; CoC considered both plans and voted on 11th-12th November 2019 (31st meeting), rejecting Appellant's plan and approving STPL's plan by 95.15% voting share. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evaluation matrix pre-disclosed to parties; scoring results of 31st CoC meeting showing STPL scored higher across quantitative and qualitative parameters; email rejection dated 13.11.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed CA No. 157/CTB/2019 for approval under Section 31; Appellant filed CA (IB) No. 160/CTB/2019 under Rule 11 and Section 60(5) challenging the evaluation matrix and seeking reconsideration; NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed the application on 30.01.2020.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can review or interfere with the evaluation matrix and commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in selecting and approving a resolution plan over another.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating the feasibility, viability, and qualitative/quantitative matrix of resolution plans is non-justiciable and cannot be interfered with by adjudicating authorities absent specific violations under Section 30(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial review under Section 31(1) and Section 61(3) is strictly circumscribed to the limited parameters of Section 30(2); it does not empower tribunals to substitute their business judgment or question CoC deliberations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A resolution applicant possesses no vested right to have its plan approved; in the absence of demonstrable material irregularity by the RP during CIRP, CoC's scoring under an evaluation matrix is conclusive. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Adhering to the Supreme Court rulings in K. Sashidhar and Essar Steel, the CoC's approval of STPL's plan by 95.15% majority fell squarely within its commercial domain, and NCLT rightly refused to intervene.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 272 of 2020 is dismissed; impugned judgment dated 30.01.2020 upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: IMR Metallurgical Resources AG appealed an order of NCLT Cuttack Bench rejecting its intervention application seeking reconsideration of its resolution plan for Ferro Alloys Corporation Limited. The Appellant alleged that the CoC and RP applied the evaluation matrix unfairly, favoring Sterlite Power Transmission Limited despite Appellant offering higher upfront cash. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a resolution applicant has no vested right to consideration and that the commercial wisdom of the CoC—exercised here by a 95.15% vote—is non-justiciable under Sections 31 and 61(3) of the IBC, following established Supreme Court precedents in K. Sashidhar and Essar Steel.

case_title: Mukesh Kumar Aggarwal vs. Anurag Gupta & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mukesh Kumar Aggarwal (director/shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Anurag Gupta (Financial Creditor and former Director); Respondent No. 2 is M/s B.K. Educational Services Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Board of Directors of Corporate Debtor passed a resolution on 01.09.2015 authorizing directors to raise unsecured loans carrying 12% interest to settle overdue lease amounts payable to Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) for plot allotment and construction of a school building. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 disbursed an aggregate amount of Rs. 20,46,500 directly to GNIDA on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, which remained unpaid and exceeded the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 lakh. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board Resolution authorizing loans passed on 01.09.2015 with repayment agreed post-institutional finance or by 30.06.2016; MoU entered on 27.01.2016 regarding inter-se shareholder liabilities; Section 7 petition filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board Resolution dated 01.09.2015; bank statements showing direct disbursement from Respondent No. 1 to GNIDA on behalf of the Corporate Debtor; balance sheets for 2015, 2016, and 2017 reflecting short-term borrowings from directors to the extent of Rs. 9 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed C.P. No. IB-422(P.B.)/2018 under Section 7 against Respondent No. 2; NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi admitted the petition on 10.10.2019 holding the amount disbursed constituted a financial debt in default.
legal_issues: Whether money disbursed directly by a Director to a statutory authority (GNIDA) on behalf of the Corporate Debtor to clear lease liabilities and save plot allotment constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, entitling the director to maintain a Section 7 petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Funds advanced by a director/promoter directly to a third party to discharge the corporate debtor's pressing liabilities and preserve its business assets possess the commercial effect of a borrowing and qualify as financial debt under Section 5(8). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8)(f), an advance that improves the financial health of the company has the commercial effect of borrowing and constitutes financial debt, even where no interest is charged or where the director acts in a distinct creditor capacity. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bank statements verifying direct fund flow on behalf of the debtor coupled with audited balance sheets showing short-term borrowings from directors provide conclusive proof of disbursement and default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The disbursement by Respondent No. 1 to GNIDA was a valid financial debt in default; inter-se shareholder disputes under an MoU do not vitiate the corporate debtor's statutory liability under Section 7.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1264 of 2019 is dismissed; impugned admission order dated 10.10.2019 upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Mukesh Kumar Aggarwal, director of B.K. Educational Services Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Principal Bench's admission of a Section 7 application filed by Anurag Gupta, a shareholder and former director who had disbursed Rs. 20,46,500 to GNIDA on behalf of the company. The Appellant argued the transaction was governed by a private MoU and did not constitute financial debt. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that payments made by a director to clear liabilities and safeguard company assets have the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8) of the IBC (relying on Shailesh Sangani), and that the recorded balance sheets and bank transfers established financial debt and default.

case_title: Anamika Singh & Ors. vs. Shinhan Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are individual lenders (Smt. Anamika Singh and 8 others); Respondent No. 1 is Shinhan Bank (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Sungil (I) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 3 is Mr. Rajesh Parakh (Resolution Professional); original Section 9 petitioner was M/s Vaiva Metals and Alloys Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants disbursed short-term loans via cheques/RTGS to the Corporate Debtor at exorbitant monthly interest rates (ranging between 3.3%, 4%, and 5% per month, equating to 40% to 60% per annum) without supporting board resolutions or proper formal corporate loan agreements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor to repay loans, leading Appellants to lodge claims before RP; Appellants claimed principal plus interest at 40% to 65% per annum; RP initially admitted only principal and kept interest in abeyance. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 01.06.2018; 1st CoC held on 25.07.2018 with Shinhan Bank holding 100% vote share; 2nd CoC on 13.08.2018 where RP admitted Appellants and diluted Shinhan Bank to 0.25%; 3rd CoC on 29.08.2018, 4th on 12.09.2018, and 5th on 29.09.2018; transactions of Appellants 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 9 fell within the 2-year lookback period preceding 01.06.2018, while Appellants 1, 5, and 8 were entered into prior to 01.06.2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Cheque/RTGS receipts; emails dated 18.07.2018 and 04.12.2018; CoC reconstitution report dated 29.11.2018 showing interest was exorbitant and unapproved; absence of debtor board resolutions authorising borrowing at 40-60% interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CA No. 184 of 2018 under Section 60(5) challenging CoC reconstitution and Appellants' status; NCLT New Delhi (Court No. IV) on 09.07.2019 and 29.07.2019 ruled Appellants were not Financial Creditors but unsecured creditors due to extortionate interest under Section 50 and declared the 2nd to 5th CoC meetings void.
legal_issues: Whether individual lenders advancing monies at exorbitant monthly interest rates (40% to 65% per annum) without corporate board sanction qualify as Financial Creditors entitled to sit on the CoC, whether such transactions constitute Extortionate Credit Transactions under Section 50 of the IBC, and whether a financial creditor can maintain an avoidance application under Section 60(5) in the absence of an application by the RP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Loan transactions bearing unconscionable and exorbitant interest rates entered into without proper corporate authority constitute extortionate credit transactions and cannot entitle lenders to status or voting membership as financial creditors on the Committee of Creditors; where transactions fall within the statutory lookback period, they are void under Section 50, whereas for transactions outside the lookback period, the extortionate interest is disallowed, restricting claims purely to principal as unsecured debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 50(1) limits the avoidance lookback period to two years preceding the insolvency commencement date, but Section 60(5) confers residuary jurisdiction on the NCLT to determine issues of priority, validity of debt, and CoC constitution upon an application by an aggrieved financial creditor even if the RP fails to act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal examines commercial reasonableness; advances made at usurious interest rates (40-65% per annum) without corporate necessity or valid board resolutions indicate collusion rather than bona fide financial debt under Section 5(8). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Loans of Appellants 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 9 were within two years of CIRP and properly set aside as extortionate and void; loans of Appellants 1, 5, and 8 predated two years, precluding complete avoidance under Section 50(1), but the unconscionable interest is struck down, leaving them only as unsecured creditors for principal with zero CoC representation.
operative_order: Appeals are disposed of with modifications to the NCLT order: transactions of Appellants 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 9 are set aside as extortionate credit transactions under Section 50(1) and declared illegal and void; Appellants 1, 5, and 8 are held to be unsecured creditors for principal amount only and disentitled to interest; declarations that CoC meetings held on 13.06.2018, 29.08.2018, 12.09.2018, and 29.09.2018 are non est and resolutions passed therein nullified are affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Shinhan Bank challenged the inclusion of nine individual lenders in the CoC of Sungil (I) Pvt. Ltd. whose claims for short-term loans carried exorbitant interest of 40% to 65% per annum and had diluted the bank's voting share from 100% to 0.25%. The NCLAT upheld the finding that loans carrying such usurious interest without corporate board approvals constituted extortionate transactions. Exercising jurisdiction under Section 60(5) read with Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, the Tribunal set aside the transactions of six appellants falling within the two-year lookback period under Section 50(1) as illegal and void, while limiting the remaining three appellants whose loans predated the lookback period to unsecured creditors for principal amount only, completely excluding them from the CoC.

case_title: Yamini Bipinchandra Shah & Ors. vs. Trimbak Estates Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are legal heirs (wife and sons) of Late Mr. Bipin Chandra Shah (founder shareholder/director holding 50% equity); Respondent No. 1 is Trimbak Estates Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Kamalkumar Shankarlal Bhageria (co-founder director); Respondents 3 to 50 are subsequent transferees and allotted shareholders. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Target company incorporated on 30.08.1995 with Rs. 1 lakh authorized share capital; founder shareholders Bipin Chandra Shah and Kamal Kumar Bhageria initially held equal 50% shares (100 equity shares each). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and illegal dilution of shareholding from 50% down to 1% on 11.12.2002 (by unnotified allotment of 9,800 shares to Respondents 3 and 4), further diluted to 0.12% in FY 2005-06, and to 0.10% (1/50th) in FY 2011-12, accompanied by the removal of Bipin Chandra Shah from the register of members. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bipin Chandra Shah fell ill in 2002-03 and died on 15.02.2004; legal heirs sought transmission on 11.03.2006; company denied shareholding on 29.05.2006; Civil Suit No. 942 of 2007 dismissed in default on 25.04.2007; CP No. 16 of 2011 dismissed on 12.03.2012 with liberty; shares transmitted to Appellants on 08.05.2013; present Company Petition filed in September 2013. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Allotment sheets, share registers showing dilution of shareholding, succession records, letters dated 11.03.2006 and 29.05.2006, and previous procedural orders from the City Civil Court and CLB. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 108/2013 under Sections 397/398 of Companies Act 1956; Respondents filed CA No. 314/2013 seeking dismissal in limine under Section 399; NCLT Mumbai allowed CA No. 314/2013 on 26.03.2018 and dismissed the petition on grounds that Appellants failed to meet the 1/10th threshold on petition filing date and for 9-year delay.
legal_issues: Whether the qualification threshold of holding 1/10th shareholding under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 must be assessed on the date of presentation of the petition or on the date the alleged acts of oppression causing dilution took place, and whether the petition was barred by limitation and laches at the preliminary stage.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement via illegal dilution of shareholding, maintainability under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 is a mixed question of fact and law that must be determined based on the petitioner's shareholding on the date the oppressive dilution occurred, rather than the date of filing the petition, and should be adjudicated along with merits at final hearing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 399 eligibility cannot be mechanically applied at the petition presentation date when the substantive grievance itself is that oppressive and fraudulent allotments reduced the petitioner below the statutory 10% threshold; otherwise, oppressed shareholders would be left without a statutory remedy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where continuous oppression, series of unauthorized share allotments, and contested accrual of the right to apply under Article 137 are pleaded, limitation is a mixed question of law and fact not amenable to summary rejection on preliminary application. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT Mumbai erred in dismissing the petition in limine under Section 399 based on post-dilution shareholding and preliminary delay; the impugned order was non-speaking regarding allotment validity, requiring remand for a full hearing on merits.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 250 of 2018 is allowed; impugned order dated 26.03.2018 is set aside; CP No. 108 of 2013 is remanded to NCLT Mumbai Bench for fresh decision on merits; parties directed to appear before NCLT Mumbai on 15.07.2020; no order as to costs.
summary: Legal heirs of a 50% founder shareholder in Trimbak Estates Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing their oppression and mismanagement petition in limine for lack of maintainability under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956, and delay. The NCLAT set aside the dismissal and remanded the matter, establishing that where an applicant alleges unlawful dilution of shareholding below 10%, Section 399 eligibility must be determined as on the date of the alleged oppressive action rather than the petition presentation date. The Tribunal also held that maintainability and limitation in continuous oppression are mixed questions of fact and law that must be adjudicated at final hearing.

case_title: Sandeep Kumar Bhagat vs. Punjab National Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sandeep Kumar Bhagat, suspended director of Corporate Debtor Shree Sai Prakash Alloys Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor and sister companies from Punjab National Bank between 2004, with enhancements up to 11.06.2012, and debt restructuring on 25.07.2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account declared NPA on 31.03.2015; date of default recorded as 12.05.2015; total claimed default amount was Rs. 84,46,17,450.68. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Letter acknowledging debt sent on 03.03.2018; Section 7 application filed on 19.05.2018 (registered July 2018); group OTS of Rs. 60 Crores approved by Bank on 27.12.2018, accepted by debtor on 10.01.2019; Bank revoked OTS on 31.07.2019; Gauhati High Court ordered status quo in WP(C) 6029/2019 on 19.08.2019 till 26.08.2019; NCLT admitted CIRP on 23.08.2019; Bank encashed Rs. 1 Crore renewal cheque on 21.08.2019 / 10.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 2 defective (proposed IRP omitted mandatory declaration regarding absence of pending disciplinary proceedings); debtor acknowledgment letter dated 03.03.2018; OTS sanction letter dated 27.12.2018 showing payment of Rs. 6.79 Crores; subsequent deposit of Rs. 1 Crore; High Court status quo order dated 19.08.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PNB filed CP(I.B.) No. 24/GB/2019 under Section 7; NCLT Guwahati admitted petition on 23.08.2019 despite the High Court status quo order and defective Form 2 declaration.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, whether the admission order was invalid for ignoring a High Court status quo order, and whether non-compliance with the Form 2 disciplinary declaration under Section 7(5) constituted a fatal or curable defect requiring remand.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A written proposal and acknowledgment of liability made within three years of default resets the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963; however, an order admitting a Section 7 petition in disregard of an active High Court status quo order and without curing mandatory procedural defects under Section 7(5)(a) cannot be sustained. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) mandates confirmation that no disciplinary proceedings are pending against the proposed IRP; under the proviso to Section 7(5)(b), failure to furnish this declaration is a curable defect requiring the Adjudicating Authority to issue a seven-day notice to rectify rather than proceeding directly to admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: While written settlement correspondence and part-payments prove debt acknowledgment under Section 18, the tribunal must strictly enforce statutory compliance in Form 2 declarations and respect judicial stay orders from superior constitutional courts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petition was filed within extended limitation due to the 03.03.2018 acknowledgment, but the NCLT committed a fatal procedural error by admitting the petition amidst a High Court status quo order and without rectifying Form 2 defects, necessitating remand.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1003 of 2019 is allowed; impugned admission order dated 23.08.2019 is set aside; matter is remanded to NCLT Guwahati Bench to pass an order afresh after providing an opportunity to cure defects and allowing parties an opportunity to dispassionately consider OTS renewal; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 29.06.2020; no order as to costs.
summary: Punjab National Bank initiated Section 7 CIRP against Shree Sai Prakash Alloys Pvt. Ltd. for a default of Rs. 84.46 Crores. The suspended director appealed the admission order on grounds of limitation, violation of a Gauhati High Court status quo order, defective Form 2 IRP declaration, and ongoing OTS settlement negotiations. The NCLAT held that while the debt was not barred by limitation because the debtor's written OTS communications extended time under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, the NCLT erred in admitting the application without giving notice to cure the defective IRP declaration under Section 7(5) and in total disregard of the High Court's status quo order. The admission was set aside and remanded.

case_title: The Registrar of Companies, West Bengal vs. Karan Kishore Samtani
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is The Registrar of Companies (ROC), West Bengal; Respondent is Karan Kishore Samtani, former director holding directorships across multiple companies. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate compliance and maximum permissible directorships under the Companies Act, 2013; Respondent held directorship in more than 20 companies simultaneously after 31.03.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Contravention of Section 165(1) read with Section 165(3) for continuing directorship in excess of 20 companies for a total of 272 days (from 01.04.2015 to 28.12.2015), attracting a mandatory statutory minimum fine of Rs. 5,000 per day under Section 165(6), totaling Rs. 13,60,000. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 165 came into force on 01.04.2014 requiring compliance/resignation within one year (by 31.03.2015); ROC issued show cause notice on 27.01.2016; resignation from Fabius Properties Pvt. Ltd. accepted on 29.12.2015 and Form DIR-12 filed on 10.02.2016; compounding application filed under Section 441(1). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Show cause notice dated 27.01.2016; Form DIR-12 filed on 10.02.2016; ROC report; compounding representation admitting contravention for 272 days. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent applied for compounding before NCLT Kolkata in CP No. 690/KB/2017; NCLT allowed compounding on 03.04.2018 subject to payment of a compounding fee of only Rs. 50,000; ROC appealed to NCLAT challenging reduction below statutory minimum.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal, while exercising powers under Section 441(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, has the jurisdiction or discretion to impose a compounding fee less than the minimum statutory fine prescribed under Section 165(6) of the Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When compounding an offence under Section 441(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal has no legal jurisdiction or discretion to reduce the compounding fee below the mandatory minimum fine explicitly prescribed by statute for that offence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 165(6) explicitly mandates that contravention of Section 165(1) shall be punishable with a fine 'which shall not be less than five thousand rupees' per day; the word 'shall' establishes a mandatory statutory minimum which the tribunal cannot dilute under the guise of judicial discretion. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of whether default is contumacious or in conscious disregard of legal obligation; holding excess directorships past the statutory one-year transition period demonstrates conscious disregard, disentitling the party from claiming technical or venial breach exemptions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed an error apparent on the face of the record in imposing a compounding fee of Rs. 50,000 instead of the mandatory statutory minimum of Rs. 13,60,000 for 272 days of default, requiring enhancement of the fee to the statutory floor.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 13 of 2019 is allowed; NCLT order dated 03.04.2018 set aside; compounding fee modified to the statutory minimum of Rs. 13,60,000 (at Rs. 5,000 per day for 272 days); Respondent directed to pay balance Rs. 13,10,000 within 60 days before NCLT Kolkata after adjusting Rs. 50,000 already paid; ROC to ensure compliance; no costs.
summary: The Registrar of Companies, West Bengal appealed an NCLT Kolkata order compounding an offence under Section 165(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 (holding more than 20 directorships) by imposing a fee of only Rs. 50,000. The ROC contended the minimum penalty prescribed under Section 165(6) was Rs. 5,000 per day, amounting to Rs. 13,60,000 for 272 days of continuous violation. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and enhanced the compounding fee to the statutory minimum of Rs. 13,60,000, ruling that the Tribunal possesses no statutory discretion under Section 441(1) to reduce the compounding amount below the mandatory minimum fine prescribed by the legislature.

case_title: Tata Consultancy Services Limited vs. Vishal Ghisulal Jain, Resolution Professional of S.K. Wheels Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Tata Consultancy Services Limited (service client); Corporate Debtor is S.K. Wheels Private Limited; Respondent is Vishal Ghisulal Jain (Interim Resolution Professional/Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Build phase agreement dated 24.08.2015 and subsequent Facilities Agreement dated 01.12.2016, where Corporate Debtor agreed to provide premises, IT hardware, air conditioning, maintenance, and staff for TCS client examination centers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged contractual deficiencies and service disruptions by Corporate Debtor, culminating in electricity disconnection in April 2019 due to non-payment of electricity charges during CIRP; TCS sought contract termination. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 against Corporate Debtor on 29.03.2019; TCS issued termination notice under Clause 11(b) on 10.06.2019 / 11.06.2019; RP filed M.A. No. 2954/2019 before NCLT on 28.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Build Phase Agreement dated 24.08.2015; Facilities Agreement dated 01.12.2016; deficiency correspondence dated 11.10.2018 and 19.11.2018; termination notice dated 10.06.2019 issued post-admission; proof of cured deficiencies during CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed M.A. No. 2954/2019 seeking an interim stay of the termination notice; NCLT Mumbai Bench on 18.12.2019 stayed the termination notice and directed TCS to adhere to the contract; TCS appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 to stay a contractual termination notice issued by a third party against the Corporate Debtor during the moratorium period in order to maintain the debtor as a going concern.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To effectuate the central statutory objective of the IBC to preserve the corporate debtor as a going concern, the adjudicating authority has the power to stay the termination of critical commercial and facilities contracts during the moratorium period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 moratorium read alongside the statutory duties cast upon the Resolution Professional under Section 25 (to take custody of assets, preserve business records, and run the debtor as a going concern) empowers tribunals to restrain contractual termination that threatens the enterprise's survival. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the contractual termination post-CIRP admission would frustrate the preservation of the company's business operations and whether past operational defaults were cured by the RP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was bound to function and continue its business activities post-CIRP admission, making the NCLT's stay of TCS's termination notice legally valid to keep the Corporate Debtor an ongoing concern.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 237 of 2020 is dismissed; impugned order of NCLT Mumbai dated 18.12.2019 staying the termination notice and enforcing the contract is upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Tata Consultancy Services Limited appealed against an order of NCLT Mumbai staying its contractual termination notice issued to S.K. Wheels Private Limited (under CIRP) under a Facilities Agreement. TCS argued that termination for material contractual breaches was not barred by the Section 14 moratorium. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 14 read with Section 25 of the IBC, the primary statutory objective is to preserve the Corporate Debtor as a going concern. Consequently, the Adjudicating Authority was justified in restraining termination to ensure business continuity during CIRP. (Note: This principle was subsequently overturned by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 1994 of 2020).

case_title: The Registrar of Companies, West Bengal vs. Sabyasachi Bagchi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is The Registrar of Companies (ROC), West Bengal; Respondent is Sabyasachi Bagchi, an individual holding directorships across multiple companies. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate statutory compliance regarding limits on directorships under Section 165 of the Companies Act, 2013; Respondent held directorship in 17 companies when the provision came into force on 01.04.2014, vacated 3 companies by 31.03.2015, but continued holding excess directorships past the statutory one-year transitional period. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Contravention of Section 165(1) read with Section 165(3) for 326 days (from 01.04.2015 to 21.02.2016), attracting a statutory minimum fine of Rs. 5,000 per day under Section 165(6), totaling Rs. 16,30,000. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 165(1) enforced on 01.04.2014; compliance required by 31.03.2015; show cause notice issued by ROC; resignation from 4 remaining excess directorships executed on 22.02.2016; ROC filed criminal complaint before Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Kolkata; compounding application filed under Section 441(1) during prosecution. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ROC show-cause notice, reply of Respondent, ROC inspection report on compounding application, and resignation filings dated 22.02.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed Company Petition No. 190/KB/2018 under Section 441(1) before NCLT Kolkata; NCLT allowed compounding on 11.07.2018 subject to paying a compounding fee of only Rs. 25,000 (calculating default as 21 days); ROC appealed under Section 421 against fee reduction below statutory minimum.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal, while compounding an offence under Section 441(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, possesses the jurisdiction or discretion to impose a compounding fee less than the mandatory minimum fine prescribed under Section 165(6) of the Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When compounding a statutory offence under Section 441(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal has no legal jurisdiction or discretion to reduce the compounding penalty below the mandatory minimum fine explicitly prescribed by the legislature for that offence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sub-section (6) of Section 165 explicitly provides that contravention shall be punishable with a fine 'which shall not be less than five thousand rupees' per day; the statutory floor is mandatory and cannot be diluted by judicial discretion. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Holding directorships in excess of statutory limits past the one-year grace period indicates conscious disregard of statutory obligations, precluding the party from seeking mitigation under the plea of technical or venial breach. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT committed an error apparent on the record by miscalculating the default period as 21 days instead of 326 days and imposing a fee of Rs. 25,000; the compounding fee must be enhanced to the statutory floor of Rs. 5,000 per day totaling Rs. 16,30,000.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 12 of 2019 is allowed; NCLT Kolkata order dated 11.07.2018 is set aside; compounding fee is modified to the statutory minimum of Rs. 16,30,000; Respondent is directed to pay the balance amount of Rs. 16,05,000 within 60 days before NCLT Kolkata after adjusting Rs. 25,000 already paid; ROC to ensure compliance; no order as to costs.
summary: The Registrar of Companies, West Bengal appealed an NCLT Kolkata order compounding an offence under Section 165(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 by imposing a fee of only Rs. 25,000 on Sabyasachi Bagchi for holding excess directorships. The ROC argued the default persisted for 326 days, attracting a mandatory statutory minimum of Rs. 5,000 per day totaling Rs. 16,30,000 under Section 165(6). The NCLAT allowed the appeal and enhanced the fee to Rs. 16,30,000, holding that the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction under Section 441(1) to reduce compounding fees below the statutory floor.

case_title: NTPC Ltd. (Sipat Project) & Ors. vs. Rajiv Chakraborty, I.R.P. of Era Infra Engineering Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Operational Creditors (NTPC Ltd. across various projects and Aravali Power Company Pvt. Ltd.); Corporate Debtor is Era Infra Engineering Ltd.; Respondent is Rajiv Chakraborty, Interim Resolution Professional/Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying infrastructure, engineering, and procurement contracts between Appellants and the Corporate Debtor involving operational claims, disputed loss, and damages. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disputed claims regarding losses and damages asserted by Appellants as operational debts against the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under CP (IB)-No. 190(PB)2017 before NCLT Principal Bench. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Claims submitted to the Resolution Professional for unliquidated damages/losses; Information Memorandum reflecting disputes and claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed applications before NCLT Principal Bench seeking admission of disputed damage claims; NCLT dismissed applications on 10.02.2020 directing that information regarding disputes and damage claims be reflected in the Information Memorandum; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Professional during CIRP functions as an adjudicating authority empowered to admit or reject disputed claims of operational creditors for loss and damages, and whether an appeal lies against non-admission before approval of a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1.
