ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional is an administrative facilitator tasked solely with collecting, collating, and verifying claims, and does not possess adjudicatory powers to admit or reject disputed claims during CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unlike a Liquidator who is empowered under Section 40 to determine claims, the IBC does not provide an adjudicatory role or an appellate mechanism against claim collation by an RP during the CIRP stage; claim grievances can only be raised before the Adjudicating Authority when the Resolution Plan is considered under Section 31. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Operational creditors asserting unliquidated damages or disputed future claims cannot compel admission during the CIRP collation phase; reflective inclusion in the Information Memorandum sufficiently protects stakeholder information. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal seeking mandatory admission of disputed damage claims prior to resolution plan approval is premature and unfounded, as the NCLT properly directed inclusion of disputed claim information in the Information Memorandum.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 491, 492, 493, 494 & 495 of 2020 are dismissed; liberty granted to Appellants to raise claim admissibility issues before the Adjudicating Authority at the appropriate Section 31 stage; interim directions vacated.
summary: Operational Creditors including NTPC appealed an NCLT Principal Bench order refusing to direct the Resolution Professional of Era Infra Engineering Ltd. to admit their disputed claims for loss and damages. The NCLAT dismissed the batch of appeals, holding that an RP is not an adjudicating authority and has no power to admit or reject claims, but is only mandated to collect and collate information for the Information Memorandum. The Tribunal ruled that disputes regarding claim admission can only be adjudicated by the NCLT at the stage of resolution plan approval under Section 31.

case_title: Prashant Properties Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vijaykumar V. Iyer, RP of the Corporate Debtor & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Prashant Properties Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor and alleged trademark holder); Respondent is Vijaykumar V. Iyer, Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Trademark user rights and Permitted User Agreement concerning the brand 'Elegant' and 'Family of Marks' utilized by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational claims and disputed trademark usage rights asserted after CIRP resolution. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by NCLT on 08.04.2019; RP issued public notice on 18.04.2019; Appellant filed CA No. 124/KB/2020 in pending CA(IB) No. 937/KB/2018 seeking intervention post-approval; limitation to appeal approval order under Section 61 expired. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Permitted User Agreement, forensic consultant and RP transaction audit reports, and the approved Resolution Plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA No. 124/KB/2020 in CP(IB) No. 595/KB/2017 before NCLT Kolkata; NCLT dismissed the application on 26.02.2020 holding that it had no jurisdiction to review its own decision post-plan approval; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an Operational Creditor can seek intervention or challenge trademark rights and claims after the Resolution Plan has already been approved by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31(1) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a Resolution Plan is approved by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31(1), it becomes final and binding on all stakeholders, rendering the Adjudicating Authority functus officio and barring creditors who participated in the CIRP from asserting subsequent collateral challenges. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 31(1), approval gives finality to the resolution process; an approved plan cannot be reviewed or modified through miscellaneous intervention applications once the statutory period for filing an appeal under Section 61 has elapsed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A creditor participating throughout the CIRP cannot plead ignorance of proceedings or maintain post-approval intervention applications seeking to alter contractual allocations approved under the plan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly refused to review its plan approval order, as the plan had attained absolute finality and the Appellant failed to challenge the approval order under Section 61 within limitation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 513 of 2020 is dismissed; impugned order dated 26.02.2020 upheld; no costs.
summary: Prashant Properties Pvt. Ltd., an operational creditor claiming ownership of the 'Elegant' trademark, challenged an NCLT Kolkata order rejecting its post-approval intervention application. The Appellant contended that trademark user rights did not pass to the Successful Resolution Applicant. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that once a Resolution Plan is approved under Section 31(1) of the IBC and remains unappealed within the Section 61 limitation period, it attains complete finality, becomes binding on all stakeholders, and cannot be reopened or reviewed.

case_title: Praveen Kumar Nanda Kumar vs. VSL Securities Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Restoration Application No. 01 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 308 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Praveen Kumar Nanda Kumar (Promoter of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is VSL Securities Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Corporate Debtor is M/s Unishire Housing LLP; Respondent No. 3 is Haribabu Thota (RP); Respondent No. 4 is K. Dushyantha Kumar (Liquidator); intervening creditor was M/s Altico Capital India Ltd.. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities extended by VSL Securities Pvt. Ltd. to Corporate Debtor M/s Unishire Housing LLP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Corporate Debtor leading to total claims received of Rs. 2,35,72,27,259 against available liquid assets of only Rs. 29,60,000. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 on 31.07.2019 in CP No. 172 of 2019; CIRP period expired without any viable resolution plan; CoC resolved to recommend liquidation by a 70.97% majority vote. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports showing liquid assets of only Rs. 29.60 lakhs against claims exceeding Rs. 235.72 Crores; CoC voting records demonstrating 70.97% majority resolution recommending liquidation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench passed an order on 08.01.2020 sending Corporate Debtor into liquidation; Appellant filed appeal challenging liquidation, which was dismissed and restored via Restoration Application No. 01 of 2020.
legal_issues: Whether the decision of the Committee of Creditors recommending liquidation of the Corporate Debtor by a majority of 70.97%, due to lack of viable resolution plans and extreme asset-liability mismatch, is open to judicial review.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors recommending liquidation of a corporate debtor after evaluating assets, liabilities, and absence of viable resolution plans is a business decision not amenable to judicial review. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 33, upon expiry of the CIRP period without any approved resolution plan, the recommendation of the CoC with the requisite statutory majority requires the Adjudicating Authority to order liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where CIRP admission stands unassailed, the statutory period expires without resolution plans, and liquid assets represent a negligible fraction of admitted debt, the CoC's business evaluation is conclusive. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC validly exercised its commercial wisdom with a 70.97% majority to liquidate the Corporate Debtor, and no grounds existed to interfere with the NCLT's liquidation order.
operative_order: Restoration Application allowed and appeal restored to file; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 308 of 2020 is dismissed on merits; no costs.
summary: The promoter of Unishire Housing LLP appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor, alleging irregularities in admitting claims of certain financial creditors during CIRP. The NCLAT restored and dismissed the appeal on merits, holding that the CIRP period had lapsed with no resolution plans, liquid assets amounted to only Rs. 29.60 lakhs against claims of Rs. 235.72 Crores, and the CoC had resolved by 70.97% to liquidate. The Tribunal reiterated that the CoC's business decision recommending liquidation is based on commercial wisdom and is immune from judicial review.

case_title: Ms. Leena D. Bagwe vs. The Registrar of Companies, Mumbai
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ms. Leena D. Bagwe (representing the struck-off company); Respondent is The Registrar of Companies (ROC), Mumbai. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Maintenance of corporate status and statutory compliance; company incorporated on 17.12.1991. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to file annual statutory returns since incorporation, leading to striking off by ROC Mumbai on 04.12.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Incorporated 17.12.1991; struck off 04.12.2018; revival petition filed under Section 252 in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual returns non-filing records, ROC strike-off notification dated 04.12.2018, and restoration application records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed C.P. No. 1461/252/MB/2019 before NCLT Mumbai Bench under Section 252 seeking restoration; NCLT allowed restoration on 07.01.2020 subject to paying onerous costs of Rs. 7 Lakhs; Appellant appealed to NCLAT challenging the cost quantum.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal exercised sound judicial discretion in imposing costs of Rs. 7 Lakhs as a condition precedent for restoring the struck-off company under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Costs imposed by an Adjudicating Authority as a condition for corporate restoration under Section 252 must be based on judicious consideration, proportionality, and explicit reasoning, and are subject to appellate modification if found disproportionate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252 confers equitable discretion to order restoration on terms deemed just; such discretion does not justify arbitrary or punitive costs devoid of explanatory reasons. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of justification or reasoning in the impugned order for imposing disproportionate costs warrants appellate reduction to a reasonable figure. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT gave no reasons for imposing Rs. 7 Lakhs costs; a reduced cost of Rs. 1,50,000 is just and reasonable, without prejudice to ROC recovering statutory filing fees and penalties.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 40 of 2020 is disposed of; impugned order dated 07.01.2020 is modified by substituting costs of Rs. 7,00,000 with Rs. 1,50,000; order will not prevent ROC from recovering other statutory penalties or dues in accordance with law.
summary: Ms. Leena D. Bagwe appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order that allowed the restoration of her company under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 (which had been struck off for not filing returns since 1991) but conditioned it upon paying costs of Rs. 7 Lakhs. The NCLAT modified the order, reducing the costs from Rs. 7,00,000 to Rs. 1,50,000, holding that the imposition of costs must be judicious and reasoned. The Tribunal clarified that this reduction would not preclude ROC from recovering standard statutory dues and penalties.

case_title: Mr. Abhijit Guhathakurta, Monitoring Agency of the Corporate Debtor vs. Royale Partners Investment Fund Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in Comp. App. 287/2020 is Abhijit Guhathakurta (Monitoring Agency/erstwhile RP of the Corporate Debtor); Appellant in Comp. App. 327/2020 is Royale Partners Investment Fund Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Intervenor is IDBI Bank representing the Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation of approved Resolution Plan for the Corporate Debtor requiring payment of Rs. 420 Crores upfront consideration, issuance of Rs. 480 Crores unlisted NCDs, and deposit of Rs. 48 Crores balance performance bank guarantee. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the Successful Resolution Applicant in remitting the upfront consideration of Rs. 420 Crores within the mandatory 30 business days from the plan approval date (25.11.2019), which expired on 10.01.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved the plan on 10.01.2019; NCLT approved it under Section 31 on 25.11.2019; appellate challenge by ArcelorMittal dismissed on 16.12.2019; Monitoring Agency filed MA 249/2020 on 15.01.2020; Bench reserved orders on 30.01.2020; reconstituted Bench stayed proceedings via MA 515/2020 on 12.02.2020; original Bench delivered implementation order on 18.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Process Document dated 04.10.2018; approved Resolution Plan dated 25.11.2019; Letter of Intent dated 10.01.2019 stipulating cash balances accrue solely to financial creditors without deduction; emails and data-room transmission logs dated 29.11.2019, 24.12.2019, and 16.03.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Monitoring Agency filed MA 249/2020 for plan enforcement, reserved by erstwhile NCLT Mumbai Bench II; Resolution Applicant filed MA 515/2020 before reconstituted Bench II which stayed MA 249/2020 on 12.02.2020; erstwhile Bench subsequently allowed MA 249/2020 on 18.02.2020 directing implementation within 7 days.
legal_issues: Whether a newly reconstituted coordinate bench of the NCLT has jurisdiction to stay proceedings and pronouncement of orders in a matter already heard and reserved by an erstwhile bench; whether a Monitoring Agency has locus standi to seek enforcement of an approved resolution plan; and whether cash balances of the corporate debtor can be set off against the upfront consideration payable by the resolution applicant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under principles of judicial discipline and decorum, a coordinate bench of a tribunal cannot stay proceedings or interfere in a matter heard and reserved for orders by another coordinate bench of the same tribunal; furthermore, an approved resolution plan is unconditionally binding on the resolution applicant without any implied condition precedent of post-approval data handover or unilateral set-off of cash accruals. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC mandates that an approved plan binds all stakeholders; Section 23 read with Section 25 empowers the Monitoring Agency and RP to take all necessary steps, including filing miscellaneous applications before the NCLT, to enforce execution of the resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Express terms of the approved Resolution Plan, Process Document, and Letter of Intent govern the transaction; where clauses explicitly assign pre-implementation cash balances to financial creditors, parole assertions of contrary adjustments cannot be entertained. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order dated 12.02.2020 staying MA 249/2020 was an illegal nullity violating judicial comity, while the order dated 18.02.2020 directing immediate payment of upfront consideration, NCD issuance, and performance guarantee without cash balance set-offs was fully justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 287 of 2020 is allowed and the stay order dated 12.02.2020 in MA 515/2020 is set aside; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 327 of 2020 is dismissed, upholding the direction ordering Royale Partners Investment Fund Ltd. to implement the approved Resolution Plan forthwith; no order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT addressed two connected appeals arising from the CIRP of a corporate debtor. In Comp. App. 287/2020, the Tribunal set aside an interim order of a reconstituted NCLT Mumbai bench that stayed an application reserved for orders by an earlier coordinate bench, holding it violated judicial discipline. In Comp. App. 327/2020, NCLAT dismissed the appeal of the Successful Resolution Applicant (Royale Partners), holding that the Monitoring Agency possessed locus standi to enforce the plan, that data delivery was not a condition precedent to payment, and that cash balances could not be deducted from the Rs. 420 Crores upfront consideration.

case_title: Food Corporation of India vs. Excel Crop Care Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Compensation Application (AT) No. 01 of 2019 in Competition Appeal (AT) No. 79-81 of 2012
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant is Food Corporation of India (FCI); Respondents are manufacturers of Aluminium Phosphide (ALP) Tablets, namely Excel Crop Care Ltd. (R-1), UPL Limited (R-2), and Sandhya Organic Chemicals (P) Ltd. (R-3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Procurement tenders floated by FCI for purchasing Aluminium Phosphide (ALP) Tablets for grain preservation during the tender periods 2009-10 and 2011-12. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Quantified overcharge loss claimed: Rs. 3,23,15,250 from R-1; Rs. 3,06,43,000 from R-2; Rs. 57,79,000 from R-3 (cumulative direct loss of Rs. 6,87,37,250), plus 18% compound interest (Rs. 18,98,70,828) and legal costs, aggregating Rs. 26,12,00,141. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CCI found bid rigging and price fixing under Section 3 on 23.04.2012; COMPAT upheld contravention findings on 29.10.2013 but adjusted penalties based on relevant turnover; Supreme Court affirmed the liability findings and penalty formula on 08.05.2017; FCI filed Section 53N Compensation Application on 11.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Actual procurement prices vs competitive cost analysis based on CCI findings; tender documents from 2009-10 and 2011-12; Supreme Court judgment dated 08.05.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: FCI filed Compensation Application (AT) No. 01 of 2019 under Section 53N before NCLAT; Respondents raised preliminary objections on maintainability arguing doctrine of merger, bar of limitation (asserting 3 years expired from COMPAT's 2013 order), and impermissibility of a single application against multiple enterprises.
legal_issues: Whether a Compensation Application under Section 53N of the Competition Act, 2002 is maintainable following final determination of contravention by the Supreme Court under the doctrine of merger; whether the application was barred by limitation or laches; and whether a single joint compensation application against multiple cartelizing enterprises is legally permissible.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory compensation claim arising from anti-competitive findings is maintainable upon the final disposal of appeals by the Supreme Court under the doctrine of merger, and the reasonable period of limitation of three years is computed from the date of the Supreme Court's final judgment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 53N(1) requires a claim to 'arise from' findings of the CCI or Appellate Tribunal; when such findings are appealed under Section 53T, they remain in legal jeopardy until merged into the Supreme Court judgment, which forms the definitive accrual point for limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of an explicit limitation period in Section 53N, courts adopt the general three-year standard under Article 137 of the Limitation Act as a measure of reasonable dispatch; deficit filing fees do not warrant summary dismissal and are curable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the cause of action achieved finality on 08.05.2017 and the application was filed within two years and two months on 11.07.2019, it was timely; joint filing against co-cartelists arises from common operative facts and is maintainable.
operative_order: Preliminary objections on maintainability are rejected and Compensation Application (AT) No. 01 of 2019 is held maintainable; Registry directed to issue an Office Memorandum if any deficit fee is due for rectification within 14 days, with liberty to amend pleadings within one week thereafter; application directed to be listed for hearing on merits in usual course.
summary: Food Corporation of India filed a Compensation Application under Section 53N of the Competition Act, 2002 claiming Rs. 26.12 Crores from three ALP tablet manufacturers for losses caused by cartelization and bid-rigging in 2009 and 2011 tenders. The Respondents challenged maintainability, arguing that Section 53N does not contemplate applications post-Supreme Court decisions, that the 2013 COMPAT order had merged into the 2017 Supreme Court judgment, and that the claim was time-barred. The NCLAT held that under the doctrine of merger, limitation commenced only upon the Supreme Court's final judgment dated 08.05.2017, making the application filed on 11.07.2019 well within the reasonable three-year period, and affirmed that a joint claim against co-cartelists is valid.

case_title: Mr. Srikanth Dwarakanath, Liquidator of Surana Power Limited vs. Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Srikanth Dwarakanath (Liquidator of Surana Power Limited); Respondent is Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL), a secured operational creditor claiming a lien/charge. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply and erection contracts for thermal power equipment; consortium lending facilities where 10 other financial creditors held a prior hypothecation deed over assets dated 24.09.2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation of Surana Power Limited following unsuccessful CIRP; BHEL obtained an ex-parte arbitral award on 24.01.2018 recognizing a lien over equipment and partially erected plant facilities, representing 26.24% in value of secured assets. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9 on 20.01.2019; liquidation ordered post-CIRP failure; 10 out of 11 secured lenders holding 73.76% value relinquished security interest to the liquidation estate; BHEL notified refusal to relinquish on 23.08.2019 and intention to realize security under Section 52 on 27.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Hypothecation dated 24.09.2010; Arbitral Award dated 24.01.2018; BHEL letters dated 23.08.2019 and 27.01.2020; relinquishment declarations of 73.76% secured creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed Misc. Application No. 1052 of 2019 before NCLT Chennai seeking permission to sell the assets as a slump sale under Regulation 32; NCLT dismissed the application on 20.11.2019 holding BHEL had an unbridled right under Section 52 and its lien took preference; Liquidator appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a single dissenting secured creditor holding an arbitral lien over non-exclusive assets representing 26.24% in value can refuse relinquishment under Section 52 and stall the liquidation process when 73.76% of secured creditors have relinquished their security interest under Section 53.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A single secured creditor holding a non-exclusive pari passu charge cannot unilaterally exercise realization rights under Section 52 of the IBC contrary to the will of the supermajority (over 60%) of secured creditors who have opted to relinquish their security interest to the liquidation estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 52(4) of the IBC mandates that enforcement of security interest must be in accordance with applicable enforcement law; where multiple creditors share charges, Section 13(9) of the SARFAESI Act applies, requiring approval of secured creditors representing not less than 60% in value to enforce or realize secured assets. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the liquidator's records establish that an arbitral lien does not confer an exclusive first charge and creditors representing 73.76% of the asset value have relinquished security, the dissenting creditor cannot meet the 60% SARFAESI threshold to enforce independently. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: BHEL lacked the requisite 60% voting value to realize the shared secured assets independently under Section 13(9) of the SARFAESI Act read with Section 52(4) IBC; the relinquishment decision of the 73.76% majority binds BHEL, allowing the liquidator to proceed with the sale.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1510 of 2019 is allowed; impugned order of NCLT Chennai dated 20.11.2019 is set aside; Liquidator is directed to proceed and complete the liquidation sale of the Corporate Debtor's assets in accordance with law; no order as to costs.
summary: The Liquidator of Surana Power Limited appealed an NCLT Chennai order dismissing his application to sell company assets where 10 secured creditors (representing 73.76% in value) relinquished their security interest, but BHEL (holding 26.24% via an arbitral lien) refused to relinquish, opting to realize its security under Section 52 of the IBC. The NCLAT reversed the NCLT order, holding that under Section 52(4) read with Section 13(9) of the SARFAESI Act, realization of shared or non-exclusive secured assets requires the consent of at least 60% of secured creditors by value. Since BHEL held only 26.24%, the decision of the 73.76% majority to relinquish was binding on BHEL, enabling the Liquidator to proceed with the liquidation sale.

case_title: Arpit Agarwal vs. Skytech Constructions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Arpit Agarwal (homebuyer/allottee); Respondent No. 1 is Skytech Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (developer company); Respondents 2 to 4 are directors (Rakesh Chawla, Mayank Chawla, Renu Chawla); Respondent No. 5 is M/s Jatasya Promoters Pvt. Ltd.. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking of Unit No. G-402, 4th Floor, in 'Skytech Matrott Project', Sector 76, Noida; Appellant paid Rs. 48.99 lakhs in June and July 2012, representing 95% of the total property consideration, under an agreement for construction and sale. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure of the builder to deliver the flat by the agreed March 2013 deadline; builder alleged delay due to NGT orders and farmers' agitation, and claimed possession was offered on 05.08.2015 and 17.07.2017 without buyer taking handover. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Advance payment made June-July 2012; promised delivery March 2013; possession offer letters issued 05.08.2015 and 17.07.2017; cross criminal complaints and FIRs lodged in March-May 2015; NCDRC complaint filed 19.06.2015; Company Petition filed 01.09.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Payment receipts totaling Rs. 48.99 lakhs; Builder Buyer Agreement; FIRs and criminal complaints under Section 190/200 CrPC; possession letters dated 05.08.2015 and 17.07.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 234(ND)/2017 before NCLT New Delhi under Sections 73, 74(3), 75, and 447 alleging unadjusted property advances constituted public deposits; NCLT dismissed the petition on 20.11.2018 without examining the deposit question to avoid multiplicity with pending NCDRC proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can dismiss a company petition alleging unlawful acceptance of deposits under Section 2(31) and Section 74(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 merely due to pendency of concurrent consumer proceedings, and whether property advance constitutes a 'deposit' under the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority exercising company jurisdiction cannot abdicate its statutory obligation to adjudicate substantive company law violations regarding illegal deposits merely because concurrent consumer or criminal proceedings are pending between the parties. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(31) read with Rule 2(c)(xii) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014 defines 'deposit' to exclude genuine property advances only when conditions regarding project approvals and proper appropriation are satisfied; determining this requires examination of transaction nature and company jurisdiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an applicant raises specific statutory grievances under corporate penal provisions (Sections 73, 74, and 75), the tribunal is obligated to examine the factual records and record a conclusive finding rather than dismissing in limine on multiplicity grounds. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in dismissing the petition without deciding whether the advance constituted an illegal public deposit and whether it had jurisdiction, requiring remand for a full rehearing on merits.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 37 of 2019 is disposed of; impugned judgment dated 20.11.2018 is set aside; matter is remitted back to NCLT New Delhi to rehear the parties on the question of 'deposit' under Section 2(31) read with Rule 2(c)(xii) and determine jurisdiction to dispose of the petition as per law.
summary: Arpit Agarwal, an allottee who paid Rs. 48.99 lakhs towards a flat, filed a company petition under Sections 73, 74(3), and 75 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging that Skytech Constructions fraudulently received public deposits. The NCLT dismissed the petition on the ground that multiple proceedings, including a consumer complaint before NCDRC, were pending. The NCLAT set aside the dismissal, ruling that the NCLT failed to determine the central statutory question of whether the unadjusted real estate advance constituted a 'deposit' under Section 2(31) read with the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, and remanded the matter for fresh adjudication on merits.

case_title: G.T. Polymers vs. Keshava Medi Devices Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is G.T. Polymers (Operational Creditor, partnership firm); Respondent is Keshava Medi Devices Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regular supply of packaging raw material (ribbon packed film used for precision medical devices) under 5 commercial invoices raised between 30.08.2016 and 20.12.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total operational debt claimed in default was Rs. 23,22,537 principal plus interest, totaling Rs. 31,73,578 (balance confirmation signed for Rs. 23,04,537 as of 31.03.2018); debtor admitted partial payments of Rs. 3,05,395 on 25.07.2017 and Rs. 5,00,000 on 18.11.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised Aug-Dec 2016; balance confirmation as of 31.03.2018; Section 8(1) demand notice issued 07.09.2018 (received 28.09.2018); debtor replied disputing debt on 05.10.2018; debtor filed civil suit in Chennai on 11.10.2018; Section 9 application filed in February 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: 5 unpaid commercial invoices; debtor's running ledger accounts (2016-2018); bank statements from Kotak Mahindra Bank; Central Sales Tax Form-C acknowledging all 5 invoices; signed balance confirmation letter dated 31.03.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed before NCLT Hyderabad/Amaravati; NCLT rejected the application on 30.09.2019 holding the claim fell within the ambit of a disputed claim due to allegations of forgery and civil suit pendency.
legal_issues: Whether a civil suit filed by the Corporate Debtor subsequent to the receipt of a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) and Section 9 of the IBC, and whether unsubstantiated allegations of document forgery without documentary support satisfy the Mobilox standard of a plausible dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A dispute or civil suit initiated after the receipt of a statutory demand notice under Section 8 does not constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the IBC; bald, unsubstantiated assertions of fraud or forgery unsupported by evidence are spurious defenses that cannot derail Section 9 admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(1) and Section 9(5)(2)(d), the 'existence of a dispute' must pre-date the receipt of the demand notice; suit filed subsequent to notice receipt is legally irrelevant to establish pre-existing dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox test requires a plausible contention supported by objective evidence; where Central Sales Tax Form-C delivered by the debtor references the disputed invoices and running ledgers corroborate the debt, a mere uncorroborated denial or plea of forgery is feeble and spurious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The operational debt exceeded Rs. 1 lakh, default was proven by Form-C and ledger records, and no genuine dispute existed prior to demand notice receipt, rendering the Section 9 application fit for admission.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1266 of 2019 is allowed; impugned order of NCLT Amaravati dated 30.09.2019 is set aside; case is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the Section 9 application after giving notice to the Corporate Debtor to provide an opportunity for settlement prior to formal admission; no costs.
summary: Operational Creditor G.T. Polymers appealed against an NCLT Amaravati order rejecting its Section 9 application against Keshava Medi Devices Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid invoices of Rs. 23,22,537. The NCLT had rejected the petition citing a disputed claim based on the debtor's allegations that a balance confirmation was forged and that a civil suit was pending. The NCLAT set aside the rejection, ruling that the civil suit was filed after receipt of the Section 8 demand notice and could not constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6). Holding that the debtor's Form-C sales tax filings and running ledgers proved the debt, the Tribunal found the defense spurious and remitted the matter for admission.

case_title: Sandeep Kumar Bhagat vs Punjab National Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shree Sai Rolling Mills (India) Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Punjab National Bank is the Financial Creditor; Sandeep Kumar Bhagat is the Appellant and Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities to the tune of Rs 35,80,00,000/- from the Respondent Bank between 20th May 2005 and 29th August 2014 upon execution of security documents and creation of security interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Financial Creditor claimed an outstanding default amount of Rs 45,33,35,395.58; the account was declared NPA on 31st March 2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was filed on 09th July 2018 (registered as CP (IB) No. 24/GB/2019). During pendency, an OTS of Rs 60 Crores for group companies was approved on 27th December 2018 and accepted on 10th January 2019, but revoked on 31st July 2019; on 19th August 2019, the Gauhati High Court in WP(C) No. 6029 of 2019 ordered parties to maintain status quo till 26th August 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's written OTS proposal letters dated 05th March 2018 and 13th March 2018 acknowledging liability prior to the expiry of 3 years from NPA; payment of Rs 6.79 Crores under OTS and subsequent encashment of Rs 1 Crore by the Bank on 21st August 2019; defective Form 2 declaration by proposed IRP lacking the statutory statement on pending disciplinary proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 23rd August 2019 despite the High Court's status quo order; the Suspended Director appealed against admission.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition under IBC is maintainable and validly admitted when the proposed IRP's Form 2 declaration fails to comply with Section 7(5)(a) requirements, whether an acknowledgment of liability via an OTS proposal within three years from NPA extends limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and whether the Adjudicating Authority could admit the application in violation of a subsisting High Court status quo order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A defect in the proposed IRP's declaration under Form 2 is a curable defect under the proviso to Section 7(5) requiring seven days' rectification notice rather than an outright invalidation of the application; furthermore, a written acknowledgment of debt/OTS proposal executed before the expiration of the three-year limitation period from NPA triggers a fresh period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) mandates satisfaction that the application is complete and no disciplinary proceedings are pending against the proposed IRP, read with the first proviso requiring mandatory notice to rectify defects; Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC Section 7 proceedings via Section 238A, meaning a signed acknowledgment of liability computes a fresh period of limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary verification of written OTS communications and payment encashments to establish subsistence of debt acknowledgment within limitation, alongside scrutiny of Form 2 to evaluate curable statutory non-compliance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was within limitation due to Section 18 acknowledgment, but the admission order was legally flawed for failing to provide statutory opportunity to cure Form 2 defects under the proviso to Section 7(5) and for disregarding the High Court's binding status quo order.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned admission order dated 23rd August 2019 is set aside, and the matter is remanded back to NCLT Guwahati Bench to pass an order afresh after providing an opportunity to rectify defects and providing one more opportunity to the parties to consider renewal of OTS; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 29th June 2020; no order as to costs.
summary: Punjab National Bank filed a Section 7 IBC application against Corporate Debtor Shree Sai Rolling Mills (India) Pvt. Ltd. for default on credit facilities of Rs 45.33 Crores, following an NPA declaration on 31st March 2016. Suspended Director Sandeep Kumar Bhagat appealed the NCLT Guwahati Bench's admission order, alleging limitation bar, defective IRP declaration under Form 2, and breach of a Gauhati High Court status quo order. NCLAT held that the petition was within limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act due to written OTS proposals in March 2018. However, because the Form 2 defect was curable under the Section 7(5) proviso and the admission violated the High Court status quo order, NCLAT set aside the admission order and remanded the matter back.

case_title: Sandeep Kumar Bhagat vs Punjab National Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shree Sai Smelters (India) Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Punjab National Bank is the Financial Creditor; Sandeep Kumar Bhagat is the Appellant and Suspended Ex-Director of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities to the tune of Rs 15,25,00,000/- were availed by the Corporate Debtor from Punjab National Bank between 20th May 2005 and 20th August 2014 upon execution of security documents. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs 17,52,42,104.49 occurred on 27th July 2015, on which date the account was classified as NPA. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor filed Section 7 application on 19th May 2018 (registered as CP (IB) No. 23/GB/2019); consolidated OTS was sanctioned on 27th December 2018, accepted on 10th January 2019, and revoked on 31st July 2019; Gauhati High Court passed status quo order in WP(C) No. 6029 of 2019 on 19th August 2019 operative till 26th August 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Written letter of acknowledgment and OTS proposal dated 13th March 2018 executed within 3 years of NPA; deposit of Rs 6.79 Crores under OTS; tender and acceptance of Rs 1 Crore cheque by the Bank on 21st August 2019; Form 2 declaration omitting confirmation regarding absence of pending disciplinary proceedings against proposed IRP Anil Agarwal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 23rd August 2019 despite knowledge of the High Court's status quo order; the Ex-Director challenged the admission.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, whether acknowledgment via an OTS proposal extended limitation under Section 18, whether the non-compliance of Form 2 under Section 7(5)(a) vitiates the admission order, and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting the application during the operation of a High Court status quo order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of liability in writing made within the prescribed period of limitation creates a fresh period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act for applications under Section 7 IBC; additionally, an incomplete IRP declaration in Form 2 constitutes a curable defect necessitating statutory notice to rectify under the proviso to Section 7(5). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) conditions admission on completeness of the application and absence of disciplinary proceedings against the proposed IRP, triggering the first proviso's mandatory cure period; Article 137 read with Section 238A of the IBC and Section 18 of the Limitation Act resets limitation from the date of a written acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of written settlement proposals acknowledging debt within 3 years of default date, alongside documentary review of statutory declaration forms filed under Adjudicating Authority Rules. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the application was not time-barred due to valid Section 18 acknowledgment, the admission order was unsustainable as the Adjudicating Authority overlooked curable Form 2 defects under the proviso to Section 7(5) and violated the binding status quo order of the High Court.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 23rd August 2019 is set aside, and the matter is remanded back to NCLT Guwahati Bench to pass an order afresh after affording opportunity to cure defects and giving parties one more opportunity to consider renewal of OTS; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 29th June 2020; no order as to costs.
summary: Punjab National Bank initiated Section 7 IBC proceedings against Shree Sai Smelters (India) Ltd. for an unpaid debt of Rs 17.52 Crores following an NPA classification on 27th July 2015. The suspended director appealed the admission order passed by NCLT Guwahati Bench on 23rd August 2019. NCLAT held that the petition was not barred by limitation because the debtor acknowledged liability in writing on 13th March 2018 under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. However, NCLAT found that the IRP's Form 2 declaration was defective and curable under the Section 7(5) proviso, and the NCLT had erroneously passed the admission order while a Gauhati High Court status quo order was in force. The admission order was set aside and the matter remanded.

case_title: S.P. Velumani & Anr vs Magnum Spinning Mills India Pvt. Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: S.P. Velumani (19.55% shareholder, founder promoter, director) and V. Prabha (2.31% shareholder) are Appellants/Petitioners; Magnum Spinning Mills India Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1; M. Parthiban and six others are Respondent directors/shareholders. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and operation of a closely held private spinning mill incorporated on 29th October 2010 where Appellants held 21.86% equity and Respondents held approximately 77% equity. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute arose over altering bank cheque-signing authority, writing off Rs 48,41,801/- as bad debts in FY 2017-18, alleged bogus cotton purchases, and unapproved compound wall construction. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting altering bank mandate held on 22nd August 2016; Appellant sent objection letters to the bank on 30th August 2016 and 06th September 2017; Company Petition CP No. 17/2017 filed under Sections 241-242 in 2017; impugned order passed by NCLT Chennai on 11th July 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered office entry registers, CCTV footage, and signed vouchers proving Appellant No. 1's attendance at the premises on 22nd August 2016; absence of promoter agreements or Articles granting exclusive veto/signatory rights; chartered engineer/surveyor confirmation proving no encroachment on poramboke land. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 17/2017 alleging oppression and mismanagement; NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed the petition on 11th July 2019 holding acts were business decisions not amounting to oppression; Appellants appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether altering bank account signatory authority from an exclusive/mandatory individual director to any two directors constitutes an act of oppression under Section 241/242, whether isolated operational acts and commercial decisions such as writing off bad debts constitute oppression, and whether a minority shareholder has an inherent right to proportional board representation in a private company.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Alteration of bank operating mandates and writing off bad debts are purely internal business and commercial decisions within the board's domain and do not constitute oppression and mismanagement unless proved to be a continuous, harsh, wrongful, and colourable exercise of power. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 require a continuing course of oppressive, harsh, and wrongful conduct prejudicial to company or public interest; isolated operational acts or democratic majority decisions under corporate articles do not satisfy the statutory threshold of oppression. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The petitioner must produce concrete evidence demonstrating complete unlawful exclusion or fraudulent diversion of funds; in the absence of contractual veto rights or evidence of colourable exclusion, majority board decisions are valid. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The alteration of bank operation to a democratic 'any two directors' format and commercial write-offs were legal board actions, not acts of oppression; dismissal of the petition was fully justified.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, the impugned order of NCLT Chennai dated 11th July 2019 in CP No. 17/2017 is upheld, and no order is made as to costs.
summary: Appellants holding 21.86% equity in Magnum Spinning Mills India Pvt. Ltd. filed a petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging oppression and mismanagement, primarily challenging a board resolution dated 22nd August 2016 that altered the bank account signatory mandate from requiring Appellant No. 1's mandatory signature to any two directors, along with allegations of bad debt write-offs and unauthorised construction. NCLT Chennai dismissed the petition. On appeal under Section 421, NCLAT held that bank signatory mandates and bad debt write-offs are commercial decisions within the board's business domain and cannot be characterized as oppressive without evidence of harsh, wrongful, or colourable conduct. Finding no merit in the claims, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Quinn Logistics India Private Limited & Ors vs The Registrar of Companies, Hyderabad
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 1, subsidiary of Quinn Logistics Sweden AB) and its nominee directors Robert Philip Dix, Paul McGowan, and Bryan O'Neill (Appellants Nos. 2 to 4); Registrar of Companies, Hyderabad is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regulatory corporate governance and statutory requirement of holding Annual General Meetings for the calendar years 2012, 2013, 2014, and 2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to convene and conduct AGMs for four consecutive years; default under the 2013 Act ran from 01st April 2014 to 09th July 2017; maximum statutory penalty computed by RoC was Rs 2,35,90,000/- per appellant (total Rs 9,43,60,000/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Swedish parent went bankrupt on 06th July 2011; nominee directors appointed at EGM on 18th February 2012; Form DIR-12 registered on 08th February 2017; AGMs conducted on 10th July 2017; compounding applications filed pursuant to NCLT order dated 11th August 2017; NCLT Hyderabad passed compounding order on 19th July 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence of civil litigation, interim injunctions, and resistance from ex-directors preventing access to bank accounts and portal registration till 2017; subsequent compliance and auditing of accounts made good on 10th July 2017; compounding applications C.A Nos. 118, 114, 120, and 116/441/HDB/2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad allowed compounding of defaults under Section 166 (Companies Act 1956) and Section 96(1) (Companies Act 2013) subject to payment of compounding fee of Rs 27,09,000/- per appellant (total Rs 1,08,36,000/-); Appellants appealed seeking further reduction.
legal_issues: Whether the compounding penalty of Rs 27,09,000/- imposed on each appellant by NCLT Hyderabad for failure to hold Annual General Meetings under Section 166 of the 1956 Act and Section 96 of the 2013 Act was exorbitant and failed to consider mitigating factors beyond the directors' control.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While compounding statutory company law offences, tribunals must maintain consistency and consider mitigating factors, gravity, period of default, and whether the default was made good, but an imposition of less than one-fifth of the statutory maximum constitutes an adequately lenient exercise of judicial discretion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Defaults in holding AGMs transition from Section 168 (Companies Act 1956) to Section 99 (Companies Act 2013) with effect from 01st April 2014, and compounding under Section 441 permits discretionary compounding fees within prescribed statutory ranges. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison of the imposed penalty against the statutory maximum benchmark (evaluating if the fine falls below 1/5th of maximum liability) and assessment of parity with prior coordinate bench precedents. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT took an appropriately lenient view by levying Rs 27,09,000/- per appellant against a maximum leviable fine of Rs 2,35,90,000/- (less than 1/5th), requiring no appellate interference.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, the NCLT Hyderabad compounding order dated 19th July 2019 is upheld, and no order is made as to costs.
summary: Appellants Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. and its nominee directors challenged an order of NCLT Hyderabad that compounded their non-compliance in failing to hold AGMs for years 2012 to 2015 upon payment of Rs 27,09,000/- each (total Rs 1,08,36,000/-). Appellants sought a reduction arguing that delay was unintentional and caused by external control hurdles and litigation following the bankruptcy of their Swedish parent company. NCLAT held that the NCLT had already taken a lenient view by imposing a penalty well below one-fifth of the maximum statutory liability of Rs 2,35,90,000/- per appellant. Concurring with the NCLT's balanced exercise of discretion, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Corporation Bank vs Uluberia Metaliks Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporation Bank is the Financial Creditor/Appellant; Uluberia Metaliks Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Banking credit/loan facilities secured by a mortgage in favour of the Financial Creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The loan account was declared NPA on 14th August 2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account classified as NPA on 14th August 2012; Section 7 IBC application filed by Corporation Bank on 20th December 2018 (over six years following NPA date). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank mortgage documents claimed by Appellant to grant a 12-year limitation period under Article 62 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) dismissed the Section 7 application as barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act relying on B.K. Educational Services and Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave; Corporation Bank appealed the dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether Article 62 of the Limitation Act (providing a 12-year period for suits enforcing payment of money secured by a mortgage) applies to an application under Section 7 of the IBC, or whether such applications are governed strictly by the three-year period under Article 137.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications under Section 7 of the IBC are governed exclusively by Article 137 of the Limitation Act (three-year limitation period running from the date of default), and the 12-year limitation period under Article 62 cannot be invoked because Article 62 applies solely to suits, not applications. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications fall within the residuary Article 137 of the Limitation Act; the right to sue accrues when default occurs, and IBC provisions cannot be utilised to give a new lease of life to debts that are already time-barred. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Determining whether the Section 7 petition was filed within three years of the date of default/NPA declaration, disregarding mortgage-suit limitation rules. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The account became NPA on 14th August 2012 and the Section 7 petition was filed on 20th December 2018 (exceeding three years); Article 62 does not apply to Section 7 IBC applications, rendering the claim hopelessly time-barred.
operative_order: The appeal is declined admission and disposed of accordingly; the dismissal of the Section 7 application is affirmed; no orders as to costs.
summary: Corporation Bank appealed against the dismissal of its Section 7 IBC application against Uluberia Metaliks Pvt. Ltd. by the Adjudicating Authority on grounds of limitation. The loan account had become an NPA on 14th August 2012, whereas the Section 7 application was filed on 20th December 2018. The Bank argued that the existence of a mortgage granted a 12-year limitation period under Article 62 of the Limitation Act. Following the Supreme Court ruling in Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave, NCLAT held that Article 62 applies only to suits and that Section 7 applications fall strictly under Article 137, which prescribes a three-year period from default. Consequently, NCLAT declined to admit the appeal and dismissed it.

case_title: Bijay Pratap Singh vs Unimax International & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Unimax International (registered partnership firm) is the Operational Creditor; Soho Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Bijay Pratap Singh is the Appellant (shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Punkaj Jain is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of aluminium/M.S. shuttering material and framework systems with standard accessories by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor for the 'Misty Heights' project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of a principal sum of Rs 61,24,637/- (stated in Part-IV) along with interest at 24% p.a. (Rs 22,04,870/-), totaling Rs 83,29,507/- as the closing balance for FY 01.04.2017 to 31.08.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Goods supplied up to last invoice dated 23rd May 2017; demand notice issued under Section 8(1) on 10th December 2016 and delivered to the registered office; CP (IB) No. 415(PB)/2019 filed under Section 9; NCLT Principal Bench admitted the petition on 30th September 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor produced invoices and delivery challans showing receipt of goods; an appreciation letter from the Corporate Debtor praising material quality; three post-dated cheques dated 22nd November 2018 totaling Rs 6 Lakhs issued by Corporate Debtor which dishonoured (leading to Section 138 NI Act proceedings); registered office postal service records; alleged defect complaint letters dated 02.07.2016 and 27.07.2016 claimed by the creditor to be forged and manufactured. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi admitted the Section 9 petition on 30th September 2019 finding undisputed supply and default; Appellant shareholder appealed against the admission.
legal_issues: Whether postal delivery of a Section 8 demand notice returned as 'unclaimed' at the registered office of the corporate debtor constitutes sufficient and valid service under law, and whether allegations of defective goods supported by disputed correspondence constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute under the rule in Mobilox Innovations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of a statutory demand notice sent by registered post to the registered office of a corporate debtor constitutes sufficient and proper service under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 20 of the Companies Act, even if returned unclaimed; furthermore, vague or manufactured assertions of defect not supported by contemporaneous cogent evidence do not constitute a real pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) read with Rule 5 does not make omission of hand or email delivery fatal where registered postal service to the registered office is established; a 'dispute' under Section 5(6) and Section 8(2)(a) must truly exist in fact and not be a spurious or illusory defense. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of postal records, registered company addresses, and subsequent conduct (including issuance of cheques and appreciation letters) to discard manufactured afterthoughts of pre-existing disputes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default exceeding statutory thresholds were clearly proved, service of statutory notice was legally complete, and no genuine pre-existing dispute existed prior to default; admission of CIRP was fully warranted.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs; IA No. 426/2020 and IA No. 3687/2019 are closed; Resolution Professional permitted to claim CIRP fees and expenses from 30.09.2019 onwards before the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: Operational Creditor Unimax International filed a Section 9 IBC petition against Corporate Debtor Soho Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid invoices of Rs 61.24 Lakhs plus interest for supply of aluminium shuttering materials. Following admission by NCLT Principal Bench, the Corporate Debtor's shareholder appealed, arguing that the Section 8 demand notice was not served (returned unclaimed) and that pre-existing disputes existed regarding defective goods. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that registered postal delivery to the registered office is deemed sufficient service under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 20 of the Companies Act. NCLAT further held that the alleged dispute was illusory and spurious, especially given post-dated cheques and appreciation letters issued by the debtor.

case_title: Sudhir Haribhai Patel & Ors vs Atlas Copco (India) Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Atlas Copco (India) Ltd is the Respondent Company; Jayshree Damani, Yashita Damani, Janak Mathuradas, Sanjay Asher, Arun Kejriwal, Sudhir Haribhai Patel, Deep Janak, and Jawahir Jagatsinh Merchant are the Appellant minority shareholders. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Selective reduction of equity share capital under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 by extinguishing 3.68% public shareholding (delisted company) at a fair equity value of Rs 1854/- plus Rs 246/- premium (offering Rs 2100/- per share). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over valuation of Rs 2100/- per share (Appellants claimed independent valuation of Rs 3627/-) and selective reduction extinguishing 8,29,613 shares. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Delisted from BSE/Pune SE in May 2011; notice of EGM issued on 18th September 2018; special resolution passed at EOGM on 25th October 2018; Company Petition No. 4475/2018 filed before NCLT Mumbai; impugned order allowing capital reduction passed on 10th December 2019; registered with ROC Pune on 27th December 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Scrutinizer's report confirming e-voting in favour by certain appellants; attendance slips; independent valuation report dated 14th September 2018 by M/s BSR & Associates LLP; company undertaking affidavit dated 08th November 2019 allowing dissenting objectors to retain their shares. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the capital reduction under Section 66(3) subject to the company's undertaking to let dissenting shareholders retain shares; seven sets of minority shareholders appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether NCLT has substantive statutory powers under Section 66(3) to approve a capital reduction scheme subject to conditions or undertakings allowing dissenting shareholders to retain shares, and whether minority shareholders can challenge an expert independent valuation without demonstrating that it is ex-facie perverse or unreasonable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses wide substantive powers under Section 66(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to approve a capital reduction on such terms and conditions as it deems fit, including accepting an undertaking to allow dissenting minority shareholders to retain shareholding; an expert valuation report cannot be rejected unless demonstrated to be unreasonable, perverse, or unfair. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66 does not mandate separate meetings of promoter and non-promoter classes of shareholders; Section 66(3) read with Rule 6 of Reduction Rules vests the Tribunal with broad discretionary authority to impose conditions ensuring fairness. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Onus rests strictly on the objecting shareholder to prove that the company's registered valuer report is perverse; speculative third-party private valuations based on incomplete data are insufficient to displace an expert valuation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The special resolution was validly approved by 99.84% votes, the valuation of Rs 2100/- per share was fair and well-founded, and the undertaking allowing dissenting objectors to retain shares adequately safeguarded minority interests.
operative_order: All seven appeals are dismissed; interim stay orders vacated; no order as to costs.
summary: Atlas Copco (India) Ltd, a delisted entity, passed a special resolution under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 to reduce its share capital by extinguishing the 3.68% public minority shareholding at Rs 2100/- per share (based on a valuation of Rs 1854 plus premium). NCLT Mumbai approved the reduction subject to the company's undertaking permitting dissenting shareholders to continue holding their shares. Several minority shareholders appealed under Section 421 challenging the valuation and the modification of the resolution via undertaking. NCLAT dismissed all appeals, holding that Section 66(3) vests wide powers in the Tribunal to approve capital reductions with equitable conditions, and that the valuation by BSR & Associates LLP was sound and not shown to be perverse.

case_title: Power2SME Pvt. Ltd. & Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. vs Allied Strips Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Allied Strips Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Power2SME Pvt. Ltd. is an Operational Creditor/Appellant in CA 680/2019; Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. is an Operational Creditor/Appellant in CA 688/2019; Sandeep Mahajan is the Resolution Professional; G.P. Global Energy Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA); Committee of Creditors represented by Canara Bank is Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of raw materials (HR coils) on credit during corporate distress, along with supply of petroleum/oil products. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor owed Rs 1993 Crores total debt (Secured Financial Creditors owed Rs 1654.69 Crores; Operational Creditors statutory dues Rs 218.94 Crores; other Operational Creditors Rs 203.41 Crores; employees Rs 7.07 Crores); liquidation value of Corporate Debtor was Rs 188.75 Crores. Under the approved resolution plan of Rs 235.86 Crores, Financial Creditors received 13.69% and Operational Creditors received 0.46%. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 16th March 2018; resolution plan approved by CoC with 99.84% vote; NCLT Principal Bench approved the plan on 30th May 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Final list of creditors showing Power2SME's claim admitted at Rs 47,59,89,098/- and IOC's claim admitted at Rs 39,01,99,828/-; hypothecation deed dated 01.12.2016 in favour of Power2SME which created only a subservient charge without bank NOCs; IOC's admission reconciliation error proving an admitted operational debt of Rs 73,07,76,273/-. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi approved the resolution plan in CA-62 (PB)/2019 on 30th May 2019; two operational creditors appealed alleging unfair and discriminatory treatment under Section 30(2)(b).
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor holding a subservient charge over hypothecated stock is entitled to equal treatment and distribution parity with secured financial creditors holding prior first and second charges, and whether differential percentage distribution between financial and operational creditors violates the amended Section 30(2)(b) and the Essar Steel principles.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The principle of equitable treatment under Section 30(2) does not mandate equal or proportionate recovery across different classes of creditors; the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors determines distribution, and an operational creditor with a subservient charge cannot demand parity with first-charge secured financial creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) requires payment to operational creditors to be not less than the liquidation value under Section 53; when liquidation value attributable to operational creditors is nil, approval of a differential commercial payout by the CoC is legally valid. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of charge priority and liquidation value allocations; an operational creditor who has already lifted and recovered hypothecated goods cannot re-assert parity with secured lenders who suffered substantial haircuts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC acted within its commercial wisdom in approving the resolution plan, which conformed to Section 30(2); however, an admitted clerical/typographical error in the quantum of an operational creditor's admitted claim must be rectified pro-rata.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 680 of 2019 is dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 688 of 2019 is disposed of with directions to correct IOC's admitted claim in the creditors' list to Rs 73,07,76,273/- and calculate its proportionate resolution plan entitlement accordingly.
summary: Operational creditors Power2SME Pvt. Ltd. and Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench order dated 30th May 2019 approving G.P. Global Energy Pvt. Ltd.'s resolution plan for Allied Strips Limited. Power2SME alleged discrimination, arguing it was a secured operational creditor entitled to equal treatment with secured financial creditors (who received 13.69% compared to 0.46% for operational creditors). NCLAT dismissed Power2SME's appeal, holding pursuant to the Essar Steel ruling that equitable treatment does not mean equal distribution across unequal classes, and noting Power2SME's charge was subservient to the lenders' prior charges. In IOC's appeal, NCLAT directed the RP to rectify a typographical error in IOC's admitted claim to Rs 73.07 Crores and disburse its proportionate dividend.

case_title: Arti Meenakshi Muthiah vs MCTM Global Investments Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: MCTM Global Investments Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 (closely held family company); Arti Meenakshi Muthiah is the Appellant (17% shareholder, daughter of R-2); Kamala Muthiah is Respondent No. 2 (66% shareholder, mother); Nandini Valli Muthiah is Respondent No. 3 (17% shareholder, sister); Ms Gomathy Subramanian is Respondent No. 4 (additional director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and asset administration of a closely held family investment company with paid-up capital of Rs 6,67,130/- following the demise of founder M.Ct. Muthiah in September 2006. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Grievances regarding joint holding transfers, purchase of Alagappa Road property for Rs 15.25 Crores with a temporary Rs 2.47 Crore company advance to R-3, funding of Learning Curve Foundation Trust, and altering bank operation signatories. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share transfer to joint holding on 28th June 2013; Board resolution authorizing surplus fund investment on 01st February 2013; property sale deed dated 15th April 2013; board meeting appointing R-4 on 06th January 2015; Company Petition TCP 163/2016 (CP/23/2015) filed before CLB/NCLT Chennai; impugned dismissal order passed on 04th September 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board resolution dated 01.02.2013 authorizing investment of surplus funds; proof of full repayment of Rs 2.47 Crore advance within one month by R-2 through personal asset liquidation; corporate records proving independent Trust (LCF) had no formal corporate affiliation with R-1; minutes of board meeting dated 06.01.2015. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397/398; NCLT Single Bench Chennai dismissed the petition and all interim applications on 04th September 2018; Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether intra-family transfers of majority shares into joint holdings without prejudice to minority shareholding, commercial real estate investments using surplus funds that were fully repaid, appointment of an additional director by majority, and adding bank account signatories constitute acts of oppression and mismanagement under corporate law.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial investment decisions taken under valid board authorizations, especially where temporary advances are fully reimbursed, do not constitute oppression and mismanagement; furthermore, adding an authorized bank signatory while preserving the minority director's signing capacity does not amount to actionable oppression. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397 and 398 require establishing that company affairs are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or oppressive to members; bona fide commercial decisions and internal administrative arrangements approved by majority cannot be impeached under the guise of oppression. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of financial records, bank statements, and board resolutions demonstrating whether actual corporate prejudice or loss occurred, and whether minority shareholder rights were unlawfully curtailed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The shareholdings of the Appellant remained intact at 17%, the property purchase was a valid commercial decision with advances fully repaid, the appointment of an additional director was lawful, and bank account mandate adjustments were non-oppressive; NCLT's dismissal was just and proper.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs; interim order passed on 06.02.2020 is vacated.
summary: Appellant Arti Meenakshi Muthiah (17% shareholder) filed a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement against her mother, sister, and MCTM Global Investments Pvt. Ltd. under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, citing the transfer of shares into joint names, appointment of an additional director, purchase of real estate property at Alagappa Road involving an advance to Respondent No. 3, and bank mandate alterations. NCLT Chennai dismissed the petition. On appeal under Section 421, NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that the share transfers caused no legal prejudice to the appellant's 17% stake, the property acquisition was a legitimate commercial board decision with the temporary advance fully repaid, and adding bank signatories did not constitute oppression.

case_title: Babasaheb Sawalaram Chaware vs Punjab National Bank & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Harneshwar Agro Products Power and Yeast (I) Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Punjab National Bank is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Babasaheb Sawalaram Chaware is the Appellant (Suspended Director); Jigar Shah is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Extension, renewal, and revision of term loan, working capital loan, and cash credit facilities by Punjab National Bank and a consortium of banks to the Corporate Debtor starting in 2005. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: As of 06th January 2019, outstanding default dues across three term loan accounts stood at Rs. 45,82,14,984/-; the account was declared NPA on 31st March 2011. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 31st March 2011; loan recall notice issued on 29th August 2011; notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued on 12th November 2011 for Rs. 12,82,06,949/-; Original Application OA 89/14 filed before DRT (which later abated); Section 7 IBC petition filed on 11th January 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Repeated written OTS compromise proposals and acknowledgments submitted by the Appellant/Corporate Debtor dated 03.12.2012, 18.03.2013, 25.11.2013, 02.05.2015, 21.03.2016 (noting Rs. 4 Crores paid), 24.05.2016, 01.07.2016, and 10.07.2018; simple mortgage deed dated 28th March 2008; unproven vague assertions of coercion and duress. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 7 petition in CP (IB) 162/MB/2019 on 26th June 2019; Suspended Director appealed against admission.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 IBC application was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, whether continuous written OTS proposals and partial repayments extend limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and whether the abatement of recovery proceedings before the DRT bars an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Continuous written compromise and OTS proposals acknowledging liability, accompanied by part payments, constitute valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act that continually reset the limitation period; furthermore, the abatement of recovery suits or proceedings before a Debts Recovery Tribunal does not extinguish the debt or bar an independent application under Section 7 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to Section 7 IBC proceedings to renew the limitation period upon signed acknowledgment; abatement of an OA before the DRT does not eliminate the existence of outstanding financial debt and default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of continuous written correspondence, OTS requests, and partial payments made prior to the expiration of limitation periods, while discarding unsubstantiated, vague pleas of coercion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was continuously acknowledged in writing from 2012 through July 2018, bringing the Section 7 petition filed on 11th January 2019 well within limitation, and the abatement of DRT proceedings was immaterial.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the NCLT Mumbai admission order dated 26th June 2019 is upheld; no orders as to costs.
summary: Punjab National Bank filed a Section 7 IBC application against Harneshwar Agro Products Power and Yeast (I) Ltd. for outstanding dues of Rs. 45.82 Crores, following an NPA classification on 31st March 2011. The suspended director appealed the NCLT Mumbai Bench's admission order, arguing that the claim was time-barred and that recovery proceedings before the DRT had abated. NCLAT held that successive written OTS proposals, compromise requests, and part payments submitted by the Corporate Debtor between 2012 and July 2018 constituted valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, keeping the claim alive. NCLAT further held that abatement of DRT proceedings does not preclude IBC resolution, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Ritu Rastogi Resolution Professional, Benlon India Ltd. vs Riyal Packers
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Benlon India Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Ritu Rastogi is the Appellant (Resolution Professional); Riyal Packers is the Respondent; Surender Kumar Chawla is the Successful Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Benlon India Ltd. and submission/approval of a resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory CIRP timeline reaching the outer threshold of 330 days; CoC approved the resolution plan within extended timelines on 05th February 2020, leaving only one day before expiry of the CIRP period to file the approval application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved the resolution plan on 05th February 2020; Section 31 application filed by the RP before the Adjudicating Authority on 17th February 2020 (a delay of 10 days beyond the extended period). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved resolution plan of Surender Kumar Chawla; administrative necessity of completing statutory formalities, including obtaining the mandatory performance guarantee from the resolution applicant prior to placing the plan before the Adjudicating Authority. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority refused to condone the 10-day delay in filing the Section 31 application and rejected the request to extend CIRP; the RP appealed invoking Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules to extend the CIRP timeline beyond the 330-day outer limit to condone a 10-day delay by the Resolution Professional in filing a Section 31 application for an already CoC-approved resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In exceptional cases where the Committee of Creditors has approved a resolution plan within the prescribed or extended CIRP timeline, the Appellate Tribunal may exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 to extend time beyond the 330-day outer limit where only a short period is required to complete statutory formalities, preventing the unjust liquidation of a viable corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in Essar Steel, the 330-day timeline under Section 12 is generally mandatory but admits judicial discretion in exceptional circumstances to avoid frustrating the core objective of the IBC, which is corporate resolution over liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Determining whether the delay is short, whether it is justified by bona fide administrative and statutory compliance (such as securing performance guarantees), and whether resolution serves the legitimate interests of all stakeholders. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP acted diligently and was delayed by only 10 days due to mandatory performance guarantee procedures; refusing extension would defeat the purpose of the Code by driving the debtor into liquidation.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order is set aside, the CIRP period is extended by 10 days up to 17th February 2020, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to consider the Section 31 application for approval of the resolution plan in accordance with law.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Benlon India Ltd. appealed an order of the Adjudicating Authority which refused to entertain an application under Section 31 of the IBC for approval of a CoC-approved resolution plan due to a 10-day delay beyond the CIRP timeline. The CoC had approved the plan on 05th February 2020 within the sanctioned extension, but the RP was left with only one day to secure the performance guarantee and file the application, leading to filing on 17th February 2020. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel and invoking Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, NCLAT set aside the impugned order, condoned the 10-day delay, extended the CIRP period up to 17th February 2020, and directed the NCLT to consider the plan on its merits.

case_title: Dr Naveen Chaudhari vs Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Limited & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Noida Medicare Centre Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Limited (acting as Trustee of Suraksha ARC-012) is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Dr. Naveen Chaudhari is the Appellant (Director of Corporate Debtor); Chandra Prakash is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor from Kotak Mahindra Bank in 2015, which were subsequently assigned via Assignment Agreement dated 29th September 2017 to Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account classified as NPA on 30th June 2016; Financial Creditor claimed default of over Rs. 9 Crores under the assignment deed and revoked concessions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30th June 2016; Assignment Agreement and Restructuring Agreement executed on 29th September 2017; revocation of restructuring concessions on 12th February 2019; Section 7 IBC application filed on 16th July 2019; NCLT New Delhi Bench V admitted petition on 27th May 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assignment Agreement dated 29.09.2017; Restructuring Agreement dated 29.09.2017 showing payments of Rs. 1.17 Crores towards outstanding dues and Rs. 33.50 Lakhs processing fees; revocation letter dated 12.02.2019 citing repayment defaults. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench V admitted the Section 7 petition in (IB) 2039 (ND)/2019 on 27th May 2020; Appellant director appealed against the admission order.
legal_issues: Whether disputes concerning compliance, breach, and revocation of a subsequent Restructuring Agreement under Sections 37 and 55 of the Indian Contract Act preclude or bar the admission of an application under Section 7 of the IBC by an assignee financial creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For the purposes of admitting an application under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is only required to determine the existence of a financial debt and a default exceeding the statutory threshold; collateral disputes arising out of subsequent restructuring agreements or breach of contract principles do not negate default on the underlying assigned financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An assignee of financial debt validly steps into the shoes of the original lender; where debt and default under Section 7 are established above the Section 4 threshold, the Adjudicating Authority has no mandate to adjudicate contractual performance disputes under Sections 37 and 55 of the Indian Contract Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the validity of the Assignment Agreement and admission of outstanding unpaid financial liabilities exceeding statutory minimums. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The assigned debt from Kotak Mahindra Bank remained unpaid and in default well beyond statutory thresholds; contractual disputes under the Restructuring Agreement were irrelevant to the Section 7 admission.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the admission stage without being admitted; the NCLT admission order dated 27th May 2020 is affirmed.
summary: Dr. Naveen Chaudhari, Director of Noida Medicare Centre Ltd., appealed against the NCLT New Delhi Bench V order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by assignee Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Limited. The Corporate Debtor defaulted on loans obtained from Kotak Mahindra Bank (declared NPA on 30th June 2016), which assigned the debt to Suraksha ARC on 29th September 2017. The Appellant argued that a restructuring agreement was executed on the same day, that part-payments were made, and that disputes existed regarding contractual obligations under Sections 37 and 55 of the Indian Contract Act following revocation of concessions. NCLAT held that collateral disputes concerning a restructuring agreement are irrelevant under Section 7 so long as the assigned financial debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold are established, and dismissed the appeal.
